fields.text: The Coup Across Usea
lines: The Coup Across Usea

fields.text:
The official chronology records that on 30 May 1997 a coup broke out across Usea, and that Unified Command defeated it with Scarface 1. In Farbanti the first reports arrive by teleprinter in fragments, contradicting one another: barracks seized here, a broadcasting station there, a government that has fled or has not.

For two days the Erusean cabinet does not know how far the coup reaches. The foreign ministry cannot reach half its embassies. The intelligence service has lists of names, most of them out of date. The general staff reports that every Erusean garrison is quiet, and the cabinet notices that the general staff is the only body in a position to say so.

That is the real lesson of the coup for Erusea, whatever happened to its neighbours. A government's safety depends on the loyalty of the men with the guns, and loyalty is a thing nobody can inspect from the capital. The palace, the cabinet and the officers' clubs all reach this conclusion at once, and each of them draws a different conclusion from it.

By the end of the week the coup has been defeated. The questions it raised in Erusea have not.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1997 / 05.30. Erusea's response is provisional gameplay.

guns, and loyalty is a thing nobody can inspect from the capital. The palace, the
cabinet and the officers' clubs all reach this conclusion at once, and each of
them draws a different conclusion from it.
By the end of the week the coup has been defeated. The questions it raised in
Erusea have not.
Official: ACES Chronicle, 1997 / 05.30. Erusea's response is provisional
gameplay.

fields.text: Stonehenge
lines: Stonehenge

fields.text:
The official chronology records that on 19 June 1998 the Federation of Central Usea completed Stonehenge in a desert region of neutral San Salvacion: eight railguns, built as an international project under the Federation's leadership, to shoot down the fragments of Ulysses before they strike.

The newsreels show the guns from a distance, each one longer than a city block, aimed at an empty sky. In Erusea the pictures are watched with relief and with something less comfortable. The battery will save lives, perhaps millions of them. It is also the most powerful weapon ever built on the continent, built on neutral soil by Erusea's largest neighbour, and nobody in Farbanti was asked where it should go or who should control it.

The general staff's engineers study the published specifications and say little in public. The foreign ministry's diplomats say a great deal in public and little that anyone remembers. In the newspapers the debate is simple and loud: the battery is a shield, or the battery is a gun pointed at the sky that could be pointed anywhere.

The official position, for now, is gratitude. Whether gratitude is what Erusea feels is a question the government would rather not ask its citizens, and one that the next years will answer for it.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1998 / 06.19, and Super Weapons, Stonehenge. Erusea's response is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Night of the Fragments
lines: The Night of the Fragments

fields.text:
The official chronology records that on 8 July 1999 Ulysses passed the Earth's Roche limit and broke apart. For a decade the government has planned for this night. Now it learns which plans were real.

Across the world the fragments fall where the astronomers said they might, and some where they said they would not. Stonehenge fires into the sky above San Salvacion. The radios carry reports from every continent, then from fewer, then only the national stations reading lists of the districts that have lost contact. Erusea's shelters fill and empty. Its trains run on the emergency timetable. Its hospitals take whoever comes.

In the weeks that follow the scale of the catastrophe becomes clear, and so does its shape. The fragments have killed, burned and flooded across the continent. Harvests are lost. Whole towns are homeless. And the displaced are moving, in columns of cars, carts and people on foot, toward any border where the lights are still on. Erusea's lights are on.

The government has done what it prepared to do. It now faces something it did not prepare for: the arrival, at its border and in its towns, of a continent's worth of people who have nowhere else to go.

The cabinet meets every day. The decade that began with a court ledger ends with a refugee register.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08. Erusean relief measures are provisional gameplay; no impact sites are scripted.

fields.text: The Officers' Oath
lines: The Officers' Oath

fields.text:
The ceremony takes place in the palace courtyard on a grey morning, with the regimental colours lowered and the general staff in the front rank. Each officer steps forward, uncovers and swears, in the old words, to serve the Crown and the Crown alone. The old words have not been used in living memory. The chancery found them in the archive.

Nobody pretends the ceremony is merely traditional. The oath binds the officers to the throne, not to the general staff, and certainly not to any constitution the country might one day write. Every officer who swears it understands this. So does every officer who finds a reason to be on leave that week.

The general staff makes no objection. Its chief swears first, in a clear voice, and is photographed shaking the monarch's hand. The photograph appears in the court gazette and in every officers' mess, and some of the younger officers are seen looking at it for a long time.

An oath is a promise. The palace has collected several thousand of them. Whether they will be kept depends on what is asked of the men who made them, and when.

fields.text: The Royal Ulysses Commission
lines: The Royal Ulysses Commission

fields.text:
The royal commission meets for the first time in the palace library, among the old survey maps, with the official chronology's single terrible sentence pinned to the door: on 20 April 1996 Central Usea announced that Ulysses would strike the Earth.

The commission's powers are broad. It may requisition land, materials and labour. It may order shelters built, grain bought and evacuation routes surveyed. It answers to the palace alone, which means it can move faster than any ministry and that any failure will carry the Crown's name.

Its members are chosen by the chancery: engineers from the royal academies, two retired generals, a banker, a bishop and the director of the national observatory, who arrives with a briefcase of orbital calculations and no patience for speeches. In the first session he explains that the fragments will fall over years, unevenly, and that the commission's job is not to stop them but to make sure the country is still standing when they stop.

The commission's first decree orders a shelter in every district town. Its second orders the palace granaries filled. The court notices that the decrees are signed by the monarch personally, every one.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20. The royal commission is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Loyal Regiments
lines: The Loyal Regiments

fields.text:
The official chronology records that a coup broke out across Usea on 30 May 1997. In Farbanti the palace does not wait to learn how far it reaches. Before the first night is over the chancery has drawn up a list, compiled from the oath registers, the garrison reports and the household guard's own files, of the regiments whose officers can be trusted absolutely.

The list is short. It is meant to be. The loyal regiments are moved to the capital's barracks within the week, and their commanders are received at the palace one by one. They are thanked, decorated and told, without anyone saying so directly, that the Crown now depends on them.

The regiments that are not on the list notice. Some of their officers write letters protesting their loyalty. Others say nothing and are watched more closely for it. In the officers' clubs a new phrase circulates, half joke and half complaint: the list. Who is on the list, who has fallen off it, who might be added after the next manoeuvres.

The palace has made itself safer by dividing the army into those it trusts and those it does not. It will now have to decide what to do with the men on the wrong side of that line, and with the ones who plotted with neighbours abroad.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1997 / 05.30. The Crown's measures are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Crown's Protest
lines: The Crown's Protest

fields.text:
The Crown's statement is read by the chancellor from the palace steps, which has not been done for a foreign affair in living memory. Erusea welcomes any measure that protects the peoples of Usea from the fragments of Ulysses. Erusea notes, however, that Stonehenge was planned, sited and built under the leadership of a single power, on neutral soil, without the participation of the continent's other great nation.

The statement goes on for four more paragraphs, each one more courteous and more pointed than the last. It asks for nothing specific. It does not need to. Its purpose is to put on the record that Erusea was not asked, and that Erusea minds.

In the capital the newspapers that support the palace print the statement in full under a photograph of the railguns. The others print it under a photograph of the palace steps. In the Federation's capital the statement is received with diplomatic silence, which the Erusean ambassador reports as anger.

The protest costs Erusea nothing today. It has, however, given a royal voice to a feeling that was already loose in the country: that the continent's future is being decided elsewhere, by people who do not count Erusea among the deciders. That feeling will outlast the fragments.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1998 / 06.19. The Erusean protest is provisional gameplay with no official source.

fields.text: The Unbroken Crown
lines: The Unbroken Crown

fields.text:
The decade's last royal audience is held in the long room where the Crown's question was first asked. On the table are the documents that answered it: the decree register, the intendants' reports, the oath lists, the commission's shelter census and the accounts of the palace granaries, opened to the districts when the sky fell.

The palace has governed Erusea through the hardest decade in its history, and it has done so by prerogative. The ministries answer to the chancery. The districts answer to the intendants. The officers have sworn to the throne and, so far, kept their word. When the fragments came, the relief carried the palace's name, and the country remembers it.

Not everything has gone well. The liberal clubs are quieter, not gone. The general staff is loyal, but it has learned to think of itself as the Crown's most indispensable servant, which is a dangerous thing for a servant to think. And the country is angry: at the fragments, at the camps on the border, at the neighbours who built a battery without asking. Anger, the chancellor reminds the room, is easier to borrow than to repay.

The monarch closes the audience with one sentence for the minutes. The Crown has kept Erusea whole. It intends to keep it whole in the decade to come, whatever that decade asks.

fields.text: The Drafting Commission
lines: The Drafting Commission

fields.text:
Forty-one people sit around the commission's table: jurists, district notables, two palace secretaries, a union organizer, a bishop and three professors who have been writing constitutions for Erusea in their spare time for twenty years and are finally being asked to read them aloud.

The first week is spent agreeing on the order of business. The second is spent on the preamble, which every member wants to write and nobody wants to vote on. In the third week the commission discovers the questions that matter: whether the monarch keeps a veto, whether the assembly controls the army's budget, whether the districts elect their own governors and whether the franchise includes everyone over twenty-one or only those who pay taxes.

Outside the hall the country follows the debates in the newspapers, which print the minutes in full. The liberal clubs hold rallies for a broad franchise. The landed families hold dinners for a narrow one. The general staff holds nothing at all and lets it be known that it is watching the clause on military appointments.

The commission's chair, an elderly jurist with a famously short temper, tells the press that a constitution is a treaty between people who do not trust each other. Erusea, the chair says, has plenty of material.

fields.text: The First Assembly
lines: The First Assembly

fields.text:
Erusea votes on a spring day, in schools, church halls and railway waiting rooms, in queues that stretch around the block in the cities and across the square in the villages. Many voters have never cast a ballot before. Some bring their children to watch. The count takes three days, and on the fourth the results are posted on the palace gates.

No party has won outright. The liberals are the largest group; the monarchist leagues are close behind; the rest are scattered among labour societies, district lists and a handful of nationalists who campaigned against the constitution itself and won seats under it anyway. The assembly will have to govern by coalition from its first day.

The monarch receives the leaders of the largest groups one after another and asks the liberals to form a cabinet responsible to the assembly. It is the first time in Erusea's history that a government owes its office to votes rather than to the palace. The palace secretaries hand over their keys with formal courtesy. Several of them are hired by the new ministers the following week, because nobody else knows where the files are.

The general staff issues a statement pledging its loyalty to the Crown and the charter, in that order. The new defence minister reads it carefully and keeps it in a drawer.

Erusea is now a constitutional monarchy. Its assembly is untested, its parties are young and its decade is about to get much harder. But it has chosen its government, and that cannot be unchosen without someone breaking a promise the whole country watched being made.

fields.text: The Ulysses Committee
lines: The Ulysses Committee

fields.text:
The official chronology records that on 20 April 1996 Central Usea announced that Ulysses will strike the Earth. Erusea's assembly hears the news in session. The speaker suspends the debate on the fisheries bill, and for an hour nobody says anything useful.

By the evening sitting the parties have agreed, for the first time in the assembly's short life, on something important. A standing committee with members from every group will plan for the fragments, in public, with published numbers. It will have authority to commission shelters, buy grain and coordinate the provincial relief boards, and it will report to the assembly every month.

The committee's hearings become the most watched programme on Erusean television. Astronomers explain orbits. Engineers explain concrete. District officials explain why their shelter is behind schedule, and are asked by deputies from the other parties why their district's contractor is the mayor's cousin. It is slow, quarrelsome and, to the surprise of the general staff, effective.

The palace watches the hearings too. So do the officers' clubs, where the conversation is less admiring. A country that plans its survival by committee, one colonel remarks, had better hope the sky is patient.

fields.text: Defend the Assembly
lines: Defend the Assembly

fields.text:
The official chronology records that a coup broke out across Usea on 30 May 1997. In Farbanti the news arrives during an evening sitting of the assembly. Within an hour there are rumours of troop movements near the capital, of officers meeting in a hotel, of a broadcasting station that has stopped broadcasting.

The speaker refuses to adjourn. The cabinet calls the police and the garrisons whose commanders it trusts, and then, because it does not know how far the trust extends, it calls the public. By midnight there are thousands of people in the square outside the chamber: students, union men, shopkeepers, veterans, families who brought blankets. Nobody organized them. They simply came.

No troops arrive. Perhaps none were ever coming; perhaps the crowd changed some minds. In the morning the general staff reports that every garrison has remained at its post, and the cabinet thanks it formally and privately asks the intelligence service for the names of the officers who met in the hotel.

The assembly survived the coup year without a shot fired in Erusea. It now has to decide what to do with the officers who considered firing them, and how to make sure that next time nobody needs to bring a blanket.

fields.text: The Stonehenge Debate
lines: The Stonehenge Debate

fields.text:
The official chronology records that Central Usea completed Stonehenge on 19 June 1998. In Erusea's assembly the news begins a three-day debate that the newspapers later call the best the chamber has ever held and the worst for anyone's nerves.

The nationalist deputies want a protest. Erusea, they say, has been excluded from the defence of its own continent, and a battery that can shoot at the sky can shoot at anything. The liberal and labour benches want a welcome: the battery will save lives, perhaps Erusean lives, and the country's dignity is not worth the fragments it will stop. The monarchist leagues propose a compromise that satisfies no one: welcome the battery and ask, politely, for a seat on whatever body oversees it.

The compromise passes, narrowly, with an amendment from the opposition that the government report every six months on the battery's operation and on Erusea's requests. The general staff's observer in the gallery leaves before the vote.

The debate settles nothing about the battery. It settles something about Erusea: that its great questions are now decided by vote, in public, by people who disagree. Whether that is strength or weakness, the chamber will be asked again.

fields.text: The Constitutional Settlement
lines: The Constitutional Settlement

fields.text:
At the end of the decade the assembly holds a short ceremony that nobody planned. The constitution's original copy is brought out of the archive and laid on the speaker's table, and the deputies file past it in silence: liberals, monarchists, labour men, district notables, even the nationalists who campaigned against it and now sit under its protection.

The charter has survived a coup year without a shot fired, a fragment year without a famine and a refugee crisis without a riot. The courts stand apart from the ministers. The districts have elected boards. The monarchy stands above the parties and is more popular than any of them. It is not a perfect settlement. It is a working one, which in Erusea is rarer.

The settlement is untested in one respect. The assembly has never had to decide on a war. The camps on the border are full, the continent is broken and the grievances in the country are real. The peace caucus says the charter will hold. The general staff says nothing, and has learned to say nothing in a way the deputies find louder than speeches.

The speaker closes the ceremony with a line from the preamble that the commission spent a week arguing over: that Erusea's government belongs to those who will live under it. The deputies applaud. Outside, the camps wait.

fields.text: The Regency Ordinance
lines: The Regency Ordinance

fields.text:
The ordinance is signed in the long room on a Tuesday afternoon, with the chief of staff standing at the monarch's shoulder and the palace secretaries waiting outside. It runs to two pages. A regency council of serving officers will govern in the Crown's name. The ministries will be reorganized as directorates of a command administration. The council will report to the throne, which will remain the head of state and the source of all legitimacy, in principle.

The council's members are not named in the ordinance. They are known by their offices: the chief of staff, the commanders of the army, the air arm and the navy, the director of military intelligence and two colonels from the staff college who drafted most of the memorandum. Their first act is to confirm every civil servant in post, which reassures the ministries more than any proclamation could.

The country receives the news with the same weary recognition it showed when the colonels first appeared in the corridors. There are no demonstrations, because demonstrations require permits and the permits office now belongs to a directorate. The liberal clubs close. Some of their members leave the country. Most stay, and wait.

The regency has promised order, efficiency and security in a dangerous decade. It now has to deliver them, with no assembly to blame and no palace to hide behind.

fields.text: The Requisition Boards
lines: The Requisition Boards

fields.text:
The first requisition board sits in a former customs house in the capital, three officers at a long table with a stamp, a ledger and a sentry at the door. By the end of the month there is one in every district. They may requisition trucks, warehouses, fuel and labour for national purposes, with receipts redeemable after the emergency.

The receipts become a currency of their own. Shopkeepers trade them, banks discount them and a satirical weekly prints its own, redeemable 'after the regency'. The weekly is closed. The receipts keep circulating.

The boards work, in the narrow sense that the directorates get what they ask for when they ask for it. Arms plants receive steel before furniture makers. Trains move the army's freight first. The general staff's logisticians, who have spent careers explaining why things take time, discover that most of the time was spent asking permission.

In the districts the boards are feared and, more quietly, admired. They are the regency's real face: efficient, unaccountable and very hard to argue with. The council's economists warn that a country run on receipts will eventually be asked to pay them.

Provisional gameplay: no official source describes Erusean politics before 2003; this is a provisional gameplay branch.

fields.text: Civil Defence Command
lines: Civil Defence Command

fields.text:
The official chronology records that on 20 April 1996 Central Usea announced that Ulysses will strike the Earth. The regency answers within a day, in the way it knows best. A Civil Defence Command is created with a general at its head, a staff in the old war ministry and every district placed under its orders.

The command's first directive is twelve pages long and contains no adjectives. Every town will have a shelter. Every district will hold grain for ninety days. Every road out of every city will have an evacuation timetable. Every school will practise its drills twice a year. The directive gives deadlines, names responsible officers and lists the penalties for missing them.

The country grumbles, digs and complies. The drills are resented: sirens at dawn, soldiers at the crossroads, children marched to shelters in their nightclothes. They are also fast, faster every time, and the newspapers that are still allowed to print figures print them with something like pride.

The regency's critics, abroad and in the closed clubs, say that a government that treats its citizens as soldiers will one day ask them to be soldiers. The command's general, asked about this by a foreign journalist, answers that the fragments do not care about the distinction.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20. The regency's command is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Martial Law
lines: Martial Law

fields.text:
The official chronology records that a coup broke out across Usea on 30 May 1997. The regency council meets within the hour, with the director of military intelligence reading the teleprinter reports aloud as they arrive. By midnight the council has signed a set of martial law ordinances that the staff college drafted three years ago and never expected to use.

There is a certain irony in the situation, which the council's members notice and do not discuss. The regency is the one government on the continent that cannot be overthrown by its own army, because it is its own army. It is not afraid of a coup. It is afraid of contagion: of plotters abroad with friends in Erusean barracks, of junior officers who look at a council of generals and see a precedent.

The ordinances close the borders to unregistered travel, put the broadcasting stations under military guard and give the intelligence service authority to detain any officer who has corresponded with foreign plotters. Several dozen are detained in the first week. Most are released. A few are not.

By the end of the week the coup abroad has been defeated. The ordinances remain in force for a year, because a regency that has learned to fear its own officers does not unlearn it quickly.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1997 / 05.30. The regency's ordinances are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Railgun Study
lines: The Railgun Study

fields.text:
The official chronology records that Central Usea completed Stonehenge on 19 June 1998: eight railguns in a desert region of neutral San Salvacion, built to shoot down the fragments of Ulysses. The regency's general staff asks its engineers a question that the rest of the continent is too polite to ask aloud: what else could those guns do?

The study takes four months. It uses only published specifications, newspaper photographs and the calculations of the national observatory, and it is classified at the highest level the regency possesses. Its conclusions are technical and cautious. A battery that can reach fragments in orbit can, in principle, reach aircraft at altitude. Its fire would be decisive over a wide area. Its owner would control the sky above much of the continent.

The council reads the study in silence. Nobody proposes anything. Nobody needs to. The study is filed, and its conclusions are taught at the staff college the following year as an exercise in strategic geography, with the names of the countries removed.

The regency's official position on Stonehenge is gratitude, expressed in a short telegram. Its unofficial position is a file in a safe in the old war ministry, and the knowledge that the most powerful weapon on the continent belongs to someone else.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1998 / 06.19, and Super Weapons, Stonehenge. The staff study is provisional gameplay, not a record of Erusean planning.

fields.text: The Regency's Mandate
lines: The Regency's Mandate

fields.text:
The council's statement is broadcast at noon on the last day of the decade, read by an announcer in uniform. The regency, it says, has carried Erusea through the most dangerous decade in its history. It built the shelters on time. It kept the army loyal in the coup year. It fed the displaced when the fragments came. It has earned the mandate it was given, and it will keep that mandate for as long as Erusea needs it.

There is no mention of the Crown's seals, or of the date the council once published for returning them. The palace issues no statement. The officers who believed in the date say nothing in public. In private, some of them begin to keep diaries.

The country's reaction is the familiar one. The regency is efficient, unloved and, for now, unchallenged. The camps on the border are run by the army. So are the railways, the broadcasting stations and the grain stores. The council's critics have mostly gone abroad or gone quiet.

The regency enters the new decade with more power than any Erusean government has held since the monarchy's founding, and with one problem it cannot order away: a government that justifies itself by danger needs the danger to continue.

fields.text: The Seals Returned
lines: The Seals Returned

fields.text:
The ceremony is brief. The chief of staff enters the long room with the seals of office in a leather case, places them on the table in front of the monarch and steps back. The council's members follow, one by one, and lay their commissions beside the seals. Then they salute, turn and leave by the side door, and the palace secretaries come in by the front.

The council has kept its promise. The fragments have fallen, the camps are run by civilians and the seals have returned to the Crown. The monarch governs through a restored Crown Council, and the officers return to their barracks with a decade of governing behind them and, for most of them, considerable relief.

Not all of them. Some officers believe the regency was right to govern and wrong to stop. Some believe it should never have begun. A few believe that the Crown, having been rescued by the army once, can be rescued again, and that next time the rescue need not end. The restored council is aware of all three groups and has no plan for any of them yet.

In the streets the reaction is relief, cautious and quiet. People have learned not to celebrate too loudly in front of soldiers. They have also learned that the soldiers can be persuaded to leave, which is a lesson no Erusean government will be able to unteach.

Provisional gameplay: an alternate-history government change with no official source; the restored council is an unnamed office.

fields.text: The Crown's Acceptance
lines: The Crown's Acceptance

fields.text:
The official chronology records that Central Usea completed Stonehenge on 19 June 1998. The Crown's statement is short, warm and read from the chancery rather than the palace steps. Erusea welcomes the battery as the continent's shield against the fragments, thanks the nations that built it and asks only to be kept informed of its operation.

The general staff calls it weakness in a memorandum that reaches the newspapers within a day. The court gazette calls it statesmanship. The Federation's ambassador calls at the palace with a personal letter of thanks from the Federation's government, which the chancery frames and hangs in the corridor outside the long room.

In the country the statement is received with relief by people who wanted the fragments stopped and with resentment by people who wanted Erusea to be asked. Both groups are large. The palace has chosen to speak for the first, knowing the second will not forget.

The acceptance has bought Erusea goodwill in the continental capitals and a quiet border for the fragment years. Whether it has bought anything at home, the next decade will tell.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1998 / 06.19. The Crown's acceptance is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Relief Trains
lines: The Relief Trains

fields.text:
The official chronology records that Ulysses passed the Roche limit on 8 July 1999. Within a day the rail ministry has pulled the military timetable out of its safe and put it into force for a purpose its authors never imagined: relief.

The trains run day and night. Outward, they carry tents, water tanks, field kitchens, medicine and engineers. Inward, they carry the injured, the orphaned and the displaced, many of them from beyond Erusea's borders, to hospitals and schools in the undamaged districts. The station masters keep their own registers, because nobody else is keeping any.

The railway workers are the heroes of the fragment months. They work double shifts without being asked, sleep in signal boxes and drive engines that the ledger said should have been retired years ago. A locomotive driver who runs a relief train through a burning valley becomes, for one week, the most famous person in Erusea. The rail ministry refuses to release the driver's name, at the driver's request.

When the trains finally return to the ordinary timetable, the country has learned what its railways are for. It has also learned how many people are now living in the camps at the end of the line.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08. The relief timetable is provisional gameplay; no impact sites are scripted.

fields.text: A Kingdom After Ulysses
lines: A Kingdom After Ulysses

fields.text:
The decade of the court ledger is over. Ulysses passed the Roche limit on 8 July 1999, as the official chronology records, and the world it fell on is not the world the palace planned for. Erusea enters the new decade as a kingdom governed by prerogative, with its regiments sworn to the throne and its relief stores carrying the Crown's name.

The kingdom has survived. Its neighbours, some of them, have not survived intact. The continent is full of ruined harvests, broken towns and people walking toward any border where the lights are on, and Erusea's lights are on. The camps at the frontier grow by the week. The palace's granaries, which fed the districts through the fragment months, are nearly empty.

In the long room the conversation has changed. The questions of the 1990s were about who governs. The questions of the new decade are about what Erusea is owed and by whom. The court gazette prints letters from district towns that took in the displaced and want to know who will pay. It prints editorials about the battery in San Salvacion, built by others, aimed at the sky, guarding a continent that did not ask Erusea's opinion. It prints nothing about the general staff, which is busier than it has been in years.

The Crown governs a country that is proud, frightened and angry, and it has spent a decade teaching that country to look to the throne for answers. The throne will now be asked for them.

The official chronology records what comes next for Erusea's border on 21 April 2000. What comes after that depends, in part, on what the Crown chooses to say.

fields.text: An Assembly After Ulysses
lines: An Assembly After Ulysses

fields.text:
The constitutional decade ends with the assembly in emergency session. The official chronology records that Ulysses passed the Roche limit on 8 July 1999. Erusea's charter survived the fragment months; the question now is whether it can survive their consequences.

The reception camps opened by the relief act are full, and still the columns arrive. The provincial boards are exhausted and the treasury warns that the next supplementary budget will not pass. In the gallery, every day, sit the mayors of the border towns, who voted for the charter and now want to know why their schools are dormitories.

The parties have begun to divide along a line the constitution never anticipated. The liberal and labour benches insist that Erusea keep its doors open and its promises. The monarchist leagues want quotas. The nationalist deputies, who campaigned against the charter and now sit under it, want the border closed and the continent made to pay for a disaster it caused Erusea to share. Their speeches are the most reported in the country.

The official chronology records that Erusea stopped taking in refugees on 21 April 2000. Under this charter that decision, or any other, will be taken by vote, in public, by people who will have to explain it to the voters at the next election. The assembly has never been asked a harder question. It has never been better placed to answer it honestly.

fields.text: A Regency After Ulysses
lines: A Regency After Ulysses

fields.text:
The regency enters the new decade with the fragments behind it and its mandate in front. The official chronology records that Ulysses passed the Roche limit on 8 July 1999. The council's directorates fed the displaced, ran the trains and kept order, and the council has told the country so every evening since.

The camps at the frontier are run by the army. So are the crossings, the roads behind them and the registers of who is allowed through. The council's border command reports that the columns are growing, that the camps cannot be expanded indefinitely and that the neighbouring governments have stopped answering letters about who will pay.

The council's propaganda office has found its theme. Erusea, it says, prepared for the fragments when others did not, and is now asked to carry the cost of their failure. The battery in San Salvacion, built by others, could not stop the sky from falling on Erusea's neighbours; it stands now as a monument to a continent that decided Erusea's future without Erusea. The theme is popular in the barracks and, more worryingly for the council's critics, in the towns.

A government that justifies itself by danger needs the danger to continue. The regency's danger has changed shape. The official chronology records what Erusea does about its border on 21 April 2000, and what it does about its neighbours in the summer of 2003. The council has filed studies for both.

fields.text: The Camps Along the Border
lines: The Camps Along the Border

fields.text:
The camps began as a few fields of tents beside the frontier crossings in the summer of the fragments. They are now towns without names: rows of tents and huts, water tankers, latrines, a clinic, a school that meets in the open, a market where the displaced sell what they carried to the people who carried nothing.

Nobody planned them. The district authorities put up the first tents because people were arriving and it was raining. The army dug the first drains because the district authorities asked. The charities came next, then the journalists, then the officials from the capital with clipboards and questions about who was responsible.

The official chronology records that Erusea stopped taking in refugees on 21 April 2000. Whatever happens at the frontier, the people already inside it are here and will be here for years. Someone must register them, feed them, keep the disease out of the camps and the anger out of the towns next to them. Someone must decide whether the camps are a waiting room or a beginning.

The interior ministry asks the cabinet to choose. The cabinet asks for a week. The camps do not wait.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2000 / 04.21 is the official anchor for the border; camp administration is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Home Front Council
lines: The Home Front Council

fields.text:
The council meets for the first time in the old stock exchange, the only hall in the capital large enough for everyone who claimed a seat. Ministries, districts, unions, employers, the charities from the camps and the general staff's logisticians sit at tables arranged in a square, so that nobody is at the head.

Its mandate is practical. The camps need food that the farms are struggling to grow. The factories need hands that the camps can supply, if the unions agree and the law allows. The railways need coal that the mines are short of men to dig. Every problem touches every other problem, and for two years each ministry has solved its own by making somebody else's worse.

The council solves very little in its first month. In its second it agrees on a single register of labour, food and transport, the first time Erusea has counted all three in one book. In its third it begins, cautiously, to make decisions that stick.

The general staff's representatives take careful notes on everything. When a journalist asks one of them why the army is so interested in rations and train schedules, the officer answers that the army is interested in everything that keeps a country standing. The answer is printed. It is read in several capitals.

Provisional gameplay: Erusean domestic administration from 2000 to 2003 has no official source.

fields.text: The Casualty Lists
lines: The Casualty Lists

fields.text:
The lists are posted every Friday at noon, on boards outside every town hall in Erusea. They are printed in small type, alphabetically, by district: killed, wounded, missing. On the first Friday the boards are half empty. By the autumn the town halls need second boards.

People gather before noon and wait in silence. When the clerk pins up the new sheets, the crowd moves forward, and for a few minutes the only sound is people reading. Then someone finds a name. The others step back to give them room, and go on reading.

The government argued for a month about whether to publish the lists at all. The general staff wanted them withheld until the end of each campaign. The interior ministry warned that rumours would be worse than names. In the end the lists were published because the families demanded them, and because a country at war needs to know what the war is costing even when the knowledge hurts.

The lists change the country. They make the war real in every district, every Friday. They make the communiques harder to believe and the speeches harder to make. And they make Erusea's families, more than its ministers, the judges of whether the war was worth fighting.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER: Erusea is at war. The lists are provisional gameplay; no casualty figures are scripted.

fields.text: The Crown at War
lines: The Crown at War

fields.text:
The official chronology records that in the summer of 2003 Erusea invaded neutral San Salvacion and seized Stonehenge, turning its railguns against aircraft. The order went out under royal decree, as the Crown's mobilization laws require. The palace is now at war, and everything it does is war policy.

The Privy Council sits every day, with the chiefs of staff at the table and the minutes kept secret for the first time since the decade of the court ledger. The household guard has been expanded to a brigade. The court gazette prints the communiques beside the royal decrees, and the decrees grow longer.

The monarch visits the forward airfields and the field hospitals and is photographed at both. The photographs are popular. So, for the first months, is the war: the grievance that the Crown spoke for has become a campaign, and the campaign is going well. In the officers' clubs the toasts are to the throne.

The chancery's oldest secretaries have seen enough reigns to be uneasy. A Crown that leads a war is judged by the war. Victories add to the throne's prestige; defeats subtract from it, and a defeat large enough subtracts the throne itself. The secretaries keep their worries out of the minutes. They begin, quietly, to put the palace archive in order.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER: Erusea invades San Salvacion and seizes Stonehenge. The government's conduct is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Assembly at War
lines: The Assembly at War

fields.text:
The official chronology records that in the summer of 2003 Erusea invaded neutral San Salvacion and seized Stonehenge. Under the charter, the decision passed through the assembly. The debate lasted two days and the vote was closer than the government admits; the peace caucus voted against, and three of its members resigned their seats rather than vote at all.

The assembly is now a war council. It sits every day and votes on every major supply bill, and its committee of inquiry examines every significant loss in public, with the generals as witnesses. The generals hate the hearings. The families of the soldiers watch every one of them.

Erusea is the only country in the war that fights it with a free press and an opposition in the chamber, and the government is not sure whether this is a strength or a weakness. The communiques are checked against the correspondents' reports. The casualty lists are read aloud at the start of every sitting. Every month the peace caucus tables a motion asking the cabinet to seek terms, and every month it fails by a smaller margin.

The charter was written for a country at peace. It is now being tested by the one thing its authors feared most, and the test will be judged, as everything in the new Erusea is judged, by vote.

fields.text: The Regency at War
lines: The Regency at War

fields.text:
The official chronology records that in the summer of 2003 Erusea invaded neutral San Salvacion and seized Stonehenge, turning its railguns against aircraft. For the regency council, the war is the plan it filed a decade ago, updated, approved and executed by the same officers who drafted it.

There is no assembly to persuade and no palace to consult. The council issues orders, the directorates carry them out and the propaganda office explains them afterwards. The army fights the war the general staff has studied for twenty years, against an enemy it has war-gamed for ten, and in the first months it fights it very well.

The council's problem is not at the front. It is in the country, which has been governed by soldiers for so long that it no longer distinguishes between the war and the government. Every shortage is the regency's. Every casualty is the regency's. Every rumour from the front is a rumour about the regency, and the propaganda office's denials are believed less with every Friday's lists.

The council has always said it governs because Erusea is in danger. Erusea is now in the greatest danger of its history, and the council is responsible for it in every sense of the word.

fields.text: Aegir Fleet Command
lines: Aegir Fleet Command

fields.text:
The Aegir fleet has a commander, a staff, a home anchorage and a name that the official chronology will one day record. What it does not yet have is a doctrine for the war it may be asked to fight: a war against a coalition of continental powers that between them control the sea lanes, the ports and, if they can take it back, the sky.

The fleet's officers divide along the old lines. The battle-line school wants to find the enemy's main force and destroy it in one engagement, before the coalition's greater numbers can tell. The fleet-in-being school wants the Aegir fleet to stay in harbour under strong defences, forcing the enemy to guard against it everywhere, and to sail only when the odds are certain.

Both schools agree on the fleet's weaknesses. Its home anchorage can be found. Its escorts are too few. Its sailors are well trained and inexperienced. And a fleet, unlike an army, cannot be rebuilt in a season: whatever is lost is lost for a decade.

The fleet commander's staff presents both doctrines to the government and asks for a decision. The government asks the commander for a recommendation. The commander, who has read history, recommends whichever doctrine keeps the most ships afloat.

fields.text: After Comberth Harbor
lines: After Comberth Harbor

fields.text:
The official chronology records that on 23 November 2004 ISAF sank the Aegir fleet at Comberth Harbor. The news reaches the capital in a single signal from the harbour's naval station, and then nothing more for six hours.

When the reports finally come, they come all at once: the strike, the fires, the hulls settling in the harbour, the crews swimming for the quays. The fleet that was planned in the 1990s and built over a decade, the fleet whose name the country learned from the newspapers and the recruiting posters, is gone in a morning.

In the naval ministry the officers count what is left. Some escorts were at sea. Some submarines were on patrol. Some sailors were ashore, on leave, in hospital, at training schools inland. They will need ships, or other duties, or simply to be told what happened by someone who was not on the quay.

In the country the loss is felt as a wound to pride as much as to strength. The Aegir fleet was a promise that Erusea could stand among the great powers. The government must decide what to say about it, and what to do with the sailors who survived it.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2004 / 11.23. No naval losses are scripted by this event.

fields.text: The Air Doctrine Board
lines: The Air Doctrine Board

fields.text:
The air arm's commanders meet in a bunker under the capital's main airfield, where the ventilation hums and the coffee is terrible. On the wall is a map of the continent with Stonehenge's range drawn on it in red, a circle wider than most of the countries inside it.

The official chronology records that Erusea seized the battery and turned its railguns against aircraft. The question for the board is how the air arm fights alongside it. One faction wants to concentrate the best pilots in elite squadrons and win the sky the old way, aircraft against aircraft. The other wants to fight under the battery's umbrella, drawing the enemy into the railguns' reach and letting the battery do the work that pilots would otherwise die doing.

Both factions are right about the other's weakness. Elite squadrons can be worn down by numbers. An umbrella lasts only as long as the battery stands, and the enemy knows exactly where the battery is.

The board's chair, who flew interceptors in the 1990s and has buried more pilots than most officers have commanded, writes the decision in one line and signs it. The air arm will fight the war it can win, for as long as it can win it.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER: Erusea used Stonehenge's railguns against aircraft. The board and its doctrines are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Megalith Directorate
lines: The Megalith Directorate

fields.text:
The official record describes Megalith as an Erusean fortress built to bring down orbiting Ulysses fragments. The directorate created to answer for it inherits a site, a staff of engineers, a budget that appears in no published estimate and a question that its first director asks aloud at the first meeting: what is Megalith for, now?

Its original purpose was a defence against the sky. Fragments of Ulysses still orbit the Earth, decaying slowly, and some will fall. A fortress that can bring them down safely is a service to Erusea and to everyone downrange. The engineers who built it believe in that purpose, and many of them chose this work because of it.

But Erusea is at war, and in war everything is weighed for its military use. The general staff has asked for the site's specifications twice. Military intelligence has placed counter-intelligence officers in the engineers' quarters. The directorate's budget is now approved by a committee that includes two generals and no astronomers.

The directorate's first report states the facts and avoids the question. It lists the staff, the security arrangements and the scientific programme. In its final paragraph it notes, without comment, that a fortress able to bring down fragments is a fortress that someone may one day ask to do something else.

fields.text: The Young Officers
lines: The Young Officers

fields.text:
The counter-intelligence officers at Megalith file their reports every Monday. Most of them are routine: who visited the engineers' quarters, which telephone lines were used, how many crates arrived and how many left. In the autumn, the reports begin to include something else.

Some of the young officers in the site's garrison talk, late at night, about what they would do if the war were lost. They do not talk about surrender. They talk about honour, about the fragments still in orbit and about the fortress they are guarding. Their conversations are recorded and transcribed and sent to the capital, where they are read, filed and not acted upon.

The official chronology records that after Erusea's surrender young officers seized Megalith. The reports on the director's desk do not predict that. They describe a mood: young officers who have given years to a war, posted to a place nobody is allowed to know about, beginning to believe that the place itself is the last thing they can defend.

The director must decide what to do with the reports. Transfers would scatter the group. Arrests would make martyrs. Doing nothing would leave a garrison of believers guarding the most dangerous site in Erusea.

fields.text: The Occupation Authority
lines: The Occupation Authority

fields.text:
The official chronology records that Erusea invaded neutral San Salvacion and seized Stonehenge in the summer of 2003. Behind the advancing columns lie towns, roads, farms and people who did not choose this war and now live under Erusean guns.

The occupation authority is created by decree in the first week. Its mandate is to govern what the army holds, under the laws of war, without annexing anything. Erusea claims no territory, the decree says; it holds ground for the duration. The distinction matters to the lawyers in the foreign ministry and to the diplomats in the neutral capitals. Whether it matters to a farmer whose truck has been requisitioned is another question.

The authority's officials face the same choices every occupying power has faced. Military administration is fast and firm, and it makes enemies. Civil commissioners are slower and more acceptable, and they need the army's protection anyway. Curfews keep the streets quiet and the resentment loud. Food distribution keeps people alive and makes them dependent.

Erusea's soldiers did not train to govern foreign towns. They are learning, under the eyes of the neutral relief agencies, the foreign press and the people they govern, all of whom are keeping records.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER. Occupation administration is provisional gameplay; no ownership, core or border changes are scripted.

The occupation authority is created by decree in the first week. Its mandate is
to govern what the army holds, under the laws of war, without annexing
anything. Erusea claims no territory, the decree says; it holds ground for the
duration. The distinction matters to the lawyers in the foreign ministry and to
the diplomats in the neutral capitals. Whether it matters to a farmer whose
truck has been requisitioned is another question.
The authority's officials face the same choices every occupying power has
faced. Military administration is fast and firm, and it makes enemies. Civil
commissioners are slower and more acceptable, and they need the army's
protection anyway. Curfews keep the streets quiet and the resentment loud.
Food distribution keeps people alive and makes them dependent.
Erusea's soldiers did not train to govern foreign towns. They are learning, under
the eyes of the neutral relief agencies, the foreign press and the people they
govern, all of whom are keeping records.
Official: ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER. Occupation administration is
provisional gameplay; no ownership, core or border changes are scripted.

fields.text: Under Oversight
lines: Under Oversight

fields.text:
The official chronology records that Farbanti fell and Erusea surrendered on 19 September 2005, and that on 26 September young officers seized Megalith, which ISAF destroyed. In the weeks that followed, Erusea formed a provisional autonomous government under ISAF oversight.

The government is Erusean. Its ministers are Erusean, its civil servants are the same people who ran the ministries before the war and its decisions are made in Farbanti. But every decision is reviewed by the oversight commission, every weapon is registered, every unit's demobilization is inspected and every budget is read by officials from the countries Erusea fought.

The country receives the arrangement with exhaustion more than anger. The war is over. The casualty lists have stopped. The prisoners are coming home by train, and the stations are full of families who have waited two years. Most people want work, food, heating for the winter and a government that will not ask them to fight again. The provisional government can offer most of that, if the commission allows.

Not everyone accepts the surrender. Officers who believed in the war are leaving the army with bitterness and their service pistols. Veterans' leagues are meeting in back rooms. The government knows all this, and must decide whether to cooperate fully with its supervisors or to give them as little as it can.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19 and 09.26. The provisional government is shown through flags and ideas; there is no forced government swap.

fields.text: A Provisional Order
lines: A Provisional Order

fields.text:
A year after the surrender the provisional government has something it did not have at the start: a working order. The disarmament registry is complete. The conscripts have been discharged and most of them have found work. The veterans' pensions are paid, late and short but paid. The oversight commission's reports have become routine, which is the highest praise a supervisor can give.

It is not sovereignty in the old sense. Erusea cannot raise an army beyond the limits the commission sets, cannot sign treaties without review and cannot forget, for a single day, that it lost. But the ministries work, the trains run and the schools have reopened, including the ones in the border towns that were dormitories for the displaced a decade ago.

The government watches the veterans' leagues closely. Most of their members want pensions, medals and to be left alone. A few want another war, and some of those have found each other. The government's intelligence officers read their newsletters and attend their meetings, and send reports to a government that has learned to take reports seriously.

The provisional order is fragile, imperfect and supervised. It is also functioning, which a year ago few people in Farbanti believed it could.

fields.text: The Victor's Peace
lines: The Victor's Peace

fields.text:
In this alternative history the war ends with Erusea's armies holding the field. The coalition's governments have asked for terms. Erusea's negotiators arrive at the conference with maps, demands and a mandate from a country that has paid for its victory in casualty lists posted every Friday for two years.

Erusea annexes nothing. Its garrisons stay in the occupied districts as guarantors of the peace, under published terms, and the general staff insists that they stay until the treaties are signed and kept. The defeated governments remain in office, humiliated and resentful, and the neutral capitals watch Erusea for any sign that its peace is an empire by another name.

At home the victory is celebrated and then, quickly, counted. The war cost more than the propaganda admitted. The camps are still full. The factories that ran three shifts for the war need new orders. The veterans want work, and some of them want parades.

The government must decide what kind of victor Erusea will be. A magnanimous peace would buy goodwill and leave the country's grievances unanswered. A hard peace would answer them and buy a generation of enemies. The general staff, the assembly or the palace, whichever governs, will be remembered for the choice.

Provisional gameplay: an alternative outcome; in the official chronology Erusea surrendered on 19 September 2005.

fields.text: The Continental Order
lines: The Continental Order

fields.text:
Two years after the victory, the shape of Erusea's peace is clear on the map, though no border on it has moved. Erusean garrisons sit in the neighbours' capitals and at their railway junctions. Treaties limit the neighbours' armies and guarantee Erusea's trade. Debts, of one kind or another, run toward Farbanti from every direction.

The foreign ministry calls it the continental order. The neighbours' newspapers, where they are allowed to, call it an occupation. The neutral capitals call it an arrangement and wonder how long it will last.

Inside Erusea the order is popular and expensive. The garrisons need regiments that the economy needs as workers. The treaties need inspectors. The debts need collecting, and the collectors are not welcome. The general staff warns that resentment is growing in every capital where Erusean soldiers stand, and that a peace held by garrisons is a peace that ends when the garrisons leave.

Erusea has won the war that the official chronology says it lost. It now faces the problem that every victor in history has faced: winning was the easy part.

Provisional gameplay: an alternative outcome; in the official chronology Erusea surrendered on 19 September 2005.

fields.text: The Line Holds
lines: The Line Holds

fields.text:
The fighting has stopped without a decision, or never began. Erusea's army and its neighbours' face each other across a line drawn by the armistice or by the accord: on the maps it is a dotted line, on the ground it is wire, trenches, watchtowers and an empty field that nobody farms any more.

Nobody has agreed to call the line a border. The armistice commission meets monthly and settles incidents: a patrol that strayed, a shot fired at night, a farmer who crossed to fetch a cow. The prisoner lists are exchanged and compared, and the names of the missing are read on both sides.

At home the armistice leaves everyone dissatisfied. Those who wanted the war won feel cheated. Those who wanted it never fought feel vindicated and bitter. The army stays on the line at a cost the treasury cannot sustain forever, and the reservists who man it want to go home to farms and factories that need them.

The government must decide whether to keep the line manned at full strength until a treaty is signed, or to thin it and send the reservists home to rebuild. Either choice is a bet on the other side's patience.

Provisional gameplay: an alternative outcome to the official chronology, in which the war ends with Erusea's surrender in 2005.

fields.text: The Long Armistice
lines: The Long Armistice

fields.text:
The armistice line has held for another year, and then another. The watchtowers are still manned. The wire is still there. But the field between the lines is being farmed again, by both sides, under an informal arrangement that the commission pretends not to know about.

The prisoners have come home. The missing have been counted, and the counting has ended, which is its own kind of grief. The reservists rotate through the line every two years and complain about the food, which the officers take as a sign that morale is normal.

In the capital the arguments have changed. The question is no longer whether the war will resume but what the armistice should become. Some deputies, officers and ministers want a treaty, a border and an end. Others want the line kept as it is, a permanent reminder of an account not yet settled. A few want the account settled by other means, and say so in public, and are watched.

An armistice that lasts long enough starts to look like a peace. Erusea must decide whether it wants it to become one.

fields.text: After the Megalith
lines: After the Megalith

fields.text:
The official chronology records that on 26 September 2005 young Erusean officers seized Megalith, and that ISAF destroyed it. In the days that follow, the directorate that answered for the fortress has nothing left to answer for but its records.

They fill a lorry: personnel files, budgets, engineering logs, the counter-intelligence reports that described the young officers' mood a year before they acted. The director delivers them to the provisional government in person and asks that they be kept, not destroyed. Somebody, the director says, will want to know how this happened, and the answer is in the files.

The engineers who built Megalith to bring down the fragments of Ulysses are scattered: some detained, some questioned and released, some simply gone home to towns where nobody knows what they did. Many of them still believe that the fortress could have been what they built it to be. The ruins say otherwise.

The provisional government files the records and does not publish them. Not yet. A country that has just surrendered has enough to explain. But the files exist, and in time they will be read.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.26. The handover of the directorate's records is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Federal Question
lines: The Federal Question

fields.text:
The cabinet room is too small for the meeting it is holding. Ministers sit along the table, their deputies along the walls, and behind them the files that have followed every government since the Federation was formed: the treaty commitments, the regional grievances, the defence estimates, the arguments about who pays for what. Central Usea is the largest state on the continent. It chairs the Treaty Organization, it leads the faction its partners joined, and it has no plan for what happens when something truly large goes wrong.

The question on the table is not new. It has been asked after every flood, every border scare and every budget that collapsed in committee. How should a federation this size govern itself in an emergency? One answer is that it already does: the presidency and the Assembly have managed every crisis of the last decade, slowly, imperfectly and lawfully. A second answer comes from the staff colleges and from some of the ministers who served in them: an emergency needs a single authority, and a statute that says when the soldiers take over is better than an improvised one. A third answer comes from the Assembly's back benches: if the Federation must face a crisis, it should face it with every party in government, so that nobody is left outside to blame the rest.

The cabinet secretary has prepared a paper on each answer, and each paper is honest about its costs. Keeping the present government costs speed: every emergency decision will pass through the presidency, the ministries and, where the law requires it, the Assembly, and the law requires it often. A directorate costs consent: the regions, the courts and the newspapers would accept military authority only for as long as they believed the emergency was real. A unity cabinet costs coherence: every party would bring its own priorities to the table, and a government of rivals would argue about every decision before it took one. The papers recommend none of the three. They ask the cabinet to decide which cost it is most willing to pay.

None of the three is a plot. Each has its supporters inside this room. The cabinet agrees on only one thing tonight: it will choose before the emergency comes, not during it.

Provisional gameplay: the 1991 government is mod provenance; the three paths are provisional gameplay, and two of them are alternate history. No source shows a Central Usea regime change before ISAF's founding on 22 August 2003.

fields.text: The Emergency Powers Debate
lines: The Emergency Powers Debate

fields.text:
The draft runs to forty pages. Its first article defines a continental emergency; its second says who may declare one; its third, which the press will quote for a decade, says that during an emergency the executive authority of the Federation passes to a directorate formed around the commanders of Unified Command. The presidency remains. The Assembly remains. Neither governs until the directorate hands the authority back.

The officers who wrote it insist that it is a fire code, not a coup. A federation of this size, they argue, cannot evacuate a coast or answer a rebellion through committees that meet twice a week. They point to the regional governments that disagreed for three weeks over a flood relief convoy, and to the Assembly sessions that ended without a vote while the water rose. Write the rules now, they say, while nobody is frightened, and the rules will be fairer than anything improvised in a panic.

The opposition reads the same forty pages differently. A statute that hands power to soldiers when soldiers declare an emergency, they say, is not a fire code. It is a door, and someone will walk through it. The cabinet's own lawyers note, carefully, that the draft contains no expiry date and no court with the power to end the emergency.

Outside the cabinet the draft leaks within a week, as drafts do. The regional governments ask whether a directorate would respect their constitutions. The courts ask whether they would still sit. Unified Command's own commanders, consulted informally, are divided: some welcome a clear chain of authority in a crisis, others warn that an army which governs in an emergency will be blamed for every hardship the emergency brings. Nobody outside the drafting committee asks the question the committee keeps returning to, which is what would happen if the emergency never ended.

The cabinet sends the draft to committee with instructions to keep it. The argument has only begun.

Provisional gameplay: alternate history. No source shows a Central Usea regime change before ISAF's founding on 22 August 2003.

fields.text: All-Party Talks
lines: All-Party Talks

fields.text:
The invitations go out on federal letterhead to every party with a seat in the Assembly, including two that have not spoken to the governing majority in years. The talks will be held in a committee room rather than the cabinet room, at a table with no head, and the first session will have no agenda beyond a single question: if the Federation faced a disaster tomorrow, who would each party trust to lead it?

The answers are less hostile than anyone expected. The regional parties want a guarantee that the provinces will not be overruled by the capital in an emergency. The opposition wants seats in any cabinet that asks it to share responsibility. The smaller parties want to be consulted before announcements rather than after. Nobody, it turns out, wants to be the party that refused to sit down while the country prepared for the worst.

What they want in return is the problem. A unity government means dividing the portfolios, and every portfolio given to a partner is one taken from the majority that won the last election. The presidency's advisers warn that a cabinet of rivals will argue for weeks over every decision. The Assembly's elders reply that a cabinet of rivals cannot easily be brought down by the rivals it contains.

The presidency's staff draw up a map of the Assembly that looks nothing like the usual seating plan. It shows which party is strong in which region, which ministries each could plausibly run and which pairs of parties have never sat in the same cabinet. The map is covered in pencil within a day. By the end of the week it has become the working document of the talks, and the staff who drew it spend their evenings explaining it to party whips who have never before had to count anyone's seats but their own.

The first session ends late. The second is already scheduled.

fields.text: The Course Held
lines: The Course Held

fields.text:
The cabinet secretary's annual memorandum is usually read by the cabinet and nobody else. This year it is leaked within a day, and the newspapers print it in full, because for once it reads less like an administrative note and more like a chapter of history.

It lists the decade's emergencies in order. The rebellion in the southern islands at the end of 1995, ended by the Southern District and Unified Command. The announcement of April 1996, when the Federation told the world that Ulysses would strike. The coup of May 1997, which broke out across Usea and was defeated by Unified Command. The completion of Stonehenge in June 1998. After each entry it records the same thing: the presidency governed, the Assembly sat, the courts opened in the morning. Nothing was suspended that the constitution did not allow to be suspended.

The memorandum does not claim that this was efficient. It admits the weeks lost to committees and the convoys that waited for signatures. It argues only that a government which kept its own rules through all of this has earned the trust it will need when the fragments fall.

The opposition calls the memorandum self-congratulation. The public, by the polls, calls it reassuring.

trust it will need when the fragments fall.

fields.text: The Directorate
lines: The Directorate

fields.text:
The declaration is read at noon on every federal channel. A continental emergency exists. Under the emergency statute, executive authority passes to a directorate formed around Unified Command. The presidency will continue its ceremonial and diplomatic duties. The Assembly will continue to sit, and may debate whatever it wishes, but it will not govern until the directorate returns the authority it has taken.

Within the hour the directorate's first orders reach the ministries. Movement permits for the evacuation zones will be issued by district commanders. Requisition orders for transport take effect immediately rather than after a thirty-day notice period. Public announcements about the emergency will come from a single information board. The orders are clear, numbered and signed, and in the ministries that have spent years arguing over who signs what, some officials are quietly relieved.

Others are not. Two regional governments issue statements reserving their constitutional rights. A newspaper prints the forty pages of the statute on its front page under a single word: Read. In the Assembly, the opposition demands to know when the emergency will end. The directorate's answer is that it will end when the danger has passed, and that it will say so.

Abroad, the treaty partners are informed before the declaration is read, and their governments respond with careful statements: they note the emergency, they trust that the Federation's commitments are unchanged and they look forward to working with whatever authority now speaks for it. Erusea says nothing at all in public. In the directorate's first briefing, an intelligence officer reports that Erusean diplomats have asked their counterparts in three capitals whether the Federation's army now governs it, and that nobody has yet given them a satisfying answer.

Outside the capital, life continues. The trains run. The schools open. A great many people discover that the government has changed and that their day has not.

fields.text: The Directorate Review
lines: The Directorate Review

fields.text:
The statute required a review once the emergency eased, and the drafters wrote that clause to be inconvenient. The directorate must report to the Assembly in open session: what it decided, what it spent, whom it detained and why the emergency should continue, if it should.

The report is long and, by the standards of emergency governments, honest. Stonehenge is complete. The evacuation plans are written, rehearsed and funded. The districts that went silent during the coup of 1997 are back under federal administration. Against this the opposition lays its own list: the newspapers that were warned, the officers removed without hearings, the regional governments overruled. Both lists are true.

The debate runs for three days. The directorate's officers answer every question put to them, which surprises the members who expected to be ignored. On the third evening the Assembly's speaker reads the statute's final article aloud: the authority taken in an emergency may be returned by the directorate, or it may be extended by the directorate, and the Assembly may only advise.

Ulysses will arrive in a year. The directorate must now decide what kind of government will meet it.

Provisional gameplay: alternate history. No source shows a Central Usea regime change before ISAF's founding on 22 August 2003.

fields.text: Authority Returned
lines: Authority Returned

fields.text:
The directorate's last order is three lines long. The continental emergency declared under the statute is ended. Executive authority returns to the presidency and the Assembly. The staff of the directorate will return to Unified Command within thirty days.

The handover is undramatic by design. Ministers who have spent years carrying out orders sit down again at the cabinet table to issue their own. The district councils are dissolved, and the regional governments resume the duties they had before. The information board is closed, and the newspapers go back to asking questions first. The evacuation plans the directorate wrote stay in force, because they are good plans, and the incoming cabinet has no wish to rewrite them a year before the impact.

The officers go back to their headquarters. Some are bitter, convinced that they have been dismissed on the eve of the emergency they prepared for. More are relieved. Unified Command was built to fight, not to govern, and several of its senior officers say privately that they never want to sign a ration order again.

The opposition's leaders, invited to the handover, are given the directorate's files in full: every order it issued, every requisition, every detention and every warning sent to a newspaper. The files run to thousands of pages, and the opposition's researchers find in them both less than they feared and more than they would like. Most of the directorate's work was administrative, dull and competent. Some of it was not, and those pages will be read aloud in the Assembly for months.

In the Assembly the opposition, which has spent the directorate's whole tenure demanding this moment, finds that it has nothing left to demand. The speaker calls the first ordinary session in years. It begins, as ordinary sessions do, with a quarrel about the agenda.

Provisional gameplay: alternate history. No source shows a Central Usea regime change before ISAF's founding on 22 August 2003; the restored presidency is the mod's 1991 government.

fields.text: The Directorate Extended
lines: The Directorate Extended

fields.text:
The renewal is announced as a technical matter. The emergency has not passed; Ulysses has not yet arrived; therefore, under the statute, the directorate remains. The announcement is two sentences long and contains no date.

The reaction is not technical. The Assembly passes a resolution, by a large majority, asking the directorate to state when it will return authority. The directorate replies that it will do so when the debris has fallen and the evacuees are home, and that it cannot know when that will be. Both the resolution and the reply are printed in every newspaper, and the newspapers are not warned for printing them, which some commentators take as a sign of restraint and others as a sign of confidence.

Inside the ministries the extension changes little. The district councils go on meeting. The evacuation timetables go on being rehearsed. What changes is the mood in the officer corps. Officers who joined the directorate as a temporary duty begin to talk about it as a career, and officers who opposed it begin to keep their opinions to themselves.

Abroad, the extension is noticed. The treaty partners, who accepted the directorate as an emergency measure, begin to ask in private how long an emergency can last. Their questions are polite, and the directorate answers them politely, but the partners' liaison officers report home that the Federation's government has stopped describing itself as temporary. That observation travels, as observations do, and by the end of the year it has reached capitals far beyond the treaty.

The directorate's own staff has drafted a further review for the year after the impact. Nobody outside the directorate has seen it.

Provisional gameplay: alternate history. No source shows a Central Usea regime change before ISAF's founding on 22 August 2003.
