fields.text: A Country Between Neighbours
lines: A Country Between Neighbours

fields.text:
The new year's cabinet paper in Chopinburg was short, because the country is small, and blunt, because its authors had nothing to lose. It began with a map. Central Usea lay across the highlands to one side, larger than Chopinburg many times over. Ugellas lay beyond the passes on another. Platania shared the industrial coast and the empty shore between them. Chopinburg sat in the middle, with an inland capital, a rubber island, three tired shipyards and a seat on a treaty council where everyone else was bigger.

The paper did not pretend this was a weakness to be overcome. It was a fact to be used. The island's rubber was wanted by every factory on the continent. The northern yards could repair the neighbours' ships. The highland crossings carried more trade than anyone admitted. And the treaty council, for all its size, needed members willing to do the dull work of drafting rules that larger members preferred to argue about.

What the paper could not say was which of these things should come first. The estate houses wanted the island settled in their favour. The yard unions wanted orders. The customs service wanted the highlands closed, and the highland families wanted them open. The cabinet resolved, as small cabinets do, to begin everything at once and to count the money weekly.

Provisional gameplay: no source covers Chopinburg; its geography and starting position are mod provenance (history/countries/CHO - Chopinburg.txt, history/states).

fields.text: The Split Island Question
lines: The Split Island Question

fields.text:
The surveyors came back from Split Island with sunburn, fevers and three hundred pages of findings, and the findings were worse than anyone had expected. The island's rubber field is one of the richest on the continent. Its ownership is a tangle of old estate grants, unwritten tenancies and debts that pass from father to son. Most of the trees are tapped by families who do not own the ground beneath them and are paid in scrip redeemable only at the estate store.

Three answers are now before the cabinet, and each has its champions. The estate houses propose that the state simply confirm their holdings in law, collect a fixed royalty and leave the plantations to people who have run them for generations. The tappers' associations, backed by the island's priests and schoolteachers, propose a smallholders' charter: title to the ground for the families who work it, and credit banks to help them keep it. fields.text: The Yard Books
lines: The Yard Books

fields.text:
The books of the three northern yards arrived in the capital in tea chests, and the clerks who opened them found the history of an industry in slow decline. The yards had built coasters and tugs for a generation, then repaired them, then repaired other people's, then very little at all. The cranes still worked. The slipways were sound. The riveters and fitters who knew how to use them were growing old.

Yet the books also showed something the cabinet had not expected. Merchant captains from Platania, Ugellas and Central Usea still asked for berths in the northern yards, because the work there was good and cheap and the harbour master did not lose papers. A small, steady trade in repairs had kept the yards alive without anyone in the capital noticing.

The yard managers' covering letter makes two requests. The first is for apprentices, before the old hands retire and take their skills with them. The second is for a decision: should the yards make a living mending the neighbours' fleets, or should they try once more to build ships of their own? The managers note, politely, that they would like an answer before the next order book closes.

fields.text: The Highland Crossings
lines: The Highland Crossings

fields.text:
On paper, the highland border with Central Usea and the passes toward Ugellas carry a modest trade in timber, wool and machine parts. In practice, the customs service estimates that three cargoes cross unrecorded for every one that crosses with a manifest. Mule trains move by night along paths no surveyor has mapped. Whole villages on both sides of the line live from the difference between one country's prices and the other's.

The Interior Ministry wants this ended. It proposes a customs cordon: a post at every crossing, a licence for every mule train, mounted rangers on the high paths and a firm rule that what cannot be declared cannot cross. The Ministry of Trade argues the opposite. The highland families have traded across the line for longer than either state has existed. A trusted traders' pass would let known hauliers cross without search, bring the trade into the open, and cost far less than a cordon.

Neither ministry pretends its plan is free of risk. A cordon will be resented in the highlands and may push the smugglers onto worse paths with worse cargoes. A pass will be abused by some of the people who carry it. The highland villages, consulted for once, have replied that they will live with whatever the capital decides, as they always have, but would prefer to be asked again before it changes its mind.

The old mountaineer training, the General Staff adds, would serve either plan.

fields.text: The Smallest Chair at the Table
lines: The Smallest Chair at the Table

fields.text:
Chopinburg's delegation to the Central Usean Treaty Council travels with two officials, one typist and a briefcase of positions that rarely survive the first morning. The council's large members arrive with staffs of dozens. Their delegates speak first, speak longest and expect the small members to listen. Chopinburg has listened for years. The foreign service now asks whether listening is the best use of its chair.

There are two ways, the service suggests, for a small member to matter. The first is to become indispensable to the large members: to send the country's most capable clerks to staff the council's committees and draft its papers, so that every rule passes through Chopinburgian hands before it reaches the chamber. The second is to stop acting alone. The council's other small members share Chopinburg's interests in transit, relief and fair contributions. If they agreed their positions before each session and voted together, the large members would have to consult them as a bloc.

The first path needs talent the country can barely spare. The second needs partners who may not always keep their word. Either way, the delegation will have to grow, and the Treasury has already asked how much a typist costs in the council city.

The cabinet notes that neither path requires Chopinburg to change its obligations under the treaty, only to take them more seriously than the larger members do.

fields.text: The Exchange Hall and the Union Hall
lines: The Exchange Hall and the Union Hall

fields.text:
Two buildings stand on opposite sides of the capital's main square, and between them they now hold more authority than the government that sits behind them. The exchange hall is where rubber is priced, contracts signed and credit extended. The union hall is where the yard crews, estate tappers and highland hauliers meet, vote and decide when to stop work. For most of Chopinburg's history the two halls have quarrelled. This year they have each proposed to govern.

The exchange houses argue that the country lives by its trade, and that those who manage the trade should manage the state. They offer a directorate: the estate houses, exporters and bankers sitting together, setting prices, balancing accounts and running the country with the care of a well-kept ledger. They promise stability, solvency and an end to strikes.

The unions argue that the country lives by its work, and that those who do the work should choose who governs it. They offer an assembly: elected delegates from every yard, estate and haulage depot, a cabinet that meets in the union hall in public, and a national ballot within a year. They promise fairness, openness and an end to scrip.

The present government, which owes its existence to neither hall, has discovered that it cannot govern against both. It can choose one. It can try to keep the balance a while longer. The square between the halls has been very crowded every evening this month.

fields.text: The Directorate Takes the Seals
lines: The Directorate Takes the Seals

fields.text:
The handover took place in the exchange hall at the close of trading, so as not to disturb the morning's prices. The outgoing ministers signed the transfer at a table usually reserved for contracts. The directorate, seated in a row beneath the price board, signed it as one body and did not give speeches. Its first notice was posted on the exchange floor ten minutes later: the government of Chopinburg was now the Rubber Exchange Directorate, all ministries would continue their work, and the price of island latex would be published at noon as usual.

The directorate speaks as an office, and its members prefer it so. They are the heads of estate houses, exporting firms and banks, and they intend to run the country as they run their businesses: carefully, quietly and with the accounts in order. Within a week the Treasury had a new set of books. Within a month the strikes at the northern yards had been settled by a wage agreement the unions had not been asked to sign.

The union hall has not been closed. Its meetings continue, its newspapers print, and its delegates are invited to submit proposals in writing. Very few of them have done so. The highland families, who distrust both halls equally, report that the customs posts have become more polite and more expensive.

Abroad, the change has been welcomed by the buyers. Platanian and Central Usean trading houses have asked for seats on the exchange floor, and the directorate is considering what such seats should cost.

fields.text: The Assembly Meets in the Union Hall
lines: The Assembly Meets in the Union Hall

fields.text:
The assembly's first session began at the change of shift, so that the night crews from the northern yards could attend before going home. The hall was full by six in the morning. Estate tappers had come by the first ferry from the island, highland hauliers by lorry, and dockworkers from every berth. The outgoing ministers were invited to sit in the front row. Most of them came.

The assembly governs as an office. Its delegates are elected by their yards, estates and depots and can be recalled by them; the cabinet it appoints meets in the union hall itself and reads its decisions aloud every week to anyone who cares to listen. Its founding resolution sets a national ballot within a year, open to every adult citizen, and forbids the assembly from postponing it.

The exchange houses have not been abolished. They have been invited to send observers to the cabinet's weekly reading, and to explain, in public, why the scrip still circulating on Split Island should not be redeemed in money at their expense. The observers have attended. Their explanations have not been well received.

The country is noisier than it was. Strikes have stopped, but meetings have multiplied. Foreign buyers ask whether contracts signed with the old government will be honoured, and the assembly answers that they will, provided the wages paid under them are honest. Whether the union hall can become a parliament before the year is out is the question every newspaper in Chopinburg is now asking.

fields.text: The Announcement Next Door
lines: The Announcement Next Door

fields.text:
The announcement came from Central Usea on the twentieth of April, and in Chopinburg it was heard first on the highland posts, where the border guards keep their radios tuned to the neighbours' stations. The asteroid Ulysses would strike the Earth. Astronomers had calculated its path; governments across the continent were being told to prepare. By evening the news had reached the island ferries, the northern yards and every cafe in the capital.

Chopinburg has no great observatories and no railguns. It has an inland capital, a rubber island exposed to the sea, three shipyards and a seat on a treaty council whose larger members will make the decisions that matter. The cabinet's first meeting after the announcement was given over almost entirely to a single question: where in a small country can people be kept safe from a disaster no one can yet locate?

Two answers emerged. The coastal provinces want an evacuation plan: ferries, lighters and the estate railway organised to move the island and the shore inland at short notice. The capital's officials want the reverse: prepare the inland city's schools, cellars and warehouses as refuges and bring the coast to them. Both plans cost more than the budget can bear, and both depend on warnings that may arrive late.

The northern yards have offered a third idea: old hulls fitted as floating stores that can move away from whatever coast is struck. The cabinet has asked them to cost it.

fields.text: The Night the Sky Broke
lines: The Night the Sky Broke

fields.text:
On the eighth of July Ulysses broke apart, and its fragments lit the sky over Usea from one horizon to the other. Chopinburg watched from rooftops, harbour walls and the decks of the shelter hulls. No one in the capital could say that night where the fragments had come down, and the first reports, when they came, contradicted one another.

What reached Chopinburg first was not news but absence. Ferries ran late, then not at all, and the island's harbours, which live on the daily boats, began to count their flour and fuel by the sack. On the second day the first boats arrived from the neighbours' damaged ports, crowded with people who had nowhere else to go. On the third day the price of flour doubled in the capital.

The preparations of three years are now being tested in ways no plan anticipated. The government has the shelter hulls, the stores and whatever the treaty council can be persuaded to send. It does not yet have a clear idea of how long the strain will last, or how many more boats will come. The cabinet has decided to treat every decision as temporary, and to take them quickly.

Provisional gameplay: Chopinburg's response is unsourced; the impact date is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08).

fields.text: War Beyond the Highlands
lines: War Beyond the Highlands

fields.text:
Erusea has invaded San Salvacion and seized the railgun site at Stonehenge, and Central Usea is gathering a coalition to drive it out. The news reached Chopinburg the way news always does, across the highlands, and with it came the realisation that the country's largest neighbour is now at war.

Chopinburg is a treaty member, not a combatant. Its obligations under the council do not include joining the coalition, and the cabinet has no intention of joining it. But neutrality next door to a belligerent is a demanding thing. Central Usean officers have asked about the highland roads. Merchant captains have asked whether the northern yards will refit hulls for war work. Agents from every side are buying rubber in the exchange at prices that make the estate houses dizzy.

The General Staff proposes to close the highland passes to every army and to keep the mountain companies on their posts through the summer. The yard managers propose something different: to refit merchant hulls as unarmed hospital ships at cost, for whoever asks, so that the yards serve the war's wounded without serving its armies. The Treasury proposes to sell rubber to all comers at the published price and to refuse every private arrangement.

None of these proposals excludes the others entirely, but each sets a tone. The cabinet must decide what kind of neutral Chopinburg will be before its neighbours decide for it.

Provisional gameplay: Chopinburg's response is unsourced; the war date is official (ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER, 2003 / 08.22).

fields.text: Chopinburg After the War
lines: Chopinburg After the War

fields.text:
The war is over. Erusea has surrendered, Central Usea is counting its losses, and the highland posts have returned to their peacetime strength. Chopinburg was never invaded, never bombed and never asked to choose a side in a way it could not refuse. In a decade that took so much from its neighbours, that is no small thing.

It is also not the end of the story. The neighbours' ports are full of damaged ships, and the northern yards have more work than they can handle. The treaty council, which spent the war arguing about transit and relief, now wants to argue about reconstruction, and Chopinburg's clerks and caucus partners have opinions ready. The island's rubber is in demand for every rebuilt factory on the continent.

The question the cabinet now faces is what a small country owes the large ones that fought the war, and what they owe it in return. Some ministers want to offer the yards and the clerks freely, as a down payment on goodwill. Others want to be paid, politely and in full, as a small country always should be.

Provisional gameplay: Chopinburg's response is unsourced; the end of the war date is official (ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19).

fields.text: The Harbour Ledger
lines: The Harbour Ledger

fields.text:
Platania has always kept its accounts at the harbour office in Scardilli, in tall ledgers bound in green cloth, and every government has eventually discovered that those ledgers describe the country better than its census. This year the harbour master has been asked to do something new: to count not only cargoes and tonnage, but people, districts and debts, from the Pantellia Islands to the farthest farms of the Scofields Plateau.

The first volumes are unflattering. Scardilli is rich, crowded and owed money by almost everyone. Casale moves the ore and grain of the plateau to the sea and keeps little of the profit. The islands land their catch in the capital because they have no cold stores of their own. The plateau feeds the country and mines its ore, and sends fewer members to the assembly than a single harbour ward. Beyond the plateau lies the inland march, a country of passing traffic and very few settled towns.

fields.text: The Houses of Scardilli
lines: The Houses of Scardilli

fields.text:
There are eleven great merchant houses in Scardilli, and between them they own most of the warehouses on the quays, most of the lighters in the harbour and a remarkable share of the debts owed by everyone else in Platania. They have survived wars, crashes, fires and at least two governments that promised to break them. They have also, more than once, failed all at once and taken half the country's savings with them.

Three proposals now lie before the government, and each has its party. The free-traders want Scardilli declared a free port, with no duties on goods in transit and the harbour's revenue drawn from fees alone. They argue that a busy port pays for everything, and that the houses will grow too rich to fail. The older houses want the opposite: chartered guilds with fixed shares of each trade, merchant courts and an end to the ruinous competition that brought the last two collapses. A third party, drawn from the ministries and the yards, wants the state to buy hulls of its own and run a national shipping line, so that Platanian trade no longer depends on foreign charters or on the houses' good humour.

Each proposal would change who holds power in Scardilli. The free port would favour the newest houses and the foreign agents who trade with them. The guilds would favour the oldest houses and freeze the order of the harbour as it stands. The national line would bring the state into the harbour as a competitor, and the houses have not forgotten what happened to the last government that tried.

The harbour office's advice is brief. Whatever is chosen must be chosen soon. The exchange is already pricing in each outcome, and uncertainty is the one cargo nobody in Scardilli can insure.

fields.text: What the Islands Want
lines: What the Islands Want

fields.text:
The ferry from Scardilli to the Pantellia Islands takes most of a day in good weather and does not run at all in bad. That single fact explains a great deal about island politics. Islanders are Platanian, and very few of them would say otherwise. But they have spent generations waiting for decisions made on the mainland, by officials who come out on the morning boat and leave on the evening one.

The island councils have sent the government a petition, signed in every harbour on the chain. It does not ask for independence, and its authors are careful to say so in the first paragraph. It asks for an island charter: an elected board to run the harbours, the fisheries and the schools, a subsidised ferry that runs on a timetable, and cold stores so that the catch can be landed at home. It is a modest document, and in Scardilli it has caused alarm out of all proportion to its contents.

The War Ministry's reply is that the islands guard the approaches to the capital and cannot be left to an elected fisheries board. It proposes the opposite course: govern the islands as any other province, with officials from Scardilli, a proper garrison and a naval station watching the sea lanes. The islanders, it notes, would also gain a slipway and fuel bunkers, which is more than their board could ever afford.

Both proposals claim to be the best way of keeping the islands Platanian. The cabinet suspects that one of them is right, and that choosing the wrong one would be remembered on the islands for a very long time.

fields.text: The Survey of the Plateau
lines: The Survey of the Plateau

fields.text:
The survey teams spent a full season on the Scofields Plateau, and they came back with two reports that seem to describe different countries. The geological report describes ore beds of real value, reachable by modest workings and a rail spur to Casale. The agricultural report describes the farms that feed the capital: good soil, short of water, short of credit and permanently in debt to buyers in Scardilli who set the price of grain before it is harvested.

The plateau has noticed the surveyors, and it has noticed what they were counting. Its farm councils have begun to ask why the country's food and ore both come from the plateau while its money, its members and its ministries all stay on the coast. The mining towns ask the same question in rougher language. Casale, which carries the plateau's produce to the sea and keeps little of the profit, has started to ask it too.

The ministries see two ways forward. The plateau can be developed for its ore, with concessions, a mining board and an ore road to the coast. That would bring money and work quickly, and it would bring the merchant houses onto the plateau as investors. Or the plateau can be developed for its farms, with public granaries, fixed purchase prices and a rural credit bank that lends against the harvest. That would bring security more slowly, and it would take the price of bread out of the houses' hands.

The two plans are not compatible, at least not with the money available. Whichever is chosen, the plateau will remember who chose it, and why.

fields.text: A Market Called a Council
lines: A Market Called a Council

fields.text:
Platanian delegates to the Central Usean Treaty Council have a reputation in the chamber. Other members arrive with security papers and emergency plans; the Platanians arrive with tariff tables. They have always treated the council as a trading forum first and a defensive arrangement second, and their colleagues have mostly been grateful that someone is willing to read the customs schedules.

This session, the delegation has asked the government for instructions on a question it can no longer avoid. The council is drafting common rules for trade between its members. Some members want a common outer tariff, so that treaty goods move freely inside and outside goods pay at the border. Others want the council to guarantee open sea lanes and open harbours to every flag, members and outsiders alike, on equal terms.

For Platania the choice is not abstract. A common tariff would protect the plateau's grain and ore against cheaper imports, and Platanian customs officers would be well placed to draft the schedule. Open sea lanes would suit the harbour of Scardilli, whose wealth comes from carrying everyone's cargo, and the pilots and salvage crews whose rules the council would probably adopt.

The delegation's own preference is plain from the way its letter is written. It has asked for instructions all the same, because the plateau and the port are both reading the newspapers, and both will hold the government responsible for the answer.

fields.text: The Yards and the Navy
lines: The Yards and the Navy

fields.text:
The Scardilli yards reopened this week with new cranes on the fitting-out basin and a covered slip large enough to take a frigate. The harbour came out to watch the first plates lifted into place, and the newspapers have already begun to argue about what the yards should build.

There are two schools of thought in the Admiralty, and each has written a paper. The first holds that Platania lives by the sea lanes and should be able to defend them: a small blue-water squadron of escorts, able to sail with merchant convoys beyond the coast and to show the flag in foreign harbours. It would be expensive, and it would need years of exercises before it was any good, but it would give Platania a voice at sea.

The second holds that Platania cannot afford to rule the open sea and should not try. It proposes a coastal flotilla instead: fast boats, minelayers, shore radar on the Pantellia Islands and a chart of every channel that could be closed in a crisis. It would make Platanian waters too costly to enter uninvited, and it would cost less than half as much as the squadron.

The merchant houses favour the squadron, because it would protect their ships wherever they sail. The islanders favour the flotilla, because it would be based on their coasts. The Treasury favours whichever is cheaper, and has said so in a third paper that nobody requested.

fields.text: The Bridge at Seals Bridge
lines: The Bridge at Seals Bridge

fields.text:
The old timber crossing at Seals Bridge has failed in every flood season anyone can remember. When it fails, the coast road and the plateau road become two separate countries for a month, and the price of bread in Scardilli rises while the plateau's grain waits on the far bank. Every government has promised a proper bridge. This one has built it.

The new crossing is steel on concrete piers, wide enough for two lorries and a rail track, and high enough to clear any flood the engineers could find in the records. It was paid for partly by the treasury and partly by a levy on the island and plateau trade it now carries, which the islanders and the plateau farmers both noticed and both paid.

At the opening, a delegation from the islands and a delegation from the plateau crossed from opposite banks and met in the middle, which was the engineers' idea and turned out to be a good one. The newspapers printed the photograph on their front pages. For a few days, at least, Platanians talked about the country as one place rather than three.

fields.text: Port, Plateau and Islands
lines: Port, Plateau and Islands

fields.text:
The assembly in Scardilli was designed for a country of merchants, and for a long time that is what Platania was. It is no longer the only thing Platania is. The plateau has its granaries or its mines, its credit bank or its ore road, and its farm councils and mining towns have learned to organise. The islands have their charter or their station, their harbours and their ferries. The houses of Scardilli have their exchange. Each has grown stronger in its own way, and each now wants the government to reflect the Platania it lives in.

Three answers are being argued in the newspapers and the cafes. The houses and the ratepayers of the ports want a mercantile senate, elected by those who pay the harbour rates, with the assembly beneath it. They argue that commerce built the country and that a government of merchants will at least know how to balance its books. The islanders and many in the smaller towns want a compact: an executive in which port, plateau and islands each hold a veto, so that no region can govern the others again. The plateau's farm councils, mine crews and the dockworkers of Scardilli and Casale want a cooperative union, which would take the government out of the houses' hands entirely.

Each answer frightens someone. The plateau fears a senate of ratepayers, because it pays few harbour rates. The houses fear a cooperative union, for obvious reasons. Almost everyone fears that a compact of vetoes would never decide anything at all, though the islanders point out that this might be an improvement.

The present government has said little, except that the assembly as it stands cannot carry the argument much longer. The exchange, as usual, has already begun pricing the outcome.

fields.text: The Mercantile Senate Sits
lines: The Mercantile Senate Sits

fields.text:
The senate met for the first time in the old exchange hall, because the assembly chamber was too small and because the houses wanted it that way. Its members were elected by the ratepayers of the ports, which means by the people who pay the harbour rates, which means very largely by the merchant houses, their clerks and their creditors. Nobody pretended otherwise.

The senate governs as an office, and its members are not named in its decrees. Its first acts were characteristically businesslike. It published the national accounts in full, set the harbour rates for the coming year and appointed a commission to draft its own charter, with a clause requiring every public contract above a fixed sum to be tendered openly. The newspapers, most of which are owned by one house or another, approved.

Outside Scardilli the welcome was cooler. On the plateau the farm councils called the senate a counting house with a flag, and pointed out that the franchise excluded most of them. On the islands, the harbour boards asked what a senate of ratepayers would do for fishermen who pay rates on very little. The senate's answer, delivered in its first communique, was that a prosperous harbour would pay for everything else, and that it intended to be judged by results.

The houses have governed Platania indirectly for most of its history. Now they govern it directly, in public, and must answer for it at the next ballot.

fields.text: The Compact Is Signed
lines: The Compact Is Signed

fields.text:
The compact was signed at Seals Bridge, on a table set up in the middle of the new crossing, because none of the three regions would agree to sign it in either of the others. The delegates of the port, the plateau and the islands each brought a copy, each read it aloud and each signed all three. It took most of a day. Nobody complained, because the whole point of the compact is that nothing will be done quickly again.

The compact executive governs as an office, and its members are not named in its acts. Its articles divide revenue by a formula that everyone has read and nobody fully understands, require unanimity on taxes and on any change to the compact itself, and allow any region to suspend a law that falls on it alone until the executive has met again. In practice this means that the islands can stop a fisheries law, the plateau can stop a grain law and the port can stop a harbour law, and all three can stop a budget.

Critics in Scardilli call it a recipe for paralysis, and they may be right. Its supporters reply that Platania has tried every other recipe, and that a government which cannot act against any region is at least a government no region needs to fear. The islanders, for once, are the most enthusiastic Platanians in the country.

The first meeting of the executive lasted eleven hours and produced a single decision: to meet again in a month. The newspapers reported this as a failure. The delegates seemed to regard it as a success.

fields.text: The Cooperative Union Takes Office
lines: The Cooperative Union Takes Office

fields.text:
The union took office in Casale rather than Scardilli, which told the country most of what it needed to know. The farm councils of the plateau, the mine crews of the ore road and the dockworkers of both ports had been organising together for years, and when the government finally fell they were the only organisation in the country with branches in every district.

The union's council governs as an office, and its members are not named in its decrees. It describes itself as a congress of cooperatives rather than a party, and its founding programme reads like one: the plateau mines to the miners who work them, the plateau harvest to boards that sell bread at a fixed price, the docks to the cooperatives that load the ships. The merchant houses keep their ships and their warehouses. They lose the right to set the price of everything else.

Scardilli received the news in silence. The exchange suspended trading for a day, then reopened with prices that suggested the houses expected to survive, if not to thrive. Some houses have begun moving their registrations abroad. Others have quietly asked the union which of their trades it intends to leave alone, and have been surprised by how long the answer is.

On the plateau there were bonfires. In the islands, where the union has few members, the harbour boards asked to be consulted before anything changed. The union council has promised that they will be, and has sent a delegation out on the morning ferry to prove it.

the docks to the cooperatives that load the ships. The merchant houses keep
their ships and their warehouses. They lose the right to set the price of
everything else.
Scardilli received the news in silence. The exchange suspended trading for a
day, then reopened with prices that suggested the houses expected to survive,
if not to thrive. Some houses have begun moving their registrations abroad.
Others have quietly asked the union which of their trades it intends to leave
alone, and have been surprised by how long the answer is.
On the plateau there were bonfires. In the islands, where the union has few
members, the harbour boards asked to be consulted before anything changed.
The union council has promised that they will be, and has sent a delegation out
on the morning ferry to prove it.

fields.text: Warning from the Sky
lines: Warning from the Sky

fields.text:
The announcement reached Scardilli from Central Usea on the twentieth of April, on the morning shipping broadcast, between the weather forecast and the harbour notices. The asteroid Ulysses would strike the Earth. Governments across the continent were being told to prepare. The broadcast continued with the tide tables, because nobody in the studio knew what else to do.

Platania is a country of harbours, and its first instinct was to look to the sea. The harbour office has already drawn up lists: every hull in Platanian registry, its tonnage, its crew and the number of passengers it could carry in an emergency. The Admiralty has added the island ferries and the coastal craft. On paper, Platanian shipping could move the population of several coastal towns in a matter of days.

The plateau's answer is different. The coast, its councils argue, is the most exposed place in the country, and the sea may not be safe if fragments fall into it. The plateau stands high above the coast and far from it. Shelters, wells and stores built there could receive the harbour towns, and the bridge at Seals Bridge, if it stands, could carry them. The plateau farmers make the point with some satisfaction. For once the country may need them more than they need the port.

Nobody in Platania knows where Ulysses will fall. The government has ordered both plans costed, and has asked the newspapers not to print the shipping lists until a decision is made. They have printed them anyway.

Provisional gameplay: Platania's response is unsourced; the announcement date is official (ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20).

fields.text: The Fall and the Ships
lines: The Fall and the Ships

fields.text:
On the eighth of July Ulysses broke apart in the sky, and the night over Platania turned white. Islanders watched from the harbour walls; the plateau watched from its fields. Nobody in the country could say where the fragments had come down, and by morning the rumours had outrun every radio report.

Then the ships began to arrive. The first came into Scardilli two days later, a coaster built for forty passengers carrying more than three hundred people who would not say where they had come from or what they had left behind. More followed every day: fishing boats, ferries, a freighter with families sleeping in its holds. Platania had prepared its ships to carry its own people away from danger. It had not prepared its harbours to receive everyone else's.

The harbour office is improvising. Warehouses have become dormitories, the exchange hall a clinic, and the bridge road towns are taking in families by the hundred, many of whom arrived with nothing but the clothes they stood in. Grain is being moved down from the plateau faster than the farmers would like. The capacity built over three years of preparation is being spent in weeks.

Two questions cannot wait. The first is how long Platania can keep its harbours open to every ship that reaches them. The second, which the ministries are already asking quietly, is what happens when the ships keep coming after the space runs out.

Provisional gameplay: Platania's response is unsourced; the impact date is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08).

fields.text: War on the Continent
lines: War on the Continent

fields.text:
The war has come to Usea. Erusea has moved against San Salvacion and seized the railgun site at Stonehenge, and Central Usea is gathering a coalition to drive it back. Platania is not a party to the fighting. It holds no alliance obligations beyond its treaty council seat, and its government has said, repeatedly and in writing, that it intends to remain neutral.

Neutrality is easier to declare in a harbour than to keep in one. Within weeks, agents of every kind appeared at the exchange, buying freight space, fuel and insurance for cargoes whose destinations they preferred not to discuss. Insurance rates for Platanian ships doubled, then doubled again. The Admiralty reports unidentified submarines in the approaches to the islands. The treaty council, meanwhile, is debating what its members owe one another in a war that none of them chose.

Two courses are open. Platania can sail under its own flag, lit and marked, carrying civilian cargo for any buyer who can prove it is civilian, and accept that some will lie. Or it can grant the coalition, now calling itself ISAF, the use of Scardilli for hospital ships and supply tenders under Platanian harbour rules, without joining the alliance. Either choice will be watched by both sides, and either will be remembered.

The harbour master has posted a single notice on the quays in the meantime. No warship of any flag will enter Scardilli without permission, and no wounded sailor will be refused a berth.

Provisional gameplay: Platania's response is unsourced; the war date is official (ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER, 2003 / 08.22).

fields.text: Platania After the War
lines: Platania After the War

fields.text:
The war is over, and Platanian ships are still at sea, carrying grain to harbours that have reopened and survivors home to coasts that are beginning to rebuild. Platania was never invaded and never bombed. Its ships sailed through the worst of the fighting under their own flag, and some of them did not come back. The harbour office is compiling a list of their names for the exchange hall wall.

Peace has brought its own arguments. The houses want the insurance rates to fall and the convoys to stand down. The plateau wants the grain it sent to the coast during the war to be paid for at a fair price. The islands want their harbours, which carried more than their share of the refugee traffic, to be rebuilt first. All three are right, and the treasury cannot pay for all of it at once.

Whatever government Platania chose in the 1990s now faces the question every government faces after a war: what the peace is for. The country that came out of the decade is not the country that entered it. It has a bridge, a navy of sorts and a great many new citizens who arrived by sea. It also has a seat at a treaty council whose members now owe it favours, which in Scardilli is the most valuable cargo of all.

Provisional gameplay: Platania's response is unsourced; the end of the war date is official (ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19).

fields.text: The Executive Takes Stock
lines: The Executive Takes Stock

fields.text:
The report reached the State Executive in four bound volumes and a single page of summary, and it was the summary that kept the lights burning late in Ganzir. Ferustia had survived the rebellion. It had not survived it intact. The furnaces of the capital district were banked, the machine shops of Ilsede worked half weeks, and the plantations of Sandbury and Mount Waia sold their latex to whichever buyer reached the estate gates first.

Everyone in the room knew the deeper problem. For years the country had been governed as if the emergency would end next month. Decrees written for a crisis had become the law of daily life: the industrial ledger that recorded every loss, the rebellion decrees that treated the Dorondian border as a front, the musters that expected every citizen to answer a call to arms. None of them had been designed to last. All of them had.

The summary closed with a question rather than a recommendation. Ferustia could keep governing by emergency, which it knew how to do, or it could begin the slow work of governing as an ordinary state, which no one in the room had done before. The executive chose to begin with the inventory itself: every works, every pass, every border post and every ministry, counted honestly, before any promise was made.

fields.text: The Ledger of Loss
lines: The Ledger of Loss

fields.text:
For the first time since the rebellion, the Ministry of Industry has published a ledger with more entries in the column of things repaired than in the column of things lost. The ledger is a modest document. It counts furnaces relit, machine tools recovered, rail spurs reopened and contracts signed. Its importance is that it exists at all.

The emergency ledger it replaces was written in the worst months, when the works of Iggingen and the districts around it passed under Dorondian administration and took a third of the country's heavy industry with them. Every allocation since then has been made against that loss. Coal went first to the plants that could replace what was gone; skilled workers were directed to them by decree; the rest of the economy waited. It kept Ferustia alive. It also kept Ferustia poor.

Retiring the emergency ledger does not restore what was lost. It changes the question. The plains economy will now be judged by what it can make, and the ministry will plan for growth rather than for survival. Some managers welcome the change. Others, who spent a decade defending their allocations, are less certain that a normal economy will remember them.

fields.text: The Iggingen File
lines: The Iggingen File

fields.text:
The file is thin, and that is the first thing the executive notices. Years of speeches about Iggingen have produced very little paper about it. There are maps, lists of works and their pre-rebellion output, names of families who left and families who stayed. There is almost nothing about what Ferustia could actually do.

The officials who assembled it have been unusually frank. The works of Iggingen run under Dorondian administration, and they run well. The district's people have lived under that administration for most of a decade. The rebellion decrees still describe the matter as a rebellion in progress, but the posts on the Altoora road describe it as a border, and the soldiers who man them describe it as a long, dull watch.

The file does not recommend a policy. It sets out two. Ferustia can build habits with Dorondo, a commission and crossings and hearings, and accept that the question will be settled slowly or not at all. Or it can keep the grievance alive, keep the posts manned and keep its claim in every speech, while promising never to fire first. Neither path, the officials note, involves taking anything back. That was never on the table.

The executive reads the file twice and sends it, unannotated, to the cabinet. Its covering note asks only that the ministers decide which of the two habits Ferustia can keep for twenty years, since whichever they choose will almost certainly last that long.

fields.text: The Garrison and the Citizen
lines: The Garrison and the Citizen

fields.text:
Ferustians like to say that their country has no army, only citizens who own rifles. It is not quite true, and it has not been true for a long time. The martial clubs and village musters that grew up in the rebellion still drill on Sundays, but the men who taught them are ageing, and the young learn more about marching than about anything a modern war would require.

The General Staff and the Ministry of the Interior have each sent the executive a plan. The Interior wants the musters registered as a citizen reserve with civilian officers, short annual camps and a duty to run civil defence in a crisis. The General Staff wants the money instead: fewer, better soldiers on long service, trained in the passes, with the musters left to wither.

The arguments are about more than soldiers. A citizen reserve keeps every household inside the state's defence and keeps the army small and civilian. A professional corps makes the army an institution of its own, competent and separate, and some in Ganzir remember what institutions of that kind have done elsewhere in Usea. Others reply that an untrained militia is a comfort, not a defence.

The cabinet will have to choose, because the budget cannot carry both. Whatever it decides will shape more than the army. It will decide whether the next crisis finds a Ferustian on every street with a warden's armband, or a few thousand professionals in the passes and a great many civilians waiting to be told what to do.

fields.text: A Seat Outside the Room
lines: A Seat Outside the Room

fields.text:
The Central Usean Treaty Council met again last week. Ferustia read about it in the newspapers. Most of its neighbours sit at that table; their delegates agree on transit rules, emergency arrangements and the movement of goods that Ferustian lorries will later be asked to obey. Ferustia was not consulted, because Ferustia is not a member.

No one in Ganzir proposes joining. Membership would bring obligations the executive has no wish to accept and arguments it has no wish to have. The question is narrower. Should Ferustia ask to observe, with no vote and no obligations, so that it hears decisions before they reach its borders? Or should it stand apart entirely, keep larger reserves of its own and trade on whatever terms it can win alone?

The Foreign Ministry favours observation, and says so at length. The Treasury favours self-reliance, and says so with figures. The executive notes that both arguments assume the same thing: that the council matters to Ferustia whether or not Ferustia matters to the council.

There is a practical side to the question as well. Ferustian freight crosses member states on every route to the sea. If the council tightens its transit rules, Ferustian lorries will wait at the border for papers they did not know they needed. An observer would know in advance. A country standing apart would need fuel and spare parts enough to wait out the delay, and the Treasury has already priced that reserve to the last drum.

fields.text: The Question of the Executive
lines: The Question of the Executive

fields.text:
The State Executive was created to govern a country in rebellion. It has done so for most of a decade, and it has done so competently enough that few Ferustians can remember any other kind of government. That is precisely the problem now being discussed in every cafe in Ganzir and every mess hall in the passes.

Three answers are on offer. The jurists and the provincial notables want a constitutional convention: a written charter, courts, provincial seats and a free press, with the executive's powers handed to a presidium until the first ballot. The commanders of the mountain garrisons propose something simpler. They have kept the passes open and the border quiet; let them govern as a council, by plain ordinances, until the country is ready for more. The factory delegates and rail crews of the plains have a third answer, and they are loudest of all: a commune of elected assemblies in every works and estate, with the old ministries answering to them.

Each faction has its strength. The convention has the provinces and the newspapers. The garrisons have discipline and the passes. The commune has the plains, which means it has the trains, the furnaces and the plantations. None of them can govern without the others' consent for long, and all of them know it.

The executive itself has said little. Its last communique notes only that the present arrangement was always meant to be temporary, and that a temporary arrangement which lasts too long becomes a kind of answer of its own.

fields.text: The Convention Sits in Ganzir
lines: The Convention Sits in Ganzir

fields.text:
The delegates arrived by every route the country still had: the Mount Waia line, the desert road, buses from the plantation towns and a single chartered aircraft from the eastern border. Some wore suits that had not been out of a wardrobe since before the rebellion. Some wore the work clothes they had left the estates in that morning. All of them were seated in the old assembly hall in Ganzir, which had been cleaned for the occasion and still smelled faintly of the archive boxes stored in it for years.

The State Executive's last act was to hand its seals to a presidium elected by the delegates. The presidium is an office rather than a person, and it was designed that way on purpose. Its members serve together, sign together and will be replaced together when the first republican ballot is held. The convention's first resolution forbids any of them from standing in that ballot.

Outside the hall the mood is cautious rather than jubilant. Ferustians have seen emergencies declared and extended before. The newspapers, already enjoying a freedom the charter has not yet formally granted, ask the questions everyone is asking: who will command the garrisons, who will pay for the courts, and whether a republic drafted in a single summer can survive its first winter.

The convention's answer, for now, is the charter itself. Its clauses will be debated one by one, in public, and printed every evening.

the desert road, buses from the plantation towns and a single chartered aircraft
from the eastern border. Some wore suits that had not been out of a wardrobe
since before the rebellion. Some wore the work clothes they had left the
estates in that morning. All of them were seated in the old assembly hall in
Ganzir, which had been cleaned for the occasion and still smelled faintly of the
archive boxes stored in it for years.
The State Executive's last act was to hand its seals to a presidium elected by
the delegates. The presidium is an office rather than a person, and it was
designed that way on purpose. Its members serve together, sign together and
will be replaced together when the first republican ballot is held. The
convention's first resolution forbids any of them from standing in that ballot.
Outside the hall the mood is cautious rather than jubilant. Ferustians have seen
emergencies declared and extended before. The newspapers, already enjoying
a freedom the charter has not yet formally granted, ask the questions everyone
is asking: who will command the garrisons, who will pay for the courts, and
whether a republic drafted in a single summer can survive its first winter.
The convention's answer, for now, is the charter itself. Its clauses will be
debated one by one, in public, and printed every evening.

fields.text: The Garrison Council Takes the Seals
lines: The Garrison Council Takes the Seals

fields.text:
There was no parade. The commanders of the mountain garrisons arrived in Ganzir in staff cars, met the State Executive in its offices for three hours and left with its seals. By evening the radio was reading the Garrison Council's first ordinance: all ministries were to continue their work, all border posts were to remain manned, and all political meetings were to be registered with the nearest garrison office.

The council's members are not named in its ordinances. It speaks as an office, and its commanders have let it be known that they prefer it that way. They are men who have spent careers in the passes, where a road is either open or closed and an order is either obeyed or not. They believe the country needs that clarity more than it needs a debate, and many Ferustians, tired of a decade of emergency, are inclined to agree.

Others are not. The provincial notables who wanted a convention have been told that a convention can wait. The factory delegates of the plains have been told that their meetings are welcome if they are registered. Both have noticed that the council's ordinances are short, specific and enforced by soldiers.

The council's first month passes quietly. Trains run on time. The ration queues shorten. The newspapers print the ordinances in full and very little else. Whether that silence is consent or caution, the council does not ask.

fields.text: The Commune Is Proclaimed
lines: The Commune Is Proclaimed

fields.text:
The proclamation was read from the steps of the Ganzir rail works at the change of shift, so that both shifts could hear it. The delegates of the works, the railways and the plantations had met through the night. By morning they had a council, a programme and a name taken from the plains' own old usage: the Ferustian Commune.

The State Executive did not resist. Its ministries were told to continue their work under the supervision of delegates elected in each department, and most of them did, some with enthusiasm and more with resignation. The garrisons in the passes sent a short message acknowledging the council's authority over civil affairs. What they meant by civil affairs was left, for the moment, undefined.

The council speaks as an office and its members are not named. The commune's founding text is clear on this point: delegates hold office only while their assemblies want them, and any assembly can recall its delegate by a simple majority. Critics call this a recipe for paralysis. Supporters call it the only kind of government the plains have ever trusted.

In the plantation towns the estate workers have begun meeting in the same halls where concession agents once read out the price of latex. They intend to read out the price themselves from now on, and to decide for themselves, in open meeting, what it ought to be.

fields.text: The Sky Over the Plains
lines: The Sky Over the Plains

fields.text:
The announcement came from Central Usea on the twentieth of April, and it was carried in Ganzir by every radio set that worked. The asteroid Ulysses would strike the Earth. Astronomers had calculated its path; governments across the continent were being told to prepare. For a few hours, the cafes of the capital were silent.

Ferustia is a landlocked country. It cannot evacuate to the sea, it builds no railguns and it has no seat on the councils where the great defensive works will be planned. What it has is mountains, plains and time. The Interior Ministry's first estimate is that the country has three years to prepare, and that no one knows yet where the fragments will fall.

Two schools of thought formed within a week. One holds that the Waiapolo range is the country's natural shelter: mine galleries and railway tunnels can be stocked with water and beds for the plains towns. The other holds that concentration is the greater danger, and that the state should spread its stores, clinics and workshops across every district so that no single blow can cripple it.

The executive has ordered both plans costed. It has also ordered that nothing be said in public about where Ulysses will fall, because no one in Ferustia knows. The rumours have begun anyway, as rumours do, and the Interior Ministry has started keeping a file of them alongside the costings.

Provisional gameplay: Ferustia's response is unsourced; the announcement date is official (ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20).

fields.text: The Night of the Fall
lines: The Night of the Fall

fields.text:
On the eighth of July Ulysses passed the point from which it could no longer hold together, and the sky over Usea filled with light. In Ferustia people watched from rooftops and hillsides. No one in Ganzir could say that night where the fragments had come down; the first reports contradicted one another, and the radio stations of the coast fell silent one by one. By morning the plains were quiet, and for a few hours that seemed to be the end of it.

It was not. Within three days the trains from the coasts stopped running to timetable, then stopped running at all. The markets in Ganzir ran short of flour, then of fuel. On the fifth day the first refugees reached the eastern crossings, on foot and on carts, from towns whose names the border guards did not recognise. The executive's shelter plans had prepared Ferustia to survive a blow. They had not prepared it for the blow to fall on everyone else.

The ministries now face a different task: keeping the trains moving over the passes, feeding the plains and deciding what to do about the people who keep arriving. The capacity built over three years of preparation is being spent faster than anyone planned. No one in Ganzir yet knows how long the strain will last.

The first decisions cannot wait for that answer. Trains must be assigned before the grain spoils in the plains depots, and the crossings must be told today whether to let the walkers through. The executive's staff have drafted both orders. They have left the signatures blank.

fields.text: Between the Fronts
lines: Between the Fronts

fields.text:
The war has come to Usea, and for once Ferustia is not at the centre of anyone's quarrel. Erusea's armies have moved against San Salvacion and the railgun site at Stonehenge, and Central Usea is gathering a coalition to push them back. Ferustia is not a party to any of it. It has no treaty obligations, no faction and no wish to acquire either.

That does not mean the war can be ignored. Ferustia's airspace sits across routes that transport aircraft would like to use. Its roads link countries that may need to move supplies. Its markets are suddenly full of agents buying rubber, fuel and spare parts for armies that would rather not say where they are going. Every request is polite. None of them is entirely innocent.

The General Staff wants the passes closed and the anti-aircraft batteries manned: armed neutrality, strictly enforced. The Foreign Ministry argues that a neutral that helps no one will be remembered by everyone. Both agree on one point. Whatever Ferustia decides, it must decide it openly and enforce it equally, because a neutral that bends for one side will soon be treated as a belligerent by the other.

In the meantime the border posts have been given a single instruction, read to every shift: no foreign soldier crosses with a weapon, and no wounded man is turned away, whatever uniform he wears.

Provisional gameplay: Ferustia's response is unsourced; the war date is official (ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER, 2003 / 08.22).

fields.text: Ferustia After the War
lines: Ferustia After the War

fields.text:
The war is over, and the reports from the coasts are still being counted. Ferustia never joined the alliances that fought it. Its passes stayed open or closed as its own government decided, and its hospitals treated the wounded who reached them. In a continent that has lost so much in a single decade, that alone makes the country unusual.

It also makes it visible. Delegations from neighbours that never noticed Ferustia before now arrive in Ganzir asking for rubber, rail capacity and the services of its engineers. The country that spent the 1990s mending its own fractures is being asked to help mend everyone else's. Some in the cabinet see an opportunity. Others see a burden that a small, landlocked state cannot carry for long.

The questions that defined the decade have not gone away. The Iggingen file is still open, whatever form it has taken. The arguments about the executive, the garrisons and the assemblies continue in whatever institutions the country chose. But they are now the arguments of a state at peace, and for the first time in a generation the people of the plains can afford to have them slowly.

Provisional gameplay: Ferustia's response is unsourced; the end of the war date is official (ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19).

fields.text: The Ledger of Steel
lines: The Ledger of Steel

fields.text:
The ministry's clerks needed eleven weeks and a borrowed room in the harbour customs house to assemble it, and when they were finished the ledger filled two shelves. It recorded every furnace in the inland mill towns, every slipway on the peninsula and in Zapland, every oil well in the harbour hills, every arsenal in the Yinshi Valley and every contract that bound them to buyers abroad. No government of Albard had ever seen the whole of its own economy on paper at once.

The figures were remarkable. Albard rolls more steel than several of its larger neighbours, pumps its own oil and builds its own ships. It is, by any measure the ministry could devise, the richest of the small Usean states. It is also a country where almost all of that wealth belongs to a few dozen houses whose books the government had never been permitted to read until now.

The ledger raises more questions than it answers. Who decides what the yards build? Who sets the wages in the mills? Who chooses the buyers for the arsenals' shells? For a generation the answer has been the houses themselves. The new government has opened the books. What it does with what it found will define the decade.

fields.text: Three Yards, One Purse
lines: Three Yards, One Purse

fields.text:
Albard has three shipyards and the money to make one of them excellent. The Payton yards are the oldest and the most crowded, hemmed in by the city that grew up around them. The peninsula yards have room to expand and a skilled workforce that has never had enough orders. The Zapland yards, on the Roca Roja border, have the deepest water and the worst roads. Each builds ships. None builds them well enough to win contracts from the larger coastal powers.

Three proposals reached the cabinet within a week. The shipping houses want merchant hulls: tankers for Albard's oil, ore carriers for its steel trade, coasters for every neighbour's cargo. The naval staff wants escorts, arguing that a harbour this rich is an invitation to anyone with a gunboat. The yard managers themselves propose the least glamorous option of all: become the drydock of the coast, repairing whatever limps into port, a business that never depends on a single buyer's fortunes.

Each proposal comes with a constituency. The merchant hulls would please the houses and the oil exporters. The escorts would please the officers and, quietly, some of the treaty council's members. The repair yards would please the unions, because repair work keeps crews employed through every slump.

Whatever the cabinet chooses, the other two will have to wait. The purse is deep, but it is not bottomless, and half-built programmes in three yards would be worse than one finished programme in one.

fields.text: The Mill and Yard Unions
lines: The Mill and Yard Unions

fields.text:
The furnace crews of the inland mill towns and the riveters of the three yards belong to the oldest unions in Albard. They have their own halls, their own newspapers and strike funds large enough to keep a yard idle for a season. They also have long memories. Every plan in the government's programme, from relined furnaces to new slipways, depends on their members turning up for work.

The union secretaries came to the ministry with a single demand: a national wage board on which they would sit as equals with the owners and the government, setting wages for the mills and yards every spring. The owners' associations came the next day with the opposite demand: the open shop, in which every yard and mill hires whom it pleases on whatever terms it can agree, and the government stays out of it.

Both sides have a case. A wage board would make strikes rarer and costs higher, and it would give the unions a permanent voice in the country's economic policy. The open shop would raise output and lower costs, and it would almost certainly put more men on the picket lines in the first years. The ministry's own economists cannot agree which would be better for Albard in the long run.

What everyone agrees on is that the question cannot be left open. A government that refuses to answer it will find the answer chosen for it, in the yards, by whichever side is better organised that winter.

fields.text: The Arms Ledger
lines: The Arms Ledger

fields.text:
The Yinshi Valley arsenals make rifles, shells and mortar bombs. They make them well, and they sell them to whoever pays: neighbouring armies, police forces, and buyers whose credentials the arsenals' sales offices have never felt obliged to examine closely. The opening ledger of this programme listed their customers for the first time. Several ministers asked to read the list twice.

Nothing on it is illegal under Albardi law, because Albardi law has never said anything about it. That is the problem the cabinet must now solve. The arsenals employ thousands in a valley that borders both Bulgurdarest and Roca Roja, and their export earnings pay for a good deal of the programme. They are also the part of the economy most likely to draw Albard into quarrels that are not its own.

Two policies are on the table. The first is open trade: sell to recognised governments that ask, under export licences published every quarter, so that every neighbour knows exactly what every other neighbour has bought. The second is an embargo: the arsenals supply Albard's own forces and no one else, and whatever they no longer sell abroad is mounted at home, around the harbour.

Neither policy is free. Open trade keeps the valley prosperous and makes Albard useful to its neighbours, but it ties the country's reputation to the use its customers make of its shells. An embargo keeps Albard's hands clean and its neighbours less armed, at the cost of the valley's best customers and a good deal of goodwill.

fields.text: What the Money Buys
lines: What the Money Buys

fields.text:
Albard pays more into the common funds of the Central Usean Treaty Council than any other small member, and its delegates have begun to ask what the money buys. The council's agenda is set by its larger members. Its relief arrangements, transit rules and emergency plans are drafted in committees where Albard is one voice among many, however much it contributes.

The delegation in the council chamber has sent home two proposals. The first is to pay more: fund the council's common programmes generously and openly, become its paymaster, and expect the agenda to reflect it. Money given in public, the delegation argues, is influence earned in public, and no one can accuse Albard of buying favours it has paid for at the front door.

The second proposal is the opposite. Albard should pay its share and not a coin more, and insist that every member's contribution is audited and published. If the larger members are getting more from the council than they put in, the audits will show it, and Albard will have its influence from the facts rather than from its cheque book.

The Treasury favours the second proposal for obvious reasons. The Foreign Ministry favours the first, because it believes the council will matter far more in the coming years than anyone in Payton yet realises. Either way, the delegation has asked for an answer before the council's next session.

where Albard is one voice among many, however much it contributes.
The delegation in the council chamber has sent home two proposals. The first is
to pay more: fund the council's common programmes generously and openly,
become its paymaster, and expect the agenda to reflect it. Money given in
public, the delegation argues, is influence earned in public, and no one can
accuse Albard of buying favours it has paid for at the front door.
The second proposal is the opposite. Albard should pay its share and not a coin
more, and insist that every member's contribution is audited and published. If
the larger members are getting more from the council than they put in, the
audits will show it, and Albard will have its influence from the facts rather than
from its cheque book.
The Treasury favours the second proposal for obvious reasons. The Foreign
Ministry favours the first, because it believes the council will matter far more in
the coming years than anyone in Payton yet realises. Either way, the delegation
has asked for an answer before the council's next session.

fields.text: Who Owns Albard?
lines: Who Owns Albard?

fields.text:
The question was printed on a union poster in the Payton harbour districts, and within a month it had become the name of a national argument. Albard is rich. Its programme of relined furnaces, new slipways and refineries is working. The argument is about who deserves the credit, and therefore who deserves to govern.

The great steel and shipping houses say plainly that the prosperity is theirs. They built the mills, they financed the yards and they found the buyers. They propose to govern openly through a single board, as they have governed the economy quietly for decades. The mill and yard unions answer that nothing was built without their members' hands, and propose a labour commonwealth in which an elected council of the unions governs and the houses pay their share. The harbour lawyers and provincial notables propose a third answer: a charter republic of written rights and contested elections, in which no house and no union governs by right.

The present government was never designed to settle such a question. It was a placeholder administration, competent at opening ledgers and signing contracts, and it has no mandate to choose among the factions now demanding that it choose. Its ministers have begun to say so in public, which is itself a kind of answer.

Each faction has its strength. The board has the money and the shipping lines. The commonwealth has the yards and the mills, which means it has the country's output. The charter has the courts, the newspapers and the provinces. Albard cannot be governed for long against any of them, and every faction knows it.

fields.text: The Board Takes the Chair
lines: The Board Takes the Chair

fields.text:
The Steel and Shipping Board met for the first time in the boardroom of the oldest shipping house in Payton, around a table that had been used for exactly this purpose, informally, for half a century. The difference was that this time the ministers attended as guests. By the end of the afternoon the board had accepted the seals of government and issued its charter: ministries become departments, ministers become managers, and every department reports quarterly against a published plan.

The board speaks as an office and its members are not named in its communiques. They are the heads of the great houses, or their appointed representatives, and they have let it be known that they prefer to be judged by results rather than by personalities. Their first plan promises higher output from the mills, longer order books for the yards and a steady price for Albardi oil.

The unions have responded cautiously. The board's charter says nothing about wages, and the union secretaries have noticed. The harbour lawyers have responded less cautiously, pointing out that a government accountable only to its own shareholders is not accountable at all. The newspapers, most of which are owned by houses represented on the board, have responded with enthusiasm.

In the harbour districts, the reaction is a shrug. The houses ran the country before; now they run it openly. Whether that is better or worse, the first quarterly report will tell.

fields.text: The Commonwealth Is Declared
lines: The Commonwealth Is Declared

fields.text:
The labour council was elected in a single weekend, in union halls from the inland mill towns to the Zapland slipways, and it met for the first time in the largest of them: the riveters' hall on the Payton waterfront, where the strike of a generation ago had been planned. Its first act was to declare the Labour Commonwealth. Its second was to send a delegation to the shipping houses to explain what that would mean for them.

The commonwealth's charter guarantees the houses their property, provided that property is used and its workers are paid. It does not guarantee them their profits, which will be taxed to fund the yards, the mills and the apprentice halls. The houses' representatives listened politely, asked for the terms in writing and left to consult their lawyers. Several of them have since moved their head offices to the peninsula, though not yet abroad.

The council speaks as an office and its members are not named. Union delegates hold their seats only while their halls want them, and the charter allows any hall to recall its delegate by a simple majority. The council's first sessions have been long, loud and broadcast on the harbour radio, which has found itself with the largest audience in its history.

In the mill towns, the mood is jubilant. In the yards it is more practical. The committees want to know when the new orders will arrive, and who will sign them now that the houses no longer do.

fields.text: The Charter Republic
lines: The Charter Republic

fields.text:
The proclamation was read on the steps of the harbour customs house, the building where the opening ledger had been compiled, and the choice was deliberate. The Charter Republic, its sponsors said, would govern the way that ledger had been written: in public, with every figure checked and every claim open to challenge. A cabinet answerable to an elected charter assembly would govern until the charter was written and ratified by national vote.

The cabinet speaks as an office, and its members have agreed not to stand in the first ballot under the charter they are drafting. The assembly that will write it was elected on the broadest franchise Albard has ever known, including the mill towns and the Zapland shore, where many voters had never cast a ballot before. Its sessions are open, its minutes are printed and its debates are long.

The great houses have accepted the republic with visible reluctance. A charter of written rights protects their property, but it also promises commercial courts independent of them and accounts that must be published. The unions have accepted it with visible suspicion, since a republic in which no house governs by right is also one in which no union does.

In the harbour cafes, the argument has already moved on to the charter's clauses: the franchise, the courts, the published accounts. That, its sponsors say, is exactly the point of a republic built in public.

fields.text: The Warning Reaches Payton
lines: The Warning Reaches Payton

fields.text:
The treaty council's message arrived on the twentieth of April, relaying an announcement from Central Usea that the government at first assumed must be mistaken. The asteroid Ulysses would strike the Earth. Astronomers had calculated its path; every member of the council was being asked to prepare. The Payton stock exchange closed early that afternoon and did not open the next day.

Albard has more to prepare with than most of its neighbours. Its mills can roll plate, its yards can build hulls and its oil fields can fuel whatever is built. What it does not have is any certainty about where the fragments will fall, and the government's planners have been told that no one else has that certainty either. They must prepare for a blow that might land anywhere, or nowhere at all.

Two plans reached the cabinet within a month. The mills propose to roll shelter plate for every coastal town: buried bunkers with steel roofs, water tanks and beds for the harbour districts, so that the population can stay where it is and wait out the worst. The yards propose an evacuation fleet: a reserve of hulls ready to carry the coastal towns inland by river and along the shore, so that the population can leave if the warning becomes a strike.

The cabinet cannot afford both on the scale either requires. Whichever it chooses, the mills and yards that lose the argument will be asked to help with the other, and the treaty council will be told that Albard is ready to share whatever it builds.

Provisional gameplay: Albard's response is unsourced; the announcement date is official (ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20).

fields.text: The Night the Sky Broke
lines: The Night the Sky Broke

fields.text:
On the eighth of July Ulysses passed the point from which it could no longer hold together, and the sky over Usea filled with falling light. In Payton the harbour crowds watched from the quays until the police cleared them. By morning the harbour's lights were still burning, and for a few hours that seemed enough.

It was not. The reports that reached the harbour over the following days described a continent whose sea lanes were disrupted, whose coastal towns had suffered in ways no one had yet measured, and whose markets had stopped functioning almost overnight. Ships that should have arrived did not. Ships that did arrive carried passengers rather than cargo, people who had boarded anything that would float and pointed it toward the nearest lights.

Albard's preparations had made it ready to protect itself. They had not made it ready to be one of the few places on the coast still working. The yards, the oil fields and the mills are suddenly the most valuable relief assets within hundreds of kilometres, and every neighbour is asking for them at once. The capacity built over three years is being spent faster than anyone planned.

The first decisions cannot wait. The relief convoys must be assigned and the harbours must be told what to do with the ships now anchoring in the roads. After Erusea's refugee decision, the government expects more of them, not fewer.

Provisional gameplay: Albard's response is unsourced; the impact date is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08).
