fields.text: A Rich Harbour in a War
lines: A Rich Harbour in a War

fields.text:
The war has come to Usea. Erusea's armies have moved into San Salvacion and seized the railgun site at Stonehenge, and Central Usea is gathering a coalition to push them back. Albard is not a party to any of it. It has no faction, no alliance and no intention of acquiring either.

That does not make it irrelevant. Albard has steel, refined fuel and three working shipyards, and every army on the continent would like a share of all three. Purchasing agents have arrived in Payton within weeks, some in uniform and more in suits, asking for plate, for fuel, for repair berths and for the services of the yards' engineers. Every request is polite and every contract would be profitable. None of them is entirely innocent.

The naval staff wants armed neutrality, strictly enforced: no warship of any side in Albard's harbours, patrol craft in the roads and batteries on the shore. The shipping houses and the yards argue that ordinary commercial contracts, delivered at Albard's own quays, are what a neutral trading state has always done, and that ISAF in particular will remember who sold to it when it most needed to buy. The unions want to know who will work the double shifts either choice will require.

Everyone agrees on one point. Whatever Albard decides, it must enforce it openly and equally, because a neutral harbour that bends for one side will soon be treated as an enemy port by the other.

fields.text: Albard After the War
lines: Albard After the War

fields.text:
The war is over, and Albard has come through it with its harbours full and its order books longer than at any time in its history. Its yards repaired ships, its mills rolled plate and its oil fields fuelled whatever the government's neutrality allowed them to fuel. In a continent that has lost so much since the night the sky broke, that makes the country conspicuous.

It also makes it the subject of a new argument. Albard's neighbours are poorer than ever, and many of them believe that some of Albard's prosperity was made from their misfortune. Delegations arrive in Payton asking for credit, steel and the services of the yards on terms that the houses, the unions and the treasury all find difficult to accept. The treaty council has begun to ask the same questions more formally.

The questions that shaped the decade remain. Who owns Albard, and who governs it, has been answered in whatever form the country chose. But a rich country among poor neighbours must now decide what it owes them, and whether generosity is a duty, an investment or a mistake. For the first time, the answer will be argued by a country at peace.

fields.text: The Harbour Ledger
lines: The Harbour Ledger

fields.text:
Every spring the Port Office of Dorondo City publishes its ledger, and every spring the republic reads it the way other countries read the speeches of their presidents. It lists the ships that entered the great anchorage, the cargoes they carried, the berths that stood empty and the wages paid on the quays. This year's ledger is the thickest in a decade. Dorondo is rich, and the ledger says so in tonnes.

It also says other things, in smaller type. The yards of the Lowlands are working at the limit of their slipways. The dock unions have filed more grievances than in any year since the old tribunals were abolished. The works of Iggingen, inland on the desert side of the republic, send their products to the coast on a single road that the Ferustian border posts can watch from their towers. And the republic's defence, as the ledger notes without comment, consists largely of the hope that no one will want to disturb a country that trades with everyone.

The cabinet has asked the Port Office for something it has never produced: not a record of the year, but a plan for the decade. What should the anchorage become? Who should the docks answer to? How should the republic govern a district that its neighbour still calls its own? The Port Office has replied, with some dignity, that it counts ships and does not make policy. The cabinet has replied that it will have to start.

fields.text: Three Plans for the Anchorage
lines: Three Plans for the Anchorage

fields.text:
The survey of the great anchorage took the harbour engineers four months and filled a room of the Port Office with charts. The anchorage is the finest on this coast: deep water close to shore, shelter from the winter gales, and berths enough for a fleet far larger than the one Dorondo actually owns. For most of the republic's history that surplus was simply wealth. Ships came, paid their dues and left.

The engineers' report sets out three ways to make the anchorage work harder, and they cannot all be afforded. The shipping houses want an open registry: low fees, light inspection and a Dorondian flag on any hull whose owner will pay for it. The yard owners of the Lowlands want the money spent on slipways and repair basins, so that the ships which call here are also built and mended here. The harbour pilots, who have guided ships through the approaches for generations, want a modern pilots' service with radar, night lights and the authority to close the approaches in an emergency.

Each plan has its party in the assembly and its column in the newspapers. The registry would bring the most money fastest. The yards would bring the most work. The pilots' service would bring the least of either, and the pilots argue that it is the only plan which would still matter if the coast were ever in danger.

The cabinet must choose one. The other two will wait, perhaps for a decade, and their supporters will not let anyone forget it.

fields.text: The Dock Unions Ask to Be Heard
lines: The Dock Unions Ask to Be Heard

fields.text:
The delegation from the dock unions arrived at the assembly with a petition of forty thousand signatures and a request that was, by their standards, modest. They did not ask for higher wages. They asked for a standing tribunal: a court of wages and conditions where a stevedore's grievance could be heard before it became a strike.

Dorondo had such tribunals once. They were abolished in a quieter decade, when the shipping houses argued that an open harbour needed open hiring and the unions were too weak to object. They are not weak now. Almost a quarter of the republic votes for parties that call themselves socialist or communist, and most of those votes are cast within sight of the cranes. A strike on the quays would close the anchorage in a day.

The shipping houses have answered with a petition of their own, shorter and better printed. They ask the government to keep the harbour an open shop, to protect men who work without a union card, and to give the port a constabulary of its own so that a picket line cannot become a blockade. They point out, correctly, that the republic's prosperity rests on ships choosing to come here rather than elsewhere.

The cabinet has both petitions on the same table. It knows that whichever it grants, the other side will remember at the next election, and at every election after that.

forty thousand signatures and a request that was, by their standards, modest.
They did not ask for higher wages. They asked for a standing tribunal: a court of
wages and conditions where a stevedore's grievance could be heard before it
became a strike.
Dorondo had such tribunals once. They were abolished in a quieter decade,
when the shipping houses argued that an open harbour needed open hiring and
the unions were too weak to object. They are not weak now. Almost a quarter of
the republic votes for parties that call themselves socialist or communist, and
most of those votes are cast within sight of the cranes. A strike on the quays
would close the anchorage in a day.
The shipping houses have answered with a petition of their own, shorter and
better printed. They ask the government to keep the harbour an open shop, to
protect men who work without a union card, and to give the port a constabulary
of its own so that a picket line cannot become a blockade. They point out,
correctly, that the republic's prosperity rests on ships choosing to come here
rather than elsewhere.
The cabinet has both petitions on the same table. It knows that whichever it
grants, the other side will remember at the next election, and at every election
after that.

fields.text: Governing Iggingen
lines: Governing Iggingen

fields.text:
Iggingen has been governed from Dorondo City for most of a decade, and for most of that decade it has been governed as an afterthought. The district's works are productive, its people pay their taxes, and its administration is run by officials on temporary postings who expect to return to the coast. The Ferustian government still describes the district as its own. The people of Iggingen have mostly stopped asking who is right and started asking who will fix the road.

The Ministry of the Interior has proposed that the republic finally decide how Iggingen is to be governed, without touching the question of whose it is. There are two models on the table. The first would give the district an elected council of its own, with powers over schools, roads and the works, so that its people govern their own affairs whatever the maps in other capitals say. The second would give it a prefecture: a single appointed administration answering directly to the capital, efficient and accountable, and entirely Dorondian.

Neither model changes a border. Both change how the district lives. An elected council would be harder to direct but easier to defend in any future conversation with Ferustia. A prefecture would be simpler to run and would make clear, to anyone watching from the desert posts, that the republic intends to stay.

The ministry adds a note. Whatever the government chooses, the works themselves will need a decision soon: their military contracts are ending.

fields.text: Families Across the Line
lines: Families Across the Line

fields.text:
The letters arrive at the Iggingen district office in the hundreds now. Most of them are about the same thing. A daughter married across the desert road before the rebellion; a father is buried in a Ferustian village; a family's land lies on one side of the posts and its house on the other. Each letter asks for a pass, a permit or simply an explanation of why a journey of an afternoon has become impossible.

The district administration has no authority to answer them. Crossings on the desert road are a matter for the governments in Dorondo City and Ganzir, and those governments have not spoken to each other about the border in any formal way since the rebellion. The posts on both sides are manned. The soldiers on both sides are bored. Occasionally one of them waves.

The cabinet has two proposals. The Foreign Ministry suggests that Dorondo offer to sit on a standing border commission with Ferustia: monthly meetings, a crossings register, and a promise to settle small disputes before they become incidents. The Ministry of Defence suggests the opposite. It would fortify the desert line properly, with entrenched posts and a reserve on the coast road, on the grounds that a republic with little army needs walls more than conversations.

Neither ministry proposes to change the border. Both believe their plan is the one that keeps it quiet, and both have a drawer full of the same letters.

fields.text: A Small Republic and a Large Treaty
lines: A Small Republic and a Large Treaty

fields.text:
Dorondo joined the Central Usean Treaty Council for the same reason it joined every trade convention on the coast: membership was cheap, the meetings were useful and the alternative was to be discussed in rooms where it had no voice. For years the republic sent a modest delegation, voted with the majority and went home. The arrangement suited a country whose army was small and whose ships were everywhere.

The Foreign Ministry now argues that the council has become something more than a convenience. A small, rich republic cannot defend its anchorage alone, and every treaty clause on transit, emergency shipping and mutual assistance is, in effect, part of Dorondo's defence. The ministry wants a full delegation: permanent staff, a seat on every committee, and the republic's shipping lawyers drafting the clauses that its ships will later sail under.

The Treasury disagrees, politely. A full delegation costs money and commits the republic to positions it may later regret. Dorondo, the Treasury argues, should remain a quiet member: present, reliable, and free to make its own arrangements with neighbours such as Delarus, Calladen and Rohden, desk by desk and contract by contract, without asking a committee's leave.

Both ministries agree that the council matters. They disagree about whether Dorondo should be heard in it, or merely protected by it, and about which of the two a small republic can actually afford for the next twenty years.

fields.text: The Republic at the Crossroads
lines: The Republic at the Crossroads

fields.text:
The republic's assembly has not produced a stable majority in three sessions. The coalitions that governed Dorondo through its prosperous decade were built on a simple bargain: the shipping houses kept the anchorage busy, the government kept taxes low, and the docks were left to argue with the houses on their own. The bargain has broken. The unions are too strong to be ignored, the houses too rich to be overruled, and the voters too divided to give anyone a mandate.

Three answers have formed in the cafes and committee rooms of the capital. The moderate parties of the centre and the left propose a social compact: a written bargain between the houses, the unions and the state, with pensions, elected port boards and a standing tribunal, renewed at every election. The labour federations propose something more radical. Let the docks, the yards and the fleet be run by councils of the people who work them, federated into a workers' government that answers to the quays rather than to the counting houses.

The third answer comes from the Port Office and the senior civil service, and it is the least popular and the most carefully argued. Suspend the quarrel. Let an emergency cabinet of administrators govern by decree for a fixed term, run the harbour as a public authority, build a reserve fund against hard years, and return the republic to its politicians once the books are balanced.

Each answer has its newspapers and its crowds. None has a majority. The assembly must choose one anyway, or watch the anchorage choose for it.

fields.text: The Social Compact
lines: The Social Compact

fields.text:
The compact was signed in the great hall of the Port Office, under the ledger boards where the republic has recorded its ships for a century. Representatives of the shipping houses, the dock unions and the government signed in turn. The document they signed is long, and much of it concerns pensions, apprenticeships and the hours of a night shift. Its first clause is short. Disputes on the quays will be settled at the tribunal, not on the picket line, and the republic will guarantee that the tribunal's awards are paid.

The new cabinet that governs under the compact is an office rather than a person. Its ministers are drawn from the parties that signed, and its programme is the compact itself. Elections will continue on their usual calendar; the compact's authors were insistent that a bargain renewed by voters every few years is stronger than one imposed once.

Not everyone is pleased. The more radical federations call the compact a truce that the houses will break as soon as trade falls. Some shipowners call it a surrender to the unions. In the cafes of the waterfront the most common view is cautious approval: the cranes are moving, the tribunal is sitting, and for the first time in years no one expects a strike next month.

The compact's critics and its friends agree on one thing. It will be tested not in a good year but in a bad one.

fields.text: The Workers' Federation
lines: The Workers' Federation

fields.text:
The general meeting of the dock federations began at dawn and ended after midnight, and by its close the republic had a new government. Delegates of the quays, the yards of the Lowlands and the crews of the merchant fleet voted to form a council of the workers' federation and to take the ministries under its direction. The previous cabinet resigned before the vote was counted. The army, such as it is, stayed in its barracks.

The council speaks as an office. Its members are delegates who can be recalled by the federations that sent them, and its founding resolution forbids any of them from holding office for more than two years. Its programme is plain: the docks and the yards to be run by councils of those who work in them, the merchant fleet to become a cooperative of its crews, and the anchorage to remain open to every ship that pays its dues, whatever flag it flies.

That last point matters more than the rest. The council knows that Dorondo's wealth depends on ships choosing to come here, and that the shipping houses of other countries are watching. Its first communique is addressed to them rather than to its own people. The harbour is open, the dues are unchanged, and the pilots will guide every ship as before.

Whether the houses believe it will be measured, as everything in Dorondo is measured, in the next season's ledger.

fields.text: The Emergency Cabinet
lines: The Emergency Cabinet

fields.text:
The assembly voted for its own suspension by a narrow margin and in a sullen mood. The motion, drafted by the Port Office and the senior civil service, transfers the government to an emergency cabinet for a fixed term. The cabinet will govern by decree, run the harbour as a single public authority, and build a reserve fund against the next hard year. When its term expires, the assembly will sit again.

The cabinet is an office. Its members are administrators rather than politicians, and its decrees are signed collectively so that no single official can be blamed or praised. It meets in the Port Office rather than the assembly building, which some see as a statement of priorities and others as an insult. Its first decrees are dull by design: tariffs fixed for three years, the tribunal suspended but its awards honoured, the harbour accounts published monthly.

The unions call it a government of clerks. The shipping houses call it a government of tax collectors. Both are partly right. The cabinet's answer is that a republic which cannot form a majority still needs someone to keep the cranes moving, and that a fixed term with published accounts is the most honest form of emergency available.

Dorondians are a commercial people. Most of them have decided to judge the cabinet the way they judge a ship's master: by whether it brings the cargo in.

fields.text: The Warning from Central Usea
lines: The Warning from Central Usea

fields.text:
The announcement from Central Usea reached the Port Office by teleprinter on the twentieth of April, and the harbourmaster read it aloud to the night shift. The asteroid Ulysses would strike the Earth. No one could yet say where the fragments would fall, but every government on the continent was being urged to prepare.

A port republic thinks first about the sea. Within a week the Port Office had produced two plans. The first treated the anchorage as Dorondo's lifeboat: every hull in the merchant fleet registered for an evacuation, fuel reserved, routes charted to safer coasts, and a schedule that could empty the capital's waterfront in a matter of days. The second treated the anchorage as the thing to be protected. It would cut shelters into the rock beneath the quays, stock them with water and stores, and keep the people of Dorondo City close to the harbour that feeds them.

The arguments were technical and quickly became political. The evacuation plan depended on ships that belonged, in large part, to private houses and foreign owners. The bunker plan depended on engineering the harbour had never attempted. Both were expensive. Neither could be finished in a hurry.

The cabinet has three years, if the astronomers are right, and money for one plan. It has asked the harbourmaster which he would choose. He has asked, reasonably, to know where the fragments will fall first. No one can tell him.

fields.text: Ships Out of the Dark
lines: Ships Out of the Dark

fields.text:
On the eighth of July Ulysses broke apart, and the night sky over the coast filled with light. In Dorondo City people watched from the quays and the rooftops until dawn, and no one on the waterfront could say where the fragments had come down. The next morning the radio carried only fragments of its own: stations that did not answer, schedules that were cancelled, ports that did not reply to the Port Office's telegrams. The ledger boards still showed the previous day's arrivals.

By the third day the arrivals were different. Ships came in without cargo manifests, crowded to the rails with passengers. Fishing boats came in from coasts whose names the harbour pilots knew only from charts. Some carried injured people; some carried whole villages. The masters asked the same question at every berth: could they land, and would they be allowed to stay?

The republic had planned for a blow. It had not planned to become a harbour of refuge for every ship that could still find its way into the approaches. Within a week the Port Office had lost count of the landings, the markets of the capital had run short of flour and fuel, and the hospitals were turning patients away.

The cabinet must now decide what kind of harbour Dorondo will be. It can open the anchorage to every ship that reaches it, land everyone and count them as future citizens of a republic that has always lived by its arrivals. Or it can sort the landings, treat and feed every passenger but send onward those whom the republic cannot keep, and say so honestly at every berth. In either case the hospital ships must sail tonight.

Provisional gameplay: Dorondo's response is unsourced; the impact date is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08).

fields.text: A Neutral Anchorage
lines: A Neutral Anchorage

fields.text:
War has broken out on the continent. Erusea has moved against San Salvacion and seized the railgun site at Stonehenge, and Central Usea is assembling a coalition to answer it. Dorondo is not a party to any of this. It has no alliance obligations, no army worth the name, and no intention of acquiring either.

It does have the finest anchorage on its coast, and within days every navy and every shipping agent in Usea has noticed. Requests arrive at the Port Office by the dozen: berths for transports, repairs for damaged freighters, fuel, charts, pilots. Some are from belligerents and say so. More are from shipping houses that will not say whose cargo they carry. The insurance markets have doubled their rates for every hull that sails from the republic's quays.

The cabinet has two proposals before it. The first would make Dorondo a strictly neutral harbour: open to commerce on equal terms, closed to every warship, guarded by anti-aircraft batteries on the headlands. The second, which the Foreign Ministry favours once the coalition has a name and a command, would allow allied convoys to use designated berths for supplies and medical cargo, under Dorondian pilots and Dorondian rules, without the republic joining the alliance.

Either way, the ledger boards in the Port Office will record every arrival. The republic has decided, at least, that it will not hide what its harbour is used for.

Provisional gameplay: Dorondo's response is unsourced; the war date is official (ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER, 2003 / 08.22).

fields.text: The Ledger After the War
lines: The Ledger After the War

fields.text:
The war is over, and the first postwar ledger of the Port Office is a strange document. It records more ships than any year of the decade and less cargo; more repairs than new hulls; more passengers than the republic has ever landed in a year of peace. The great anchorage has been busy throughout the war. It has not always been profitable.

Dorondo emerges from the war unoccupied, with its harbour working and its institutions in whatever shape its government chose for them. It never joined the fighting, and its quays never stopped recording arrivals. Delegations from the coasts are already arriving to ask for berths, yards and credit for their own recovery, and the shipping houses see a decade of reconstruction contracts in front of them.

The older questions are still waiting. Iggingen is still governed from the coast, under whatever arrangement the republic chose. fields.text: The Charts of the Coast
lines: The Charts of the Coast

fields.text:
The Hydrographic Office keeps the oldest charts in the country, and in the first weeks of 1991 the cabinet asked to see all of them. Scandia exists along a single line. Every one of its provinces touches the sea, and almost every one of its citizens lives within sight of salt water. The charts show the harbours, the fishing banks, the shoals and the anchorages in patient detail. They do not show how poor the country has become.

The report that came with them did. The fishing fleet is old and largely unregistered. The oil beneath the coast has been surveyed in places and guessed at everywhere else. The smaller harbours silt up faster than the dredgers can clear them, and the capital's shipyards build more repairs than ships. Scandia's budget is the smallest of any treaty member on this part of the continent, and every ministry knows exactly how small it is.

And yet the sea is the one thing no neighbour can take from Scandia. Calladen and Bulgurdarest send cargo over Scandian quays whenever the rates are right. The banks offshore still fill nets. The cabinet's instruction to the ministries was short: start with the charts. Know every harbour, every boat and every well, and only then decide what a coastal nation with very little money should build first.

fields.text: The Price of Fish
lines: The Price of Fish

fields.text:
The cold stores have changed everything on the quays. For the first time Scandian fishermen do not have to sell their catch on the morning it lands, at whatever price the buyers on the dock decide to offer. Fish can now wait a week for a better market. That single fact has turned an old argument about who owns the boats into a new argument about who owns the catch.

The fishing villages want cooperatives. Each harbour would pool its boats, run its own auction and share its cold store, with the state lending money for nets and engines. The harbour merchants and the capital's banks want something else: incorporated trawler companies with steel hulls, deep-water range and the capital to fish banks the small boats cannot reach. The cooperatives promise to keep the villages alive. The companies promise to make the fleet profitable.

Both sides have brought figures to the Fisheries Ministry, and both sets of figures are honest. Cooperatives would land less fish but keep more families on the coast. Companies would land more fish with fewer crews, and the crews they let go would need work somewhere else in a country that has very little of it. Neither option makes Scandia rich. One makes it fairer; the other makes it busier.

The minister has asked the cabinet for a decision before the next season opens, because the banks do not wait for politics, and neither do the buyers who have already started visiting the villages with contracts in their pockets.

fields.text: Oil on the Petrol Coast
lines: Oil on the Petrol Coast

fields.text:
The drilling crews on the Petrol Coast have struck oil in quantities the surveyors had only hoped for. The coast earned its name generations ago, when tar seeped out of the cliffs and fishermen scraped it up to caulk their boats. Now the seepage has become a field, and the cabinet must decide who will pump it.

The Treasury proposes a National Oil Board. The state would own the wells, pay the crews and sell the crude itself, keeping every unit of profit for the budget. It would also bear every unit of risk, and Scandia has never run an industry larger than its fishing fleet. The Ministry of Trade proposes leases instead. Companies would bid for blocks of coast, drill at their own expense and pay the state a royalty on every barrel they lift.

The arguments are familiar from every small country that has found something valuable under its soil. A state board keeps control and learns slowly and expensively. Leases bring money and expertise quickly, and take a share of both away with them when the field runs down. The fishermen of the Petrol Coast have their own concern, which neither ministry has yet answered: what oil on the water will do to the banks their families have fished for a century.

The cabinet has promised to answer that question as well, whichever way it chooses. The fishermen have heard promises from the capital before, and have asked for this one in writing.

fields.text: What Navy Can Scandia Afford?
lines: What Navy Can Scandia Afford?

fields.text:
The Admiralty's annual return is an unusually frank document. Scandia owns a handful of patrol craft, a training ship older than most of the officers who sail in her, and a dockyard in the capital that keeps them all afloat through great ingenuity and very little money. Everything the navy does at sea, from fishery inspection to smuggling patrols, it does with too few hulls and too much coast.

Two plans are on the minister's desk. The first would turn the navy into a coast guard in all but name: cutters built for inspection, rescue and police work, armed enough to be obeyed by a foreign trawler and no more. The second would spend the same money on a small squadron of fast armed craft, trained to hold the harbour mouths at night and in bad weather. It would not win a war at sea, its advocates admit, but it would make any visitor think twice.

Underneath the plans is an older argument about what Scandian sea power is for. The coast guard plan assumes that the country's dangers are storms, smugglers and poachers, and that its navy should be useful every single day. The squadron plan assumes that one day a larger navy will come close to the coast, and that Scandia should be able to say no with something more than a radio message.

The budget allows for one plan, not both, and the Admiralty has asked for an answer before the yards need to order steel.

fields.text: A Chair at the Treaty Council
lines: A Chair at the Treaty Council

fields.text:
Scandia sends the smallest delegation to the Central Usean Treaty Council. Its delegates share a single office, take turns at the translation desk and travel second class. Yet they represent the longest coastline of any member on this part of the continent, and when the council discusses shipping, rescue or harbour fees, they are usually the only people in the room who have actually worked on a quay.

The Foreign Ministry wants to use that knowledge. It proposes that Scandia press the council to adopt common rules for harbours, sea rescue and shipping lanes, drafted largely by Scandian officials. A small member that writes the rules, the ministry argues, is no longer a small member on those subjects. The Ministry of Trade disagrees. The council, it says, is where large members make large decisions. Scandia should vote with the majority, ask for little and spend its effort on direct arrangements with the neighbours whose cargo actually crosses its quays.

The disagreement is partly about money. Leading the council's maritime work would require more officials than the delegation has, and more travel than its budget allows. Bilateral deals with Calladen and Bulgurdarest would cost almost nothing and pay quickly in handling fees.

The cabinet must decide whether Scandia's chair at the council is a platform or a formality. Its delegates have asked, politely, to be told which before the next session.

fields.text: Who Governs the Harbours?
lines: Who Governs the Harbours?

fields.text:
On paper Scandia is governed from the capital by a cabinet answerable to an assembly that has not been elected in years. In practice it is governed from the harbours. The harbourmasters decide who berths and who waits. The fishing guilds decide who sails and who mends nets ashore. The shipping houses decide which cargo moves and at what price. The cabinet signs what they agree, and the arrangement has worked well enough that nobody has bothered to change it.

The decade's work has changed it anyway. The cold stores, the oil wells, the rescue service and the navy have all needed decisions that no single harbour could make, and every one of them has exposed how little authority the cabinet really holds. Two answers are now being argued in every customs house on the coast.

The first comes from the dockers, the younger fishermen and the newspapers of the capital. They want a Coastal Commonwealth: an elected parliament in which every port, however small, sends a member, councils in every harbour, and open registers of who owns every ship, berth and licence. The second comes from the harbour guilds themselves. They propose a regency council, an old form from the harbour charters, in which the great harbour offices govern together above party, in trust for the coast, with elections set aside until the country is stronger.

Both sides claim to speak for the sea. The cabinet, which speaks for very little, has agreed only that the question can no longer be avoided.

fields.text: The Coastal Commonwealth
lines: The Coastal Commonwealth

fields.text:
The Commonwealth was proclaimed from the steps of the capital's fish market at dawn, when the auction bell rang and the largest crowd in the city was already awake. The old cabinet resigned the same morning and handed its seals to a provisional cabinet of the Commonwealth, which governs as an office until the first parliament is elected. Its members have agreed not to be named in its decrees.

The new charter is short and practical. Elections every four years. Free association for fishermen, dockers and seamen. Public accounts for every harbour board. And, most controversially, open registers: anyone may now walk into a customs house and learn who owns a ship, a berth or a fishing licence. Some old harbour fortunes, the newspapers note cheerfully, are about to become a great deal more visible.

Not everyone is cheering. The harbourmasters have accepted the change with careful neutrality, which in Scandia is a form of protest. The shipping houses have asked how open registers will affect their foreign customers. The guilds, who proposed a very different constitution, have said only that they will watch how the Commonwealth governs a bad winter.

The first bad winter is never far away on this coast. The provisional cabinet has six months to draft electoral rolls for every port, and the fishing season starts in four. Nobody on the quays expects the two calendars to agree.

fields.text: The Harbour Regency
lines: The Harbour Regency

fields.text:
The regency council first met in the old customs house of the capital, in a room hung with the harbour charters that gave it its form. Its seats belong to offices rather than persons: the senior harbourmasters, the wardens of the fishing guilds, the master of the shipping register and the senior captain of the fleet. Whoever holds those offices sits on the council. No one else does, and no one is named.

The guilds call the arrangement a regency because it governs in trust, for the coast as a whole, rather than for any party or district. Critics in the capital call it a committee of harbourmasters with a grand title. Both descriptions are accurate. The council has promised an advisory assembly, charters that bind its own members, and elections when the country is stronger. It has not said when that will be.

In the harbours, the change is barely visible. The people who decided who berthed and who sailed still decide it; now they do so with the seals of the state. The cabinet's ministries continue their work under the council's instructions, and the first of those instructions concern dredging, quotas and the navy's cutters.

The dockers' newspapers, which wanted a Commonwealth, have been told they may keep publishing. They have printed the charters in full on their front pages, with the clauses about elections underlined twice in red ink.

fields.text: Warning to a Coastal Nation
lines: Warning to a Coastal Nation

fields.text:
The announcement came from Central Usea on the twentieth of April: the asteroid Ulysses would strike the Earth, and every government on the continent was being told to prepare. In the capital, the news was read out on the quays over the loudspeakers normally used for storm warnings. The fish auction stopped. For the first time anyone could remember, the boats stayed in harbour on a fair-weather day.

No one in Scandia knows where the fragments will fall. That uncertainty is the whole of the problem. Scandia is a country made of coastline, and every Scandian has heard what a large enough blow at sea could do to a shore. The weather service has no model for it. The radar chain can watch the sky but cannot change what it sees. The rescue service, built to save a boat at a time, has been asked how it would save a town.

Two plans emerged from the first emergency cabinet. The Interior Ministry wants every coastal town assigned high ground behind it, stocked with food and water, with a road kept clear so that people can leave the shore within an hour. The Harbour Board wants the harbours hardened instead: shelters behind the sea walls, deep cellars in the customs houses and boats on call to move people along the coast.

Both plans assume the worst without knowing what the worst will be. The cabinet has ordered both costed, and has asked the radar crews to keep watching.

fields.text: The Night the Sky Fell
lines: The Night the Sky Fell

fields.text:
On the eighth of July Ulysses broke apart over the world. Scandia's radar crews tracked the light for hours, plotting what they could and recording what they could not explain. When dawn came the duty officers were still at their screens, and the harbours were still waiting for the warning they had spent three years preparing to give.

The news arrived by radio, in fragments. Coasts and cities across Usea had suffered terribly; the details changed with every bulletin. Within days the shipping lanes emptied and the markets for Scandian fish and oil simply stopped. By the end of the first week, boats began to arrive in Scandian harbours: fishing boats, ferries and small craft carrying families who had left other coasts with whatever they could carry.

The rescue service that was built to save one boat at a time is now being asked to receive hundreds. The cold stores built for the catch are being emptied for the relief kitchens. Every ministry's preparations assumed a single blow and a single recovery. What has come instead is a long strain with no clear end, and the capacity the country built over three years of preparation is being spent faster than anyone planned.

The cabinet has drafted orders for the fishing fleet and the harbours. It must now decide whether the harbours will stay open to everyone who reaches them, and for how long.

fields.text: A Neutral Coast
lines: A Neutral Coast

fields.text:
The war has come to Usea. Erusea's armies have moved against San Salvacion and seized the railgun site at Stonehenge, and Central Usea has founded a coalition, ISAF, to push them back. Much of what follows will be fought at sea and in the air. Scandia is not a party to any of it. It has no faction, no alliance obligations and no wish to acquire either.

A neutral coast is still a coast that every navy can see. Warships of more than one flag will pass within sight of the headlands. Supply ships will want fuel, pilots and berths. Agents are already in the capital asking about fishing boats for charter, with crews who know the shoals and do not ask questions. Every request is polite. None of them is entirely innocent.

The Admiralty wants Scandian waters closed: no warship of any flag enters without permission, the headland batteries manned and the radar chain reporting every contact. The Foreign Ministry argues that a neutral who helps no one will be remembered by everyone, and that clearly marked hospital ships could be given harbour rights without compromising anything. The fishing guilds want only to know that their boats will be kept out of every warship's way.

Whatever the cabinet decides, the harbourmasters have been given one instruction for every shift: no armed vessel berths without written permission from the capital, and no one in the water is left there, whatever flag they sailed under.

fields.text: The Coast After the War
lines: The Coast After the War

fields.text:
The war is over, and the shipping lanes are filling again. Scandia's harbours stayed open or closed exactly as its government decided. Its rescue crews pulled sailors of more than one flag out of the water, and its fishing fleet kept working, in escorted groups, through every season of the war. In a continent that has lost so much in a single decade, a coast that kept its lights on is worth something.

It is also worth noticing. Shipping companies that never called at Scandian harbours now ask about berths and handling fees. Neighbours inland want their cargo moved through Scandian quays. The treaty council has asked Scandian officials to help write the rules for a busier sea. The country that spent the 1990s counting its boats is being asked to help run a coastline larger than its own.

The arguments that defined the decade have not gone away. The harbours still argue with the capital, the fishermen still argue with the shipowners, and the oil on the Petrol Coast still divides the people who live beside it. But they are the arguments of a coastal nation at peace, and for the first time in years the boats can sail on a fair-weather day without anyone looking up at the sky first.

fields.text: A Door to the Sea
lines: A Door to the Sea

fields.text:
The bonded zone on the capital's quays opened with very little ceremony: a fence, a gate, a customs office and a sign in three languages. Inside the fence, goods bound for the inland countries can be landed, stored and loaded onto wagons without paying Scandian duty. Outside it, Scandia collects a modest handling fee and a great deal of goodwill.

The idea is older than the fence. For generations, cargo for Calladen and Bulgurdarest has crossed Scandian quays and paid Scandian duty twice, once on the way in and again whenever the paperwork went wrong. Shippers learned to avoid the coast when they could. The free port is an admission that Scandia earns more by being an easy door than by being an expensive one.

Not everyone agrees. The customs service has lost a source of revenue it guarded for decades, and the merchants of the capital worry that foreign goods passing through untaxed will find their way into Scandian shops. The Treasury replies that the handling fees already exceed the duty that was actually collected, and that a busy quay employs more dockers than an empty one.

On the first morning a train of empty wagons stood waiting at the gate. By evening it had left, full, for the inland border.

fields.text: Six Borders and a Register
lines: Six Borders and a Register

fields.text:
There is an old joke in the capital that Bulgurdarest is not a country but a timetable. It is not entirely unfair. Six neighbours meet at its frontiers: Calladen, Albard, Scandia, Ferustia, Central Usea and Roca Roja. Their freight crosses its railways, their traders fill its market towns, and their quarrels are argued in its cafes by people who have relatives on both sides.

The administration that took office in 1991 inherited all of this and very little paper about it. No one could say with confidence how many trains crossed the frontiers in a week, how much the customs posts collected, who owned which seam on Mount Sartan, or why the great halls of Expo City stood half empty. The ministries had kept the country running. They had not kept count.

The cabinet's first decision was therefore a modest one. Before choosing what Bulgurdarest should become, it would find out what it was: every road and railway, every customs post and its takings, every mine and every hall. The register would be published. Its compilers were warned that it would make many people angry, and told to compile it anyway.

fields.text: What the Crossings Earn
lines: What the Crossings Earn

fields.text:
For one full season, every customs officer in Bulgurdarest counted. They counted lorries and wagons, barges and handcarts; they counted what was declared and estimated what was not. The results arrived in the capital on a single sheet of figures, and the Finance Ministry read it twice before it believed it.

Bulgurdarest moves far more freight than it ever recorded, and earns far less from it than it should. Ferustian rubber, Albard steel and Calladen grain all cross its frontiers, and much of it crosses through a fog of local fees, informal payments and posts that close whenever their officer has business elsewhere. The country is already the region's crossroads. It simply has not decided to be paid for it.

Two proposals have come back with the figures. The Railway Board wants bonded yards at the frontier junctions: sealed sidings where foreign freight changes trains without paying duty, for a handling fee, so that Bulgurdarest becomes the switching yard of the whole region. The Trade Ministry wants something simpler and more radical: one low tariff, published, the same at every crossing for every neighbour, with the market towns left to grow on the traffic.

Both promise more money than the fog. Both would put some officials out of work, and those officials have already begun to explain, loudly and at length, why neither can possibly succeed in a country like this one.

fields.text: The Halls of Expo City
lines: The Halls of Expo City

fields.text:
Expo City was built for a single season of crowds, long before anyone now in government was born. Its pavilions still stand, its avenues are still lined with lamps, and its great central hall still seats more people than live in most Bulgurdaresti towns. For most of the year it is empty. Caretakers sweep the floors and tourists photograph the fountains, and the city council pays the heating bills with a sigh.

The new fair charter is meant to change that. The board it creates has been told to fill the halls, and the board has divided almost at once over how. One faction wants a market: buyers and sellers from every neighbouring country, contracts signed on the fair floor, hotels full and the city earning its keep. The other wants a showcase: engineers, universities and laboratories from across Usea exhibiting what they can build, with Bulgurdarest hosting the conversation that follows.

The two are not quite opposites. A market attracts the money that a showcase needs, and a showcase gives a market something worth buying. But the halls can only be arranged one way at a time, the board's budget can only be spent once, and both factions believe the other's version of the fair would be a slow way of emptying it again.

The board has asked the cabinet to choose, and promised to make the best of whichever answer comes back.

fields.text: Who Owns the Mountain
lines: Who Owns the Mountain

fields.text:
The geologists' map of Mount Sartan is the first complete one ever made, and it is beautiful: oil in the lower strata, aluminium ore and iron in the seams above, all of it traced in colour through a mountain that men have been digging into for a century. It is also deeply alarming, because it shows how much of that century was wasted.

The mountain has been worked by a dozen small companies, most of them now bankrupt or nearly so. Their galleries cross one another, their spoil heaps block one another's roads, and their accounts are a matter for the courts. The pit villages that depend on them have learned to distrust every new owner, and they have usually been right to.

Three proposals now lie before the cabinet. The Ministry of Industry wants a State Mining Trust: buy out the failing companies and run the mountain as a single enterprise with a single plan. The miners' unions want the pits to belong to the villages that work them, as cooperatives, with state credit and a state buyer for their ore. And a group of foreign mining houses has offered to lease the upper seams at their own expense, paying royalties to the treasury for every tonne they lift.

Each offer solves a different problem. The trust solves disorder, the cooperatives solve distrust, and the leases solve the treasury. None solves all three, and the mountain cannot be divided three ways.

fields.text: A Table on Neutral Ground
lines: A Table on Neutral Ground

fields.text:
Bulgurdarest has never been powerful enough to frighten its neighbours or rich enough to buy them. What it has, by accident of geography, is a seat at the centre of their quarrels. Every dispute between any two of its six neighbours eventually produces traffic through Bulgurdarest: refugees, smugglers, journalists, and sooner or later diplomats looking for somewhere to meet that is not the other side's capital.

The Foreign Ministry has proposed making a policy of what has so far been an accident. Bulgurdarest would offer neutral ground: a place where any two neighbours may talk, with hosts who take no side and want nothing from the outcome except quiet borders. It would not mediate wars, guarantee borders or join anyone's alliance. It would provide a table, an interpreter and a closed door.

The ministry is divided on how. One school wants the table to be public: meetings in the capital with the press in the gallery, on the theory that promises made in the open are harder to deny at home. The other wants quiet rooms and couriers, on the theory that the most useful conversations are the ones that never officially happened. Both schools agree on the danger. A host who is caught favouring one guest will not be invited to host again.

The cabinet has approved the principle. The method is still being argued over, in private, which some ministers consider an answer in itself.

fields.text: The Member Everyone Needs
lines: The Member Everyone Needs

fields.text:
The Central Usean Treaty Council meets with its larger members at the head of the table and its smaller members along the sides. Bulgurdarest sits along the side. It cannot outvote anyone, it cannot outspend anyone, and when the larger members agree among themselves, its delegates learn about it from the communique.

The Foreign Ministry believes this can be changed without changing Bulgurdarest's size. The country's frontiers touch more members than almost anyone else's, and its railways carry more of their trade. A delegation that understood transit better than anyone else, or one that could deliver the votes of the other small members, might make itself the member that every agreement has to pass through.

Two strategies are on offer. The first is to champion the council's transit clauses: propose one set of rules for moving goods across every member's frontier, and offer Bulgurdaresti officials to draft and administer them. The second is to organise the small members into a caucus that agrees its positions in advance, so that the larger members must negotiate with a bloc rather than pick off its parts one by one.

Either strategy would make Bulgurdarest more visible on the council. Either would also make it some enemies there. The larger members are not accustomed to negotiating with the side of the table, and they are unlikely to enjoy learning how. The delegation has been told to be patient, polite and very well prepared.

fields.text: Who Governs the Crossroads?
lines: Who Governs the Crossroads?

fields.text:
The administration that took office in 1991 was meant to be a placeholder. It has governed competently enough, kept the trains moving and the customs posts open, but it has never quite explained what it is or why it should continue. Now that the country is busier, richer and more visible than at any time in living memory, three very different groups have decided that they should explain it instead.

The royalists point out that the Tsardom of Bulgurdarest was never formally abolished, merely set aside, and that a crown council of notables could govern in its name without the expense or the embarrassment of a monarch. The railway unions, the miners of Mount Sartan and the workers of the Nervada factories answer that the country is a timetable, and that the people who run the timetable should run the country: a people's republic, governed by committees. The customs service says the least and perhaps means the most. It is the one institution that functions at every frontier, it has kept the country's accounts for a decade, and its senior officers have quietly let it be known that they could govern as a directorate until politics can be trusted again.

Each group has its strength. The royalists have the notables and the capital. The unions have the railways, which is to say they have everything that moves. The customs service has the frontiers, which is to say it has the money.

The administration has made no reply. Its silence is being read, in every cafe in the capital, as an admission that it no longer knows the answer.

fields.text: The Crown Council Sits
lines: The Crown Council Sits

fields.text:
The crown council met for the first time in the old palace of the capital, in a hall that had not been heated for a generation. Its members are notables: magistrates, senior officials, the heads of old families and newer fortunes, chosen by a procedure the royalist societies had drafted years ago and kept in a drawer against exactly this day. They govern in the name of the crown of Bulgurdarest.

They do not name a monarch. This is deliberate, and it is the council's cleverest decision. A named monarch would need a dynasty, a household, a claim to defend and enemies to answer. A crown governed by a council needs only a charter and a seal. The council is the crown, as far as the state is concerned, and its members serve together, sign together and can be replaced together without anyone needing to be crowned or deposed.

The country's response has been mixed but calm. Some Bulgurdarestis welcome the crown as a symbol above party, or at least welcome the idea of one. The railway unions have denounced the council as a club for the rich, and the customs service has said nothing at all, which the council has chosen to take as consent. In the market towns, the change is mostly noticed because the stamps on official letters now carry a crown.

The council's first instruction to the ministries is to continue their work exactly as before. Its second is to prepare a charter defining what the crown may do. It has promised that the charter will be short.

fields.text: The People's Republic Is Proclaimed
lines: The People's Republic Is Proclaimed

fields.text:
The proclamation was read at the Nervada junction at the hour when the most trains were standing in the station, so that their crews could carry the news down every line in the country. By evening it had reached the capital, Mount Sartan and Expo City, and by the following morning every frontier post had a copy pinned beside the timetable.

The People's Republic of Bulgurdarest is to be governed by a presidium answerable to elected committees in every works, depot and pit. The presidium is an office, not a person; its members serve together and can be recalled together by a congress of committee delegates. The railway unions, the miners and the Nervada workers who wrote the proclamation insist that this is the point. No one will rule the crossroads alone again.

The old administration handed over its ministries without resistance and, it must be said, with some relief. The customs service accepted the presidium's authority in a short letter that promised continuity of duties and committed to nothing else. The royalist societies held a dignified protest in the capital and then went home. The neighbours, who depend on Bulgurdaresti railways for a good deal of their trade, have asked only that the trains keep running.

The presidium's first decree guarantees that they will. Its second orders every committee to meet within a month, and to send its delegate to the capital with a list of what its works needs and what it can give.

fields.text: The Directorate Takes the Frontiers
lines: The Directorate Takes the Frontiers

fields.text:
There was no proclamation. The senior officers of the customs service met the outgoing administration in the Finance Ministry, signed a transfer of authority drafted by their own legal department, and returned to their offices. The radio announced that evening that Bulgurdarest would be governed by a Customs Directorate until further notice, and played the same music it always played.

The directorate is an office, not a person, and its members have gone to some trouble to stay unnamed. They are career officials who have spent decades at the country's frontiers, inspecting wagons, collecting duties and learning exactly where every rule could be bent and by whom. They do not claim to represent anyone. They claim to know how the country works, and to be able to make it work honestly.

Many Bulgurdarestis find this oddly reassuring. The crown council would have been a club for notables, the people's republic a government of the railway unions. The directorate is merely the customs service, and the customs service, whatever else is said about it, has always opened on time. The royalists and the unions are less reassured. Both have noticed that the directorate controls the frontiers, the frontiers control the money, and the money controls everything else.

The directorate's first act is to announce that it will publish every rule it enforces, in full, in a single code. Its second is to begin writing that code, which its officers estimate will run to some nine hundred pages.

fields.text: The Crossroads and the Sky
lines: The Crossroads and the Sky

fields.text:
The announcement came from Central Usea on the twentieth of April: the asteroid Ulysses would strike the Earth. In Bulgurdarest it was heard on station loudspeakers as well as radios, because the railway staff turned up the volume and the crowds on the platforms stopped to listen. By the end of the afternoon the first special trains had been requested, though no one yet knew where they should go.

The government's planners understood their country's particular danger within a day. Whatever fell from the sky, and wherever it fell, the crossroads could be overwhelmed by what followed. Six neighbours, some of them with long coasts and great cities, would have reasons to send their people somewhere safer. Many of those people would travel by rail, and most of the region's railways run through Bulgurdarest. A crossroads in a catastrophe is a funnel.

Two plans were drafted within a month. The Railway Board proposed an evacuation junction: emergency timetables that could turn every line one way, reserve rolling stock parked at every frontier, and reception halls at every major station. The Ministry of the Interior proposed something more local. The galleries under Mount Sartan run for kilometres; cleared, shored and stocked, they could shelter the mining towns and much of the capital.

The first plan assumes that the danger will come from outside and must be moved through. The second assumes that it may come from above and must be survived at home. No one in the capital yet knows which assumption is correct, and both plans cost more than the government has.

Provisional gameplay: Bulgurdarest's response is unsourced; the announcement date is official (ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20).

fields.text: The Night the Sky Broke
lines: The Night the Sky Broke

fields.text:
On the eighth of July Ulysses broke apart over the world. In Bulgurdarest people watched the sky from station platforms, rooftops and the slopes of Mount Sartan. No one in the capital could say where the pieces had come down, and the radio could only repeat that the night was over. By morning the stations were quiet. By the next morning they were not.

The trains began arriving on the second morning. They came from every border at once, and they came full: families with whatever they could carry, the injured, the elderly, crews who had driven through the night because no one had told them to stop. The emergency timetables, if they had been prepared, were tested to their limits within a week. If they had not, the stationmasters improvised, and some of their improvisations were remarkable.

The government now faces the question it has been dreading since 1996. Bulgurdarest can keep its crossings open, run its trains for anyone who reaches them and become the region's refuge and corridor at once, accepting the strain on its food, its housing and its patience. Or it can close its frontiers to all but the sick and the children, protect what it has, and accept that its neighbours will remember the decision for a generation.

In the meantime, the Expo City halls have been opened as depots. No one ordered it. The caretakers simply unlocked the doors when the first relief lorries arrived, and the board has decided not to ask whose idea it was.

Provisional gameplay: Bulgurdarest's response is unsourced; the impact date is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08).

fields.text: Between Six Borders
lines: Between Six Borders

fields.text:
War has come to Usea. Erusea's armies have moved against San Salvacion and seized the railguns of Stonehenge, and Central Usea is gathering a coalition to drive them back. Bulgurdarest is a party to none of it. It has signed no alliance, accepted no obligation and has no intention of acquiring either.

It is, however, a crossroads, and in wartime a crossroads is a prize. Six neighbours' supply lines touch its railways. Their refugees reach its frontiers. Their agents buy fuel, steel and spare parts in its markets, and their diplomats arrive in the capital with polite requests that grow less polite with every week the war continues. The country that spent the 1990s learning to be paid for its traffic must now decide what traffic it will carry at all.

The frontier service proposes the simplest rule: every train inspected, no weapon, soldier or munition allowed through, whoever's it is. The Foreign Ministry argues for a narrower exception. ISAF has asked to move its wounded and its medical supplies by Bulgurdaresti rail, under Bulgurdaresti crews and inspectors, without any military cargo and without any alliance. A neutral, the ministry argues, can still be humane.

Both sides agree on one thing. Whatever Bulgurdarest decides, it must apply the rule to every army equally and be seen to do so, because a crossroads that bends for one side will soon find itself treated as part of the other.

fields.text: The Busiest Crossroads in Usea
lines: The Busiest Crossroads in Usea

fields.text:
The war is over. Bulgurdarest was never invaded, never bombed and never forced to choose a side, and it emerges from the war with its railways intact in a region where many are not. Every neighbour needs to rebuild. Almost every road to rebuilding runs through the crossroads.

The trains have never been fuller. Steel, cement, timber and machinery cross the frontiers in quantities the customs posts struggle to count, and the old complaint that Bulgurdarest earns too little from its traffic has been replaced by a new one: that it earns too much, and that its neighbours have noticed. Every delegation that arrives in the capital to arrange transit also arrives with a list of grievances from the war years.

The country's institutions, whatever form they have taken by now, face the test that the 1990s prepared them for. The register, the fair, the mountain and the table on neutral ground were all built for a busy, quarrelsome region. That region has arrived. The question is whether Bulgurdarest can stay a crossroads rather than becoming a battlefield of other people's peace.

Provisional gameplay: Bulgurdarest's response is unsourced; the end of the war date is official (ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19).

fields.text: The Chromium Archipelago
lines: The Chromium Archipelago

fields.text:
The executive office at Wyatt occupies the top two floors of the old customs house, and from its windows a visitor can watch most of the islands' economy load itself onto other people's ships. Ore trains come down from the Calafia pits at dawn. By noon the freighters are low in the water. By evening the money has been counted, and most of it has already been promised.

Spayca has more chromium than any other state in Usea and more merchant hulls than a country of its size has any right to own. It has no land border, no seat on the Central Usean Treaty Council, and a government that has never been asked what it is for. The executive governs because it always has. The mining towns of Calafia and Alta accept this as long as the pay arrives; Adamas Minor, with its oil rigs and its one airfield, accepts it as long as Wyatt leaves it alone.

The review the executive has ordered will not change any of this by itself. It will write down what the office does, what it has promised, and to whom. The clerks have been told to be thorough. Several of them have already asked whether that is wise.

The islands are rich, isolated and undecided. Every faction in Wyatt agrees that this cannot last. None of them agrees on what should replace it.

fields.text: The Free Port Charter
lines: The Free Port Charter

fields.text:
The charter was read aloud on the steps of the customs house, which is where Wyatt has always announced the things it wanted the harbour to hear. It runs to forty articles. The first makes Wyatt a free port. The second creates elected councils on each of the four islands. The thirty-eighth, which nobody read aloud, abolishes the executive office as an office and turns its staff into a ministry.

The traders who wrote most of it are delighted. Open exchanges mean published prices, and published prices mean that a broker in New Rudigo can compete with a broker in Wyatt. The island delegations are delighted for different reasons: for the first time Calafia and Alta will elect the people who decide what happens to their pits, and Adamas Minor will elect someone who has actually been there.

Not everyone is delighted. The concession holders, who negotiated their licences with the executive in private, now find that every renewal will be argued in a council chamber. The smelter owners worry that open exchanges will price island ore for foreign buyers, not island works. And the dockers, who were not asked, note that the charter says a great deal about ports and very little about the people who work in them.

The new Council of Ministers sits for the first time tomorrow. Its first decision will be how quickly to call the elections the charter promises. Its second will be how to explain to the islands that a charter is a beginning and not a result.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Spaycan free port is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: The Mineral Board
lines: The Mineral Board

fields.text:
The Mineral Board met for the first time in the boardroom of the largest concession company at New Rudigo, because it had a long table and the executive's offices did not. Eleven chairs. Seven belong to concession holders, two to the smelter owners, one to the oil leaseholders on Adamas Minor and one, at the foot of the table, to the executive office, which will keep the seals and do as it is told.

The Board's argument is simple and has the merit of being true: the islands live on ore, and the people who know most about ore are the people who mine it. Quotas will be set by those who understand production. Prices will be negotiated by those who understand buyers. Politics, the chairmen say, has cost the islands money for long enough.

What the Board does not say, because it does not need to, is that it will also decide who works, at what wage, and what happens to a pit committee that objects. The dockers at Wyatt struck for two days when the Board was announced. The strike ended when the ore trains stopped and the quays had nothing to load.

Abroad, the Board's arrival is read as stability. Contracts will be honoured. Shipments will arrive on time. At home it is read as the old arrangement made honest: the islands were always governed by the people who own the pits, and now they are governed by them in writing.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Mineral Board is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: The Dock and Mine Compact
lines: The Dock and Mine Compact

fields.text:
The Compact was signed in the union hall at Haja by delegates from every pit on Alta and Calafia and every quay at Wyatt and Innsmouth. It took eleven hours. The miners wanted a single wage scale; the dockers wanted control of the loading schedules; the smelter hands wanted to be counted as miners rather than dockers, and were. Nobody wanted the executive office, but everyone agreed that somebody had to keep its records.

What emerged is a government by committee. Each pit and each quay elects delegates; the delegates elect a Coordinating Committee; the Committee governs the islands until a congress can be called to write something more permanent. The executive's clerks have been kept on. Several of them seem relieved to be told plainly what to do.

The concession holders have not been expropriated, yet. They have been told that their licences will be honoured, that their ore will be loaded at the Compact's rates, and that their foremen will now answer to a pit committee. Two companies have already announced that they are reconsidering their investment in the islands. The Committee has announced that it is reconsidering their licences.

The Compact has the support of most of the people who live on the islands and the hostility of most of the people who buy from them. It has inherited a merchant fleet, an ore trade and a credit rating. It will need all three, and it will need the buyers on the continent to believe that a committee can keep a delivery schedule.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Compact is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: Who Owns the Ore
lines: Who Owns the Ore

fields.text:
The survey teams came back from Calafia with more than the executive expected. The seams run deeper than the concession maps show and further under Alta than anyone had guessed. At the present rate of extraction the islands will be exporting chromium for longer than anyone now living will be alive to see.

That is the good news. The difficult news is in the second volume of the survey, which sets out who actually benefits. The concession holders pay a flat licence fee that has not changed in years. The ore leaves the islands unrefined. The steel made from it is sold back to Spayca at continental prices. The survey's authors, who are engineers and not politicians, have written this down without comment, which has made it more effective than any pamphlet.

Two answers are now being argued in Wyatt. The first is to keep the concessions and charge properly for them: royalties by the tonne, a public exchange, a reserve. The second is to found national smelters at Alta, keep the ore on the islands and sell steel instead of rock. The first is quicker and safer. The second is slower, more expensive and, its supporters say, the only way the islands will ever be more than a quarry.

Both answers begin with the survey. Neither can be taken back once the contracts are signed.

concessions and charge properly for them: royalties by the tonne, a public
exchange, a reserve. The second is to found national smelters at Alta, keep the
ore on the islands and sell steel instead of rock. The first is quicker and safer.
The second is slower, more expensive and, its supporters say, the only way the
islands will ever be more than a quarry.
Both answers begin with the survey. Neither can be taken back once the
contracts are signed.
Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Spaycan Register
lines: The Spaycan Register

fields.text:
The harbourmaster's office at Wyatt has kept a list of Spaycan hulls for as long as there has been a harbourmaster. It is not a registry. It records which ships called and what they paid, and it has never been used to answer the question the executive now wants answered: how many ships do the islands own, where are they, and what would happen if they stopped?

The answer, once the clerks have finished, is surprising even to people who expected to be surprised. Spaycan owners operate enough tonnage to carry a large share of the ore, fuel and general cargo moving between the continental ports. Many of these hulls never call at the islands at all. They are registered at Wyatt because the fees are low and the questions few, and they earn their keep carrying other people's goods.

This is a source of income and a source of exposure. A fleet that carries for everyone is useful to everyone, and in a crisis it will be wanted by everyone. Insurance, protection and the question of whose cargo a Spaycan ship will carry are about to become matters of state.

The register is only a list. What the islands do with it will decide whether the fleet is an asset or a hostage.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: An Invitation from the Council
lines: An Invitation from the Council

fields.text:
The trade desks on the continent have done their work: they sell ore, and they listen. What they have heard most often, from port officials and shipping agents alike, is that the Central Usean Treaty Council is drafting common rules for the ports of its members. Spaycan hulls will have to follow those rules whether or not Spayca has any say in them.

One of the desks has gone further and brought back an informal suggestion. The council could admit Spayca as an observer: no vote, no obligations under the council's treaties, but a seat at the table when shipping is discussed. It would be the first time the islands had sat in any continental body.

The executive's oldest advisers are against it. An observer seat today becomes a membership application tomorrow, they argue, and a member is expected to take sides. The islands have survived by never being on anyone's side. The answer, if there must be one, is to say so in law: permanent neutrality, written down, so that no future government can drift into a bloc.

The younger officials reply that neutrality written down is still neutrality nobody else has agreed to respect. The decision belongs to the focus that follows. This event only records that the question has now been asked.

Provisional gameplay: the Central Usean Treaty Council is the mod's CNEA membership (mod provenance).

fields.text: The Ulysses Briefing
lines: The Ulysses Briefing

fields.text:
The announcement from Central Usea reached Wyatt at the same speed as it reached everywhere else: by radio, then by telex, then by every newspaper on the islands under the same headline. An asteroid called Ulysses will strike Earth. The Federal Republic has said when, approximately, and has said that it is preparing. It has not said what anyone else should do.

The executive convened a briefing the next morning. It was attended by the harbourmasters, the radar officers from Calafia, two engineers from the survey teams and, because nobody thought to stop them, a delegation from the mining towns who wanted to know whether the pits could be used as shelters. Nobody in the room could answer the most important questions. Spayca has no observatory. Its radar sees aircraft, not stones falling from orbit. Its civil defence plan was written for storms.

What the islands do have is a great deal of rock, a great many ships and miners who know how to dig. By the end of the morning the briefing had produced a list: count the population and the cellars; join the radar, the tide boards and the air watch into one reporting office; buy fuel and food while they are cheap; give every hull in the register a role. None of it will stop an asteroid. All of it might matter afterwards.

The briefing's last note is a reminder that the islands do not know where the fragments will fall, and must not pretend to.

Provisional gameplay: the Ulysses announcement is official (ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20); Spayca's response is not.

fields.text: Ore for the Railgun Project
lines: Ore for the Railgun Project

fields.text:
The purchasing agents for the FCU-led international railgun project arrived at Wyatt without much ceremony. They want chromium, a great deal of it, refined to a specification the islands can only partly meet. They are prepared to pay, they say, a fair price. They are also prepared to explain at some length why the project matters to everyone in Usea, including the islands, and why a fair price might reasonably be lower than a market price.

The executive's position is awkward. The railgun project is the most serious answer anyone has proposed to Ulysses, and refusing to supply it would be remembered. But Spayca is not a party to the project, has no say in where the guns are built or who controls them, and owes nothing to its organisers. The islands are also preparing their own shelters, which need the same steel.

Three answers are on the table. Sell at market price, as Spayca would sell to anyone. Sell at cost, as a contribution that the islands can point to afterwards. Or keep the ore for the hillside shelters and the islands' own preparations, and let the project buy elsewhere.

This decision does not change the project's timetable or its completion. It only decides what the islands will be able to say about their part in it.

Provisional gameplay: Stonehenge as an FCU-led international project is official (ACES Chronicle, 1998 / 06.19; Super Weapons, Stonehenge); Spayca's ore contracts are not.
