fields.text: The Impact Night
lines: The Impact Night

fields.text:
The Wyatt reporting office went on the air at dusk and did not go off it until long after dawn. Every hour it read the same short bulletin: what the continental stations were reporting, what the islands' own watch posts had logged, and what the office did not know. It did not know very much. That, the duty officer said on the third broadcast, was the most important thing anybody could tell the islands.

The islands' watch posts logged lights in the sky and readings on instruments that nobody had calibrated for this. The harbourmasters logged the tides. The radar officers on Calafia logged a great deal of interference and very little else. The office broadcast all of it, unedited, with the time attached, so that whatever happened next the islands would have a record.

By morning the continental stations were reporting damage in places the islands trade with, and asking for help. The first requests came in by radio from port authorities who knew Spaycan freighters by name. They want fuel, food and medical stores, and they want ships that can carry them.

The bulletins will be read again for years. The question now is what the islands do with the freighters they have been counting since the briefing.

Provisional gameplay: the impact is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08); no impact site or damage on Spayca is asserted.

fields.text: Ships Turned Away
lines: Ships Turned Away

fields.text:
The first ship arrived at Wyatt in the early morning, low in the water and with no cargo manifest. Its master explained to the harbour pilot that Erusea had closed its doors to refugees and that the port he had been bound for had refused him a berth. He had fuel for three more days. He had nearly four hundred people aboard.

By the end of the week there were nine such ships in the roads off Wyatt and more reported at sea. Some had been chartered by relief organisations, some by the refugees themselves, and some by owners who had seen a market. The harbourmaster has put them all at anchor and sent water out. He has asked the executive what he is supposed to do next.

There are two answers and neither is comfortable. The islands could open the harbours: let the ships berth, land their passengers, and house and feed them in towns that are already crowded. Or the islands could offer transit: fuel, water, food and repairs at the quays, and then the ships sail on to someone else's harbour.

Whatever the islands decide will be noticed on the continent and in the ships still at sea.

Provisional gameplay: the Erusean refugee closure is official (ACES Chronicle, 2000 / 04.21); the ships at Wyatt are not.

fields.text: News from San Salvacion
lines: News from San Salvacion

fields.text:
The news came in on the trade desks' telex before it reached the radio: Erusean forces have crossed into San Salvacion and taken the railgun installation the islands once sold ore to build. The trade desks' next messages were about prices. Chromium has jumped. So have insurance rates for any hull bound for a continental port.

Spayca is not a party to this war and has no intention of becoming one. But its freighters carry cargo for ports on both sides, its ore goes into steel that both sides will want, and its harbours are the nearest neutral anchorage for anyone who needs one. Within a week, agents of both sides had called at Wyatt. Each was polite. Each wanted to know whom the islands intended to sell to.

The executive has three choices and has been warned that none of them is neutral in the way the islands would like. It can embargo ore to all belligerents, losing money and keeping its word. It can sell to every buyer who pays and collects, which is profitable and will be called something else on the continent. Or it can try to do both, case by case, which will satisfy nobody.

Whatever the islands decide, the war will be decided elsewhere.

Provisional gameplay: Erusea's invasion of San Salvacion and seizure of Stonehenge is official (ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER).

fields.text: The Archipelago After the War
lines: The Archipelago After the War

fields.text:
The war is over, and the islands are taking stock. The trade desks have reopened. The insurance pool has paid its last claims and is counting what it has left. The harbourmaster at Wyatt has stopped recording which flag each ship flies before he records what it carries.

What Spayca sold, and to whom, is now a matter of record, and the record is being read on the continent. Governments that bought island ore during the war remember the price. Governments that were refused remember that too. The islands' neutrality has survived, more or less, but it has acquired a history, and histories are argued over.

At home, the war years have changed the islands in ways that the executive is only beginning to measure. The merchant fleet is smaller and older. The pits are deeper. The people who came on the refugee ships, those who stayed, have children in island schools. The shelters behind Wyatt are now storerooms, and nobody is quite ready to fill them in.

The review that began the islands' long decade asked what the government was for. The answer is now written in ten years of decisions. Spayca will go on selling ore to Usea. What Usea thinks of Spayca is a question for the years after this one.

Provisional gameplay: the war's official end is ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19; Spayca's part in it is not.

fields.text: Counting the Crossroads
lines: Counting the Crossroads

fields.text:
The survey teams stood at every frontier post for a full season with clipboards and counters, and when they had finished the National Administration discovered something it had suspected for years and never measured: Calladen is a corridor that happens to have a country attached. Freight from Scandia, Dorondo, Ferustia and Bulgurdarest crosses its three districts on the way to somewhere else, and a large share of it never stops long enough to pay anything.

The capital district handles the heaviest traffic, most of it from the Dorondan frontier, which runs almost into the city. Port Edwards, the smaller harbour, sees inland freight that could not afford the capital's quays. The interior district, inland and unglamorous, turns out to be the place where nearly every route meets, and where nearly every delay begins.

The customs service has four sets of rules, one for each neighbour, written at different times by different governments. Inspectors apply whichever set they learned first. Hauliers know which posts are slow, which are expensive, and which can be persuaded.

The survey's authors end with a sentence the Administration has had printed and pinned in every ministry: a crossroads that does not know its own traffic is not governed by anyone.

Provisional gameplay: Calladen's states, resources, neighbours and 1991 government are mod provenance (history/states 15, 355, 393; history/countries/CAL - Calladen.txt; adjacency from the province map).

fields.text: Two Customs Doctrines
lines: Two Customs Doctrines

fields.text:
The draft customs code reached the Administration's desk with two final chapters, because its authors could not agree on one. Both chapters accept the same basic idea: Calladen will have one code for all four frontiers instead of four. They disagree about what that code should be for.

The first chapter proposes open transit. Goods crossing Calladen would travel on a single declaration and a single seal, inspected only when an officer has a reason. Hauliers would save days on every journey. The neighbours would come to rely on Calladen's corridors, and Calladen would earn its living from volume. Its critics point out that a country which inspects nothing will soon carry things it would rather not, and that a corridor everyone relies on is a corridor everyone will want to control.

The second chapter proposes bonded corridors. Transit goods would travel only on fixed routes between licensed depots, sealed at one frontier and opened at the other. It is slower, and hauliers will complain. But the state would know what crosses it, could charge for the privilege, and could close a corridor without closing the country.

The customs service is divided. So are the neighbours' trade attaches, who have begun to call at the capital district with opinions of their own.

fields.text: The Electoral Charter
lines: The Electoral Charter

fields.text:
The charter was adopted in the old assembly hall in the capital district, which had been used as a records office for so long that the clerks had to move filing cabinets to make room for the delegates. It is short. It restores elected assemblies in the three districts, creates a cabinet answerable to them, and fixes a calendar of elections that no government can postpone by decree.

The jurists who wrote it insist that it changes less than it seems. The National Administration remains; its officials keep their posts; the customs code and the corridors are untouched. What changes is who the Administration answers to. Until now it answered to itself. From now on it answers to people who use the roads.

That is precisely what worries its opponents. The engineers who run the corridors fear that elected assemblies will spend the transit revenues on whatever wins votes in the capital district, and leave the interior junction to decay. The frontier commanders fear that elected politicians will open the frontiers to anyone with a ticket and close them only after something has gone wrong. Both have said so publicly. Both have been told that they may stand for election.

The neighbours are watching with interest. Calladen's elections will be the first in the region in some time, and the hauliers who cross its frontiers every day will be watching the polling stations at the posts, where commuters can vote on their way across.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Electoral Charter is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: The Transit Directorate
lines: The Transit Directorate

fields.text:
The Transit Directorate held its first meeting in the drawing office of the railway administration, because it had the largest tables in the capital district and nobody saw any reason to move them. Seven directors: the chief engineers of the railways and the roads, the head of the customs service, the harbourmaster of the capital district, the depot superintendent of the interior junction, and two senior officials of the National Administration who had spent their careers keeping all of the others supplied.

Their argument is that Calladen is a machine for moving freight, and machines are run by engineers. Elections would interrupt the timetables. Frontier commanders would close the crossings at the first rumour. The Directorate will govern by plan, publish its plans, and be judged by whether the trains run.

The plans are good. Within a month the Directorate has published a ten-year programme for the corridors, a new tariff schedule and a list of every depot that needs repair. What it has not published is any way for someone who disagrees to change its mind. The district councils have been reduced to advisory bodies. Their first advice, that the plan pays too little attention to the people who live along the corridors, was received politely and filed.

Abroad, the Directorate is welcomed by everyone who ships freight across Calladen. At home it is welcomed by the people who work for it, tolerated by the people who use it, and quietly resented by the people who live beside it.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Transit Directorate is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: The Frontier Security Council
lines: The Frontier Security Council

fields.text:
The Frontier Security Council was proclaimed at the main Dorondan crossing, in front of the customs house, with the barrier down and the traffic held for an hour so that everyone could hear. Its members are the commanders of the frontier posts and a handful of civilian officials who have argued for years that Calladen's borders are its only real defence and its greatest weakness.

Their case is simple and widely shared. Calladen is small, its neighbours are larger, and everything that crosses its frontiers is someone else's business conducted on Calladenian soil. A country made of borders, the council says, must be governed by the people who guard them. Every crossing will be a question of security first and of trade second. The council will govern until the frontiers are secure, and it will decide when that is.

The first measures are visible within days. Armed guards replace civilian inspectors at the busiest posts. Every traveller is asked for a destination and a purpose. The bonded routes, if Calladen has them, are patrolled; if it does not, the council announces that it will create them. Queues at the frontiers lengthen, and hauliers begin to talk openly about routes that avoid Calladen altogether.

The neighbours have reacted cautiously. None of them objects to a secure frontier. All of them have noticed that the council's speeches describe the neighbours, by name, as the source of every danger the frontier must guard against.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Frontier Security Council is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: The Council and the Crossroads
lines: The Council and the Crossroads

fields.text:
Calladen has been a member of the Central Usean Treaty Council for as long as most of its officials can remember, and for most of that time membership has meant attending meetings, signing communiques and paying a modest subscription. The customs delegation now being sent to the council's offices is the first time Calladen has gone there wanting something.

What it wants is simple to state. Three of Calladen's four neighbours, Scandia, Dorondo and Bulgurdarest, are members of the council. Ferustia is not. If the council writes common rules for transit freight, Calladen's corridors will either fit those rules or be bypassed by them. The delegation's task is to make sure the rules fit.

There are two ways to do this. The delegation could offer Calladen's own customs code as the basis for a council protocol: one set of seals and papers from one end of the membership to the other, drafted, printed and checked in Calladen. Or it could argue that transit tariffs are a matter for each member, keep Calladen's power to bargain with each neighbour separately, and accept a lot of paperwork as the price of freedom.

The council's secretariat has already let it be known that it would welcome a draft. It has also let it be known that Ferustia will not be bound by anything the council adopts.

Provisional gameplay: the Central Usean Treaty Council is the mod's CNEA membership; Scandia, Dorondo and Bulgurdarest are members and Ferustia is not (mod provenance, history files).

fields.text: The Ulysses Corridors
lines: The Ulysses Corridors

fields.text:
The announcement from Central Usea reached the capital district by radio in the middle of a working day. Ulysses, an asteroid, will strike Earth. The Federal Republic is preparing. Every other government in Usea now has to decide what preparing means for it.

For Calladen the question arrived already shaped. The country's whole life is movement: freight, commuters, trucks, trains, ships. The Administration's first emergency meeting spent less than ten minutes on the asteroid and more than two hours on the railways. If the alarm is raised, who moves first? Where do they go? What happens to the freight trains already on the lines, the trucks already at the frontiers, the travellers who happen to be in Calladen that day?

By evening there was a plan to make a plan. Every train, bus and truck would be assigned a place in an evacuation timetable. The interior district, furthest from the sea and best connected, would be the place to build shelters and keep reserves. The neighbours would be asked to agree that a traveller caught on the wrong side of a frontier would be sheltered wherever they were.

None of this will stop Ulysses. The Administration knows it and has said so. What the corridors can do is make sure that whatever happens next happens to a country that knows where its people are.

Provisional gameplay: the Ulysses announcement is official (ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20); Calladen's response is not.

fields.text: The Coup Reports
lines: The Coup Reports

fields.text:
The first reports came in on the customs telex before the radio had them: officers in several Usean states had moved against their governments, and nobody yet knew how many or where. By noon the reports were contradictory. By evening it was clear that something large was happening across the continent, and that Calladen's neighbours were as uncertain as Calladen was.

The National Administration met through the night. Nobody in the room could say whether any Calladenian officer had been approached, and nobody wanted to be the one to ask. The frontier posts were full of armed men who had spent years complaining about civilian government. The garrisons in the capital district answered to commanders the Administration knew mostly by reputation.

Two courses were argued. The first was to say nothing, trust the garrisons, and avoid giving any officer a reason to feel suspected. The second was to call every commander to the capital district, one at a time, to explain their orders and receive new ones. The first risked being wrong. The second risked insulting the people it was meant to reassure.

The Administration chose to review. Whatever the commanders thought of it, the review would at least establish who commanded what, which was more than the Administration had known the day before.

Provisional gameplay: the Usea-wide coup is official (ACES Chronicle, 1997 / 05.30); no Calladenian unit or officer is named or asserted to have taken part.

fields.text: Relief Through the Crossroads
lines: Relief Through the Crossroads

fields.text:
The night of the impact passed in Calladen with the radios on and the trains stopped. By morning the continental stations were reporting damage in places that Calladen's corridors serve every day, and by noon the requests had begun to arrive at the clearing house, the customs desks and the railway administration all at once.

Relief for Calladen's neighbours must cross Calladen. Fuel, food, medical stores and engineers are already on the move from the sea and from other frontiers, and every one of those shipments will pass through a Calladenian post, a Calladenian depot and, in most cases, the interior junction. The corridors built for trade are now the corridors of relief.

The question in front of the Administration is not whether to let relief pass. Nobody has argued that. It is how. Relief could travel free of tolls and ahead of all other freight, which would be generous, popular and expensive. Or it could pay the normal tolls and take its place in the timetable, which would keep the clearing house solvent and the ordinary freight moving, and be remembered for a long time by the neighbours.

The relief trains are already being made up at the junction while the Administration decides. Nobody in Calladen asserts that the impact damaged the country itself, and the bulletins say so plainly.

Provisional gameplay: the impact is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08); no impact site or damage in Calladen is asserted.

fields.text: Refugees at the Frontier Posts
lines: Refugees at the Frontier Posts

fields.text:
The frontier posts noticed it before the Administration did. The usual queues of trucks and commuters had begun to include families with luggage, then buses chartered by relief agencies, then whole trains whose passengers had no onward tickets. Erusea had closed its doors to refugees, and the people who might have gone there were looking for somewhere else.

Calladen does not border Erusea. It does not need to. Its corridors connect the continent, and people who have been turned away from one destination are moving along those corridors in search of another. Most of them do not want to stay in Calladen. Many of them have nowhere else that will take them.

The frontier posts are asking for instructions. The Administration has two answers before it. It could open humanitarian corridors: marked routes across the country, with food, shelter and medical posts, and permission to stay for those who have nowhere else to go. Or it could allow registered transit only: refugees cross when they are registered at the frontier and sponsored onward by the country they are going to, and wait at the posts until they are.

The first answer will crowd the interior district. The second will crowd the frontier posts. Either way, the neighbours will watch what Calladen does and plan around it.

Provisional gameplay: the Erusean refugee closure is official (ACES Chronicle, 2000 / 04.21); the arrivals at Calladen's posts are not.

fields.text: Cargo for the War
lines: Cargo for the War

fields.text:
Erusea has invaded San Salvacion and taken the railgun installation there. Calladen is nowhere near the fighting, and for a few weeks the war was something on the radio. Then the requests began to arrive at the clearing house: freight for the war, routed across Calladen because that is the shortest way, with papers that describe it as something else.

The clearing house has been asked to move fuel, vehicles, spare parts and crates whose manifests say machinery. Some requests come with official letters; some come with offers of payment that would cover the corridor budget for a year. The customs service can usually tell what a crate contains. It cannot always tell who will use it.

The Administration has two answers before it. It could adopt neutral transit rules: no cargo for any belligerent crosses Calladen, whatever its papers say, and the corridors stay open for everything else. Or it could license war freight: belligerent cargo crosses on the bonded routes, under licence, at a premium, and Calladen is paid for its geography.

The first answer will cost money and may anger whichever side was relying on the corridors. The second will make money and will be called something unpleasant by whichever side was not.

Provisional gameplay: Erusea's invasion of San Salvacion and seizure of Stonehenge is official (ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER).

fields.text: The Crossroads After the War
lines: The Crossroads After the War

fields.text:
The war is over, and the clearing house has reopened its full set of ledgers. For the first time in years the Administration can see the whole picture: what crossed Calladen during the war, what was refused, what was paid, and what was lost when the traffic stopped.

The corridors held. Trains ran, roads stayed open, and the interior junction never closed for more than a day. That is the achievement Calladen will point to. What its neighbours will point to is less simple. Every decision about who could cross and on what terms is now a matter of record, and every neighbour has its own reading of that record.

At home the war years have left their marks. The frontier posts are larger and better manned than they were. The refugees who stayed have become commuters, hauliers and customs clerks. The shelters under the interior depots are used to store wagons nobody has room for anywhere else.

Calladen began this decade by counting its traffic. It ends it knowing that the traffic is the country, and that the country is only as safe as the corridors that cross it. What it does with that knowledge belongs to the years after this one.

Provisional gameplay: the war's official end is ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19; Calladen's part in it is not.

fields.text: Three Districts, One Republic
lines: Three Districts, One Republic

fields.text:
The National Administration meets in a converted customs hall in the capital, which is close to the sea and a long way from everything else Roca Roja contains. From its windows the clerks can watch freighters load mountain ore at the quays. The ore came down from the Scofield on trucks and mules. Very few of the clerks have ever been up there.

Roca Roja is three districts that share a flag and not much else. The capital trades by sea and thinks of itself as the republic. The interior farms the long valleys that run to the Central Usean frontier and thinks of itself as the part of the republic that actually borders anyone. The Scofield highlands mine steel and aluminium ore, keep their own counsel and think of the other two as places where the ore is sold.

The Administration has governed all three for years without elections and without much objection, because it has asked very little of anyone. That arrangement is running out. The interior wants a say in frontier policy. The highlands want roads. The capital wants a seat at the treaty council that means something.

Calling the three district councils together is the first step. Nobody in the hall pretends to know what the second will be.

Provisional gameplay: Roca Roja's three states, resources, neighbours and 1991 government are mod provenance (history/states 67, 416, 465; history/countries/RJR - Roca Roja.txt).

fields.text: The Frontier Office
lines: The Frontier Office

fields.text:
The new frontier office at Roca Roja occupies a farmhouse a short drive from the Central Usean line. Its first week is spent reading. There are frontier agreements nobody has enforced, customs schedules nobody has updated, and a drawer full of complaints from farmers whose fields lie on both sides of the line and who have paid duty twice on the same harvest.

The interior's people are not anxious about Central Usea. They trade with it, marry into it and listen to its radio stations. What they want is a policy. The Federal Republic is the largest and richest neighbour Roca Roja has, and the frontier office has been asked to decide how close the republic should stand to it.

One answer is association: adopt the Federal Republic's frontier rules, its customs schedules and its road standards, and let the interior's trade cross the line as if it were not there. The other is distance: keep Roca Roja's own rules, its own customs posts and its own counsel, and be a good neighbour without becoming a dependant.

Both answers have supporters in the interior. Neither will be popular in the highlands, which suspect that whoever wins, the mountains will pay.

fields.text: The Scofield Survey
lines: The Scofield Survey

fields.text:
The survey teams spent the summer walking the Scofield passes with theodolites, notebooks and mules borrowed from the mines. They came back thinner, sunburnt and with a map that nobody in the capital had seen before. It shows forty working mines, a dozen abandoned ones, nine passes usable in winter and three usable only by people who were born there.

It also shows how the highlands actually live. Ore comes down to the interior by mule and truck on roads the mining families built themselves. Claims are held under titles written in family Bibles. Disputes are settled by the oldest miner in the valley, and the republic's courts have not been consulted in living memory.

The highlands' councils have read the survey with suspicion. A map, one of them told the survey leader, is the first thing the capital needs before it can tax you. But the same councils have asked, politely, whether the capital might now be able to build them a road.

The survey's authors recommend both: graded roads to the upper workings, and registered leases for every working claim. The highlands will have to be persuaded that the second is the price of the first, and that the capital means to keep both promises.

fields.text: The Mountain Constitution
lines: The Mountain Constitution

fields.text:
The joint session of the three district assemblies met in the capital's largest hall and lasted eleven days. The capital's delegates arrived with a draft constitution. The interior's arrived with amendments to it. The highlands' arrived with a list of questions about roads, which they insisted on reading into the record before anything else could be discussed.

By the end of the first week three proposals had emerged. The capital and the frontier towns favour a federal association: a parliamentary cabinet, a single civil service and the closest relationship with Central Usea that the treaty council allows. The rural interior and much of the highlands favour a cantonal league: three cantons, three assemblies and a League Council that may do only what all three agree. The mining towns and the interior's tenant farmers favour a commonwealth built on the mine councils, with land for those who work it.

The National Administration has said that it will hand over to whichever government the republic chooses. It has not said what it will do if the republic cannot choose.

The debate's last day ended without a vote. The delegates went home to consult their districts, which is what Roca Rojans do when they cannot agree, and which is why they have so rarely had to.

fields.text: The Federal Association Cabinet
lines: The Federal Association Cabinet

fields.text:
The Federal Association Cabinet took office in the capital on a wet morning, before a crowd that was larger than expected and mostly from the capital. Its programme fits on one page. A parliament elected by all three districts. A civil service recruited by examination and paid from one treasury. Federal standards for weights, gauges and roads, borrowed from Central Usea because Central Usea already has them. And the closest association with the Federal Republic that the treaty council allows, short of anything that would make Roca Roja less than a state.

fields.text: The Cantonal League
lines: The Cantonal League

fields.text:
The League was proclaimed in the interior, at Roca Roja itself, because the capital's delegates could not agree to hold it in the capital and the highlands' delegates refused to come down any further. Three cantons now exist where there were three districts. Each has its own assembly, its own courts, its own taxes and its own militia. The League Council in the capital may do what all three cantons allow, and nothing else.

The highlands are jubilant. For the first time the Scofield governs itself in law and not only in practice, and the capital needs the highland assembly's consent to build so much as a bridge. The interior is satisfied: its frontier policy is now its own business. The capital, which proposed none of this, has accepted it with the resignation of a city that knows it is outvoted.

The League's critics, most of them in the capital, point out that a government which can do only what three assemblies agree on will do very little. The League's defenders reply that the republic has never needed much government, and has always needed to be asked.

At the treaty council the League will speak with one voice, provided the three cantons have agreed beforehand what the voice should say. The first such agreement took nine days. The council has been patient, and several of its larger members have quietly asked whether a League that needs nine days to agree on a sentence can be relied on in a crisis.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Cantonal League is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: The Miners' Commonwealth
lines: The Miners' Commonwealth

fields.text:
The Commonwealth was founded at a mass meeting in the largest mining town of the Scofield, attended by delegates from every mine council in the highlands and from the tenant farmers' associations of the interior. The capital sent observers. They were seated, given tea and told politely that their district would have its full share of delegates once it had organised councils of its own.

The Commonwealth's programme is simple and alarming to anyone who owns land. Every mine and every mill will be run by an elected council with authority over shifts, safety and output. An elected Council of Delegates will govern the republic above them. The interior's large estates will be divided among the families who farm them, and the owners paid from mining revenue over twenty years. Elections will continue, and the Commonwealth intends to win them.

The highlands are euphoric. The interior is divided between tenants who expect land and owners who expect ruin. The capital is alarmed, and its merchants have begun asking the treaty council whether a member state may change its constitution this quickly. The council has replied, after some delay, that it may.

Across the frontier, the Federal Republic has said nothing in public. In private its officials have asked whether the Commonwealth intends to honour the frontier agreements. The Council of Delegates has answered that it intends to honour every agreement that the people of Roca Roja have reason to keep.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Miners' Commonwealth is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: Word of Ulysses
lines: Word of Ulysses

fields.text:
The announcement from Central Usea reached the capital by radio, the interior by its neighbours across the frontier, and the highlands two days later by a truck driver who had heard it in a roadside cafe and assumed everyone else had too. An asteroid called Ulysses will strike Earth. The Federal Republic is preparing. It has asked its friends to prepare too.

Roca Roja has no observatory, no early-warning radar worth the name and no idea where the fragments will fall. What it has is mountains, and the people who have dug into them for generations. Within a week the highland councils had sent the capital a message that was half offer and half demand: the old galleries under the Scofield could shelter the republic, if somebody paid to make them safe.

The district offices have drawn up their own lists. The capital wants an evacuation plan for its coast. The interior wants fuel and medical depots along its roads. The highlands want the galleries surveyed, ventilated and stocked, and they want their own people to do the work.

None of this will stop an asteroid. All of it may decide who is still standing afterwards, and the republic does not intend to pretend it knows where the fragments will fall.

Provisional gameplay: the Ulysses announcement is official (ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20); Roca Roja's response is not.

fields.text: Reports of a Coup
lines: Reports of a Coup

fields.text:
The first reports came over the radio in the early afternoon and contradicted each other by evening. A coup has broken out across Usea. Some stations reported fighting, others reported that the fighting was over, and one reported both within the same bulletin. The capital's telex machines filled with messages from neighbours asking what Roca Roja knew. Roca Roja knew nothing more than anyone else.

What the republic does know is that it has soldiers, barracks and district offices, and that nobody has ever written down precisely who may order the soldiers to do what. The garrison commanders have asked for instructions. Some of them want to put guards on every district office until the news is clearer. Others warn that soldiers on the streets of the capital will frighten people more than the radio has.

The Administration's advisers are divided. Guards are a sign of strength, and strength may prevent trouble. Guards are also a sign that the government expects trouble, and expectations have a way of being met.

Whatever happens elsewhere in Usea will be settled elsewhere. What happens in the republic's barracks tonight will be settled in the capital, by people who will have to explain their choice to all three districts in the morning.

Provisional gameplay: the Usea-wide coup of 1997 / 05.30 is official (ACES Chronicle); no rebel country is named and no event in Roca Roja is asserted.

fields.text: The Night of the Impact
lines: The Night of the Impact

fields.text:
The signal posts on the Scofield heights stayed manned through the night of the impact, though nobody was certain what they were watching for. The duty officers logged lights, pressure readings and long silences on the radio. The district offices stayed open. In the capital, people gathered on the quays and in the squares because it seemed better than being alone.

By morning the reports from the continent were arriving faster than anyone could read them. Central Usea, across the interior frontier, was asking its neighbours for help: medical stores, fuel, vehicles and roads that could carry them. The interior district assembly met at dawn and voted, without much debate, to clear a corridor across the valleys to the Federal Republic.

Up in the passes, the army's field hospitals were set up before anyone had formally ordered them. The highland brigades had rehearsed this for two years and did not wait to be asked.

The republic did not know where the fragments had fallen, or what would follow them, and said so plainly in every bulletin it broadcast. What it did know was how many trucks it had, where the roads went, and which of them were still open by noon.

Provisional gameplay: the impact is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08); no impact site or damage in Roca Roja is asserted.

fields.text: Columns on the Pass Roads
lines: Columns on the Pass Roads

fields.text:
The first column reached the head of the pass road at dusk: perhaps two hundred people, most of them on foot, some with carts, a few with nothing at all. They had been walking for weeks. Erusea had closed its doors to refugees, and the places they had tried after that had closed their doors too. Somebody had told them that the mountain republic still let people through.

By the end of the month the field hospitals in the passes were treating more refugees than soldiers, and the district offices were feeding columns that arrived every few days. The highland villages have shared what they have. Their councils have now written to the capital asking how long they are expected to go on sharing it.

Two answers are being argued. The interior has empty valleys and too few hands to farm them; the refugees could be settled there, given land and building materials, and become Roca Rojans. Or the columns could be escorted across the mountains and out the other side, fed on the way, and left to find a country that will keep them.

Neither answer is free, and neither will be forgotten by the people in the columns.

Provisional gameplay: the Erusean refugee closure is official (ACES Chronicle, 2000 / 04.21); the columns in Roca Roja are not.

fields.text: War Beyond the Frontier
lines: War Beyond the Frontier

fields.text:
The news reached the interior before it reached the capital, carried across the frontier by Central Usean radio and by farmers who had watched troop trains moving south all night. Erusea has invaded San Salvacion and taken the great railgun installation there. The Federal Republic is mobilising. Its frontier with Roca Roja, so quiet for so long, is suddenly full of vehicles.

Roca Roja is not at war and has no intention of being at war. But it shares a long frontier with a country that is, and its roads, depots and hospitals are exactly what an army's rear area needs. Within a fortnight Central Usean officials had called at the frontier office with a list. They were polite. They mentioned the treaty council more than once.

The republic has two answers available, and both have costs. It can let its roads and hospitals serve Central Usea's rear area under civil contracts, staying out of the fighting but inside the war. Or it can declare its roads neutral: no military cargo for any belligerent, civilian traffic searched and allowed through.

Either way, the passes must stay open for food, fuel and the sick. The highland brigades have already been told, and have already moved.

Provisional gameplay: Erusea's invasion of San Salvacion and seizure of Stonehenge is official (ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER).

fields.text: After the War
lines: After the War

fields.text:
The war is over, and the traffic on the interior roads is changing. Fewer military trucks, more farm carts. The frontier office has gone back to reading complaints about double duties. In the highlands the brigades are coming home, and the mine councils are asking when the roads they kept open will be repaired.

What Roca Roja did in the war years is now a matter of record, and Central Usea has read it. If the republic served the rear area, the Federal Republic remembers the roads and the hospitals, and expects the friendship to continue. If the republic kept its roads neutral, the Federal Republic remembers that too, and the treaty council's next meeting will be polite and slightly cold.

At home the three districts have changed. The interior has new villages, or new memories of columns passing through. The capital has new quays and new debts. The highlands have galleries that were dug for shelters and are now used as storerooms, and nobody is in a hurry to fill them in.

The National Administration once called the three districts together to ask what held the republic together. A decade later the answer is the mountains, and the roads through them, and the people who kept those roads open.

Provisional gameplay: the war's official end is ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19; Roca Roja's part in it is not.

fields.text: The Northern Works
lines: The Northern Works

fields.text:
The inventory took four months and filled eleven volumes. The engineers who compiled it walked every slipway in the capital, every still at White Valley and every rolling mill along the shore district, and they wrote down what they found without much regard for whose feelings it might hurt. Rohden, the first volume concludes, is an industrial port that has never been managed as one.

The yards build coastal freighters on slipways laid for a smaller trade. The refinery ships half its crude away unrefined because nobody has paid for the extra column. The mills roll plate that the yards cannot use without reworking it, because the two have never agreed a specification. Each part of the works is competent. Together they are less than the sum of their parts, and everyone who works in them knows it.

The question the inventory leaves on the Administration's desk is not technical. Someone must own the plan that joins these works together. One proposal would gather them into a public trust, run by managers who answer to the state and publish their accounts. The other would license private syndicates to run them, raise their own capital and take their own risks, under conditions the state can enforce.

Either answer will change the country. The yards employ a large share of the capital's workers, and the people who run the works are, in practice, the people who run Rohden.

fields.text: The Northern Charter
lines: The Northern Charter

fields.text:
The charter was adopted in the great hall of the capital's oldest shipyard, because no government building was large enough for the delegates who wanted to watch. It has sixty articles. The first establishes an elected parliament, the Northern Diet. The twelfth gives the works councils legal standing. The fortieth, which the employers' federation fought over for three days, requires every large works to seat elected workers on its board.

The National Administration has not been abolished. It has been turned into a civil service, with the same offices, the same clerks and a cabinet above them that must now answer to the Diet. Several senior administrators resigned when the charter was read. Most stayed, and some seem relieved to be told plainly whom they serve.

The works councils are jubilant, and cautious. They have won the right to be consulted and lost the right to call it a betrayal when they are not. The employers' federation is sullen but present: its members will stand for the Diet, and several expect to win. The shore towns, which have no works councils and no federation, want to know what the charter means for them, and have been told that the elections will answer that question.

Abroad, the charter is read as a stable country choosing to stay stable. In Delarus, which buys Rohdener steel, the reaction is relief. Inside the gates, the first test of the charter will come when the next wage round fails, as wage rounds do.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Northern Charter is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: The Industrial Concordat
lines: The Industrial Concordat

fields.text:
The Concordat was signed in the boardroom of the employers' federation, in front of the heads of the state ministries and nobody else. It is a short document. It creates chambers of industry for shipbuilding, refining and steel. It gives each chamber authority over wages, prices and the allocation of plate and fuel among its members. And it seats the chairmen of the chambers, together with the ministers, on a Council of Industry that will govern the country.

The argument for the Concordat is that Rohden already worked this way, informally and badly. The works set the pace of the country's life; the Administration followed. Under the Concordat the people who run the works will run the state openly, plan their investment together and stop competing for the same plate and the same workers. The federation calls it rationalisation. The ministries call it coordination.

The works councils call it something else. They were not invited to the signing, and their offer to send observers to the chambers was declined with a letter thanking them for their interest. Two yards struck for a week. The strikes ended when the chambers announced a wage band slightly above the old rates, which the federation's members had agreed to pay in exchange for the right to set it.

The Concordat's first year will be productive. The yards will order plate on schedule, the stills will run at capacity and the mills will roll to specification. Whether the people who do the work will accept being governed by the people who own it is a question the Council of Industry has decided not to ask aloud.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Industrial Concordat is not established in any official chronology.

The Concordat's first year will be productive. The yards will order plate on
schedule, the stills will run at capacity and the mills will roll to specification.
Whether the people who do the work will accept being governed by the people
who own it is a question the Council of Industry has decided not to ask aloud.

fields.text: The Shipyard Council
lines: The Shipyard Council

fields.text:
The Council met for the first time in a mould loft at the capital's largest yard, under the half-drawn lines of a freighter that nobody now expected to finish on schedule. Its delegates came from every yard, mill and refinery committee in the country, and most of them had walked in straight from a shift. The meeting took fourteen hours and produced one decision: the committees will run the works, and the Council will run the country until it can write a constitution.

The National Administration has been kept on, as the Council's secretariat. Its clerks have been told that they will be paid, that their records will be needed and that their former superiors will not be returning. The employers' federation has been dissolved. Its members have been invited to stay on as managers, under committees that will now decide whether to keep them. Some have accepted; others have left for Delarus with whatever they could carry.

The Council's programme is simple to state and hard to carry out. Every works will produce to a published plan. Wages will be set by the Council. Fuel, plate and labour will be allocated where the plan needs them. A guard drawn from the yard workers will protect the works and the Council from anyone who objects, at home or abroad.

The yards are cheering. The shore towns, where nobody works in a yard, are waiting to see what a government of shipwrights means for fishing boats. In Delarus, which buys Rohdener steel and borders Rohden's most industrial valley, the news has been read very carefully indeed.

fields.text: The Delarus Desk
lines: The Delarus Desk

fields.text:
The foreign ministry had never had a Delarus desk before. It had a desk for the Treaty Council, a desk for the continent and a desk for everyone else, and Delarus fell somewhere between them. Yet most of Rohden's trade that does not go by sea crosses the Delarusian border, much of it by road, and the customs posts at White Valley handle more freight in a week than the council's secretariat discusses in a year.

The new desk's first report is blunt. Rohden and Delarus need each other. Rohdener steel and refined fuel go one way; food, machinery and transit to the south come the other. Delarus is a member of Central Usea's alliance and Rohden is not, which has never mattered to the lorries but may one day matter to the governments. The rail line from White Valley stops short of the border, so every tonne is unloaded twice.

Two approaches are argued in the ministry. The first is bilateral: settle trade and transit with Delarus directly, government to government, quickly and without waiting for anyone else. The second is to work through the Central Usean Treaty Council, where both countries sit, and write rules that every member port will use, so that Rohden's advantage becomes the council's standard.

The desk recommends finishing the rail link either way. Steel does not care which route the diplomats prefer.

fields.text: The Slipway Question
lines: The Slipway Question

fields.text:
The capital's slipways were laid for the coastal freighters that carried Rohden's trade a generation ago. They are too short for the hulls the council ports now order, and the yards have been turning work away for years. Lengthening them is the obvious answer. It is also the most expensive single project the works have attempted, and it will close two of the four slips for a year.

The yard managers want the work done at once and all together, so that the capital can bid for large hulls by the end of the decade. The works councils want it phased, so that nobody is laid off while the slips are closed. The mills want the yards to agree a plate specification before the new slips are designed, because the plate they roll now has to be reworked before it can be welded.

Behind all three arguments is the same question: what kind of shipbuilder does Rohden want to be? The country could specialise in large hulls for the council ports, or in standard coastal freighters that every yard can finish, or in repairs and refits for whatever limps into the northern harbours. Each choice needs a different yard.

The first slip is already being cleared. The rest of the answer will come out of the focuses that follow.

fields.text: Crude on the Coast
lines: Crude on the Coast

fields.text:
The survey teams spent a season on the coast between White Valley and the shore district, and came back with good news and an argument. The good news is that the oil under Rohden runs further and deeper than the old wells suggested. The argument is about what to do with it.

For decades Rohden has pumped its crude and shipped most of it away unrefined, because the one still at White Valley was too small and nobody would pay to enlarge it. The buyers refine it elsewhere and sell some of it back. The survey's authors, who are engineers and not economists, have calculated how much margin leaves the coast every year this way, and printed the figure on the first page.

A new refinery at White Valley would keep that margin at home. It would also put a large chemical works next to a large town, take three years to build and need a pipeline along the shore district to reach the eastern berths. The fishermen in the shore towns have already asked who will be responsible if the pipeline leaks. The refinery's backers have promised that nobody will need to be.

Refined fuel is also, as the survey notes in its last paragraph, the first thing every government wants in a crisis. Whatever the coast decides now will matter more than anyone expects.

fields.text: The Ulysses Notice
lines: The Ulysses Notice

fields.text:
The announcement reached the capital by telex at the start of the morning shift. An asteroid called Ulysses will strike Earth, and Central Usea is preparing. By the end of the shift the works councils, the employers' federation and the Administration had each asked the same question in different words: what does a country of furnaces, tank farms and slipways do about a stone falling from the sky?

The honest answer is that nobody in Rohden knows where the fragments will fall, and nobody can find out from the north. What the country can do is decide what it will protect and how. A furnace that is banked properly can be restarted; one that is abandoned cannot. A tank farm that is drained is a hazard; one that is full is a much worse one. Every works will need orders for what to shut down, what to save and where its people will go.

The yards have tunnels, the refinery has tank pits and the mills have basements built to hold machinery that weighs more than a house. With work, they could hold people. A buried reserve of refined fuel at the capital could keep the hospitals and the trains running if the shore tank farms are lost.

The works councils want the shelters built first. The employers want the contingency orders written first. The Administration wants a budget before anything else. All three will be needed, and none of them will stop an asteroid.

Provisional gameplay: the Ulysses announcement is official (ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20); Rohden's response is not.

fields.text: The Impact Watch
lines: The Impact Watch

fields.text:
The furnaces were banked at dusk, for the first time in living memory on purpose. The yards ran skeleton shifts. The tank farms at White Valley had been drained to the minimum, and the reserve tanks at the capital were full. In a basement room under the Administration's offices, every shelter warden in the country reported in by telephone every half hour, and a clerk wrote the reports on a board that covered the whole wall.

The board recorded what the wardens saw and what the continental stations were saying, and nothing else. The watch room had been told not to guess. Lights in the sky were recorded as lights. Instrument readings were recorded as readings. Reports from the south were recorded with the station that sent them and the time they arrived.

By morning the reports from the continent were about damage, fires and cut lines in ports that Rohden trades with. The first requests arrived soon after: cranes, pumps, welding crews and above all refined fuel, from port authorities that knew Rohdener yards by name. The furnaces could be relit in a day. The question was whether to relight them for home or for everyone else.

The watch room's board was photographed before it was cleaned, and the photographs were filed with the readiness inspection reports. Nobody yet knows what they will be needed for.

Provisional gameplay: the impact is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08); no impact site or damage in Rohden is asserted.

fields.text: Arrivals from the South
lines: Arrivals from the South

fields.text:
The first arrivals came by train, on a freight service from the south that had been carrying relief supplies north and had found room for passengers on the way back. Then they came by ship, on coasters that had been turned away from Erusean ports and had kept sailing until they found one that would take them. By the end of the month the White Valley stationmaster was counting several hundred a week.

They are people from the impact areas who had hoped to settle in Erusea, until Erusea closed its doors to refugees. Many have trades. Some have relatives in the north. Most have very little else. They want work and a roof, in that order, and Rohden, which has been short of hands in its yards for a decade, seems to them a reasonable place to look for both.

Two answers are being argued in the capital. The first is to house them: reopen the old works dormitories at White Valley as hostels, feed and register everyone, and place them in work afterwards at the state's expense. The second is to register them by trade at the station and send them straight to the yards, mills and stills that need them, with housing provided by the employer.

The first is kinder and slower. The second is quicker, and the works councils have already asked what wages the new arrivals will be paid.

Provisional gameplay: the Erusean refugee closure is official (ACES Chronicle, 2000 / 04.21); the arrivals in Rohden are not.

fields.text: Wartime Orders
lines: Wartime Orders

fields.text:
Erusea has invaded San Salvacion and taken the great railgun installation there, and within a fortnight the orders started arriving at Rohden's yards. Repairs, mostly, and fuel, and plate. Some came from shipping lines whose hulls had been damaged in waters that were suddenly dangerous. Others came from navies, through agents who were careful to say only which government they represented once the price had been agreed.

Rohden is not at war. It sits on the Central Usean Treaty Council, it trades across the Delarusian border, and its yards have never been asked to choose between customers. They are being asked now. The coalition that Central Usea is building wants repair capacity in the north, away from the fighting, and Rohden's yards are the nearest and the largest. The contracts on offer would fill the slipways for years.

The works councils are divided. Some yards want the work and the wages. Others remember that a yard which repairs one side's warships is a yard the other side has a reason to strike. The shore towns want to know whether their fishing boats will still be built if the slipways are full of grey hulls.

Whatever the yards decide, refined fuel will be short. The Administration has drafted a permit system, just in case.

Provisional gameplay: Erusea's invasion of San Salvacion is official (ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER) and ISAF's founding is official (2003 / 08.22); Rohden's orders are not.

fields.text: The Works After the War
lines: The Works After the War

fields.text:
The war is over, and the yards are quiet for the first time in two years. The last repair contracts have been paid, or argued over, or written off. The fuel permits have been withdrawn. The slipways that were full of grey hulls are being cleared for freighters, and the yard managers are discovering that the freighter market has not waited for them.

What Rohden built during the war, and for whom, is now a matter of record. Shipping lines remember which yards took their work. Governments remember which yards refused it. The works councils remember the double shifts, and they have presented the Administration with a bill for overtime, hazard pay and the pensions of men who were injured on the slips.

At home, the decade has changed the country more than anyone noticed while it was happening. The arrivals from the south have become yard hands and mill hands, and some have become foremen. The shelters under the works are storerooms now. The reserve tanks at the capital are still full, and nobody has suggested emptying them.

The inventory that began the northern works' long decade asked who should own the plan that joins them together. The answer is written in ten years of decisions. The works will go on building ships for Usea. What Usea will order from them next is a question for the years after this one.

Provisional gameplay: the war's official end is ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19; Rohden's part in it is not.

fields.text: The Republic Between
lines: The Republic Between

fields.text:
The National Administration occupies the old district treasury in Voslage, the capital city of Indore, and its windows face south. On a clear day the clerks can see the hills of the frontier with San Salvacion. On every other side of the republic, a little further away, is Erusea.

Voslage has more people than any of the small states around it and fewer friends than it would like. Every one of its three districts borders Erusea. Two of them border San Salvacion as well. The republic sits on the Central Usean Treaty Council, but its seat has always been filled by clerks who take notes and sign nothing. Its government has not faced an election in living memory. It governs because it is there, and because the alternative has never been put to anyone.

The report the Administration has ordered is meant to change that, or at least to describe what would have to change. It will set out what the government controls, what it spends, and what it has been doing about two frontiers it cannot defend alone. The districts have been told to cooperate. The army has been told the same, and has asked to see the draft first.

Everyone in the capital agrees that the republic cannot go on as it is. They agree about very little else.

fields.text: The Frontier Neutrality Act
lines: The Frontier Neutrality Act

fields.text:
The Act was passed by the Assembly of Districts in a single sitting, which its supporters call a mandate and its opponents call haste. It runs to three articles. Voslage will join no alliance. Voslage will host no foreign soldier. The army of the republic exists to keep every foreign army off Voslagian roads, without exception and without preference.

The cabinet that governs under it is drawn from the frontier districts and the army staff, and it does not pretend to be anything else. Its members are farmers, customs officers and colonels who have spent their careers watching two borders. They are not interested in the Treaty Council's debates. They are interested in whether the posts on the Erusean roads have working telephones and whether the garrison at Sierraplata can reach the southern crossings in a day.

The capital's reformers, who wanted elections and a seat at the council table, are dismayed. The council's members are polite but uneasy: a member that will take no side is a member that cannot be counted on. Abroad, the Act is read with relief in some ministries and suspicion in others. A neutral Voslage is a buffer. It is also a gap.

The cabinet's first instruction is that the Act must be made to work in practice, with rules for every crossing and courts for every incident. Neutrality written in a single sitting will take years to make real, and it will be tested long before it is finished.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Frontier Neutrality Act is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: A Government Among Friends
lines: A Government Among Friends

fields.text:
The Continental Solidarity Government was formed in the old treasury on a wet evening, after the National Administration agreed, under some pressure, to stand aside until elections could be held. Its ministers are the capital's reformers, the council party and a handful of district delegates who decided that a republic between two larger states is safer inside a club than outside it.

Its programme is simple to state. Voslage will send a full delegation to the Central Usean Treaty Council, with ministers who can sign what the council agrees. It will hold elections in every district, under observers from the council's members. And it will open the port at Indore to council shipping, so that the republic is tied to its partners by trade as well as by treaty.

The frontier districts are less certain. They see a government that talks about the council and says little about the posts on the Erusean roads. The army staff, who were not consulted, have asked what the council would actually do if a crisis came to Voslage's border, and have not received an answer they find reassuring. fields.text: The Frontier Defence Directorate
lines: The Frontier Defence Directorate

fields.text:
The Directorate took office in the capital's garrison headquarters, not the treasury, which tells the republic most of what it needs to know. Its members are the senior officers of the Erusean and southern frontier commands. They have announced that they will govern until the frontiers are safe, and have not said when that will be.

Their argument is not foolish, which is what makes it dangerous. Voslage has an army on every border and a government that has never had to answer for it. The Directorate says it will answer for it. Every district will have a military governor appointed by the Directorate and responsible for order on its stretch of the frontier. Every adult of service age will be on a national register. The newspapers will be told what the frontiers look like, so that the public is not alarmed by rumours.

The districts have accepted it with more resignation than enthusiasm. The capital's reformers have mostly gone quiet; a few have gone abroad. The Treaty Council has issued a careful statement that says nothing. In Erusea and San Salvacion, governments that had grown used to a sleepy republic on their border are now reading reports about conscription registers.

The officers insist that they want no war and no territory, only a frontier that holds. Whether a government of soldiers can keep a neutral republic out of other people's wars is the question the next years will answer.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Frontier Defence Directorate is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: The Erusean Roads
lines: The Erusean Roads

fields.text:
The survey teams came back from the Erusean frontier with maps, photographs and a list that the army staff read twice before passing it to the National Administration. Voslage's frontier with Erusea is longer than the republic's official maps admit. It runs along every one of its districts. It is crossed by main roads, farm tracks, river fords and a number of paths that appear on no map at all.

Most of these crossings are watched by nobody. The main roads have posts, some of which are staffed in daylight. The rest of the frontier is watched by farmers who know which of their neighbours on the other side are cousins and which are smugglers. Trade moves on market days, mostly in cash and mostly untaxed. The frontier towns live on it, and have done for generations.

The survey does not recommend closing anything. It recommends knowing what crosses: permanent posts on the main roads, proper customs houses, radar in the coastal district and a garrison in Sierraplata that can reach any part of the frontier in a day. It also recommends licensing the market days rather than abolishing them, since abolition would only drive them into the fields.

The survey's last page notes, without comment, that none of this would stop an army.

fields.text: The Southern Crossings
lines: The Southern Crossings

fields.text:
The frontier with San Salvacion has always been the friendly one. Families live on both sides of it. Voslagian workers cross every spring for seasonal work and come home in the autumn. The road south from the capital is in poor repair, and the crossings are watched by customs officers who are more interested in lunch than in contraband.

The registration teams sent to count the traffic found more than anyone expected. Hundreds of people cross every day, in both directions. Trade with San Salvacion is larger than the republic's books show, because most of it is never recorded. Several thousand Voslagians work on the other side for part of the year, without contracts, protection or any record that they exist.

None of this is a threat. San Salvacion is neutral, small and as uninterested in Voslage's army as Voslage is in its own. The teams recommend practical work: rebuild the southern road, set up a single customs desk, register the workers through an exchange that protects their wages, and give the capital's airfield enough reach to watch the frontier from the air.

One of the officers on the team added a handwritten note to the report. A friendly frontier, he wrote, is still a frontier. The republic should plan for the day it stops being friendly, without ever saying so out loud.

Provisional gameplay: Voslage's border with San Salvacion is mod provenance (map adjacency of states 437 and 446 with 310 and 521).

fields.text: The Battery Across the Border
lines: The Battery Across the Border

fields.text:
The FCU-led railgun battery called Stonehenge is complete. It stands in the San Salvacion district that borders Voslage's own, and the army's border observers now record its guns in their daily logs alongside the weather and the traffic. They were built to fire at fragments of Ulysses. Nobody in the capital doubts that. Several people in the capital have nevertheless asked what else they could fire at.

The question is not whether Voslage likes the battery. It is how openly it watches it. The army staff have three proposals. The first is to send liaison officers to the frontier openly, ask for briefings, and treat the battery as the shared protection it is meant to be. The second is to watch it from the Voslagian side, quietly, with observers and radar, and ask nobody's permission. The third is to thin out the villages closest to it on the Voslagian side, since if anything ever goes wrong there, they will be the first to know.

None of these choices changes anything about the battery itself, who controls it or what it is used for. They only decide what Voslage can say about it later.

The impact is a year away. The guns across the border are the best answer anyone has.

Provisional gameplay: Stonehenge's completion is official (ACES Chronicle, 1998 / 06.19); its location in state 310 is the mod's provisional mapping (USEAN_CONTINENTAL_WAR.md); its visibility from Voslage is not sourced.

fields.text: The Frontier Hears of Ulysses
lines: The Frontier Hears of Ulysses

fields.text:
The announcement from Central Usea reached the capital by radio in the afternoon. An asteroid called Ulysses will strike Earth. The Federal Republic has said that it is preparing, and that the preparations will take years. It has not said what anyone else should do, and the National Administration did not wait to be told.

Voslage's civil defence plan was written for floods and was last revised before most of the officials reading it were born. It assumes that people will go to their cellars and wait. It does not assume that the republic's neighbours will be doing the same thing, or that people from those neighbours might come to Voslage's borders looking for somewhere safer to wait.

The army staff raised that point at the first meeting, and it changed the conversation. The republic must prepare its own people: registers of shelters, wardens in the capital, marked routes to the inland districts, stores of grain and fuel. But it must also prepare for others. Its frontier posts will see whatever comes, first. Its border towns will have to feed whoever arrives.

Nobody in the room knew where the fragments would fall. The briefing's final note asks the republic not to pretend otherwise, and to prepare for the people as well as the sky.

Provisional gameplay: the Ulysses announcement is official (ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20); Voslage's response is not.

fields.text: The Impact Night
lines: The Impact Night

fields.text:
The frontier posts telephoned the capital every hour through the night of the impact, and the duty officers in the old treasury wrote down everything they said. The posts reported lights in the sky, flashes on the horizon and radio stations falling silent one by one. They reported the battery across the southern border firing. They did not report anything they could not see, and the capital did not ask them to guess.

In the morning the National Administration broadcast what it knew and what it did not. It did not know where every fragment had fallen. It did know that the republic's shelters had been used, that its stores were intact, and that the frontier posts were already reporting people on the roads: families with what they could carry, lorries without papers, columns that had been walking since before dawn.

The army staff want field hospitals at the main crossings and relief columns to the border towns, at once. The treasury wants to know who will pay for them, and for how long. The districts want to know whether the people on the roads are passing through or staying.

Nobody can answer the last question yet. The first two will be answered by what the republic does in the next week.

Provisional gameplay: the impact is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08); no impact site or damage in Voslage is asserted.

fields.text: Turned Back at Erusea
lines: Turned Back at Erusea

fields.text:
The news came first from the frontier posts on the Erusean roads: Erusea has closed its doors to refugees. The columns that had been moving towards its border towns are being turned back. Within days, the posts were reporting the same columns again, this time coming down the roads towards Voslage.

They are not all from one place. Some came from the regions worst hit by the impact; some had already been on the road for months; some had been living in Erusean camps and have now been told to leave. Many have no papers. All of them need food, water and somewhere to sleep. The field hospitals at the crossings are full, and the border towns have started to close their doors.

The republic has three answers and must choose one. It can open reception camps at the frontier, register and house everyone who arrives, and pay for it. It can open a registered transit corridor across Voslage, with food and medical stops, towards whichever country will take them. Or it can do what Erusea has done and close the frontier to new arrivals, keeping those already inside and turning the rest away.

Whatever the republic chooses, it will be seen from both sides of every border it has.

Provisional gameplay: the Erusean refugee closure is official (ACES Chronicle, 2000 / 04.21); the columns at Voslage's border are not.

fields.text: War on the Southern Border
lines: War on the Southern Border

fields.text:
The posts at the southern crossings reported the first columns before dawn, moving through San Salvacion and not towards Voslage. By noon it was clear what was happening. Erusean forces had invaded San Salvacion and taken Stonehenge, the battery the republic's observers had watched for years from the Sierraplata hills.

Voslage is not a party to this war. Its government, whatever kind of government it is by now, has said so in every language its neighbours speak. But the war is being fought along its southern frontier, by an army whose country borders every one of its districts, against a neutral neighbour whose people have family on the Voslagian side. Within a week the first civilians from San Salvacion were crossing at the southern posts.

The army staff have called up the district reserves and are rotating them through the frontier posts. The civil defence office has taken the Ulysses sirens out of storage. The Treaty Council is meeting, and its members are asking each other what they will do. Before summer is over, Central Usea will found ISAF, and every small state in Usea will be asked where it stands.

Voslage's answer, so far, is that it stands on its own frontier and nowhere else. Whether that answer survives the war depends on people who are not in the capital.

Provisional gameplay: Erusea's invasion of San Salvacion and seizure of Stonehenge (ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER) and ISAF's founding by FCU President Robert Sinclair (2003 / 08.22) are official; Voslage's position is not.

fields.text: Voslage After the War
lines: Voslage After the War

fields.text:
The reservists have gone home, most of them. The frontier posts are back to their peacetime rosters, and the customs officers at the southern crossings have started taking lunch again. The capital has published the cost of the war years, and the figure is larger than anyone expected for a republic that never fired a shot across its own border.

Voslage spent those years watching two frontiers and taking in, or turning away, the people who came to them. Some of those people have stayed. Their children are in district schools, and some of them have the vote. The republic's neighbours remember what it did, and remember it differently. San Salvacion remembers the posts that opened. Erusea remembers the ones that watched. The Treaty Council remembers which members came to its sessions, and what they said.

The government in the old treasury, whatever it now is, has to decide what the republic will be in the years after this one. It can return to the quiet frontier it was before, if its neighbours will let it. It can keep the army it built, and explain why. Or it can try to turn the habits of the war years, the registers, the shelters and the corridors, into something a peaceful republic would want to keep.

The report that began this decade asked what the government was for. Ten years of frontier decisions have answered it, at least for now.

Provisional gameplay: the war's official end is ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19; Voslage's part in it is not.

fields.text: Two Islands, One Flag
lines: Two Islands, One Flag

fields.text:
The National Administration of Corscae works from a converted warehouse on the western quays, and its windows look across the strait at East Corscae. On a clear day the eastern harbour can be seen from the director's desk. On most days it cannot, and the administration governs it the way it always has: by telegram, by ferry when the weather allows, and by assuming that no news is good news.

It is rarely good news. The East pumps more oil than the West and lands more fish, and it sends both across the strait to an administration that spends most of its money on the western capital. The West has the offices, the archives, the only paved roads and the conviction that this is simply how a state is run. The two islands have shared a flag for longer than anyone can remember. They have never shared much else.

And then there is Imperator, the third island, which has no roads, no buildings and nobody living on it. Both islands claim it in principle. Neither has ever spent money on it.

The administration has decided to ask both islands what they want from the state. It knows the answers will contradict each other. The question is which island it hears first, because the island it hears second will take that as an answer in itself.

Provisional gameplay: Corscae's states, resources and 1991 government are mod provenance (history/states 62, 174, 575; history/countries/CRS - Corscae.txt).
