fields.text: The Empty Island
lines: The Empty Island

fields.text:
The survey team spent six weeks on Imperator Island and came back sunburnt, short of water and more enthusiastic than anyone expected. The island has good harbourage on its sheltered side, high ground that can see both main islands, soil that could be farmed and traces of oil under the western ridge. It has no roads, no wells, no buildings and no people. It has never had any of them within living memory.

Both islands have always claimed Imperator, the way people claim a thing they have never needed. Now that the survey has given it a value, the claims have become sharper. The West wants a station there under the administration's control. The East wants fishing rights and a share of any oil. A few people on both islands have begun to suggest something stranger: that Imperator could belong to neither, and that a third island might be the one place where West and East learn to build something together.

There are two serious proposals. One is to settle the island with families from both sides, on homestead grants, and give Corscae a third community. The other is to keep it empty and make it a reserve: fuel, stores and a watch station, held for a crisis.

First, though, someone has to build a landing stage.

Provisional gameplay: Imperator Island (state 174) has no buildings and minimal resources in the mod (mod provenance).

fields.text: The Strait Conference
lines: The Strait Conference

fields.text:
The delegates met in the ferry hall on the western quays, because it was the only building on either island that both sides agreed was neutral. The western delegation arrived with the capital's lawyers and a written constitution. The eastern delegation arrived with the harbour assemblies' secretaries and a list of grievances that ran to forty pages. The National Administration provided chairs, coffee and a clerk.

For three days nobody agreed on anything. On the fourth, the clerk circulated a single page summarising the points on which the two delegations already agreed, and it turned out to be longer than either side had expected. Both islands want the ferry run by the state. Both want the oil revenue published. Both want Imperator to belong to Corscae as a whole. Both want a voice in how the flag is used abroad. What they disagree about is who decides when they disagree.

The conference has produced a Strait Accord, which commits both islands to settle their disputes in a standing conference instead of on the quays. It is not a constitution. It is an agreement to keep talking, written down and signed.

Some delegates want to go further, and propose a federation with a cabinet answerable to both islands. Others think the accord is as much as two islands that have never trusted each other can manage.

fields.text: The Western Executive
lines: The Western Executive

fields.text:
The executive office was proclaimed in the western capital on a weekday morning, without a vote and without much ceremony. The National Administration's director read a short statement from the steps of the warehouse: the two claims had been heard, the islands could not agree, and the state could not wait for them. From today the executive office in the West would govern both islands by decree, with prefects for the eastern districts and a gendarmerie to keep the peace.

In the West the reaction was relief. The capital's officials, its merchants and most of its residents have long believed that the East was governed too loosely and argued too much. They now have a government that says so. The western newspapers printed the statement in full, and several of them printed it twice.

In the East the reaction was quieter and more dangerous. The harbour assemblies met that evening and voted to send no delegates to the executive office, which had not invited any. Fishing boats stayed in harbour for two days. Then they went back to sea, because the islands still need to eat. The eastern grievances have not gone away. They have simply lost the place where they used to be heard.

The executive promises order first and argument later. It will be judged on whether the roads it builds in the East arrive before the East decides it has nothing left to lose. The prefects have been told to spend money quickly and to listen carefully. Whether they will do either is another matter.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Western Executive is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: The Harbour Commons
lines: The Harbour Commons

fields.text:
The proclamation was read at the eastern harbour at dawn, as the boats were going out, so that the crews heard it first. The harbour assemblies of both islands, it said, would govern Corscae as they govern the boats: in common, by open meeting, with the catch, the fuel and the oil shared out by rules everyone could read. The National Administration would keep its clerks and lose its director. The western capital would keep its offices and lose its say over who sat in them.

The East took to it at once. The harbour assemblies have run the fishing fleet for generations, settling disputes over berths and nets and fuel without lawyers or officials, and they see no reason why a state should be harder to run than a harbour. Within a week every eastern village had elected a delegate to the Commons Council.

The West has been slower. Its fishing harbours have assemblies too, and several of them have sent delegates. But the capital's officials, its merchants and its oil-rig owners regard the Commons as a takeover by the East dressed up as a harbour meeting. Some rig owners have stopped pumping until they are told who will pay them. The Council has told them that the oil belongs to the islands, and that the islands will pay a fair wage to whoever pumps it.

The Commons has the loyalty of the boats and the suspicion of the capital. It will need to show that common ownership can keep a state solvent as well as keep it fed, and it will need to do so before the West decides that it has been outvoted for the last time.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Harbour Commons is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: The Two-Island Compact
lines: The Two-Island Compact

fields.text:
The Compact was signed in the ferry hall, in the same room where the Strait Conference had met, by delegates from every district of both islands. It took a further two weeks to write and another week to translate into language the western lawyers and the eastern assembly secretaries could both accept. The result is a federation. Each island will govern its own roads, schools, harbours and police through an elected island council. A federal cabinet, with equal members from West and East, will govern the strait, the flag, the oil revenue and anything the two councils cannot settle between them.

Nobody is entirely satisfied, which the delegates take as evidence that they have got it about right. The West keeps the capital and the federal offices. The East gets equal seats in the cabinet and a written share of the oil revenue for the first time. Imperator Island is declared federal territory, belonging to neither island and to both.

The National Administration becomes the federal civil service. Its director has resigned, with some dignity, and the cabinet has asked the clerk who wrote the conference's one-page summary to run the new federal secretariat. The clerk has accepted, on condition that the cabinet publish everything it decides.

The Compact's opponents are not silent. Western officials complain that the East now has a veto over everything. Eastern assemblies complain that federal cabinets are still cabinets. But both islands will vote, on the same day, for the first time.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. The Two-Island Compact is not established in any official chronology.

fields.text: Letters from the Council
lines: Letters from the Council

fields.text:
The new foreign desk was a single office with two clerks, a typewriter and a radio, and for its first month it mostly read other people's newspapers. The clerks learned a good deal. The continental states are building roads and harbours with shared money, under rules set by the Central Usean Treaty Council. Corscae is not a member, has never applied, and until now had not been sure the council knew it existed.

The council does know. A letter arrived in reply to the desk's first enquiry, courteous and practical: Corscae could apply for associate status, which carries no vote and few obligations but makes it eligible for the council's harbour and road grants. For two islands that have never had enough money to pave their own roads, the grants are not a small thing.

The islands' politicians are divided along the usual line. Western officials like the grants and dislike the obligations. Eastern assemblies like neither and point out that Corscae has survived outside every continental body for a very long time. A third view, heard on both islands, is that the islands should buy what they need on their own terms and owe nobody a vote or a favour.

The decision belongs to the focus that follows. The desk has been told to reply politely and promise nothing.

Provisional gameplay: the Central Usean Treaty Council is the mod's CNEA membership (mod provenance).

fields.text: Word of Ulysses
lines: Word of Ulysses

fields.text:
The announcement reached Corscae on the radio, as most news does, and then by a telegram from the continent that said the same thing in fewer words. Central Usea has announced that an asteroid called Ulysses will strike Earth. It has said when, approximately. It has said that it is preparing. It has not said, and could not say, what two poor islands with no shelters, no air watch and one radio station should do about it.

The National Administration called the island delegations together in the ferry hall, the only room either island trusts. For once the meeting was short. Everyone agreed that Corscae could not stop anything that fell from the sky, could not see it coming and could not move its people very far if it did. Everyone also agreed that this was no reason to do nothing.

What the islands do have is soft rock, oil-field miners who know how to dig, harbour assemblies that can organise a village overnight, and Imperator Island, empty and close at hand. The delegates left the hall with a short list: dig and stock shelters on both islands, put a radar post above the western capital, and plan to move people to Imperator if either main island has to be emptied.

The administration's notice ends with a plain warning that nobody on the islands knows where the fragments will fall, and that the state will not pretend otherwise.

Provisional gameplay: the Ulysses announcement is official (ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20); Corscae's response is not.

fields.text: The Impact Vigil
lines: The Impact Vigil

fields.text:
On the night of the impact, both islands kept vigil by the radio. The reporting office in the western capital broadcast every hour: what the continental stations were saying, what the islands' own watch posts had logged, and what nobody yet knew. The duty officer read each bulletin twice, once for each island, because the eastern villages had complained for years that the western station spoke too fast.

The watch posts logged lights in the sky and readings nobody could interpret. The harbours logged the tides. The shelters, where they had been finished, were opened, and some families spent the night in them while others watched from the hills. The office broadcast all of it, with the time attached, and made no claims it could not support.

By morning the news from the continent was of damage in places the islands trade with, and of disruption everywhere. The tankers that bring Corscae's spares and refined fuel were delayed. Prices on the continental markets had already begun to rise. The islands pump their own oil, but they cannot refine much of it, and their boats and generators run on what arrives by sea.

The administration has two immediate decisions. It must decide how to share the fuel the islands have until the tankers return, and whether to ask the continent for help it may not be able to give.

Provisional gameplay: the impact is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08); no impact site or damage on Corscae is asserted.

fields.text: Boats on the Beaches
lines: Boats on the Beaches

fields.text:
The first boat came ashore on an eastern beach at first light: an open fishing boat, badly overloaded, with a failed engine and no fuel left. The village assembly fed the passengers, found them somewhere to sleep and sent word to the western capital. Within a fortnight there had been eleven more. Erusea has closed its doors to refugees, and some of the boats that could not land there have kept going until they reached somewhere that could not turn them back.

Corscae has never received refugees in numbers and has no law that covers it. The harbour assemblies have done what they would do for any boat in trouble. The administration has sent doctors, food and a clerk to register names. Nobody has yet decided what happens next.

There are two proposals. One is to land the boats where they arrive, house the passengers in the towns of both islands, and accept that the islands will be more crowded and less certain of themselves. The other is to receive them on Imperator Island, in camps the state builds and pays for, where they will be safe and fed and kept apart from two islands that cannot agree on anything.

Both proposals are expensive. Both will be argued over on the quays. The boats, meanwhile, keep arriving.

Provisional gameplay: the Erusean refugee closure is official (ACES Chronicle, 2000 / 04.21); the boats reaching Corscae are not.

fields.text: The Strait Goes Quiet
lines: The Strait Goes Quiet

fields.text:
The news reached the islands by radio: Erusean forces have crossed into San Salvacion and taken the great railgun installation there. Corscae is a long way from San Salvacion and is not a party to anything. But within a week the islands felt the war in the only way they could, which was through the sea. The tankers that brought Corscae's refined fuel and spares were chartered by bigger buyers. Freight rates tripled. The continental markets stopped answering the foreign desk's telegrams.

The strait between the islands has gone quiet. The ferry still runs, but the fishing boats are staying closer to home, unsure which waters are safe and which harbours will take their catch. The radio carries war news every hour, and the islands listen to it the way they listened on the night of the impact, knowing that what they hear will be decided somewhere else.

The administration has two choices, and neither is free. It can allocate every barrel of island oil by the state until the war ends, keeping boats and generators running at the cost of every private use. Or it can keep the fishing fleet at sea under a neutral flag, selling the catch wherever a harbour will take it, and trust the sea to feed the islands while the continent fights.

Whatever the islands choose, they will choose it alone.

Provisional gameplay: Erusea's invasion of San Salvacion and seizure of Stonehenge is official (ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER).

fields.text: Corscae After the War
lines: Corscae After the War

fields.text:
The war is over, and the islands are taking stock. The tankers are returning, slowly and at higher prices than before. The fishing fleet is going further out again. The radio carries prices and weather instead of war news, and the reporting office in the western capital has gone back to broadcasting twice a day.

What the islands did in the long decade since the Ulysses announcement is now a matter of record. They dug shelters, built a landing stage on an empty island, rationed their oil and received boats that nobody else would take. Some of these things were done together, by both islands, and some were done by one island over the objections of the other. Both islands remember which were which.

The strait is still there. The ferry still runs. Whether it is any narrower than it was in 1991 is the question that every politician on both islands now asks, and answers according to which island they come from. Imperator, the empty island, is no longer quite empty, whether it holds homesteads, a reserve or the remains of a reception camp.

The review that began the islands' long decade asked what Corscae wanted from its state. The answer is written in ten years of decisions. What the islands want from each other is a question for the years after this one.

Provisional gameplay: the war's official end is ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19; Corscae's part in it is not.

fields.text: Shilage Restored
lines: Shilage Restored

fields.text:
The district officials who stayed at their posts met in the capital in a building that still carried the former administration's signs over the door. Nobody had thought to take them down. There were not enough chairs, and the first resolution of the provisional council was to borrow some.

Shilage is a state again because Erusea has released it. How that happened, and what was agreed, will be argued about for years; for the council it is simply the fact they wake up to. The districts are there. The roads are there. The registers, the treasury, the courts and the border posts, the things that make a place a state rather than a region, are either missing or belong to someone else.

The council's first list is short and urgent. Count the people. Recover the registers or rebuild them. Staff the border posts so that the border is a fact. Raise enough revenue to pay the people doing all of this. Every item depends on another, and none of them can wait for a constitution.

Outside the building, a crowd waited most of the afternoon to hear what the council would say. When it came out, the announcement was brief: the council exists, it intends to hand over to something better, and it would be grateful if everyone kept the roads open in the meantime.

This is an alternate branch. In the official chronology Shilage is among the small nations annexed by Erusea that declare independence only in 2019.

Provisional gameplay: Shilage's cores are mod provenance (history/states 426, 447, 607); the official 2019 / 10.01 independence declaration is outside this window (ACES Chronicle).

fields.text: The Assembly Elected
lines: The Assembly Elected

fields.text:
The election was held in schools, post offices and, in one district, a cinema, because the registers allowed it and because the council had promised. Turnout was high. Counting was slow, partly because the ballot boxes had been borrowed from three different places and opened three different ways, and partly because every party sent observers who wanted to watch every ballot.

The assembly that has emerged is a mixture of district notables, former officials, teachers, merchants and a small number of people who seem to have stood for election mainly to find out whether they could. Nobody has a majority. The largest group wants a constitution quickly and a cabinet that answers to the assembly; the second largest wants the constitution to be argued line by line in public, however long that takes.

The provisional council has dissolved itself, as it said it would. Its members have mostly been elected, which some find reassuring and others find suspicious. The new cabinet is drawn from the assembly and has promised to govern by law while the law is being written, a promise that will be tested every week.

Abroad, the election has been noticed. Several governments that had said nothing about Shilage have now said something cautious. Erusea has said that it notes the result.

fields.text: The Provisional Directorate
lines: The Provisional Directorate

fields.text:
The council's last act was to appoint five administrators as a Provisional Directorate and to give them the authority it had never quite had itself: to issue decrees, to appoint officials, and to decide when the emergency would end and elections could be held. The vote was close. Several council members left the room before it was taken.

The directorate's argument is that a state with no registers, no treasury and no army cannot afford a parliament that argues. Roads need repairing now. Officials need paying now. The border posts need orders that will not be overturned by next week's vote. A directorate can act; an assembly can only discuss.

Its first decrees are sensible and numerous. Officials keep their posts and their pay. The registers will be rebuilt district by district. Customs will be collected at every post. Public meetings require a permit, which will usually be granted. Newspapers may publish freely, provided they publish the decrees as well.

The districts have accepted the directorate with relief in some places and resignation in others. Abroad, governments that like order have noticed that Shilage has some. Governments that prefer elections have noticed that it has none, and have said so politely.

The directorate has promised elections when the emergency has passed. It has not said what passing would look like, and it has the authority to decide. In the cafes of the capital, people have started counting the decrees the way they once counted the days until the next election.

This is an alternate political path for an unsourced state. No Shilagian directorate is established in any official chronology.

fields.text: The Former Administration
lines: The Former Administration

fields.text:
The files arrived in a lorry from the frontier: pension records, land titles, a list of property that had belonged to the former administration and a much longer list of debts it had owed. The covering letter, from Erusean officials, was courteous and brief. It said that these were the records Shilage had asked for, that others would follow, and that certain questions remained open.

Shilage's officials have read the files and agree that the questions are large. Who pays the pensions of people who worked for the former administration? Who owns the buildings it left? Which debts did it incur on Shilage's behalf, and which on its own? None of these has an easy answer, and each answer will tell Erusea and everyone else what kind of state Shilage intends to be.

There are two broad paths. Shilage can seek practical terms with Erusea: agreed procedures for customs, post, rail and records, which keep things working and say nothing about the past. Or it can turn to its other neighbour, Amber, and build its trade and travel around that border instead, keeping dealings with the former sovereign to the minimum.

Neither path changes where the border is. Both will be read in Farbanti and elsewhere as a statement.

fields.text: The Night the Sky Fell
lines: The Night the Sky Fell

fields.text:
The relief office opened the morning after the impact in two rooms of the treasury building, because the treasury had telephones and the relief office did not. By noon it had a list of what the districts were reporting, a second list of what they needed, and a third, much shorter list of what Shilage could provide from its own resources.

The reports are confused and will remain so for days. Lines are down. Some districts have not reported at all, and the office cannot yet tell whether that means they are unharmed or unable to report. Radio stations from the larger states are carrying news of damage across the continent, and Shilage's officials are listening to it with the same mixture of fear and helplessness as everyone else.

What the office can do is modest. It can count. It can send the constabulary's trucks where the roads allow. It can ask the neighbours for help, knowing that they are asking the same of their own neighbours. And it can make sure that, whatever Shilage receives, it reaches the districts that need it and not the ones that shout loudest.

The relief office's first public notice says exactly that, in plain words, and asks everyone with a working vehicle to report to their district council.

Provisional gameplay: the impact is official (ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08); no impact site or damage in Shilage is asserted.

fields.text: Between the Armies
lines: Between the Armies

fields.text:
The news reached the capital by radio and then by the border posts, which reported unusual traffic on the roads within the hour. Erusea has invaded San Salvacion. The continent is at war again, and Shilage, which has never fought one as a state, lies between the belligerents' roads.

Shilage has no army worth the name, no alliance and no seat at any table where the war will be decided. It has a constabulary, a set of border posts and a government that is still learning how to govern. Both sides will want things from it: passage, supplies, silence. Neither side is likely to ask politely for long.

The government's options are few. It can declare itself outside the war, ask every army to respect its roads, and hope that a small state's neutrality is less trouble to violate than to respect. It can try to keep its head down and say nothing. Or it can wait to see which way the war goes before it decides anything at all.

Whatever it decides, Shilage will be judged afterwards by what it did in these months, by its neighbours and by its own people. The constabulary has already asked for orders in writing, so that whoever comes to the border posts can be shown exactly what Shilage has decided, and nobody at a crossing has to improvise its foreign policy.

Provisional gameplay: Erusea's invasion of San Salvacion is official (ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER).

fields.text: Shilage After the War
lines: Shilage After the War

fields.text:
The war is over and Shilage is still a state, which in the first months of the fighting not everyone had expected. Its border posts are still staffed. Its treasury is poorer and its registers are thicker. Its constabulary is more experienced than anyone wanted it to be.

The government is now taking stock. Some neighbours recognised Shilage during the war; some did not, and some recognised it in ways that were carefully worded to mean very little. The refugees who crossed its border in the closure years are now residents, and some of them are now voters, or would be if Shilage held elections. The roads that were built for trade carried armies, and are in worse repair than they were.

Above all, Shilage now has a history of its own: a few years of decisions made by its own government, for its own reasons, that nobody else can be blamed for. Its officials disagree about whether that history is a source of pride or of embarrassment, and they will go on disagreeing.

The provisional state is no longer quite provisional. What it becomes next is a question for the years after this programme, and for people who will not remember a time before the border posts were staffed.

Provisional gameplay: the war's official end is ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 09.19; Shilage's part in it is not.

fields.text: The Question Before the Council
lines: The Question Before the Council

fields.text:
The Council chamber has no windows. It was built that way on purpose, the older officers say, so that nobody inside could be distracted by the weather or the harbour. Tonight it is full: every member of the National Defense Council, observers sent by the subdivision governments, a stenographer from the evening broadcast and, for the first time anyone can remember, a delegation from the harbour unions standing along the back wall because there are no more chairs.

The 1991 returns lie on the table in sealed folders, and every party has read them as a victory. The Old Guard points to the steady majorities of the outer islands and calls them a vote of confidence. The Democratic Republicans point to the port towns and call them a demand for change. The Reformists point to the barracks and the naval academy and say nothing at all, which unsettles the room more than any speech.

The senior admiral who chairs the session reminds the chamber that the arrangement which has kept North Point out of the continent's wars was never written down. It lives in habit, in telephone calls between the Council and the subdivision halls, and in the patience of islanders who have never been asked whether they consent. That patience, the admiral says, is not a reserve the islands can draw on forever.

Nobody proposes an answer that night. The session ends after midnight with an agreement to keep talking, a promise to publish the minutes and a single question entered into the record in the stenographer's careful hand: what are the islands to become?

fields.text: The Council Answers
lines: The Council Answers

fields.text:
The Old Guard does not make speeches. It makes lists. The paper sent to every subdivision hall on the morning after the vote is three pages long and contains no adjectives: the harbours that stayed open, the wars the islands stayed out of, the ferries that ran on time.

Beneath the list is a promise, and the promise is new. The National Defense Council will remain the government of the islands' defence and foreign affairs, but it will explain itself. It will open its promotion boards to every subdivision, publish its decisions, and write down for the first time the division of powers that the islands have lived under by habit for as long as anyone remembers.

In the port towns the reaction is a shrug. The Democratic Republicans call the promise a delaying tactic and announce that they will hold the Council to every word of it. In the outer islands the reaction is relief. The fishing towns did not want a revolution; they wanted to know that somebody in the capital was listening.

Inside the Council the younger officers are quietly pleased and the older officers quietly alarmed. Both suspect that a Council which starts explaining itself will find it hard to stop. Neither group says so in the chamber, and both are already drafting the rules they hope the other will have to follow.

fields.text: The Question of Succession
lines: The Question of Succession

fields.text:
A senior general of the National Defense Council has asked to retire. The request is reasonable: the general's health is poor and the general's service has been long. The difficulty is that nobody knows how the seat is to be filled, and everybody has an opinion.

For as long as anyone can remember, seats on the Council have passed by understanding. A retiring officer recommended a successor, the Council accepted the recommendation, and the islands read the name in the evening bulletin. With the merit boards open and the compact signed, that quiet custom has become conspicuous. The port newspapers have started asking who chooses the people who choose.

Two answers are argued in the wardrooms. The senior officers favour seniority: the longest-serving officer of the retiring member's service takes the seat, and experience is rewarded over ambition. The younger officers favour rotation: seats filled for fixed terms from officers who have passed the merit boards and served in a subdivision post, so that nobody governs the islands who has not first worked in them.

The retiring general has declined to recommend anyone, which everyone in the chamber understands is itself a recommendation. The Council will have to decide on its own, and in public. Whichever rule it adopts will govern who sits at the windowless table long after everyone now in the room has gone home to the outer islands to fish.

fields.text: The Convention Sits
lines: The Convention Sits

fields.text:
The delegates fill the old customs hall from the first morning. They sit by island rather than by party, because the convention's rules say so, and within an hour the arrangement has produced alliances nobody predicted: fishing towns with fishing towns, port cities with port cities, and the outer islands with whoever promises them a ferry.

The federalists speak first. The islands, they argue, have governed themselves for generations through their own councils, and a parliament should sit only for what they share: defence, foreign relations, the harbours and the currency. A unitary state run from the capital would be the Council's old centralism in a civilian coat.

The unitarists answer that a federation of fishing towns can never raise a loan, plan a grid or build a shipyard, and that a single roll of electors is the only way to make North Point one nation instead of a collection of harbours that happen to share a flag. They are loudest in the capital and quietest in the outer islands.

The Council's observers sit in the back row and take notes. When a journalist asks one of them what the officers think, the observer replies that the officers have been asked not to think aloud, and that they are finding it very difficult.

fields.text: The First Sitting
lines: The First Sitting

fields.text:
At noon the members of the National Defense Council walk into the customs hall in dress uniform, carrying the seals of the foreign and defence portfolios in a plain wooden box. They hand the box to the provisional cabinet, salute the new Parliament of the Islands and take their seats in the public gallery. The ceremony lasts eleven minutes.

The cabinet has no famous faces. It is an office of the parliament, staffed by civil servants and delegates who have agreed to govern until the islands can elect a government of their own, and it signs its first decrees with the cabinet seal rather than any name. Its critics call it faceless. Its supporters reply that a face is the last thing the islands need while they learn to govern themselves.

In the barracks the change is received in silence. The officers obey, as the Council told them to; some of them are relieved, and a few are angry. In the port towns there is dancing on the quays. In the outer islands people listen to the broadcast, turn off the radio and go back to work, which is how the outer islands receive most news.

The new government's first sitting ends after dark. The last item on the agenda is the ferry timetable, and the debate on it is fierce.

Provisional gameplay: an alternate government path for players only; the AI keeps the 1991 government.

fields.text: The Generals Go Home
lines: The Generals Go Home

fields.text:
The question of the National Defense Council's future reaches the parliament on a wet afternoon, and the gallery is full of officers in civilian clothes. The Council still exists: a committee of senior soldiers and sailors with no portfolio, an office in the capital and the loyalty of most of the Defense Forces.

One side of the chamber wants it abolished. A civilian state, they argue, cannot keep a second government of generals in reserve, however honourable its members. If the Council remains, the next crisis will tempt someone to call on it, and the islands will have built their parliament on sand.

The other side wants it kept as an advisory body, consulted on defence and honoured for its service. The Defense Forces accepted civilian rule because the Council asked them to, they argue, and humiliating the Council would teach every barracks that obedience is repaid with contempt. Better a council of honour that advises than a council of grievance that waits.

The Council's own members say nothing in public. In private, the senior admiral tells a reporter that the officers will accept whatever the parliament decides, and would prefer to be told soon. The reporter prints the remark on the front page, and the debate that follows is the longest the new parliament has held.

Provisional gameplay: an alternate government path for players only; the AI keeps the 1991 government.

fields.text: The Directorate
lines: The Directorate

fields.text:
The vote in the Council chamber is closer than the Reformists expected and more bitter than anyone wanted. When it is done, the old division of powers is suspended by decree, and North Point is governed by a Readiness Directorate with authority over every harbour, fuel store, airfield and road in the archipelago.

The subdivision governments are not abolished. They keep their schools, their clinics and their courts, and they are told that the Directorate will consult them. They are also told that their harbour budgets, their emergency plans and their road funds now belong to a single national plan, and that the plan will be published when it is complete.

The Directorate has no leader the islands can name. Its decrees carry a seal and its spokesmen read them without giving their names. Supporters say that this is the point: the Directorate is an office of the nation, not a ladder for ambitious officers. Opponents say that a government without a face is a government without a conscience, and wonder aloud who signs the orders.

more bitter than anyone wanted. When it is done, the old division of powers is
suspended by decree, and North Point is governed by a Readiness Directorate
with authority over every harbour, fuel store, airfield and road in the
archipelago.
The subdivision governments are not abolished. They keep their schools, their
clinics and their courts, and they are told that the Directorate will consult them.
They are also told that their harbour budgets, their emergency plans and their
road funds now belong to a single national plan, and that the plan will be
published when it is complete.

and its spokesmen read them without giving their names. Supporters say that

fields.text: The Prefects Arrive
lines: The Prefects Arrive

fields.text:
In most subdivisions the Directorate's prefects are received politely, shown to their offices and given the keys to the harbour stores. The handover takes a morning and a lunch, and the councils go back to arguing about school roofs.

In two subdivisions the councils refuse. Their members lock the harbour offices, sit on the steps and read the Subdivision Compact aloud, one clause at a time, to a crowd that grows larger with every clause. Nobody is armed. Nobody leaves. The prefects wait in the ferry terminal and telephone the capital every hour.

The Directorate's staff are divided. Some argue that a plan with exceptions is not a plan, and that the councils must be made to understand that the Directorate's authority is not a matter for negotiation. Others argue that the plan is meant to defend the islands, not to fight them, and that a compromise which leaves the councils their keys and the Directorate its plan would cost nothing that matters.

Whatever the Directorate decides will be reported on every island by morning. The fishing fleet has radios, and the fishing fleet has already heard. So have the other subdivisions, which handed over their keys politely and are now waiting to learn whether politeness was the wiser choice.

Provisional gameplay: an alternate government path for players only; the AI keeps the 1991 government.

fields.text: The Directorate Looks at Itself
lines: The Directorate Looks at Itself

fields.text:
The readiness audit is complete, the hedgehog doctrine is in place and the islands' neutrality has been declared to every government with an embassy in the capital. By the Directorate's own measures, the emergency for which it was created has been met.

That is the difficulty. The Directorate's founding decree promised a review once the plan was complete, and the subdivision councils have been counting the days. The Reformists are divided. Some believe the plan is finished and that the Directorate should return the harbours and the roads to the councils with honour. Others believe the plan will never be finished while the continent is unstable and the sky is uncertain, and that a Directorate which dissolves itself now will only have to be recreated in a worse crisis.

The review sits for a month behind closed doors. The islands wait with the patience of people who have learned not to expect much from closed doors.

When the review reports, it does not dissolve the Directorate. It decides how the Directorate will govern from here on, which, the councils note, is not the same question. The Reformists who argued for dissolution accept the result in public and keep their notes, and the islands understand that the argument has been postponed rather than settled.

Provisional gameplay: an alternate government path for players only; the AI keeps the 1991 government.

fields.text: What the Islands Make
lines: What the Islands Make

fields.text:
The economic survey is delivered to the government in a single volume bound in grey card. It is the first complete account of what North Point makes, earns and imports, and its authors have resisted every temptation to make it more exciting than it is.

The islands live by the sea. Fishing, ferries, harbour dues and ship repair account for most of what they earn. The Defense Forces' airfields employ more skilled technicians than any civilian industry. Almost everything else, from fuel and steel to radios and tinned food, comes from the continent on ships that the islands do not own.

The survey concludes that the islands can afford one serious industrial programme. The shipyards want it, because the yards have kept the islands alive for generations and could build the patrol craft and coasters that North Point has always bought abroad. The airfields want it too, because their hangars already hold the most advanced skills on the islands and could grow into an aviation industry of their own.

The survey's authors decline to recommend either. Asked why, the senior author replies that economists who live on islands have learned not to take sides between the harbour and the airfield. The government will have to choose, and whichever programme it chooses, the other will spend the next decade explaining why it would have done better.

Provisional gameplay: the economic survey and both programmes are authored for this package.

fields.text: The Fleet at Anchor
lines: The Fleet at Anchor

fields.text:
The review fleet anchors in a single line off the capital on a bright, windy morning, and half the islands come out to watch. There are patrol boats, a pair of elderly escorts, minesweepers, a survey ship and a scattering of auxiliaries, all freshly painted and none of them young.

Afterwards, in the wardroom of the flagship, the naval staff argue about what the fleet is for. One school wants a coastal fleet: torpedo boats, minelayers and submarines that would make the straits a gamble for any invader, built cheaply in the island yards and crewed from the fishing towns. North Point, they say, does not need to cross oceans; it needs to make sure that nobody crosses to it.

The other school wants an escort fleet: frigates and oilers that could bring a tanker convoy across open water if the continent ever went to war. Every litre of fuel the islands burn arrives by sea, they point out, and a fleet that can close the straits is of little use if the islands are starving behind them.

The budget will pay for one of these fleets, not both. The naval staff are asked to settle the argument by the end of the month. They settle it by the end of the year.

Provisional gameplay: the review and both fleet doctrines are authored for this package.

fields.text: A Date in the Sky
lines: A Date in the Sky

fields.text:
Central Usea has announced that the asteroid Ulysses will strike the Earth. The announcement reaches the islands at midday through the continental news agencies, and the radio station reads it in full, twice, before falling silent while the engineers decide what to play next. They choose nothing. For a quarter of an hour, every radio on North Point hisses.

By evening the government and the subdivision councils are meeting together, which they have rarely done before. The astronomers' reports are carefully worded and deeply frightening. Ulysses will break apart before it reaches the ground, and its fragments will fall over a wide area. Nobody can yet say where, or how many, or how large.

North Point's islands are small, scattered and surrounded by sea. Some of them have hard rock that could be tunnelled; some have nothing but sand and fishing huts. The harbour towns are crowded and the outer islands are far apart. Whatever the government decides, it must decide for every island at once, and it must decide without a map.

The meeting ends with a single decision: the islands will prepare. The details are left for the morning, and for the years that follow. On the walk home, more than one delegate stops on the harbour wall to look up at a sky that is, for now, entirely ordinary.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20. North Point's response and every choice are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Smoke across the Strait
lines: Smoke across the Strait

fields.text:
The first reports come from fishermen. Smoke over the mainland coast, aircraft where there should be none, a radio station that stopped broadcasting in the middle of a song. By mid-morning the continental news agencies confirm what the fishing fleet already suspected: a coup has broken out across Usea.

The reports through the day are confused and contradictory. Barracks have been seized, broadcasts interrupted, airfields closed. By evening it is clear that the Unified Command is fighting back, and that it may be days before anyone knows who holds the coast opposite the islands. North Point is no part of the rising and has no intention of becoming part of it.

The harbours, though, are filling. Freighters, ferries and private yachts that were at sea when the fighting began have turned north rather than sail home into it. Their captains ask for fuel, water and permission to wait. A few of the vessels are armed, and a few of their passengers wear uniforms with the insignia hastily removed.

The government must decide what the islands' neutrality means when the fighting is not between nations but inside them. Whatever it decides tonight, the captains in the harbour and the governments on the mainland will remember it long after the rising is over.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1997 / 05.30. North Point's response and every choice are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Eight Guns in the Desert
lines: Eight Guns in the Desert

fields.text:
The news is announced with ceremony: the Stonehenge project is complete. Eight railguns stand in a desert of San Salvacion, built by an international project led by Central Usea to bring down the fragments of Ulysses before they reach the ground.

On North Point the announcement is received with relief and a certain wariness. The guns can protect only what they can reach, and nobody on the islands knows whether the islands are within that reach. What the project does have, and will need to share, is its forecasts: the trajectories its astronomers are calculating, which will say where the fragments are expected to fall and when.

The government's request goes to the mainland through every channel it has: the embassy, the treaty organisation and the scientific societies. It asks for nothing more than the forecasts, and it offers the plots from the islands' own headland radars in return. In a year when every government in the world wants the same information, nobody expects the islands to receive special treatment.

The reply, when it comes, is polite, technical and slower than anyone hoped. It is also, the island astronomers report, extremely useful, and for the first time the shelter planners can draw something on their maps besides question marks.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1998 / 06.19, and Super Weapons, Stonehenge. North Point's response and every choice are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Last Drill
lines: The Last Drill

fields.text:
At ten in the morning the sirens sound on every island at once. For once nobody looks at the sky first; they look at their watches, because the drill was announced a week in advance and the wardens want to know how long it takes.

In the harbour towns the crowds move to the tunnels and cellars in orderly lines, carrying the bags they were told to pack. On the outer islands families open their shelter kits and tune their radios to the emergency frequency. The ferries sail their evacuation routes with passengers aboard. The hospitals move their patients below ground, and a surgeon completes a real operation in an underground theatre while the sirens wail above.

When the all-clear sounds, the wardens count heads. The figures are not perfect. An old fisherman refused to leave his boat; a school took the wrong road; a ferry ran aground on a sandbar it had passed a thousand times. Every mistake is written down, and every mistake is corrected before the end of the week.

There are only months left on the calendar now. The government asks whether the islands should keep drilling until the last week, or seal the stores and let people rest.

Provisional gameplay: the drill and its outcomes are authored for this package; no impact site is asserted.

fields.text: After the Fragments
lines: After the Fragments

fields.text:
Ulysses passed the Roche limit and broke apart, and for a long night its fragments fell across the world. On the islands the sirens sounded, the tunnels and cellars filled, and the radio went silent as the station's staff went below with everyone else.

Now the shelter doors are opening. People climb out into a grey morning and look first at the sky and then at each other. The reports from the continent are fragmentary and terrible: cities without power, roads cut, harbours closed, and numbers of dead that change every hour. What happened to the islands themselves will take weeks to count, and the government refuses to guess.

The years of preparation are about to be tested. Where the shelters were dug, the drills rehearsed and the stores sealed, the islands can begin to look outward almost at once. Where the preparations were thin, the government must first account for its own people before it can think about anyone else's.

The meeting room is cold and the coffee is bad. The decision in front of the government is simple to state: where do the islands begin? Outside, the civil wardens are already going door to door with their lists, and the first ferry captains are asking the harbour offices where they should sail.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08; no impact site or damage on the islands is asserted. North Point's response and every choice are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Boats from the South
lines: Boats from the South

fields.text:
The first boat arrives at dawn: an open fishing launch with twenty people aboard, no fuel left and a sail improvised from a tarpaulin. The harbour pilot who finds it tows it in, feeds its passengers and telephones the capital. By the end of the week there have been eleven more.

Across Usea the displaced are still moving, as they have been since the fragments fell. In April 2000 Erusea's government reached its decision about the refugees at its borders, and whatever that decision has meant on the continent, some of those who cannot find a place there have started to look north across the water. They carry families, fishermen, a few deserters and a great many people who simply have nowhere else to go.

North Point has room, but not unlimited room. Rationing has only just ended, the harbours are still repairing their cranes, and the treasury is exhausted. The port towns are generous; the outer islands are anxious; the Defense Forces want to know who is coming ashore.

The government cannot turn the boats away without a decision, and it cannot postpone the decision much longer. Every night the harbour pilots go out with lamps, and every morning they bring in more boats than the night before.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2000 / 04.21; the arrivals and their numbers are provisional. North Point's response and every choice are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Relief Ledger
lines: The Relief Ledger

fields.text:
The relief ledger is finished: four volumes bound in the same grey card as the old economic survey. It lists everything the islands spent after the fragments fell, every ferry and flight, every bed in every ward, every family sheltered and every sack of grain distributed from the stores.

It is not a triumphant document. It records the mistakes beside the successes: the ferry that sailed to the wrong island, the shipment of medicine that sat in a warehouse for a fortnight, the ration board that fed its own members first. Each mistake is followed by a note of what was changed to prevent it from happening again.

The officials who compiled it have read every page, and they know how the islands will read it: on the morning ferries and in the harbour cafes, and with arguments that will last for weeks. Some of those arguments will be bitter. Most will end with a grudging admission that the islands did better than they feared and worse than they hoped.

The government must decide whether to publish every page, or keep the most painful chapters in the archive until tempers cool.

Provisional gameplay: the ledger and its contents are authored for this package.

fields.text: The Continent at the Edge
lines: The Continent at the Edge

fields.text:
The radio from the mainland has changed its tone. The bulletins that once led with relief convoys and reconstruction now lead with border incidents, troop movements and the speeches of ministers who used to speak only about rebuilding. On the islands people have started listening to the late bulletin again, which they have not done since the fragments fell.

Years after the impact, Usea has not recovered and has not forgiven. The refugee camps are still full, the ruined towns are still ruined, and the governments of the continent are suspicious of one another in ways the shared disaster did nothing to soften. The island diplomats on the mainland report that every capital is preparing for something, and that none of them will say what.

North Point is party to none of these quarrels. It is, however, an island chain within reach of all of them, with airfields, deep harbours and a fleet that knows its own waters. Sooner or later, whatever happens on the continent, someone will ask the islands which side they are on, and the islands must know their answer before the question arrives.

The government orders the Defense Forces to review their plans, and the diplomats to keep listening. At the harbours the ferry captains notice that the naval patrols have started sailing a little further out each week.

Provisional gameplay: Usea's 2001-2002 tensions have no Chronicle entry; this briefing is authored.

fields.text: Strangers in the Harbour Towns
lines: Strangers in the Harbour Towns

fields.text:
On a Saturday night in one of the harbour towns, a fight starts in a bar between a group of allied aircrew and the crew of a fishing boat. Nobody is badly hurt. The bar's windows are broken, the town's only police car is overturned, and by Sunday morning every island has heard a different version of the story.

The incident is small, but it lands on a pile of grievances that has been growing for months. Rents in the harbour towns have doubled. The roads are full of military trucks driven by people who do not know them. The ferries are crowded with allied personnel who have not yet learned that the ferries leave on time and wait for no one. The island newspapers are full of letters, some reasonable and some not.

The allied command is embarrassed and anxious. The rear base depends on the islands' goodwill, and goodwill cannot be requisitioned. The island government is anxious too: it agreed to host the allies, and the islanders are beginning to ask whether anyone asked them.

The two sides meet on Monday morning. Both know that one more bad night could turn grumbling into something much worse.

Provisional gameplay: the ISAF headquarters itself is official (ACES Chronicle, 2004 / 09.16); this incident is authored.

fields.text: Neutral Ground
lines: Neutral Ground

fields.text:
The request arrives in a diplomatic pouch from a third embassy, unsigned and typed on plain paper. It asks whether North Point would be willing to host a meeting between representatives of two governments whose names it does not give, to discuss matters it does not specify, in a place where neither side would feel threatened.

The government has offered its customs hall, its guarantees and its discretion to anyone who needs them, and this is the first answer. It could be anything: an exchange of prisoners, a humanitarian corridor, the first tentative step toward a settlement, or a trap designed to compromise the islands' neutrality in the eyes of one side or the other.

The foreign ministry is divided. Some officials want to accept immediately, on the grounds that a neutral who refuses to host talks is not much use to anyone. Others want to accept only talks about humanitarian matters, on the grounds that a neutral who becomes involved in politics will soon not be neutral at all.

The meeting room is prepared either way. The chairs are counted, the windows are checked, and the coffee is better than it has been in years.

Provisional gameplay: the neutral lane and these talks are authored; they change no war state.

fields.text: The Islands Take Stock
lines: The Islands Take Stock

fields.text:
The review is presented to the islands on the evening broadcast, in a series of programmes that runs for a week. It covers everything that has changed since the ballot boxes came ashore on the morning ferries in 1991: the government, the economy, the fleet, the shelters, the relief years and the continent's long crisis.

It is an honest document, which means it is not a comfortable one. It records the arguments the islands lost as well as the ones they won, the money spent badly as well as well, and the decisions that seemed wise at the time and look less so now. The islands listen, as they always do, and argue about it on the morning ferries, as they always do.

Fourteen years is a long time for islands that measure their history in fishing seasons. Children who were in primary school in 1991 are now old enough to serve in the coast watch. The question the Council asked on the night of the returns, about what the islands were to become, has been answered, at least for now, in a way that nobody in that windowless chamber could have predicted.

The last programme ends with the shipping forecast, as every programme on the islands always has.

Provisional gameplay: the 2005 review is authored and describes only choices made in this tree.

fields.text: Polling Day on the Ferries
lines: Polling Day on the Ferries

fields.text:
As in 1991, the ballot boxes come ashore on the morning ferries under the eye of a single corporal per island. The difference is what they are for. This time the islands are electing a parliament with the power to govern, and everyone knows it.

The campaign has been loud. Posters cover the harbour walls, the radio carries debates into the small hours and the cafes have run out of chairs. The Democratic Republicans campaign on the convention and the charter. The Old Guard, reborn as a civilian party, campaigns on caution. The Reformists campaign on readiness and win more votes in the barracks towns than the cabinet expected.

On polling day the queues form before dawn. Volunteers lay out the rolls on long tables in the subdivision halls, schoolteachers check names against the registers, and the radio announcers remind listeners every quarter hour that polling closes at dusk. The Defense Forces escort the boxes and nothing else, as they promised.

The count takes two days. Whoever has won, the provisional cabinet's last act is to hand over to them, and the islands find, somewhat to their surprise, that it does. The old Council members watch the handover from the public gallery and leave without comment, which the newspapers agree is the most eloquent thing they have said in years.

Provisional gameplay: an alternate government path for players only; the AI keeps the 1991 government.

fields.text: The Question of the Administration
lines: The Question of the Administration

fields.text:
The question was not asked in a speech. It was asked in a memorandum, circulated among the permanent secretaries of San Salvacion's ministries on a winter morning in 1991, and it ran to a single line: on what authority does this administration govern? The national administration had kept the republic neutral through the long quarrels of its neighbours, balanced its budget in most years and opened more schools than it closed. It had never held an election, and nobody inside it could remember the last time anyone had asked it to.

The answers came back within a week, and they did not agree. The ministry of justice returned a draft charter written by its own junior lawyers, who had been meeting in the evenings with schoolteachers and district clerks. The civil protection service, the one national body every district already obeyed, returned a proposal that read like an inspection manual: a Directorate, a rota, and powers defined by the emergencies they were meant to meet. From the dry interior came a letter signed by the chairs of a dozen water councils, asking why a capital that could not fill a cistern should decide anything else at all.

The administration's own answer was the shortest. It works, the memorandum's author wrote in the margin of the last reply. The continent is rearming, the economy is fragile, and neutrality is a habit that a single bad year can break. Continuity is also a choice, and from now on it will have to be defended as one.

None of these answers is a government yet. Each is a movement, a draft, a committee and a set of grievances. Which of them San Salvacion follows will decide who holds the seals when the hard years come.

Provisional gameplay: no official source describes San Salvacion's internal politics or policies; this is an authored alternative.

fields.text: The Charter Assembly Convenes
lines: The Charter Assembly Convenes

fields.text:
The Charter Assembly met in the old customs hall because no other public building in the capital had enough chairs. Delegates came from every district with their credentials pinned to their coats and the draft charter folded in their pockets, many of them reading its first article for the hundredth time. San Salvacion is a neutral republic. It takes no side in the quarrels of other nations and lends its territory to no army. The second article was shorter and more dangerous: the republic is governed by an assembly elected by its citizens.

The national administration handed over the seals on the first afternoon. There was no ceremony, only a permanent secretary placing a wooden box on the presidium's table and asking for a receipt. Most of the administration's officials stayed at their desks. They had run the country for a generation, and the assembly needed someone who knew where the files were. Some of them believed in the charter. Others believed it would fail within a year and intended to be in the room when it did.

The presidium's first decisions were modest. It confirmed the budget, renewed the neutrality law and appointed a commission to draw the electoral districts. The commission's maps would take months, and every district wanted its own boundaries drawn by its own people. The assembly also had to decide what to do with the civil protection service and the water councils, whose movements had lost the argument but not their followers.

Outside the customs hall, the capital watched with the wary patience of a city that had seen many promises. A charter is a paper. Whether it becomes a constitution depends on what the assembly does when the paper is tested, and the years ahead will test it.

fields.text: The Directorate Takes the Keys
lines: The Directorate Takes the Keys

fields.text:
The civil protection Directorate did not seize power. It inspected it. On the morning of the transfer, officers in grey service jackets visited every ministry with a clipboard, counted the keys, checked the fire exits and asked each permanent secretary to name a deputy who could act in their absence. By noon the national administration had been replaced by a rota, and the rota had been posted on the door of every public building in the capital.

The Directorate's proclamation was brief and carefully worded. It assumed the functions of government for the duration of the national emergency. It did not say what the emergency was, when it had begun or when it would end. Asked by a foreign correspondent, a Directorate spokesman explained that a small country surrounded by rearming neighbours was always in an emergency, and that the only question was whether it prepared for one.

The districts accepted the change faster than the capital did. The civil protection service had been the only national body that came when called: it had dug out villages after floods, run water convoys in dry summers and kept the shelters in repair. The Charter Movement's lawyers and the water councils protested, wrote letters and were invited to join advisory committees, which met regularly and decided nothing.

Government by checklist has its virtues. It is predictable, it does not panic and it keeps records. Whether it can govern a republic rather than an emergency is a question the Directorate has chosen not to ask.

fields.text: A Government of the Councils
lines: A Government of the Councils

fields.text:
The standing committee of the district councils arrived in the capital by bus, with a crate of water tallies, a list of unrepaired roads and no intention of staying longer than necessary. The national administration had agreed to hand over the ministries after the congress of councils made clear that the districts would otherwise stop paying for them. The committee took the keys, held its first meeting in the ministry of public works and voted to move half the ministry back to the interior.

Government by council is government by argument. Every district sends a delegate, every delegate has a mandate, and every mandate is about water. The dry districts want cisterns, the river districts want flood works and the capital wants to be remembered at all. The committee decides by majority, publishes its votes and reverses itself when the councils instruct it to, which happens often enough that ministry officials now keep two drafts of every order.

The capital is unhappy, and its newspapers say so daily. The Charter Movement calls the councils a federation of complaints; the civil protection service quietly continues its rotas under a committee it does not respect. Foreign embassies ask which office they should telephone and are given several numbers. Yet the wells are being dug, the roads repaired in the order the councils chose, and for the first time the interior can point to a government that answers when it calls.

Whether a republic can be governed from its districts depends on whether the districts can agree on anything except their grievances. The committee intends to find out.

Provisional gameplay: no official source describes San Salvacion's internal politics or policies; this is an authored alternative.

fields.text: A Mandate without a Ballot
lines: A Mandate without a Ballot

fields.text:
The national administration published its mandate on a Monday, in every newspaper and on the door of every district office. It was four pages long. It said what the administration governed, which was everything it had always governed; for how long, which was until the republic decided otherwise by lawful means; and on whose behalf, which was the citizens of San Salvacion, whose consent it did not claim but whose trust it intended to earn.

The mandate's critics noticed what it did not say. It did not say how the republic might decide otherwise, or what lawful means would be recognised, or who would recognise them. The Charter Movement called it a lease without a landlord. The water councils called it a promise from the people who had broken most of the others. The civil protection service, which had expected to be asked to govern, said nothing at all and renewed its rotas.

Inside the administration, the mandate was received as a reform. Permanent secretaries now had to publish their procedures, answer written questions from district offices and appear before an inspector they could not dismiss. Some resigned. Most adapted, as they had always adapted, and found that a published procedure was easier to defend than an unwritten one.

A mandate without a ballot is still a promise, and promises can be counted. The administration has given the republic something to count. If it keeps the count honest, continuity may yet become consent.

fields.text: What the Desert Needs First
lines: What the Desert Needs First

fields.text:
The civil survey of the desert district took a year and three vehicles, two of which did not come back under their own power. Its report ran to nine volumes. The first eight counted things: wells, cisterns, schools, clinics, roads, families and the distances between them. The ninth volume was a single chapter, and it asked the only question the government had to answer: what does the desert need first?

The water engineers answered at once. A district without water loses its people, and no road will bring them back. Wells, cisterns and pumping stations should come first, maintained by the people who use them and paid for by tariffs they set themselves. The cost would be high and the benefits local, but a district that could drink could stay.

The transport officials answered differently. A district without roads cannot sell what it produces, cannot reach a hospital and cannot be reached when something goes wrong. Roads would bring tankers, doctors and buyers. Water could follow the roads; roads could not follow the water. The cost would be high and the benefits national, and the haulage firms were already offering to carry public freight in return for concessions.

The survey's authors refused to choose. They wrote that both answers were right and that the republic could not afford both at once. The desert district has waited a long time for the capital to notice it. It will notice which answer the capital chooses.

fields.text: News from the Skully Islands
lines: News from the Skully Islands

fields.text:
The news reached San Salvacion's capital on the last day of 1995, by way of a radio bulletin and a telephone call from the border posts. Robert Tyler of Central Usea's Army Southern District had eliminated a rebel base in the Skully Islands, and Unified Command had defeated the rebels with Scarface Squadron. The bulletin was brief, the telephone call was not. The border officers wanted to know whether anyone fleeing the islands was likely to come their way, and what they were supposed to do if someone did.

Nobody in the capital knew. San Salvacion had no part in the action and wanted none. The government's first instinct was the one it always had: issue a statement of neutrality, recognise the authorities that existed and take no side. The statement was drafted within the hour. The harder question was what neutrality meant at a border post in the interior, at night, when a truck without papers stopped at the barrier.

The border posts asked for rules. Who may cross? Who must be detained? Who may be returned, and to whom? The interior ministry produced a draft that answered the first question, avoided the second and referred the third to a committee. The civil protection service offered to staff the posts with its own rota. The water councils pointed out that the posts were in their districts, and that nobody had asked them.

A rebellion on islands far away has turned into a question at San Salvacion's own gate. The answer the government gives tonight will become the rule for the years ahead.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1995 / 12.31; San Salvacion's response is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Warning
lines: The Warning

fields.text:
Central Usea announced it on the twentieth of April 1996: the asteroid Ulysses would strike the Earth. The announcement was read on every radio station in San Salvacion within the hour, and in the afternoon the telephones at the national observatory rang without stopping. The observatory had two astronomers and one telescope that could see anything useful. They spent the evening explaining to ministers, journalists and frightened callers what an orbit was and why nobody in San Salvacion could change one.

The government's first task was to decide what to tell the country. Some ministers wanted to say very little until the international estimates were firmer. Others argued that silence would be filled by rumour, and that rumour would be worse than any estimate. The civil protection service wanted to publish shelter instructions at once. The finance ministry wanted to know what the instructions would cost before anyone promised them.

The second task was to decide what to ask of the neighbours. San Salvacion was small and neutral and had always relied on being left alone. Ulysses would not leave anyone alone. Central Usea was speaking of an international response, and an international response would need land, roads, water and the consent of whoever owned them.

By midnight the cabinet had agreed only that it would meet again in the morning. The observatory's lights were still on. Above the capital, the sky looked exactly as it always had, which was the hardest thing of all to explain.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20; San Salvacion's preparations are provisional gameplay.

San Salvacion within the hour, and in the afternoon the telephones at the
national observatory rang without stopping. The observatory had two
astronomers and one telescope that could see anything useful. They spent the
evening explaining to ministers, journalists and frightened callers what an orbit
was and why nobody in San Salvacion could change one.
The government's first task was to decide what to tell the country. Some
ministers wanted to say very little until the international estimates were firmer.

worse than any estimate. The civil protection service wanted to publish shelter

would cost before anyone promised them.

was small and neutral and had always relied on being left alone. Ulysses would
not leave anyone alone. Central Usea was speaking of an international
response, and an international response would need land, roads, water and the
consent of whoever owned them.

fields.text: The Coup across Usea
lines: The Coup across Usea

fields.text:
On the thirtieth of May 1997 a coup broke out across Usea. The radio carried fragments of it all night: barracks seized in one country, a broadcasting station in another, an airfield that changed hands twice before dawn. Unified Command would defeat it, with Scarface 1 among the pilots sent against the rebels, but on that night nobody in San Salvacion's capital knew how it would end, and several officers had stopped answering their telephones.

The government met in the basement of the interior ministry because the basement had a generator. Ministers arrived one at a time, each with a different rumour. The garrison of the capital was loyal; the garrison of the capital was wavering; a battalion in the interior had declared for no one in particular and was waiting to see who won. The civil protection service had already put its own rota on the doors of every ministry and was asking for authority to keep it there.

By morning the worst rumours had proved false. A handful of officers had joined the coup, a few dozen soldiers had followed them and most had gone home when they realised nobody else was coming. The capital had not fallen. The republic had not been tested so much as frightened, and the question now was what to do with the frightened men who had briefly thought otherwise.

Every government in Usea is asking the same question this week. San Salvacion's answer will say what kind of republic it means to be.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1997 / 05.30; events inside San Salvacion are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Host Terms
lines: The Host Terms

fields.text:
Central Usea's proposal arrived in a folder thicker than most of the ministry's budgets. An international project, led by Central Usea, would place a battery of railguns in a desert region of San Salvacion to destroy the fragments of Ulysses before they reached the ground. The folder contained maps, engineering summaries, security annexes and a short letter asking for the host government's consent.

Consent was the only thing San Salvacion had to give, and the cabinet discovered that it was worth more than anyone had expected. The project needed land, which the republic owned. It needed roads, water and power, which the host district had in short supply. It needed airspace, customs exemptions, security arrangements and the promise that the host would neither obstruct the work nor claim what it produced. In return it offered protection from the sky, which was not something San Salvacion could refuse.

The cabinet divided along familiar lines. One faction wanted a sovereign lease: the site leased, not ceded, with national law, national customs and national inspectors at the gate. Another wanted joint custody: a share of the site's security and a voice inside the perimeter, at the cost of standing visibly beside the guns. A third wanted to know what would happen to the battery when the fragments had fallen, and found that nobody in the folder had answered.

Whatever the engineers' timetable, the host must decide what it is lending. Neutrality has never been tested by a guest this large.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1998 / 06.19, and Super Weapons, Stonehenge (an FCU-led international project in neutral San Salvacion's desert); the host terms are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Eight Guns in the Desert
lines: Eight Guns in the Desert

fields.text:
On the nineteenth of June 1998 Stonehenge was completed. Eight railguns stood in San Salvacion's desert, their barrels pointed at an empty sky that would, in a little over a year, be full of falling stone. Central Usea's engineers held a short ceremony. San Salvacion's delegation stood at the back, in borrowed hard hats, and was thanked in the third paragraph of the speech.

The host district had lived beside the project for long enough to know what it meant. Convoys on roads built for farm carts. Floodlights that turned the night white. A perimeter that kept moving outward, swallowing grazing land and a road the villages had used for generations. The district had also seen clinics, wages and paved streets it had asked the capital for in vain. Its people did not know whether they were protected or occupied, and most suspected they were both.

In the capital, the completion raised a question the host terms had not answered. The battery was built to defend the world from Ulysses. It stood on neutral soil, operated by foreign crews, with power enough to bring down anything that flew. San Salvacion had agreed to host it. It had not agreed to become the most strategically important desert on the continent, and it had no say over what the guns would be used for once the sky was clear.

Tonight the host district is quiet, and the guns are silent. San Salvacion must decide how to live beside them.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1998 / 06.19, and Super Weapons, Stonehenge (eight railguns); the host's response is provisional gameplay.
