fields.text: The Night of the Fragments
lines: The Night of the Fragments

fields.text:
On the eighth of July 1999 Ulysses passed the Roche limit and broke apart. In San Salvacion the night began with a light brighter than the moon and ended with a sound nobody who heard it would forget. Stonehenge fired into a sky full of falling stone, again and again, and the villages of the host district counted the shots until they lost count.

By morning the reports were confused and contradictory. Radio links to the interior failed for hours, the telephone exchanges jammed and rumours travelled faster than any official word. The government could confirm only what its own wardens and drivers had seen: a sky that had been on fire, a battery that had fired until its crews were exhausted, and roads filling with people from across the region who had not waited for instructions before leaving home.

The plans met the night they were written for. Some worked; wardens knew their streets, trains ran to their timetables and the field hospitals opened before the first ambulances arrived. Some did not; keys were held by the wrong office, convoys waited for orders that never came and a shelter built for a hundred people was found to hold three hundred. The preparation record closed at midnight. Everything done afterwards would be relief.

The morning brings its own questions. What was lost, what can be saved and what must be rebuilt are questions for the coming months. Tonight there is only the work.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08; San Salvacion's relief is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Border That Closed
lines: The Border That Closed

fields.text:
On the twenty-first of April 2000 Erusea stopped taking in refugees. The displaced of the fragment year, who had walked toward Erusea's cities, found the border closed and turned back. Many of them turned toward San Salvacion. Within a week the border posts in the interior reported columns on the roads: families with handcarts, lorries piled with furniture, children carrying younger children.

The government had planned for the fragments. It had not planned for this. The reception centres opened in the fragment year were still full. The water convoys were already stretched. The districts that would receive the newcomers were the same districts that had been stretched to breaking a year before, and their councils wanted to know who would pay.

The cabinet considered two answers. San Salvacion could be a refuge: open reception centres, register the newcomers, give them the right to work and accept that the country would change. Or it could be a corridor: feed them, treat them, give them a ticket and send them onward to whoever would take them. The first would cost money and comfort; the second would cost something harder to measure.

Erusea's decision was made in Erusea. San Salvacion's decision will be made here, and the people on the roads are waiting for it.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2000 / 04.21; San Salvacion's refugee policy is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Summer of the Invasion
lines: The Summer of the Invasion

fields.text:
In the summer of 2003 Erusea invaded San Salvacion and seized Stonehenge. The first reports came from the host district: columns on the roads, aircraft over the perimeter, the project's crews disarmed or fled. Within days the railguns that had been built to shoot down falling stone were turned against aircraft, and the sky over the desert, which had been the safest in Usea, became the most dangerous.

San Salvacion's neutrality ended without the country choosing to end it. Its letters to every capital, its sovereign lease or its joint custody, its ledger of everything given and refused: none of it stopped a single armoured column. The border posts in the interior fought for an afternoon and were overrun. The government, meeting in the same basement it had used on the night of the coup, found itself governing a country that was being cut in pieces around it.

Central Usea and its partners are already at war with Erusea, and the coalition's help will come slowly if it comes at all. The government now has to decide how it will govern what it still holds, and how it will protect the people, the records and the institutions it no longer controls. Some ministers want to hold the free districts at any cost. Others want to prepare the ministries for occupation: to keep working quietly, keep records and wait.

The war has come to the desert because of the guns in it. Whatever San Salvacion does next, it will do as a country at war.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER; the exact day and San Salvacion's response are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Liberation
lines: Liberation

fields.text:
San Salvacion was liberated in the summer of 2005. The occupier's columns withdrew from the towns they had held for two years, the guns in the desert were silent, and the government returned to a capital that had learned to manage without it. People came out into the streets, not to cheer, at first, but to look: at each other, at the damage, at the soldiers of the coalition who had come so far to reach them.

Liberation has its own disorder. Officials who stayed under occupation and kept the quiet ministries running meet officials who governed the free districts and officials who fled abroad. Each has a record, and each record says something different about the others. Collaborators, real and alleged, are denounced in the squares. Families look for relatives who were displaced by the fighting, and the count of the displaced is longer than anyone wanted to believe.

The government's first act is to read the ledgers. The ledger of the occupation lists requisitions, arrests and debts. The host's ledger lists everything San Salvacion gave the battery and everything it was promised in return. The national budget, published every year under the administration or the assembly or the councils, has not been published for two. Somebody has to decide what the republic owes, and to whom.

The country that comes out of the war is not the country that went into it. It has governed itself in pieces. It must now decide how to govern itself whole.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 07.10 (San Salvacion liberated); the reconstruction of government is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Desert after the Guns
lines: The Desert after the Guns

fields.text:
The battery in the desert was built for one crisis and fought over in another. Where the war followed its historical course, ISAF destroyed it in April 2005, and seven of its eight great batteries lie broken in the sand. Where the war took another course, or never came, the guns still stand, silent, their foreign crews gone or going. Either way, the site belongs to San Salvacion again, and San Salvacion must decide what it is.

The host district has opinions. Some of its people want the site fenced and closed for ever: a grave for those who died there and a warning to anyone who might want to build something like it again. Others point to the roads, the power lines and the water works that the battery left behind, and ask why a district that went without them for a century should leave them to rust in the name of remembrance.

The survey teams have opinions too. The site is dangerous: unexploded munitions, damaged power systems, ground nobody wants to test. Whatever the government decides, the first years will be spent making the desert safe, and the decision will shape where the surveyors start.

Above the desert, the sky is empty again. The country that hosted the guns has to decide how to live without them.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2005 / 04.02, and Super Weapons, Stonehenge (seven of eight batteries destroyed, where the war follows that course); the site's future is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Who Signs for Amber?
lines: Who Signs for Amber?

fields.text:
In Amber the government is a signature. For as long as anyone can remember, the cabinet has governed by contract: it signs for roads, for rolling stock, for grain, for the maintenance of yards it does not own, and it answers for those signatures to nobody but itself. The arrangement has made Amber rich by the standards of its neighbours and has never once asked its citizens what they thought of it.

In the first weeks of 1991 three groups asked anyway. The largest contract holders, whose firms built most of what the cabinet signed for, proposed a Chartered Development Board: a government of the people who actually build things, answerable to the contracts they sign. The freight unions, whose members moved everything the contractors built, proposed a compact: they would keep Amber moving if the state guaranteed their wages, their safety and a vote. And a league of nationalists, noisy and growing, said that Amber had sold itself one contract at a time to foreign capitals and demanded that every foreign clause be struck out.

The cabinet's answer was to keep signing. It had delivered growth without elections and without a scandal anyone could prove. It saw no reason to hand the pen to people who would use it to sign for themselves. Yet its ministers noticed that the three movements were drawing crowds, and that the crowds were not all asking for the same thing.

Someone will hold the pen when the crisis years come. Amber must decide whose hand it trusts.

fields.text: The Board Publishes Its Schedule
lines: The Board Publishes Its Schedule

fields.text:
The Chartered Development Board took office in a hired conference hall, because its members agreed that the old cabinet rooms were too small for a government that intended to build things. Twenty-one seats were filled: fourteen by the largest contract holders in proportion to the value of their public work, five by regional delegates and two by the freight unions, who did not come. The chair of the Board was elected on the first ballot by the contractors, and the regional delegates abstained.

The Board's first act was to publish a schedule. It ran to five years and four hundred pages, and it allocated every yard, road and depot in Amber to a programme of work. Nothing outside the schedule would be built, and nothing inside it would be delayed. It was, the Board explained, a manifesto that could be audited: a promise written in tonnes, kilometres and completion dates rather than slogans.

Amber's citizens found that they had a government that knew exactly what it wanted to do, and that they had very little say in it. The schedule was efficient and largely sensible. It favoured the regions where the contractors already worked and the projects they already knew how to deliver. The freight unions called it a timetable for profit. The Sovereign Contracts League called it the old cabinet in new clothes, with the foreign clauses still inside.

The Board does not mind criticism, so long as the schedule is met. It intends to be judged on its deliveries, and its first deliveries are due within the year.

fields.text: The Compact Takes the Cabinet
lines: The Compact Takes the Cabinet

fields.text:
The Labour Compact Cabinet was sworn in at the central freight yard, on a platform built from railway sleepers, in front of several thousand rail crews, dockers and warehouse staff who had stopped work for the afternoon and would make it up on Sunday. The compact's terms were read aloud before the oath: a wage floor, a national safety code, an elected chamber, and a freight workers' veto over any law that would break a strike.

The cabinet's ministers were union officials, transport engineers and two former contract managers who had changed sides. They had never governed anything larger than a pension fund. They knew, however, exactly how Amber moved, because they had moved it, and their first decisions were about the yards: rest periods, inspections and the right to stop work that would kill someone.

The contractors were alarmed and said so. A safety code would slow the freight; a wage floor would raise the price of every contract; an elected chamber would be full of people who had never signed anything. Several firms threatened to move their work abroad. The cabinet replied that the yards, the rails and the people who worked them would stay in Amber, and that the firms were welcome to take their offices wherever they liked.

Freight moves more slowly now, and fewer people die moving it. Whether Amber can afford that trade will be decided by the first election.

Provisional gameplay: no official source covers Amber; its politics, treaty role and policies are authored for this mod.

would make it up on Sunday. The compact's terms were read aloud before the
oath: a wage floor, a national safety code, an elected chamber, and a freight
workers' veto over any law that would break a strike.
The cabinet's ministers were union officials, transport engineers and two
former contract managers who had changed sides. They had never governed
anything larger than a pension fund. They knew, however, exactly how Amber
moved, because they had moved it, and their first decisions were about the
yards: rest periods, inspections and the right to stop work that would kill
someone.
The contractors were alarmed and said so. A safety code would slow the freight;
a wage floor would raise the price of every contract; an elected chamber would
be full of people who had never signed anything. Several firms threatened to
move their work abroad. The cabinet replied that the yards, the rails and the
people who worked them would stay in Amber, and that the firms were
welcome to take their offices wherever they liked.
Freight moves more slowly now, and fewer people die moving it. Whether
Amber can afford that trade will be decided by the first election.

fields.text: The League in the Ministries
lines: The League in the Ministries

fields.text:
The Sovereign Contracts League did not win an election, because there was none. It won the streets, then the newspapers, then the loyalty of enough officials that the old cabinet found its orders unanswered. When the cabinet resigned, the League's directorate moved into the ministries the same evening and hung its banners from the windows: long lists of every foreign clause in Amber's public contracts, each one marked for renegotiation.

The lists were accurate. Amber had signed contracts that gave foreign firms first claim on its freight in an emergency, that priced its grain in foreign currency and that allowed foreign inspectors into its yards. The League's conclusions were another matter. It promised that every foreign clause would be struck out and every bargain rewritten on Amber's terms, and it promised that the rewriting would cost nothing, because foreigners needed Amber more than Amber needed them.

The directorate's first letters went out within a week. Foreign partners were invited to sign new terms; partners who refused were sued, delayed or expelled. The contractors who had built Amber's prosperity were given deadlines and told that their loyalty would be remembered. The press was given instructions, and the newspapers that had made the League's name were the first to receive them.

Amber is now governed by people who believe it has been cheated, and they are partly right. Whether they can renegotiate the world without breaking the country remains to be seen.

fields.text: The Cabinet's Promise
lines: The Cabinet's Promise

fields.text:
The contracting cabinet renewed its own mandate with a promise rather than a vote. Every public contract would be published, the cabinet announced: large or small, foreign or domestic, completed or in dispute. Every bargain would be explained in plain language, with its cost, its beneficiary and the minister who signed it. The cabinet asked for nothing in return except time.

Publication proved harder than promising. The ministries held contracts in filing cabinets, in safes, in the private papers of retired officials and in the memories of clerks who had died. Some contracts had been signed twice, by different ministers, for the same work. Some had never been signed at all and had been honoured anyway, on the strength of a handshake and a dinner. The cabinet's audit office began to count them and discovered that nobody knew how many there were.

The movements that had wanted to replace the cabinet watched the audit closely. The Chartered Board movement found its own members' contracts on the list and argued for discretion. The freight unions found clauses that allowed contractors to cut safety inspections in a hurry and demanded that they be printed first. The League read every foreign clause aloud at its rallies, and the crowds grew.

The cabinet has made a promise it cannot quickly keep. If it keeps it slowly and honestly, Amber may come to trust a government it never chose.

fields.text: A Register of Usean Contracts
lines: A Register of Usean Contracts

fields.text:
Amber's firms hold contracts in half the capitals of Usea. They build roads in one country, run freight in another and maintain rolling stock for a third. Until 1991 nobody in Amber's government had tried to list them all. The register, when the trade ministry began compiling it, turned out to be the most important document the country had ever produced, because it showed what Amber had promised abroad and therefore what it could still promise at home.

The first draft listed three hundred contracts. The second draft, after the ministry asked the firms directly, listed eleven hundred. Many committed Amber's freight capacity to foreign clients for years ahead. Some committed it in an emergency, on terms that nobody in the cabinet had read. A few committed the same wagons to different clients on the same dates, and the firms involved explained that the clients would never all need them at once.

The register raised two questions. The first was practical: how much freight could Amber move for itself, once its foreign obligations were met? The second was political: who had authorised these obligations, and on whose behalf? The freight yards survey would answer the first. The treaty office would begin to answer the second, by reading every treaty Amber had signed and marking every clause that put its trains at someone else's disposal.

A country that sells its capacity must know how much it has sold. Amber is about to find out.

fields.text: Contracts after the Warning
lines: Contracts after the Warning

fields.text:
When Central Usea announced on the twentieth of April 1996 that the asteroid Ulysses would strike the Earth, Amber's freight offices received their first telephone calls before the cabinet had met. Foreign clients wanted guarantees. If the fragments came, would their contracted wagons still run? Would Amber honour its emergency clauses, or would it keep its trains at home? The clerks who answered the telephones did not know, and said so.

The yards at home asked the opposite question. If Amber's trains were needed for relief, whose relief would come first: the foreign clients who had paid in advance, or the Amber districts that had paid nothing but would need the trains most? The register of Usean contracts suddenly mattered more than any document in the country, because it showed exactly how much of Amber's freight had already been promised to someone else's emergency.

International relief was being discussed in every capital. A consortium was forming to coordinate the response, and Amber was invited to join as its freight and contracting house. Membership would give Amber a voice in where relief went. It would also bind Amber's trains to the consortium's priorities, which might not be Amber's own. The alternative was to remain an independent contractor, selling freight to whoever needed it on Amber's terms.

The asteroid has turned every freight contract into an emergency contract. Amber must decide whose emergency it will serve first.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20; Amber's response is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Contracts in the Coup Summer
lines: Contracts in the Coup Summer

fields.text:
On the thirtieth of May 1997 a coup broke out across Usea, and by the next morning Amber's lawyers were working through the night. Contracts signed with governments that had been overthrown overnight were suddenly contracts with nobody. Payments due from ministries that no longer existed were suddenly debts without a debtor. One freight consignment was halfway across a border when the government at its destination changed twice.

Unified Command defeated the coup, and within weeks most of the governments that had fallen were restored. The contracts were not so easily restored. Some coup governments had signed new orders in their few days of power, and the restored governments refused to honour them. Some of Amber's firms had accepted payment from the coup governments and now faced claims from their successors. The register of Usean contracts, so carefully compiled, had developed a new column: valid, disputed, void.

Through it all the trains kept running. Amber's freight crews had learned long ago that a train in motion is easier to protect than a train in a siding, and they kept moving consignments whose destinations were uncertain until someone told them otherwise. Nobody did, and most of the consignments arrived. The crews were thanked in the cabinet's statement, in the last paragraph.

The coup has taught Amber that a contract is only as stable as the government that signed it. The question is what Amber does with the lesson.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1997 / 05.30; Amber's contracts are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Every Government Wants the Same Trains
lines: Every Government Wants the Same Trains

fields.text:
On the eighth of July 1999 Ulysses broke apart over the Earth, and the fragments fell across Usea. Amber's yards worked through the night under orders written years before. The relief rail plan had named the trains that would run, and most of them ran, crewed by people who had rehearsed the timetable for three years and hoped never to use it.

By noon the telephones were ringing in every freight office. The consortium wanted trains wherever its relief plans pointed. Foreign clients wanted their contracted wagons. Amber's own districts, crowded with people who had fled from elsewhere, wanted everything. The relief plan had assumed that Amber would decide how its capacity was used. Within hours it was clear that every government in Usea was asking for the same trains at the same time, and that Amber had fewer trains than it had promised.

The capacity board met in the basement of the transport ministry. It could open the yards to everyone, moving relief in the order requests arrived and accepting that Amber's own districts would wait their turn. Or it could ration capacity by a published formula: domestic need first, contracts second, appeals third. The first would make Amber the hero of the relief effort; the second would make it the protector of its own people.

The trains are waiting at the yards. Whichever answer the board gives, some of the people asking will be refused.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08; Amber's relief is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Refugees on the Freight Lines
lines: Refugees on the Freight Lines

fields.text:
On the twenty-first of April 2000 Erusea closed its border to refugees, and many of the displaced of the fragment year turned toward Amber instead. They rode Amber's freight trains: on wagon roofs, in empty boxcars, on the couplings between cars. The freight crews did not stop them. Many of the crews had carried refugees before, unofficially, on the relief trains of the fragment year.

The yards became the first place the refugees stopped. Families camped in sidings, in warehouses and in the shelters built for the impact. They washed at the yard taps, cooked on the yard braziers and asked the yard foremen for work. Some of the foremen hired them, because the yards were short of labour after the fragments, and the refugees worked hard for very little.

The unions objected. A refugee who worked for half wages undercut every member of the compact or the old agreements, and the freight workers had fought too long for their wages to watch them fall. The contractors welcomed the labour and asked the government to regularise it. The League, where it had influence, demanded that the refugees be sent onward in sealed trains, fed, treated and gone.

The government must decide whether the refugees on the freight lines are workers, guests or passengers. The yards cannot hold them for long without an answer.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2000 / 04.21; Amber's refugee policy is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: War Comes to the Yards
lines: War Comes to the Yards

fields.text:
In the summer of 2003 Erusea invaded San Salvacion and seized Stonehenge, and the war reached every partner of Central Usea. In Amber it arrived as a telephone call from the transport ministry to every yard foreman in the country: dim the lights, hood the signals, prepare the shelters. The yards that had moved relief for four years were now targets, because the coalition would need them to move everything else.

The first raids came within weeks. They were small and inaccurate, and they taught Amber what the next raids would be like. A junction burned for two days. A train of empty wagons was destroyed in a siding. The crews learned to shunt in the dark, to repair track by night and to sleep in the shelters at the junctions. Accidents rose for a month and then fell, as people learned how to work in a war.

The cabinet had to decide what Amber's freight was for. The coalition wanted trains; Amber's towns wanted food. The development programme could be converted to war production under contract, with profits capped and deliveries guaranteed. Or a protected share of freight and industry could be kept for civilian life, giving the coalition less and keeping Amber's towns fed and calm.

The war has come to the yards. Amber's crews have kept the trains running through the fragments, and they intend to keep them running through this.

fields.text: The Yards after the War
lines: The Yards after the War

fields.text:
The crisis years are over. The warning, the fragments, the refugees and, for most of Usea, the war: Amber has carried all of them on its freight lines, and its yards show it. Some are patched, some are improvised and a few are ruins, and all of them are working. Crews who learned to repair track by night now repair it by day, and the shelters at the junctions are being turned into storerooms.

The question now is what to rebuild. The old yards could be rebuilt to the old plans by the old firms, quickly and familiarly, leaving every old bottleneck where it was. Or the yards could be rebuilt as a hub for the continent's reconstruction: larger, more open and designed to carry the freight that would rebuild Usea's cities. The first would serve Amber. The second would serve everyone, and would make Amber indispensable, which is not the same thing as loved.

The contractors, the freight unions and whatever remains of the League each have their own answer. The contractors want the work, and the larger the better. The unions want the jobs, and the safety code that protects them. The League's survivors want to know who will own the new yards and whose clauses will govern them.

Amber has always been a country of bargains. The bargain it strikes now will shape its next generation.

fields.text: The Reserve Question
lines: The Reserve Question

fields.text:
Ugellas does not keep its reserve in one place. It keeps it everywhere: in depots behind town halls, in tunnels under farms, in warehouses whose custodians are schoolteachers and grocers and retired sergeants. The habit is older than anyone can explain. It has made the country hard to surprise and impossible to summarise, and it has given the reserve officers who manage the depots a knowledge of the republic that no ministry can match.

In 1991 the reserve officers began to ask questions about the government. A circle of them, meeting in the evenings in a depot office, argued that a dispersed country needed a government that thought like a dispersed army: decentralised, disciplined, always ready to move, with every office holding a deputy somewhere else. They wrote their argument down and circulated it, and it was read in more depots than the government had expected.

The towns that hosted the depots had questions of their own. They had housed the reserve for decades, at a fee nobody had revised, and they wanted the reserve's money spent locally and its officers answerable locally. They formed a league, and the league asked for a federal parliament in which every town would have a seat and the capital would coordinate rather than command.

The national administration had kept the depots stocked and the borders quiet. It intended to continue, and it asked the reserve officers and the towns to be patient. Patience, in Ugellas, has always been a reserve too.

fields.text: The Council Disperses the State
lines: The Council Disperses the State

fields.text:
The Reserve Council took office without a parade. Its members arrived at the old ministries in plain cars, signed the transfer documents and left the same afternoon, each to a different town. By the end of the week the Council's first order was in force: every ministry would be dispersed, every office would hold a deputy somewhere else, and every decision would be taken where it would be carried out.

Government in Ugellas became something that happened everywhere at once. The ministry of finance moved into a depot on a hillside, the ministry of health into a school, the ministry of the interior into three separate town halls that took turns being its headquarters. Officials commuted between offices that were deliberately far apart. Letters took longer to arrive, decisions took longer to coordinate, and yet the country found itself governed by people who could see what they were governing.

The towns were divided. Some welcomed the ministries and the salaries that came with them. Others resented officials who arrived with requisition orders and left with the town's best building. The municipal league, which had wanted a federal parliament, found itself governed by a council it had not elected and could not petition, because the Council had no single address.

The Council does not believe in capitals. It believes that a country that cannot be decapitated cannot be conquered. Whether it can be governed that way is the experiment.

fields.text: The Towns Hold the Purse
lines: The Towns Hold the Purse

fields.text:
The first federal parliament of Ugellas met in the largest depot in the country, because no other building had room for a delegate from every town. They sat on folding chairs between stacked crates of tinned food and blankets, and the chamber's acoustics were terrible. The parliament elected a federal cabinet on the second day and gave it a single instruction: coordinate, do not command.

The federal charter gave each town a seat, each region a budget and the capital a telephone. The cabinet discovered that the telephone was the most important instrument of government it had. It spent its days calling towns: asking, persuading, reminding, apologising. Decisions that the old administration had taken in an afternoon now took a month, because every town had to agree or at least be seen to have been consulted.

The reserve officers were not pleased. The depots were now governed by the towns that hosted them, and some towns had ideas about what a depot should hold that did not match the reserve's lists. The circle of reserve officers, which had argued for a Reserve Council, now argued for discipline, and its members found that discipline was hard to impose on a parliament of grocers and schoolteachers.

Ugellas has a government that answers to its towns. The towns are learning that answering is not the same as agreeing.

fields.text: The Administration Renews Its Lease
lines: The Administration Renews Its Lease

fields.text:
The national administration of Ugellas renewed its mandate the way it renewed a depot lease. It conducted an inventory, held a review and signed a document. The inventory counted everything the administration governed: depots, roads, towns, people and the custodians who held the keys. The review found that the administration had governed adequately, which was what it had always found. The document was signed by the senior officials of every ministry and published without comment.

Nobody voted, and nobody was surprised. The reserve officers who had argued for a Reserve Council read the inventory and found their own depots listed accurately, which was a kind of compliment. The towns that had formed a municipal league read the review and noted that it said nothing about the fees they were paid to host the depots. Their delegates wrote to the administration, and the administration replied that the fees would be reviewed in due course.

The administration's strength is that it knows its country. Its weakness is that it knows it as an inventory: a list of things to be counted and kept, rather than a set of people with opinions. It has kept Ugellas stocked, quiet and ready for decades. It has never had to persuade anyone of anything.

The lease has been renewed. Whether the tenants accept it will depend on what the administration does with the next inventory.

fields.text: Depots No Map Shows
lines: Depots No Map Shows

fields.text:
The census of the depots began with the official list, which named four hundred sites. It ended eighteen months later with a list of eleven hundred. The census teams found depots in barns, in churches, in a disused railway tunnel and in the cellar of a hotel whose owner had been paid a storage fee for thirty years without ever being told what was in it. Most of the depots held something useful. Some held things nobody could identify.

Every depot was assigned a custodian and a deputy who lived somewhere else. A depot without a custodian, the census report concluded, was a rumour, not a reserve. Custodians were schoolteachers, farmers, shopkeepers and retired soldiers; they were paid a modest fee, given a key and a list, and told to check the list against the contents twice a year. Many of them had been doing this informally for decades and were pleased to be asked officially.

The census also raised a question about neighbours. Several neighbouring governments had heard about Ugellas's depots and asked whether they could store their own emergency stocks in them. Storage was cheap to offer and expensive to honour: a depot holding a neighbour's grain could not hold Ugellas's own, and a custodian holding a neighbour's key might one day have to choose whom to open the door for.

Ugellas now knows what it has. It must decide whom it will share it with.

fields.text: Can We Store People?
lines: Can We Store People?

fields.text:
When Central Usea announced on the twentieth of April 1996 that the asteroid Ulysses would strike the Earth, Ugellas's custodians received a circular from the national reserve office. It asked them to inventory their depots again, this time with a new column: could the depot hold people? A cellar that stored grain might shelter a family. A tunnel that stored fuel might shelter a village, if the fuel were moved somewhere else.

The neighbours who stored grain in Ugellas's depots telephoned the same week. Their governments had read the same announcement and done the same arithmetic. If the fragments came, where would their people shelter? Ugellas had more underground space than most countries its size, and its neighbours wanted to know whether a storage agreement for grain could become a storage agreement for people. Nobody had ever drafted such an agreement, and the lawyers were not sure it was possible.

The government faced a choice it had avoided for years. It could sign a Usean reserve pact, sharing its depots, its inventories and its obligation to open them with its neighbours. Its reserve would become a regional reserve, and its custodians might one day open the door to people who were not Ugellan. Or it could keep a national reserve only, selling neighbours what they needed but pledging the depots to nobody else's emergency.

The asteroid will not fall on borders. Ugellas must decide whether its depots will.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20; Ugellas's preparations are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Who Holds the Keys?
lines: Who Holds the Keys?

fields.text:
On the thirtieth of May 1997 a coup broke out across Usea. In Ugellas it arrived as a question at the gate of a depot. Shortly after midnight a lorry pulled up outside a depot in the interior, and an officer with a rifle and an order the custodian did not recognise demanded the keys. The custodian, a retired schoolteacher, telephoned the deputy, who telephoned the reserve office, which telephoned the ministry, which did not answer.

The custodian refused. The custodian told the officer that the depot would open for the person named on the list and for nobody else, and that the officer was welcome to wait until morning, when the reserve office could confirm the order. The officer waited. By morning the coup in Ugellas had collapsed, the officer had been recalled, and the custodian had become the most famous schoolteacher in the country.

Unified Command defeated the coup across Usea within days. In Ugellas the coup had never really begun, because nobody could find the keys. Officers who had joined it discovered that the depots they meant to seize were held by thousands of custodians who answered to lists rather than orders, and that a dispersed reserve could not be taken by a single telephone call.

The coup has shown Ugellas what its depots are worth. It has also shown that the keys are held by civilians, and the government must decide whether that is a weakness or a strength.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1997 / 05.30; events in Ugellas are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: A Battery in Someone Else's Desert
lines: A Battery in Someone Else's Desert

fields.text:
On the nineteenth of June 1998 Stonehenge was completed in San Salvacion's desert. Eight railguns now stood ready to destroy the fragments of Ulysses before they reached the ground, and in Ugellas's cabinet room a minister asked the question several colleagues had been thinking. If the battery could stop the fragments, why was Ugellas spending so much on depots, shelters and custodians?

The custodians answered before the cabinet did. Their association published a letter in every newspaper, signed by more than a thousand of them. A battery, they wrote, could shoot at a fragment; it could not promise to hit every one. A battery in someone else's desert would protect someone else's country first. And a battery could not feed a family whose water works had been destroyed, house a village whose roofs had fallen in, or carry the injured to a hospital. The depots could.

The reserve office added its own arithmetic. The battery would reduce the risk; it would not remove it. The depots cost a fraction of what a single railgun had cost, and they would be needed after the fragments fell whatever the battery achieved. Cutting them now would save money for a year and leave Ugellas exposed for a generation.

The battery in the desert has changed the calculation. Ugellas must decide whether it has changed the answer.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1998 / 06.19 (Stonehenge completed); Ugellas's reserve policy is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Dispersal Night
lines: The Dispersal Night

fields.text:
On the eighth of July 1999 Ulysses broke apart over the Earth. In Ugellas the sirens sounded an hour before the first fragments were visible, and families across the country walked to their assigned depots by torchlight. Each family had a card naming its depot; each depot had a list naming its families. The custodians stood at the gates with their lists and their torches and checked names as people came in.

Most of the lists were true. Families arrived at depots that had room for them, with blankets and water and a custodian who knew where everything was. Some lists were not: a depot built for forty held ninety, a tunnel listed as dry had flooded in the spring, a custodian had died and the deputy had moved away. The mobility columns spent the night carrying families from depots that were too full to depots that were not.

By morning the custodians knew what their own gates had seen and little else; the radio carried reports from across Usea, few of them confirmed. In the morning the custodians opened the depots and began to distribute what was in them. The question of how much to distribute was not on any list. The reserve was large, but it was not endless, and nobody knew whether this was the only crisis or the first.

The night is over. The depots are open. Ugellas must decide how much of its reserve to spend now, and how much to keep.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1999 / 07.08; Ugellas's relief is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Refugees at the Depots
lines: Refugees at the Depots

fields.text:
On the twenty-first of April 2000 Erusea closed its border to refugees, and some of those turned back found their way to Ugellas. They came to the depots, because the depots were where the food was and because the stories of the dispersal night had travelled. Custodians found families camped outside their gates, asking for bread, blankets and a place to sleep.

The custodians had lists, and the refugees were not on them. Some custodians opened the gates anyway, because the depots held food and the families outside were hungry. Others telephoned the reserve office and asked what to do, and the reserve office telephoned the ministry, which convened a committee. By the time the committee met, several depots had become camps, and several camps were becoming villages.

The government considered two answers. It could let the refugees settle around the depots, building villages where there had been only warehouses, and accept that Ugellas would grow by the size of a town. Or it could feed and treat the refugees and carry them onward in the mobility columns to wherever they were expected, keeping Ugellas a road rather than a destination.

The custodians are waiting for instructions. In the meantime they are doing what custodians always do: counting, feeding and keeping the gates.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2000 / 04.21; Ugellas's refugee policy is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Reserves Are Called
lines: The Reserves Are Called

fields.text:
In the summer of 2003 Erusea invaded San Salvacion and seized Stonehenge, and Central Usea's partners found themselves at war. In Ugellas the mobilisation notices went out by post and by radio. Reservists were to report to their depots, the same depots they had guarded, stocked and inventoried for a decade. Many of them reported within the day, still wearing the clothes they had been working in.

The depots that had held grain and blankets for the fragment years now held shells and fuel for the war. Coalition forces moving to the front asked to use them, and the custodians who had stored relief for their neighbours now stored munitions for the coalition. The command posts were dispersed across the country, so that no single raid could silence them. Orders arrived late, but they arrived.

Ugellas had prepared for a crisis, not for a war, and the difference was painful. The depots were scattered and small; the army needed large, concentrated stocks close to the front. The mobility columns knew the roads; they did not know how to move under air attack. The government had to decide whether to defend the depots where they stood, keeping the reserve at home, or to empty them forward to the coalition's front.

The reserve has been called. Ugellas must decide where its reserve will fight.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 2003 / SUMMER (Erusea invades San Salvacion); Ugellas's wartime exposure is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Depots after the War
lines: The Depots after the War

fields.text:
The crisis years are over. The warning, the fragments, the refugees and, for most of Usea, the war: Ugellas has met each of them from its depots, and its depots show the cost. Some are empty, their stocks spent on the dispersal night or sent forward to the coalition. Some are damaged, their tunnels cracked and their roofs fallen. Some are full of things nobody needs any more: munitions for a war that has ended, blankets for refugees who have gone home.

The country must now decide what a reserve is for in peacetime. The reserve officers want the depots restocked for the next war or the next crisis, and they point out that every crisis Ugellas has faced arrived without notice. The towns want the depots handed over for schools, clinics and workshops, and they point out that the depots were paid for by their taxes and housed in their buildings for decades.

The custodians, as always, want to know what will be on their lists. Many of them have held their keys for twenty years. They have opened their gates for families, refugees and soldiers, and they have closed them against officers with rifles. They would like to know whether they are still needed.

Ugellas survived the crisis years by being everywhere at once. It must now decide whether to stay that way.

fields.text: Who Inspects the Government?
lines: Who Inspects the Government?

fields.text:
Delarus is a country of inspectors. It inspects its accounts, its requisitions, its contracts and its promises; it inspects its shelters, its stores and its roads; it keeps dockets on everything the state has undertaken and closes them only when the work is done. Its inspectors are proud, poorly paid and very hard to bribe. In 1991 a group of them asked a question that had never been asked in public: who inspects the government itself?

The senior inspectors had an answer ready. The government should be answerable to the same rules it enforced: published accounts, an independent audit office and an elected chamber to read the audits. They wrote an Inspectors' Charter and read it aloud at their own congress, to applause that surprised even them. The charter was not radical by the standards of other countries. In Delarus, where the government had always inspected others and never been inspected, it was a revolution on paper.

The senior commanders had a different answer. Inspection, they argued, had become obstruction. Every requisition was delayed by a docket, every order by an audit, every plan by an inquiry. A small country surrounded by larger ones could not afford to govern by committee. They proposed a Command Council that would govern by order and inspect afterwards, if at all.

The present government had balanced the inspectors against the commanders for years, and it intended to go on doing so. Both sides were now asking it to stop balancing and choose.

Provisional gameplay: no official source covers Delarus; its politics, treaty role and policies are authored for this mod.

fields.text: The Audit Office Audits Its Makers
lines: The Audit Office Audits Its Makers

fields.text:
The Inspectorate Cabinet took office under the Inspectors' Charter and called elections for a chamber within six months. Its first act was to make the audit office independent: the office's director could no longer be dismissed by any minister, its budget was fixed by law, and its reports would be published in full. Its second act was to ask the audit office to audit the cabinet.

The audit was published a year later, and it was thorough. It found that the old government had kept accounts nobody could reconcile, that the commanders had signed requisitions nobody had approved, and that the Inspectorate's own movement had accepted donations it had not declared. Three ministers resigned within the week. One of them had been a senior inspector and a signatory of the charter.

Delarus discovered that it had a government that could be embarrassed, and that liked it. The newspapers printed the audits in full, and people read them on the trams. The commanders complained that every plan now took a year to approve, and they were partly right: planning was slower, and the army's officers spent more time with auditors than with their units. fields.text: Orders without Appeal
lines: Orders without Appeal

fields.text:
The Command Council took office on a weekday morning and suspended the old inspection regime by noon. Audit offices were placed under the Council's directorates. Dockets were closed, whether the work they recorded was finished or not. Inspectors were reassigned to the directorates as clerks, and many of them resigned rather than serve. The Council published its standing orders the next day: numbered, clear and binding, with no procedure for appeal.

Orders were faster now. A requisition that had taken a month to approve took an afternoon. A road that had waited three years for an inquiry was begun within a week. The army's officers, freed from the auditors, spent their time with their units, and the army improved. The Council's supporters pointed to all of this and asked whether the old inspections had ever achieved as much.

The Council's critics pointed to what could no longer be seen. Nobody outside the Council read its orders before they were carried out, and nobody inside it was required to explain them afterwards. The directorates spent money without publishing accounts. Contracts went to firms whose owners had served under the Council's members. The newspapers that reported this were warned, then closed.

Delarus has a government that can act quickly. It no longer has a government that can be inspected, and the inspectors, many of them now unemployed, are keeping their own dockets.

fields.text: Inspected and Commanding
lines: Inspected and Commanding

fields.text:
The present government renewed its mandate without new powers and without renouncing any. It promised to be inspected and to command, and to say in each case which it was doing. The promise was written into a short statement and read in the chamber of the old council of state, which had no legislative power but a good public gallery. The gallery was full of inspectors and commanders, and both groups listened for the clause that favoured them.

There was no such clause. The government's statement divided its business into two columns. Matters of command, including defence, emergency requisitions and the army's internal organisation, would be decided by order and reviewed afterwards. Matters of inspection, including public accounts, contracts and relief, would be decided only after audit. Every new matter would be assigned to a column by the cabinet, and the assignment would be published.

Both sides found reasons to object. The inspectors noted that the cabinet decided which column a matter belonged to, and that it could move anything it liked into the column of command. The commanders noted that relief had been placed among the matters of inspection, and that the next crisis would be a relief crisis. Neither side, however, could claim to have lost, and that was the government's intention.

Delarus is governed by a balance. A balance is only as stable as the hand that holds it, and the hand belongs to the present government.

fields.text: A Register of Foreign Obligations
lines: A Register of Foreign Obligations

fields.text:
Delarus had signed more treaties, guarantees and relief pledges than anyone in its foreign ministry could list from memory. Some had been signed by governments that no longer existed; some promised things Delarus no longer had; a few contradicted each other. In 1991 the foreign ministry asked its docket clerks to compile a register of every obligation Delarus had undertaken abroad and of the official who was answerable for each.

The docket clerks were trained to read treaties the way inspectors read accounts: slowly, precisely and with a strong suspicion that something was missing. They found obligations in treaties, in exchanges of letters, in the minutes of conferences and in the private correspondence of former ministers. They found a guarantee to a neighbour that nobody had remembered for twenty years and a relief pledge that had been honoured twice by different ministries.

The register gave Delarus an idea. If its clerks could read treaties so carefully, perhaps they could read other countries' treaties too. A small country could make itself indispensable by verifying the obligations of larger ones: checking that pledges were kept, that relief reached the people it was meant for, that guarantees were honoured. It would make Delarus useful to everyone, and suspected by some.

Delarus now knows what it has promised. It must decide whether to offer its inspectors to the rest of Usea.

fields.text: A Docket for Every Pledge
lines: A Docket for Every Pledge

fields.text:
When Central Usea announced on the twentieth of April 1996 that the asteroid Ulysses would strike the Earth, the pledges began within days. Governments pledged money, shelters, trains and grain; firms pledged equipment; international bodies pledged coordination. Delarus opened a docket for every pledge it heard of, recording who had promised what, to whom and by when, and then waited to see which pledges would be kept.

The docket clerks worked through the spring and summer. By autumn the dockets filled a room. Some pledges were already being honoured: shelters were being built, grain was being stored, trains were being reserved. Some had been quietly withdrawn. Many had simply never been mentioned again, and nobody had been asked to account for them. The clerks marked these with a single word: pending.

The dockets raised a question Delarus could not answer alone. The relief accounts of the Usean governments would be the largest sums of money spent on any single purpose in the continent's history. If nobody inspected them, some of the money would vanish. Delarus could offer to audit them, sending its inspectors to follow the money and say where it went. Or it could inspect only its own relief and leave foreign accounts to foreign governments.

Every pledge now has a docket. Somebody must decide who reads them.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1996 / 04.20; Delarus's dockets are provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Orders Signed the Night Before
lines: Orders Signed the Night Before

fields.text:
On the thirtieth of May 1997 a coup broke out across Usea. In Delarus it lasted less than a day. A group of officers seized a barracks and a broadcasting station, issued a proclamation and a series of orders, and were arrested the next morning when their own units declined to follow them. Unified Command defeated the coup across the continent within days. In Delarus the coup was over before most people had heard of it.

It left dockets everywhere. The officers had signed orders during their few hours of power: requisitions, transfers, appointments and one order dissolving the audit office. Some of the orders had been carried out before anyone realised who had signed them. Lorries had been requisitioned, officials had been transferred, money had been moved. The coup was over; its paperwork was not.

The government had to decide which of the coup's orders still stood. Some of them were harmless, and reversing them would cost more than leaving them in place. Some were clearly illegal. Some fell in between: a requisition that had delivered supplies to a town that needed them, an appointment of an official who had turned out to be competent. The inspectors wanted every order reviewed; the commanders wanted the matter closed.

Delarus has always believed that a signature creates an obligation. It must now decide what a signature means when the signer had no right to sign.

fields.text: The Battery's Civilian Accounts
lines: The Battery's Civilian Accounts

fields.text:
On the nineteenth of June 1998 Stonehenge was completed in San Salvacion's desert. The battery was an international project led by Central Usea, and its member governments had paid for it. Within a month several of them asked Delarus whether its inspectors could read the project's civilian accounts: the roads, the water, the housing and the services provided to the host district. The military accounts would remain secret. The civilian accounts, the members argued, should be verified by someone who had not written them.

Delarus's inspectors were flattered and cautious. A battery in someone else's desert, operated by someone else's crews, was not a matter for Delarus. The civilian accounts, however, were exactly the kind of thing Delarus was good at: roads that had been paid for and not built, water works that had been built and not paid for, housing allocated to people who did not exist. The inspectors suspected that all three would be found.

The commanders in Delarus's own government had a different worry. If Delarus's inspectors read the battery's accounts, Delarus would be seen as part of the project. If the project became a target, so might its inspectors. Neutrality was not Delarus's tradition, but caution was.

The members are waiting for an answer. Delarus must decide whether its inspectors will travel to the desert.

Official: ACES Chronicle, 1998 / 06.19, and Super Weapons, Stonehenge (an FCU-led international project); Delarus's verification role is provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Checklists Meet the Night
lines: The Checklists Meet the Night

fields.text:
On the eighth of July 1999 Ulysses broke apart over the Earth. In Delarus every relief docket was opened at once. Shelters that had been inspected with a tape measure and a torch filled with families; stores that had been counted against their dockets were opened and issued; relief convoys that had been listed for inspection left their depots and took to the roads.

The inspectors discovered which of their checklists were real. Most were. The shelters held, the stores were full and the convoys knew their routes. Some were not. A shelter that had passed inspection had been repaired with the wrong materials; a store that matched its docket had been filled with the wrong supplies; a convoy listed as ready had no fuel. The gap between the docket and the reality, which the inspectors had published every year, was suddenly a matter of life and death.

The government had to decide how relief would be run in the weeks ahead. Relief officers could be given emergency warrants to requisition what they needed and account for it later, making relief faster and accounts slower. Or every relief issue could be docketed and inspected even now, making relief slower and every sack traceable. The inspectors argued that a crisis was exactly when theft was easiest. The relief officers argued that a crisis was exactly when speed mattered most.

The fragments have fallen. Delarus must decide whether to trust its checklists or its officers.

fields.text: Stay or Move On?
lines: Stay or Move On?

fields.text:
On the twenty-first of April 2000 Erusea closed its border to refugees, and some of those turned back reached Delarus. They were docketed at the border, as everyone in Delarus was docketed: name, origin, family, health, skills and destination. The dockets were thorough, and they all ended with the same blank line. Under the heading destination, the clerks wrote nothing, because nobody had told them what to write.

The docket clerks pressed the question. A docket with a blank line could not be closed, and Delarus did not leave dockets open. Was the refugee to stay or to move on? If to stay, where, and doing what? If to move on, to where, and who would receive them? The interior ministry referred the question to the cabinet, and the cabinet referred it to a committee, and the dockets piled up in the border offices.

Two answers were proposed. Refugees could be allowed to settle in Delarus once they were registered, housed and assigned work, creating the most complete refugee register in Usea and a population that would change the country. Or they could cross Delarus under inspection, with food and care, but not stay, their dockets travelling with them to whatever country would take them.

The clerks are waiting to fill in the blank line. So are the people the dockets describe.

fields.text: The Page Marked War
lines: The Page Marked War

fields.text:
In the summer of 2003 Erusea invaded San Salvacion and seized Stonehenge, and Central Usea's partners found themselves at war. In Delarus the foreign ministry opened its obligations ledger at the page marked war and found it longer than expected. Over the years Delarus had promised the coalition supplies, transit, liaison officers and inspectors, in treaties, letters and conference minutes. Some of the promises had been made by governments that no longer existed, but they were still in the ledger.

The government had to decide which promises it would keep. The commanders wanted all of them honoured at once, by order. The inspectors wanted each one reviewed, docketed and delivered on schedule. The coalition wanted everything immediately and was not interested in the difference. Requisitions began within the week, and so did the disputes: lorries taken from farmers who needed them for the harvest, warehouses taken from firms that had been storing relief.

Requisition tribunals were set up to hear the disputes. They worked quickly, and they gave every owner a receipt that a court would honour. The commanders called them a delay; the inspectors called them the only reason the requisitions were still lawful. Delarus's shelters, inspected for the fragments, were inspected again for the raids, and fewer of them passed.

The war has its own dockets now. Delarus must decide whether to run its war effort by order or by inspection.

fields.text: Open or Sealed
lines: Open or Sealed

fields.text:
The crisis years are over. Delarus holds the most complete records of the war in Usea: requisitions, orders, losses, obligations and the dockets of every refugee who crossed its borders. Its inspectors kept them through the fragments, the refugees and the war, copying everything and storing the copies somewhere else. Now the government must decide what to do with them.

Some want the records opened. A commission could hear anyone who claimed to have been wronged: farmers whose lorries were requisitioned, families who lost relatives, refugees whose dockets were closed without their consent. It would take years and make enemies, but it would leave Delarus with an honest account of what it did. The inspectors who kept the records, many of whom worked through the war at great personal risk, want them read.

Others want the records sealed. The country has been through enough. Opening the records would reopen every quarrel, every grievance and every suspicion, and would set neighbours against each other for a generation. Sealing them for a fixed period would let the country move on, and the records would still be there when the people they describe were no longer alive to be hurt by them.

Delarus has always believed in records. It must now decide whether it believes in reading them.

fields.text: Delarus has offered a defined civil service, with its own administrative cost already paid. Acceptance records a practical relationship and limited recovery work; it is not a request to create another faction, decide the war or commit unlimited capacity. The offer lapses if either participant becomes ineligible. A refusal leaves the sender with a domestic programme to pursue.

fields.text: The Telephone That Everyone Calls
lines: The Telephone That Everyone Calls

fields.text: A district operator has pinned three unofficial numbers beside the official switchboard. They reach the people who can find a water crew, open a shelter or explain why a receiving office is shut. None appears in the national register. Publishing the contact list would make a fragile local arrangement into a public service; keeping it within the rota would leave operators freer to improvise. The choice is who can demand an answer when a familiar voice is no longer there.

fields.text: The Key in the Wrong Office
lines: The Key in the Wrong Office

fields.text: An inspection has found a sound shelter whose key is held by an office that closes before the evening protection rota begins. Everyone involved followed a written instruction. The protection service can fund a joint receiving desk and rebuild institutional capacity, or put dispatchers on an immediate priority footing so the next practical allocation need not wait. Neither course creates more staff; it changes how the existing service uses them.

fields.text: A Forecast on Every Noticeboard
lines: A Forecast on Every Noticeboard

fields.text: The warning has produced notices that disagree in small but important ways. A protection officer asks for practical instruction cards explaining where uncertainty remains. Dispatch staff ask instead for time to revise the movement chain. The first choice strengthens preparation completed before the crisis boundary; the second improves a military and service capability that remains useful afterward. Neither can promise safety simply by printing a confident sentence.

fields.text: The Receiving Office Is Full
lines: The Receiving Office Is Full

fields.text: A neighbouring service asks whether San Salvacion can accept another set of urgent requests. The local receiving desk is already carrying cases that were never assigned a destination. Officials can protect domestic continuity, or prepare a bounded offer to Central Usea with its receiving obligations written in advance. The recipient remains free to refuse. What cannot be offered is capacity that the country has only counted twice.

fields.text: A Desk Returns without Its Files
lines: A Desk Returns without Its Files

fields.text: Recovery has brought an official back to a desk whose surviving files do not match the cases being presented. Some records may be reconstructed; some cannot. An inspected restoration will rebuild local capacity and leave an honest gap in the evidence. A rapid operational restart will give dispatch work precedence and reopen the next review allocation. The service must choose what it can responsibly promise, rather than declare every missing record found.

fields.text: The Network's Ordinary Year
lines: The Network's Ordinary Year

fields.text: The national programme now has a record of what survived, what was refused and what had to be done under external conditions. Its conclusion does not decide the war or erase the settlement. The government can renew an ordinary civil service whose future funded completions support recovery, or retain a bounded readiness record at a continuing public cost. Either choice is an ongoing obligation, not a final gift from the calendar.

fields.text: Two Owners of the Same Timetable
lines: Two Owners of the Same Timetable

fields.text: A workshop's delivery book and a public receiving office both reserve the same morning movement. The workshop insists its slot has been promised for months; the office holds a more recent priority notice. Amber can publish a common record, accepting the public cost of explaining which bargain had to wait, or maintain a restricted operational schedule and concentrate on dispatch capability. The timetable is a development policy before it becomes a relief plan.

fields.text: A Guarantee Is Not an Empty Wagon
lines: A Guarantee Is Not an Empty Wagon

fields.text: A contractor has accepted a service guarantee but has no uncommitted crew to attach to it. Cancelling the whole bargain would destroy useful maintenance work; accepting its paper capacity would mislead the board. A funded inspection can restore administrative capacity and identify what remains deliverable. Alternatively the board can open the next practical allocation immediately and accept a narrower operational settlement.

fields.text: The Reserve in the Fine Print
lines: The Reserve in the Fine Print

fields.text: The international warning has reached suppliers as a new clause in their standing contracts. Some can prepare a genuine civilian reserve if they receive clear instructions before the crisis. Others argue that the existing movement chain must be made more reliable first. The capacity board must choose between a preparation credit earned within the real window and transport coordination that remains useful in later years. It cannot backdate either decision.

lines: A Manifest with No Receiving Signature

Amber can direct its development effort toward domestic services, or prepare a defined offer to Central Usea that carries a smaller administrative burden when it is sent. A funded service slot is still required, and a refused offer must return that slot rather than strand it abroad.

lines: The Contract That Outlived the Emergency

An inspected review restores administrative capacity and clarifies the development record. A faster operational settlement reopens the next review allocation and puts transport work first. Keeping both promises would simply reserve the same capacity again.

lines: The Price of Standing Capacity

The final review follows the settlement that exists, including any constraints on the country. Ministers can renew ordinary service work with continuing recovery value, or protect a readiness record at an ordinary public cost. Neither course creates another transport fleet or an unlimited claim on suppliers.

fields.text: Two Keys and One Depot
lines: Two Keys and One Depot

fields.text: Two offices hold valid instructions to draw on the same small depot. One expects to support a local receiving service; the other has reserved the space for an emergency movement. Ugellas can publish the custody record and accept its continuing public burden, or keep the working list restricted and strengthen operational coordination. The finite slot limit remains in either case. A better form is not another warehouse.

lines: The Unavailable Driver

An inspected roster can rebuild institutional capacity and improve the mobility account. An immediate operational allocation can instead resolve the next practical task without waiting for a further rota. The reserve authority must record which commitment was left unmet.

fields.text: Space Reserved before the Warning
lines: Space Reserved before the Warning

fields.text: The warning has made every unused corner of a depot look like a national reserve. Protection staff want practical instructions that turn some of that space into preparation before the deadline. Dispatchers want to concentrate on the receiving chain and the transport already available. Ugellas can improve one without pretending it has found unlimited storage, drivers or fuel. Work completed afterward will be response rather than earlier preparation.

fields.text: One Slot Offered Twice
lines: One Slot Offered Twice

fields.text: A useful mobility service can be offered abroad only if the reserve authority remains able to account for the work left at home. Officials can protect domestic dispersal, or prepare a bounded offer to Central Usea. Preparing the offer reduces its later institutional burden, but it does not create another service slot or oblige the recipient to accept. Refusal must leave the mobility programme useful.

lines: Receipts from Different Places

Inspection can rebuild local capacity around the surviving evidence. A faster operational restart can instead prioritise movement and reopen the next review allocation. The missing receipt cannot honestly be replaced by a declaration that everything arrived.

A useful national programme is one that can refuse a fifth commitment when only four slots exist. The country can renew ordinary service work whose funded completions aid recovery, or retain a readiness record with its continuing public burden. The choice preserves a limited capability rather than an endless emergency.

An immediate operational allocation instead opens the next task and strengthens coordination. Whichever course is chosen, one office will have to record a refusal.

Existing leadership retains responsibility for either decision.

Neither course can honestly turn every surviving instruction into a completed delivery.

fields.text: The Skully Islands
lines: The Skully Islands

fields.text:
On 31 December 1995, Robert Tyler, commander of the FCU Army Southern District, eliminates a rebel base in the Skully Islands. Unified Command defeats the rebel forces there through the actions of Scarface Squadron (ACES Chronicle, 1995 / 12.31).

The report names the islands and the squadron. It does not name a wider conspiracy, and it does not move the border. The same day, far to the north, other forces attack Avalon Dam. This dispatch does not concern them.

fields.text: Rebellion across Usea
lines: Rebellion across Usea

fields.text:
On 30 May 1997 a rebellion breaks out. A coup d'état is carried out all across Usea (ACES Chronicle, 1997 / 05.30).

Garrisons report officers who will not answer, and radios that have gone quiet. The council does not yet have a list of which commands have turned. Unified Command is already moving.

Provisional gameplay: the strain on administration is a balance effect. No state changes hands.

fields.text: Unified Command
lines: Unified Command

fields.text:
Scarface 1 is in the air. Unified Command asks the council for authority to break the rebellion and then send the emergency staff home.

fields.text: Who Commands the Republic?
lines: Who Commands the Republic?

fields.text: A Mandate Nobody Voted For
lines: A Mandate Nobody Voted For

fields.text:
The National Administration meets in the capital centre with an agenda its members have postponed for years. The emergency orders that suspended elections are due for renewal, and for the first time the ministry lawyers will not countersign them without a recorded cabinet vote. Aemurraq is governed by an office that sits under a democratic banner while the democratic camp itself barely registers in any count of public opinion.

Outside, the country has split almost exactly in two. Half answers to a nationalist movement that fills the squares and promises discipline, pride and an end to government by clerks. The other half belongs to a non-aligned establishment of export boards, senior officials and district notables who care more about stable prices than about any creed. Neither half trusts the Administration, and neither has yet found a lawful way to replace it.

The ministers cannot settle the country's future at one sitting. They can decide how the argument will be conducted: in public, with the press in the gallery and the movement's speakers given airtime on the state radio, or inside the ministries, where the export boards already keep their chairs. Whatever they choose will be read as a signal by both halves of the country, and by every foreign buyer of Aemurraqi oil.

fields.text: Five Districts Report
lines: Five Districts Report

fields.text:
The census teams return from the five districts with trucks full of ledgers and a list of grievances longer than the ledgers. The Capital District holds most of the civilian plants, the only air base and the fuel silo, and complains that it pays most of the taxes. District E, with its arms and civilian plants, calls its single road a scandal. District B points to the logistics centre and asks why its hill roads were laid out for mules.

The harbour district on the coast has the naval base and the yards and wants a road that does not flood every winter. District D is the strangest return of all: the largest district by far, twenty-seven provinces of desert, hill, jungle and plain with a long coastline, and no paved road, no plant and no resource the old surveys ever recorded. Its delegates arrived late because there was no way to arrive early.

The ministers must decide how to present the census. Printed in full, it will start a long quarrel about fairness among the five districts that no ministry can steer. Held inside the ministries, it will quietly shape the budget while every district assumes the worst about the others. Either way, the figures for District D will decide the road budget for the rest of the decade.

fields.text: What the Wells Really Pump
lines: What the Wells Really Pump

fields.text:
The inspectors sent to every well, pipeline and depot have finished, and their figures do not match anyone's. Output from District B, District E and the Capital District is higher than the export boards reported and lower than the ministries assumed. Several pipelines carry no meters at all. The fuel silo in the capital, which the army counts on for its trucks and fighters, is less than half full on most days of the year.

Everyone has an explanation. The boards blame old equipment and honest rounding. The ministries blame the boards. Plant managers in District E say they have been buying fuel back from exporters at foreign prices because the domestic allocation never arrived. The movement's newspapers print the gap between the two sets of figures on their front pages and invite readers to guess where the difference went.

The government now holds the only honest account of the country's oil, and must decide what to do with it. It can use the audit to reopen every export licence, which will take years and enrage the boards, or let the boards correct their own books in exchange for a quiet settlement. The figures will not stay secret either way.

fields.text: A Tanker Overdue
lines: A Tanker Overdue

fields.text:
A tanker loaded at the harbour district misses its reporting call two days out. The convoy desk at the trade ministry assumes the navy is handling it; the navy assumes the harbour police have heard from the owners; the harbour police assume the ship has simply switched off its radio to save power. For two days nobody looks. Then the owners telephone the capital and ask, politely, whether anyone knows where their ship is.

The tanker turns up drifting with engine failure, its crew safe and its cargo intact. The search that found it was organised by merchant masters on the radio rather than by any office of the state. Foreign underwriters raise their premiums on Aemurraqi cargoes the following week, and the masters' association writes an open letter asking which of the three offices is responsible for them at sea.

The new route security service is supposed to answer that question, and this is its first test. The government can publish a full inquiry naming every failure, which will embarrass three ministries at once, or settle quietly with the owners and the underwriters. The masters will judge the new service by the choice, and they talk to every crew in the fleet.
