fields.text: Muster Day in Five Districts
lines: Muster Day in Five Districts

fields.text:
For the first time in years, every volunteer on the army rolls is called to report on a single day. In the Capital District the barracks overflow and the trucks run out of seats. In District B the hill companies arrive early, in good order and short of boots. In District D, where the rolls list hundreds of names, a few dozen men walk in from the interior and ask where everyone else is.

By evening the figures are clear and uncomfortable. The four formations exist, but two of them are far below strength, and the stocks of rifles, trucks and support equipment would not outfit even the men who did report. Officers who had signed paper returns for years avoid each other in the mess. The quartermasters, who always knew, are quietly pleased that someone has finally asked them.

The general staff must report to the government, and the government must decide what the public hears. Publishing the real strength will shake confidence and invite the movement's newspapers to ask who was paid for soldiers who never existed. Reporting the paper strength keeps calm for now and leaves the army as hollow as it was this morning.

fields.text: Prices of a Distant War
lines: Prices of a Distant War

fields.text:
In March 1995 war breaks out around Belka. Aemurraq is no party to it and its frontiers are nowhere near the fighting, yet within days the war is present in every ministry. Oil prices jump on the foreign exchanges. Underwriters add war-risk premiums to routes near the fighting and to any ship whose cargo might be resold. Buyers the export boards have never met begin calling with large orders and few questions.

The arms plants in District E and the capital see overtime for the first time in years. The movement's speakers say the country should take every order it can get, since the belligerents will not thank anyone for staying poor. The establishment worries about foreign memories and about ships being stopped at sea. Several embassies ask, in identical language, what Aemurraq intends to sell and to whom.

The government must answer before the boards answer for it. It can declare at once that Aemurraq takes no side, which costs nothing today and may cost orders tomorrow, or say only that existing contracts will be honoured, which keeps every option open and satisfies nobody abroad. Either statement will be read in capitals that Aemurraq's ministers have rarely visited.

large orders and few questions.

years. The movement's speakers say the country should take every order it can
get, since the belligerents will not thank anyone for staying poor. The
establishment worries about foreign memories and about ships being stopped
at sea. Several embassies ask, in identical language, what Aemurraq intends to
sell and to whom.
The government must answer before the boards answer for it. It can declare at
once that Aemurraq takes no side, which costs nothing today and may cost
orders tomorrow, or say only that existing contracts will be honoured, which
keeps every option open and satisfies nobody abroad. Either statement will be
read in capitals that Aemurraq's ministers have rarely visited.

fields.text: The Asteroid Will Strike
lines: The Asteroid Will Strike

fields.text:
Astronomers warned in December 1994 that the asteroid Ulysses might pass close enough to strike the Earth. In April 1996 the warning becomes an announcement: it will strike, and nations must prepare. Nobody can yet say where the fragments will fall. Aemurraq has a crowded capital, towns that depend on a few wells, a merchant fleet spread across distant routes and no experience of planning for anything this large.

Every ministry discovers a plan that needs money. Engineers want shelters and sealed cisterns under the towns. Radar and observatory specialists want a warning net that can clear a district in hours. The export boards want to know whether their ships should stay in port. The treasury points out that any of these plans costs as much as a decade of road building, and that the roads are not finished.

The public reaction arrives before any plan does. Markets in the capital sell out of water containers, places of worship fill and some families in the harbour district talk of moving inland. The government must decide how to speak about a danger it cannot control: openly and at once, accepting a rush on the markets, or calmly and slowly, accepting that preparation will lag.

Provisional gameplay: date anchors only, ACES Chronicle rows 1994 / 12.10 and 1996 / 04.20; Aemurraqi preparations are gameplay.

fields.text: Queues at the Grain Markets
lines: Queues at the Grain Markets

fields.text:
Three weeks after the government began preparing in public, the markets break. Grain, flour, water containers and fuel cans sell out in the capital by noon each day, and prices for staples double within a fortnight. District towns at the end of long roads run out entirely. Traders who can afford to wait hold back stock, and everyone knows who they are.

The movement blames exporters for shipping grain money abroad. The export boards blame the ministries for frightening the public. Crews from foreign ships in the harbour district buy whatever is left and sail away with it. The district councils, where they exist, send telegrams to the capital that grow shorter and angrier as the week goes on.

The cabinet has two tools and little time. It can fix the price of staples and ration them by household, which needs clerks, inspectors and patience the country has not shown before. Or it can let prices run, import as fast as the ships can carry, and trust that high prices will draw new supply into the country before tempers break in the queues outside the market halls.

fields.text: The Night Ulysses Passed
lines: The Night Ulysses Passed

fields.text:
On 8 July 1999 the asteroid Ulysses passes through the Roche limit of the Earth. In Aemurraq the night is spent listening. Families gather around radios in the capital and the district towns, the warning chain reports every hour whether or not there is anything to report and the shelters, where they exist, hold more people than their designers ever imagined.

Merchant masters on distant routes report by radio what they can see and hear from their bridges, which is mostly rumour relayed from other ships. The route service logs every call. Officials in the capital try to separate what is known from what is feared, and find that the line moves every few minutes. Nobody in the government sleeps, and nobody pretends to.

By morning the country is still standing and still frightened. Whatever has fallen, and wherever it has fallen, the markets, the sea lanes and the insurers will carry the consequences to Aemurraq for years. The government must decide whether to keep its emergency measures in force while the world takes stock, or to stand the districts down and let ordinary life resume.

fields.text: War Comes to Usea
lines: War Comes to Usea

fields.text:
In the summer of 2003 Erusea invades the neutral country of San Salvacion, seizes Stonehenge and begins using its railguns as anti-air batteries. Usea is far from Aemurraq's districts, but Usean ports buy Aemurraqi steel and Usean lanes carry Aemurraqi oil. By the time the ministers meet, insurers have already suspended cover on several routes and doubled it on the rest.

Masters of the merchant fleet refuse Usean charters until someone tells them who will pay if their ships are lost. Buyers on both sides of the war call the export boards with orders larger than anything since the Belkan War, and the boards forward the calls to the cabinet without comment. The movement and the establishment, for once, agree on something: the country should not send soldiers. They agree on nothing else.

The government must set Aemurraq's posture before every ship in the fleet sets its own. Keeping all cargoes away from Usean waters is safe and expensive. Sailing wherever the contracts lead is profitable and dangerous. Every later choice about whom to supply will follow from what the ministers say this week.

fields.text: The Chamber Doors Stay Shut
lines: The Chamber Doors Stay Shut

fields.text:
The chamber of Aquitoria has not sat since the elections of November 1987. Its doors are locked, its benches lie under dust sheets and the Office of the Crown has governed alone through orders renewed each year by the palace lawyers. This year the lawyers have asked, for the first time, that a council of ministers sign the renewal alongside the crown.

Outside the palace the kingdom is split in a way the old orders never anticipated. Half of the country remains loyal to the crown and expects it to go on governing. The other half is divided almost equally between democrats, who want the chamber reopened and a constitution written, and communists, who want the docks and arms halls run by the people who work in them. A small non-aligned remainder wants only lower prices.

The ministers cannot settle the kingdom's future at a single sitting, but they must decide how the question will be handled. They can renew the orders quietly and let the matter rest another year, invite the three camps to argue it in public, or let the petitioners gathered at the palace gate in for a hearing that will certainly not stay polite.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: A Night at the Palace Gate
lines: A Night at the Palace Gate

fields.text:
A week after the gate was opened, the crowd of petitioners has not gone home. Dock workers, tenant farmers from the northern plain and shopkeepers from the capital port camp on the palace square with blankets, lanterns and copies of the 1987 election lists. Their requests range from the price of bread to the abolition of the crown, written on the same sheets of paper.

The palace guard is small and unused to crowds. Its officers ask whether they should clear the square before the night shifts at the arms halls finish and swell the numbers further. Loyalist notables send messages urging firmness. Democratic and communist organisers, who did not call the crowd, are working hard to take credit for it before the other camp can.

The crown office must decide before midnight. It can receive a delegation chosen by the crowd itself, which would make the gathering a precedent every later petitioner will cite, or have the guard clear the square gently and promise written replies to every sheet. Either choice will be retold in every ward of the kingdom by morning, with the details improved at each telling.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Four Provinces Report
lines: Four Provinces Report

fields.text:
The surveyors return from the four provinces with crates of ledgers. The capital port on the western coast holds most of the kingdom's people, its arms halls and civilian plants, its naval berth and one of its two supply nodes. Its wards complain that they pay most of the taxes and receive water only on alternate days each summer.

The northern coastal plain reports tenant farmers paying rents fixed generations ago and drainage ditches nobody has cleared since. The southern plain around the logistics centre is the kingdom's crossroads, with the second supply node and the far end of the railway, and its traders want more of the freight money that passes through. The eastern hills, which touch both Monstrua and Valka, report the fewest people, the poorest schools and the longest stretch of frontier.

Publishing the survey in full will start a quarrel among the provinces that no ministry can steer, because every figure will be read as an insult by somebody. Keeping it inside the ministries will shape the budget quietly while each province assumes the worst of the others. The government must choose before the newspapers obtain a copy of their own.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Six Plants Counted
lines: Six Plants Counted

fields.text:
The census of the kingdom's works is the first in a generation. Inspectors visit the three civilian plants and the three arms halls, count every press and lathe, time every shift and read every maintenance log they can find. They also walk the edges of the industrial ground and confirm what managers have long said: there is no spare land left for a seventh plant.

The findings are mixed. Some lines run well above their rated output because foremen have quietly rebuilt them over the years. Others stand idle for days while parts arrive by sea. Steel from the kingdom's own mines is good, oil is modest and rubber is scarce. The arms halls make rifles and trucks the army can use, though rarely as many as it orders.

The ministers must decide how much of this to share with the owners, the unions and the press. Publishing the census will embarrass managers and give the unions arguments for years. Sharing it only with the owners keeps the peace in the halls and leaves the workers guessing. The plants will run the same tomorrow either way; the politics will not.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Quay Stops Work
lines: The Quay Stops Work

fields.text:
Three days after the convoy register is announced, the stevedores on the capital quay stop work. They are not against the register itself. They object to the clause requiring them to report every cargo they handle, which they read, correctly, as the end of the small private trade that has topped up dock wages for decades.

Ships wait at anchor off the coast and their owners telephone the palace hourly. Shipping agents warn that charters will move to other ports if the quay is not working by the end of the week. The communist organisers, who have members in every gang, insist that the strike belongs to the dockers alone; the loyalist papers insist it was planned in a back room.

The port office can drop the reporting clause and let the register cover ships but not the men who unload them, or keep the clause and offer the gangs a wage rise to replace what they will lose. Either way, the dockers will have learned that the kingdom's trade stops when they stop, and they will not forget the lesson when the next quarrel with the port office comes round.

fields.text: Muster Day for Four Battalions
lines: Muster Day for Four Battalions

fields.text:
Every soldier of the territorial service is called to report on the same morning. The battalions in the capital port fill their barracks squares by eight. The hill battalion arrives on foot from the eastern ridges, short of boots and long on complaints. The trucks, all five hundred and sixty of them on paper, are lined up and counted in the yards of the logistics centre.

The tally taken at dusk is sobering. Both formations exist and both are understrength. Fewer than half of the trucks start on the first attempt. The rifles are sound but the reserve of ammunition would last a week of serious fighting at most. There is no artillery to count and no aircraft to inspect, which spares the general staff two separate embarrassments.

The war ministry drafts two reports. One gives the true count and asks for money; it would shake loyalist confidence and hand the crown's critics an easy headline. The other repeats the figures printed every year since 1987 and asks for nothing. Ministers must decide which report goes to the press and which goes into the safe.

fields.text: Notes from Two Capitals
lines: Notes from Two Capitals

fields.text:
Within a month of each other, envoys from Monstrua and Valka call at the crown office with notes that say much the same thing in very different tones. Each wants to know where Aquitoria stands on frontier patrols, on the exiles who cross the eastern hills and on the freight that passes through the logistics centre. Neither asks directly about the other neighbour; both clearly mean it.

The Monstruan note is short and formal, written by a government whose movement faces no organised rival at home. The Valkan note is longer and friendlier, from a government whose own public is divided almost evenly between a nationalist camp and a non-aligned one. Aquitorian loyalists, democrats and communists each read the two notes and find exactly what they feared.

The crown office must answer both before rumours answer for it. It can send identical replies promising good neighbourliness and nothing more, or answer each in its own register, warmly to Valka and correctly to Monstrua. The replies will be read in both capitals line by line, and kept on file for a long time by clerks who will quote them back whenever a frontier quarrel flares.

fields.text: Should the Kingdom Fly?
lines: Should the Kingdom Fly?

fields.text:
The new air office presents its first paper to the ministers. Aquitoria has no air base, no combat aircraft and a handful of pilots trained abroad. Its research staff studied early fighter designs years ago and filed the reports. Freight companies already ask why air cargo for the kingdom must land somewhere else and travel the last stretch by truck.

The paper sets out the costs plainly. A first runway would take farmland at the edge of the capital port. A radar set and a control tower would cost more than the hangars. Aircraft must be bought abroad, along with spares, fuel and instructors. The army notes that the same money would put every truck back on the road and buy a year of ammunition.

The ministers must decide how the plan is presented. Announced as a matter of national pride, it will draw volunteers and applause and set expectations that a few aircraft cannot meet. Presented as a quiet transport project, it will draw little attention and few recruits. Either way the runway gets built; the question is what the kingdom expects of it.

fields.text: The War Reaches the Freight Market
lines: The War Reaches the Freight Market

fields.text:
War breaks out around Belka on 25 March 1995. Aquitoria has no part in it and no frontier near it, but the war reaches the capital port within days through the freight market. Charter rates double, insurers add war clauses to routes they consider exposed, and buyers the port office has never heard of call asking for fuel, trucks and rifles.

The arms halls receive more enquiries in a week than in the previous year. Loyalist newspapers argue that the kingdom should sell to whoever pays, since nobody will thank it for staying poor. Democrats and communists, for once in agreement, warn that crates with Aquitorian markings will be found on battlefields and remembered. Foreign embassies ask, politely and in nearly identical words, what the kingdom intends.

The crown office must say something before the arms halls decide for it. A declaration of strict neutrality costs nothing today and may cost orders tomorrow. A statement that existing contracts will be honoured keeps every option open and satisfies nobody abroad. Whatever is said now will be quoted back to the kingdom for years, by friends and critics alike.

fields.text: The Announcement Reaches the Quay
lines: The Announcement Reaches the Quay

fields.text:
In December 1994 astronomers warned that the asteroid Ulysses might strike the Earth. In April 1996 the warning becomes an announcement: it will strike, and nations must prepare. Nobody can say where the fragments will fall. In Aquitoria the news arrives on the evening radio, and by morning the queues outside the grain merchants on the quay reach the harbour wall.

Ministries produce plans overnight. Engineers want shelters beneath the capital port. Planners want evacuation routes into the eastern hills. The port office wants to know whether ships should stay at sea or come home. The treasury points out that any of these plans costs more than the kingdom spends on its army in a year, and that the army also has requests.

Before any plan is approved, the government must decide how to speak to a frightened public. It can announce preparations openly and at once, accepting a rush on the markets, or urge calm while the ministries work, accepting that the public will hear rumours before it hears plans. The quay will judge the choice within a day, and the grain merchants will judge it within the hour.

fields.text: A Long Night on the Radio
lines: A Long Night on the Radio

fields.text:
On 8 July 1999 the asteroid Ulysses passes through the Roche limit of the Earth. In Aquitoria nobody sleeps. Families sit beside radios in the dock wards and the hill villages, the port office logs every call from ships at sea and the soldiers guarding the depots at the logistics centre listen to the same bulletins as everyone else.

Rumours move faster than facts. One report places fragments in the sea; another, an hour later, places them on another continent entirely. The port office separates what is known from what is feared and finds the line moving every few minutes. Ministers spend the night in the government offices above the quay, waiting for a telephone call that may never come, and sending clerks down to the harbour every hour for news the radio has not yet carried.

By morning the kingdom is still standing and still frightened. Whatever has fallen, and wherever it fell, the consequences will reach Aquitoria through freight rates, refugees and prices for years. Ministers must choose between holding the depots, curfews and drills in place until the damage abroad is known, and releasing the provinces to work, trade and sleep normally again.

Provisional gameplay: date anchor only, ACES Chronicle row 1999 / 07.08; no Aquitorian damage is claimed.

fields.text: War in Usea, Prices on the Quay
lines: War in Usea, Prices on the Quay

fields.text:
Erusea's invasion of neutral San Salvacion in the summer of 2003 puts the railguns of Stonehenge in Erusean hands, and they are soon firing at aircraft. Usea is a long way from the capital port, but freight and fuel prices respond within days, and the convoy register shows a dozen Aquitorian ships on routes that touch Usean waters.

Shipowners hold their vessels in port until the government tells them whom the kingdom will supply. The arms halls receive enquiries from buyers on both sides. The three political camps, whatever government now holds the seals, agree that no Aquitorian soldier should go to Usea. They agree on very little else, least of all on whether the kingdom should profit from the war.

The government must give the shipowners an answer this week. Keeping every Aquitorian hull out of Usean waters is safe and expensive. Letting each owner decide for himself is profitable and dangerous. Later choices about whom to supply will follow from this first answer, and so will the rates the insurers charge. The shipowners have made clear that if the government says nothing, they will each make their own choice by the end of the month.

Provisional gameplay: date anchor only, ACES Chronicle row 2003 / SUMMER; the Aquitorian response is gameplay.

fields.text: Who Governs the Duchy
lines: Who Governs the Duchy

fields.text:
The National Administration has governed Arklith since the vote of 1990, and it has done so competently enough that few people ask by what right. The ministries in Cabaria run, the yards launch their hulls and the Llano factories keep their shifts. Yet the Duchy has no election on its calendar, and the administration's own lawyers concede that its mandate rests more on habit than on any written grant.

Publishing the administration's powers has brought every faction into the open. Loyalists of the ducal house, still about a third of the country by the old measures, want the title to mean something again, either beside a council of ministers or above it. The owners of the yards, shipping lines and Nieblo mines want a board that runs the state the way they run their companies. A smaller but organised camp in the Llano and the port unions wants an elected assembly and nothing else.

Nothing has been decided yet. What the administration chooses today is how the argument will be held: openly, with the press and the provinces watching, or quietly in the corridors of Cabaria, where the great houses and the ducal household already have friends. Either choice will be remembered by the camp it disappoints.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Port and Plain
lines: Port and Plain

fields.text:
Ask in Cabaria where the country's future lies and the answer points to the harbours: Puerto Tranquilidad and Cabarion, the yards along the coast, the merchant fleet that carries Arklith's name to foreign ports. Ask in the city of Arklith on the Llano and the answer is the factories, the seven great works and the workshops around them, and a population larger than any coastal province can claim.

The state has never resolved which of the two it serves first. Officials commute by the coast railway, files go missing between offices, and both regions are convinced the other receives the larger share of the budget. Planners have drawn up three answers: move the economic ministries inland, keep everything by the harbour, or split the government between them and accept the cost of running it from two cities.

Before any of those plans is chosen, the government must decide how to frame the question. It can treat it as a technical matter of efficiency, to be settled by surveys of traffic and cost, or as a political bargain between two regions that both believe they carry the country. The surveys will be quicker. The bargain will last longer.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Order Book
lines: The Order Book

fields.text:
The inspectors' report on the twenty slipways reads like a ship's log of the last decade. Some berths at Arklith del Norte and Arklith del Sur have worked without a pause; others on the Cabar coast have built nothing larger than a tug in three years. Cranes, welding gear and dry docks vary from modern to museum pieces, often in the same yard. Payrolls are full everywhere, because no yard owner wants to be the first to dismiss skilled hands.

The order book itself is thin. Foreign shipping companies have plenty of yards to choose from, and Arklith wins contracts mainly on price, with the state's credit making up the difference. The navy has ordered little beyond maintenance. Repair work comes and goes with the passing traffic. Every owner has a plan to fix this, and every plan requires the treasury.

The government must decide how much of the report to release. Published in full, it will show foreign buyers exactly where the yards are weak, and give the unions a clear view of which berths are at risk. Kept within the ministry and the owners' association, it will guide a quieter reform, at the cost of rumours along the coast that something is being hidden.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Under Whose Flag
lines: Under Whose Flag

fields.text:
The shipping office has finished its count of the merchant fleet, and the results surprise even its own clerks. Several hundred ships carry the Arklith flag, far more than a country of eight provinces could load with its own trade. Some are owned and crewed at home and call at Puerto Tranquilidad every month. Many more belong to foreign companies that registered here for low fees and have never seen the coast.

The foreign-owned hulls pay their dues on time and ask for little. They also bring risk: old ships, crews of uncertain training and owners whose other business is not always visible. A single disaster at sea involving an Arklith-flagged ship would land on the Duchy's reputation regardless of who owned it. Meanwhile, the domestic lines complain that the open register undercuts them on every route they sail.

Two opinions dominate the shipping office. One says the register is a business like any other and should be run for revenue, with inspections tight enough to avoid scandal. The other says a flag should mean something, and that a smaller, national fleet would serve the country better in a crisis. Before choosing, the office must decide whom to consult.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Highland Ledger
lines: The Highland Ledger

fields.text:
The survey teams come down from the Nieblo with crates of core samples and notebooks full of warnings. The aluminium and tungsten seams of both highland provinces are richer than the old maps suggested, especially in the eastern valleys. The shafts that reach them are in worse condition than anyone admitted: ventilation that fails in the warm months, props past their age and escape routes that end in rock.

The highland towns depend on the mines and the arms plants beside them, which together employ most working adults in some valleys. Wages are low, prices are high and the roads to the Llano close for days at a time in the rains. The mining families have learned not to expect much from Cabaria. Their delegates have nonetheless travelled down with the survey, to make sure the report is read.

Two proposals are already circulating. The state could bring every mine and plant under one public authority, or lease the seams to the commercial houses for investment and royalties. Before either can be argued, the government must decide what it says to the delegates who are waiting in the corridor, and whether it promises them anything now.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Works Council Meets
lines: The Works Council Meets

fields.text:
For the first time, the owners of the seven great works on the Llano, the unions that organise their shifts and the city council of Arklith sit in one room with a single agenda. The meeting is stiff. Owners speak of energy prices and foreign competition; union delegates speak of housing, overtime and the workers who arrive each week from the highlands and the coast. The city's officials mostly take notes.

Beneath the formalities, everyone knows what the plain needs. Its machine tools are old, its engineers are few and its power supply falters whenever several works run full shifts at once. The works make almost everything the country uses, from buses to rifles to pump housings, and almost none of it is made as well as it could be. Foreign buyers have noticed.

The council's first decision is about its own character. It can become a planning body with access to the ministries and a budget of its own, or remain a forum where problems are aired and settled by the parties themselves. A planning body would move faster and carry the state's weight. A forum would keep the government at arm's length from wages and prices.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Army Counts Its Rifles
lines: The Army Counts Its Rifles

fields.text:
The general staff's audit runs to several volumes, and the summary is blunt. Arklith has an army sized for a small country with no enemies, which is what it believes itself to be. Garrisons in every province maintain their barracks and parade grounds. The mountain detachment in the Nieblo trains hard. Elsewhere, trucks wait for parts, artillery waits for crews and many soldiers have not fired a live round in a year.

Public interest is close to nil. War support sits near the bottom of every measure the ministries track, and most voters, asked about defence, mention the navy's escorts protecting the merchant fleet before they mention the army at all. The officers know that any request for money will be compared with the yards, the highlands and the metropolis, and lose.

The staff therefore proposes to begin with what costs least: repair, reorganisation and honest planning. The question is how loudly to say so. A public report would invite debate and perhaps support. A confidential one would avoid alarming anyone and keep the army's weaknesses away from foreign eyes, at the price of another decade of indifference.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Four Frontiers
lines: Four Frontiers

fields.text:
The frontier review lays the country's borders out on a single table in the foreign office in Cabaria. To the east, Perbla, beyond the Halloma Basin and the Cabar hills, a larger kingdom with old friends of its own. To the south, Leasath along the edge of the Llano and the Nieblo passes. Past Eastern Nieblo, Dakrain. On the southern edge of Arklith del Sur, the Gibraltar Mining Zone and its mining administration.

None of these frontiers is in dispute, and the review does not propose to change any of them. What it finds is that each is managed by a different ministry, under different rules, with different priorities. Customs officials at the Halloma crossings work to one code; border police in the Nieblo passes to another. Nobody in Cabaria has ever asked whether the four policies make sense together.

The review's authors offer two broad directions: open the crossings to trade and transit, or keep them courteous but watchful and promise nothing to anyone. Before that choice, the government must decide how much to say to the neighbours about the review itself. Openness would reassure them. Discretion would keep options available.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: War Beyond Perbla
lines: War Beyond Perbla

fields.text:
In March 1995 the Belkan War breaks out. Arklith has no part in it and no treaty that could draw it in. Yet the news lands hard in Cabaria. Perbla, on the eastern frontier, has old ties to Belka, and nobody knows how far its sympathies will go. Arklith-flagged ships sail in waters that are suddenly dangerous, and the crisis office opens with more questions than staff.

Within days the practical effects arrive. Foreign insurers raise premiums on any hull bound anywhere near the fighting. Shippers who usually book space months ahead call daily for news. Rumours spread in the Halloma Basin that the Perbla frontier will close, though nothing on the ground suggests it. In the Llano, factories that buy foreign parts begin hoarding.

The administration must decide what it will tell the country. It can speak frankly about the risks to shipping and trade, which may cause a run on stores and a rush to reflag ships. Or it can reassure first and explain later, accepting that if things go badly the public will remember being told all was well. The crisis office has drafted both statements and waits for a signature.

fields.text: The Insurers Raise the Rates
lines: The Insurers Raise the Rates

fields.text:
Two weeks into the war, the foreign insurance syndicates that cover most of Arklith's merchant fleet publish new rates. War-risk premiums on routes near the fighting rise several times over; some routes are excluded altogether. Owners of older ships find themselves uninsurable at any price. Several masters radio from foreign ports that they will not sail until someone tells them who pays if they are sunk.

The shipping lines come to Cabaria in a body. They want the state to guarantee their hulls, or at least to share the risk, and they point out that a fleet idling in harbour pays no dues and buys no fuel. The treasury answers that a guarantee is a blank cheque written on a war it cannot control. Both are right, which makes the meeting long.

There are middle courses. The state could cover only domestic-owned ships, or only routes it judges safe, or only hulls that sail under navy escort. Each would leave someone unprotected and angry. The crisis office recommends a decision within the week, before the masters abroad make it for the government by selling their ships.

Provisional gameplay: date anchor only, Chronicle row 1995 / 03.25; the insurance crisis is gameplay.

fields.text: A Date in the Sky
lines: A Date in the Sky

fields.text:
In December 1994 astronomers warned that the asteroid called Ulysses could strike the Earth. In April 1996 the warning becomes an announcement: it will. Governments are told to prepare. Nobody can yet say where the fragments will fall, or how many there will be, or whether a coast, a plain or a mountain range is the safer place to be.

In Arklith the news arrives on the evening broadcasts and reaches the morning markets as panic. Bottled water and tinned food sell out in Cabaria and the city of Arklith. Churches and union halls fill. The sky watch, a handful of amateur astronomers and radar crews, is suddenly asked questions it cannot answer. Foreign bulletins contradict each other daily, and every radio phone-in has a caller who claims to know where the fragments will land. The ports report families booking passage abroad without any idea where abroad would be safer.

The government has two tasks. The first is to plan, and engineers are already drafting proposals for shelters beneath the cities or for evacuation to the highlands and the basin. The second is to keep the country calm while it plans. How much uncertainty the government admits in public will shape whether people trust the plans when they come.

Provisional gameplay: date anchors only, Chronicle rows 1994 / 12.10 and 1996 / 04.20; the Arklith response is gameplay.

fields.text: Ulysses Overhead
lines: Ulysses Overhead

fields.text:
In July 1999 Ulysses passes through the Earth's Roche limit and begins to break apart. In Arklith, sirens are tested at noon, ships in the reserve raise steam and the sky watch moves its reports from weekly to hourly. Families who rehearsed their routes check them again. The broadcasts carry foreign bulletins, then local ones, then foreign ones again.

The plans written since 1996 are about to be judged. Shelters stand stocked, or reception towns stand ready, depending on what the government chose. Neither plan can do anything about where the fragments fall. Both depend on people trusting the instructions they receive in the next hours, and on officials resisting the temptation to improvise. In the Llano works, managers ask whether to bank the furnaces. In the highlands, miners ask whether to stay underground. Every question reaches Cabaria at once, and the crisis office answers them in order.

The government's last decision before the night is simple and difficult. It can order the plans into effect now, on the strength of uncertain warnings, accepting the disruption if nothing comes. Or it can wait for clear warnings and act on them, accepting the risk that clear warnings may come too late to matter. Neither choice will look wise to everyone in the morning.

whether to bank the furnaces. In the highlands, miners ask whether to stay
underground. Every question reaches Cabaria at once, and the crisis office
answers them in order.
The government's last decision before the night is simple and difficult. It can
order the plans into effect now, on the strength of uncertain warnings,
accepting the disruption if nothing comes. Or it can wait for clear warnings and
act on them, accepting the risk that clear warnings may come too late to
matter. Neither choice will look wise to everyone in the morning.

fragment fall in Arklith is claimed.

fields.text: Ten Years On
lines: Ten Years On

fields.text:
The review panel, drawn by lot from all eight provinces, delivers its report at the turn of the century. It is long, careful and in places harsh. It credits the decade with order and growth: the yards are busier, the Llano works more modern, the highland towns safer. It faults the state for deciding too much in Cabaria and explaining too little everywhere else.

Each camp reads the report for its own purposes. Supporters of the government chosen in the early nineties find praise; its opponents find enough criticism to quote for years. The yards and the shipping lines read the chapter on credit and guarantees with particular care. The Llano reads the chapter on industry and asks why its name appears so rarely in the recommendations.

The government must decide what to do with the report. It can adopt its recommendations wholesale, binding itself to a programme it did not write. It can thank the panel and choose selectively. Or it can submit the report to the provinces for comment, which will take months and produce a second, louder argument. The panel members, at least, have already gone home.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: A Buyer Walks Away
lines: A Buyer Walks Away

fields.text:
A foreign shipping company with two hulls half built on Arklith berths announces that it cannot pay. Its creditors abroad have seized its accounts, its directors have stopped answering letters and the hulls sit on the slipways with their plating unfinished. Suppliers who delivered steel, engines and wiring want their money. The yard wants to know who will pay its welders next month.

This is the case the yards have always feared and rarely planned for. A default on one contract can ripple through dozens of small suppliers in the coastal provinces, some of whom have no other customer. The question in the ministry is not whether the state will help, but how, and how much it will expect back when the hulls are finally sold.

Options are limited. The state can buy the hulls, finish them and sell them itself, taking the risk and any profit. It can lend the yard enough to finish them and leave the sale to the owners. Or it can let the yard and its suppliers settle among themselves, as any other business would, and accept the closures that follow.

fields.text: Freight for a Distant War
lines: Freight for a Distant War

fields.text:
In August 2003 the FCU founds the ISAF to fight Erusea on the Usean continent, and the war that follows touches every shipping market in the world. Arklith has no part in it. Its lines feel it within weeks: charter rates for bulk carriers rise, insurers redraw their maps and buyers who had hesitated over new hulls sign contracts to secure capacity before prices rise further.

The shipping office reports offers from many directions. Some are innocent: grain, machinery, building materials for economies disrupted by the fighting. Others are less clear, with cargo descriptions that could cover almost anything. The yards report a rush of repair work from ships diverted onto longer routes. In Cabaria, the old debates of 1995 return as if they had never ended.

The government must set the terms. It can let the lines take every lawful cargo, with inspections to keep them honest, or ask them to keep their ships closer to home until the war is over. Either way, it must decide quickly, because the lines are already signing contracts and the masters are already at sea.

fields.text: An Election Nobody May Hold
lines: An Election Nobody May Hold

fields.text:
The statute book of the Republic of Azbekerania still prints a general ballot every forty-eight months, with dates, polling rules and the duties of district returning officers set out in full. None of it has been used under the present suspension. The National Administration governs under the democratic banner, but when the interior ministry quietly polls the districts, the democrats register at one voter in a hundred.

The rest of the country has sorted itself into two blocs of nearly equal size. One is the reservists' leagues: former soldiers of the eight formations, their families and the towns that send them, who want the state run like a mobilisation table. The other is the civil establishment of the three industrial cities, career officials and district notables who belong to no party and distrust anyone who does. Each bloc believes the suspension favours the other.

The Administration cannot answer the calendar question in a single sitting. It can choose who gets to argue about it first. A public hearing gives the leagues a stage and the establishment a grievance. A ministerial review keeps both out of the room. Inviting both to a round table satisfies neither, but it keeps them talking rather than marching.

fields.text: The Seven Towns Report
lines: The Seven Towns Report

fields.text:
The survey parties return from the seven towns after a season on tracks that their trucks were never built for. Their reports agree on the essentials. District B, District D, District E, District F, District H, District I and District J have no paved road, no factory and no resource any geologist has recorded. Schools and clinics depend on what each town can raise for itself, which is usually very little.

The details differ. District I is bigger than any of the three cities' districts and takes days to cross. District E climbs into hills and the republic's only mountain country along the Yuktobanian frontier. District J is desert running down to a coast with no harbour. District F is small and quiet and sits in the middle of everything. District B has a coast and a frontier with Seterano and nothing to connect them.

The ministers must decide what to do with the findings. Publishing them district by district will start an argument between the three cities and the seven towns that no ministry can control. Filing them inside the ministries will let the road budget follow the figures quietly, while every town assumes it was cheated. Either way the towns now know that someone in the capital has looked.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Three Cities, One Set of Books
lines: Three Cities, One Set of Books

fields.text:
The ledger clerks finish adding up the three industrial districts and find that nobody had ever done it before. The Capital District, District A and District C each run four civilian plants and two arms plants and each draws on its own oil, steel, aluminium and rubber. Together they are the whole of the republic's industry. Separately, each city has been negotiating with foreign buyers as if the other two did not exist.

The export law sends a large share of everything abroad, and the ledger shows how much of the remainder is lost between plant gates and the customs sheds. Rubber is the tightest figure: barely enough for the army's tyres if none is sold. Fuel is the strangest, because the capital's silo is rarely more than half full while the cities export crude oil every week of the year.

The ministers can use the ledger to force the three city chambers into a single trade policy, which will take years and set the cities against the capital. Or they can hand each chamber its own figures and let the cities tidy their books quietly. The figures will reach the newspapers whichever course is chosen, and the leagues already have a reporter asking about the silo.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Eight Formations on the Road
lines: Eight Formations on the Road

fields.text:
For one week every formation of the army leaves its barracks at the same time. Three march out of the Capital Centre, three from the logistics centre in District A and two from the logistics centre in District C. Their orders are simple: reach an assembly area at the inland crossroads in District F, report strength and return. Nobody has attempted it before, and the staff suspects why.

The road from the capital is graded only for part of the way. Trucks from District A must come round by rail through District D, and the line can carry one formation at a time. Two formations arrive on schedule, four arrive late, and two never leave their railheads because the wagons went somewhere else. The engineer companies spend more of the week repairing culverts than any of them expected.

The chief of staff carries the timings to the Administration in person. They show a continental reserve that cannot yet reach the middle of its own country inside a week. Releasing them hands the leagues an argument and the city chambers a scandal about money spent on trucks that sat at railheads. Releasing only photographs of the closing parade, with bands and a fly-past from the capital wing, keeps spirits high and leaves every road as poor as before.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: A Map with Three Frontiers
lines: A Map with Three Frontiers

fields.text:
The foreign ministry's new frontier map takes up a whole wall of the cabinet room. A long red line marks the frontier with Yuktobania, running past five districts and close to two of the three industrial cities. A shorter line marks Seterano along District A and District B. A third runs with Aemurraq past the Capital District, District H and District J, closer to the capital than any minister had quite realised.

Each frontier has been handled by whoever happened to live near it. Customs officers in District C keep their own arrangements with their counterparts across the line. Farmers in District B cross to markets on the Seterano side and come back without paperwork. The garrison in the capital has never planned for a frontier only a short drive from the cabinet room. None of these habits has ever been written down.

The cabinet is asked for a single policy and finds it has three different problems. The ministers can start with the largest neighbour and accept that the other frontiers wait, or start with the frontier nearest the capital, or simply publish the map and ask the districts what they want. The map itself changes nothing on the ground; it only shows the ministers what they had not looked at.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Shots in the Dark in District D
lines: Shots in the Dark in District D

fields.text:
A night patrol near a crossing in District D meets a party of armed men moving without lights. Somebody fires; the patrol returns fire; the party scatters into the dark. At dawn the patrol finds two abandoned packs full of tinned food and cigarettes, a wounded man who will not give his name and a set of tyre tracks running toward the line. Nobody is dead, which everyone agrees is lucky.

By noon the incident has three explanations. The patrol commander says smugglers. The district notables say deserters from some army looking for work. The leagues' newspapers say something far worse and print a map with arrows on it. The frontier authorities across the line, contacted by telephone, say they know nothing and would like the wounded man returned.

The cabinet must decide how large to make the incident. A full inquiry with outside observers will take months and satisfy the careful. A quiet handover of the wounded man will end it in a day and anger the leagues. A loud protest will please the newspapers and commit the republic to a story it cannot prove. Whatever is chosen, the patrols on every frontier will learn from it what the capital expects of them.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Inquiry Reports
lines: The Inquiry Reports

fields.text:
Three weeks after the shooting in District D the inquiry delivers its report. It is shorter than anyone expected. The armed party were smugglers carrying food and cigarettes, and the first shot came from a nervous patrol member who saw a flashlight and thought it was a weapon. The wounded man was a hired porter. The tyre tracks belonged to a farm truck on the Azbekeranian side.

The observers sign the report without reservation. The leagues' newspapers, which had printed arrows on maps, print a correction on an inside page. The patrol commander is moved to a training post and his men are retrained in night procedures. The district notables in District D, who had been sure it was deserters, say very little and buy the patrol a meal.

The cabinet now holds an unusual thing: a frontier incident settled entirely by evidence. It can publish the report in full as an example of how incidents should be handled, at the cost of embarrassing its own army. Or it can thank the observers privately and file the report, keeping the patrols' pride intact and the lesson inside the general staff where it may or may not be read.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Staff Opens a War Room
lines: The Staff Opens a War Room

fields.text:
In March 1995 a war begins around Belka. Azbekerania has no part in it and no frontier near it, yet within a week the general staff has opened a war room in the Capital Centre with a wall map, a radio and a duty officer at every hour. The room exists to answer one question that nobody asks aloud in the cabinet: what happens to a small republic when the countries around it go to war?

Dispatches arrive from attaches, newspapers and shortwave bulletins, contradictory and late. The leagues demand that the reserve be called up at once, on the principle that nobody was ever criticised for being ready. The civil establishment answers that calling up the reserve would empty the plants in the three cities in the middle of a price boom. Both sides cite the same dispatches.

The cabinet must give the war room a purpose. It can be a study cell that reports quietly to the staff and costs nothing in public. Or it can be the visible centre of a raised alert, with the formations brought to readiness and the newspapers briefed each week. The first keeps the plants running; the second tells every neighbour that Azbekerania is watching.

fields.text: Ten Districts Ask What to Do
lines: Ten Districts Ask What to Do

fields.text:
In April 1996 the long-feared announcement is made: Ulysses will strike the Earth, a danger astronomers first raised in December 1994. Which regions will be hit is not yet known to anyone. Within a day every district office in Azbekerania has telephoned the capital for instructions, and the capital has discovered that it has none to read out.

The questions are practical. The capital and District C want to know whether their coasts are safe. The seven towns want to know whether anyone will bring them food if the roads fail. The general staff wants to know whether the reserve should prepare for war or for disaster, since it cannot do both well. The trade ministry wants to know whether exports will be held back, and is told to wait.

Before any plan, the cabinet must decide how to speak. It can announce preparations at once and in full, accepting queues at the markets and a rush of families from the coast inland. Or it can urge calm while the ministries work, accepting that the plan will arrive late and that rumours will fill the gap. The coastal districts will feel the choice first.

fields.text: A Rumour on the Coast
lines: A Rumour on the Coast

fields.text:
Two weeks after the government announced its preparations, a rumour spreads along the coast from the capital to District C: the fragments will fall into the sea, and the sea will come ashore. Nobody can say where it started. By the weekend the coast road inland is jammed with cars, carts and trucks, and the evacuation timetables nobody has written yet are already overdue.

In District F and District D the arrivals overwhelm towns that have never housed visitors. Prices for rooms and bread triple. Some families sleep in schools and some in their vehicles. In the capital, half-empty streets encourage looting in a few warehouses near the naval harbour, and the police ask the garrison for help. The leagues offer their members as volunteers before anyone has asked.

The cabinet has two ways to respond, neither good. It can deploy the formations to direct traffic, guard the empty streets and run feeding stations, which works and puts soldiers on every corner. Or it can broadcast the astronomers' own statements every hour and trust that facts will slowly outrun fear, which is slower and leaves the inland towns to cope alone for a while.

fields.text: A Night with the Trucks Running
lines: A Night with the Trucks Running

fields.text:
Ulysses crosses the Roche limit on 8 July 1999. Azbekerania meets the night with its engines running: the formations are drawn up beside their trucks at the Capital Centre and both logistics centres, the evacuation trains are parked in the District D sidings, and an operator sits awake in every district office with orders to report each hour, even if only to say that the hour passed.

Most of what reaches the capital is noise. Foreign stations contradict one another, amateur operators relay what other amateurs claim to have heard, and the duty officers in the plotting room stop chalking rumours on the board after the first few hours. In the seven towns, families crowd into the town offices around radio sets that arrived only months earlier and listen in near silence.

Morning comes and the ten districts are intact, tired and uneasy. Wherever the fragments came down, the consequences will travel to Azbekerania by slower roads: prices, insurance, debris reports and people on the move. The cabinet must choose between holding the formations beside their trucks for weeks while the reports settle, or releasing them to barracks and asking the districts to open their shops and schools as usual.

around radio sets that arrived only months earlier and listen in near silence.

fragments came down, the consequences will travel to Azbekerania by slower
roads: prices, insurance, debris reports and people on the move. The cabinet
must choose between holding the formations beside their trucks for weeks
while the reports settle, or releasing them to barracks and asking the districts
to open their shops and schools as usual.

fields.text: What the Railguns Teach
lines: What the Railguns Teach

fields.text:
Erusea's invasion of neutral San Salvacion in the summer of 2003, and its seizure of the Stonehenge railguns for use against aircraft, reach the ten districts as newspaper columns about a faraway continent. The Azbekeranian air staff reads them differently, because the war poses the one question its two small wings have never answered: what becomes of an air force when the sky itself is defended from the ground?

The staff splits at once. One group argues that the railguns prove the value of air defence from the ground: guns and radar are cheaper than fighters, harder to destroy and never need a pilot. The other group answers that ground defences only deny the sky directly above them, and that a country with seventy-two fighters cannot afford to stop renewing them for a decade while it buys guns.

The cabinet is asked for money before the war in Usea has run its course, and before anyone knows how it will end. It can fund a study that waits for the result. Or it can let both schools prepare competing programmes now, accepting that one of them will lose a budget fight it has been promised it might win. Either way, the air staff will argue about this war for years.

Provisional gameplay: date anchor only, ACES Chronicle row 2003 / SUMMER; the Azbekeranian response is gameplay.

fields.text: The Suspended Ballot
lines: The Suspended Ballot

fields.text:
The National Administration that governs Glaceland in 1991 carries a democratic name and a suspended election calendar. Its officials run ten districts, eighteen plants, a small navy and a smaller air arm, and they do it competently enough that few people ask who appointed them. When the question is finally asked aloud, in the capital's press and in district halls from A to J, nobody in the Administration has a ready answer.

The pollsters' figures make the problem sharper. Barely one citizen in a hundred supports the party whose name the government carries. Close to half want the country run by non-party administrators, as it effectively already is. The other half answers to a nationalist movement that promises discipline, a stronger coast and an end to government by clerks. Democrats and communists together could fill a meeting hall, not a chamber.

The Administration must decide how the question will be argued before it can decide how it will be answered. District hearings would take a season and invite every grievance in the country into the record. A decision inside the Administration would be faster and quieter, and would confirm everything its critics say about it. Both choices will be remembered when the seals change hands.

fields.text: Returns from the Districts
lines: Returns from the Districts

fields.text:
The hearing clerks return from the ten districts with crates of transcripts. The core districts, the capital and Districts B, G and I, talk about wages, rents and the plants. The empty districts talk about roads they have never had, clinics a day's travel away and young people who leave for the core and do not come back. District C, across the water, talks mostly about the ferries.

On the constitutional question the returns are as divided as the polls. Officials and managers want a board that keeps things running. Farmers and plant workers split between the nationalist petition and a scattering of voices who want a real vote. Almost every district asks first to be consulted again, and many hearings closed with a vote of thanks to the clerks for coming at all.

The Administration now holds the returns and must decide what to do with them. Publishing every transcript would show the country to itself, flaws included, and hand the opposition a library of quotations. A summary would be tidier and safer. Officials who sat through the hearings warn privately that a summary will be read as the Administration editing the districts out of their own record.

fields.text: Half a Country Without Roads
lines: Half a Country Without Roads

fields.text:
The survey teams come back from Districts C, D, F, H and J with photographs that surprise even the ministers who sent them. Half of Glaceland has no paved road network and no factory of any kind. Villages are joined by farm tracks, forest roads and boats. The frontier districts facing Sfaenland, Luremia and Kaluga could not move a convoy to their own border posts in a wet week.

The other half of the country is a different place. The capital and Districts B, G and I hold all twelve civilian plants and all six arms works, the logistics centres and nearly all the oil, steel and aluminium. District A holds the four dockyards. The core is busy, crowded and increasingly expensive to live in, and every year it draws the young out of the empty districts.

The survey's authors refuse to recommend a solution. They price roads, plants, schools and clinics for each empty district and leave the choice to the government: spread industry outward at a higher cost, or concentrate it where it already works and connect the rest by road. The empty districts are watching to see whether the survey becomes a programme or a report on a shelf.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Collection Gap
lines: The Collection Gap

fields.text:
The treasury's auditors present a short report with a long appendix. Glaceland collects roughly eighty-five of every hundred owed in tax. Public debt stands near a third of national output. Growth is steady at around three percent and inflation is low, so nothing is on fire. But the gap compounds every year, and the debt grows a little faster than the economy that must carry it.

The missing fifteen are not hidden in one place. Some is evaded by firms in the core, some is never assessed in the empty districts where the nearest tax office is a day's travel away, and some is simply lost between ministries that keep separate accounts. The oil districts pay royalties under formulas older than most of the wells. Nobody has ever audited all of it at once.

The auditors want powers to inspect firms, district offices and ministries alike. The ministries object to being audited by the treasury, and the firms object to everything. The government must decide whether to publish the report or keep it for internal use, knowing that publication makes every later tax measure easier to defend and every later scandal harder to bury.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: A Long Coast and Five Escorts
lines: A Long Coast and Five Escorts

fields.text:
The naval register is finished, and it fits on two pages. Glaceland has five escorts, two coastal submarines and a merchant fleet of about a hundred and eight hulls, many of them older than their crews. The main naval base and all four dockyards stand in District A, beside the Sfaenland frontier. District C's small post and the jetty on District H's islet complete the list.

Against that list stands the coast itself. Seven of the ten districts touch the sea, and the coastline is several times longer than all three land frontiers together. The merchant fleet carries most of the country's trade and every passenger to District C. Fishermen, smugglers and the occasional foreign survey ship use the same waters, and most of the time nobody official sees any of them.

The admirals agree on the problem and on nothing else. Some want the escorts organised around the convoys, some want submarines hidden along the mountain coasts, and some want a guard service for what actually happens at sea every day. The government is asked first for a simpler decision: whether the navy's weakness is admitted in public or kept as a matter for the defence staff.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Across the Water
lines: Across the Water

fields.text:
District C lies across the water from the rest of Glaceland: twenty-two provinces of plains and low hills, with a small naval post and a harbour town. It has no paved roads and no plants. Its farmers grow food the mainland imports, its fishermen work the surrounding waters, and every ton of anything moves by ship. When storms close the crossing, the district lives on whatever is in its warehouses.

The islanders' complaints are practical and old. Ferry fares are high and timetables unreliable. Mainland officials arrive for a week and leave before learning the names of the villages. Doctors are scarce, spare parts take weeks, and young people who cross to study in the capital rarely return. Yet the district is loyal in its own stubborn way, and asks mainly to be remembered.

The government must decide how District C is to be governed within Glaceland. A charter would let the islanders run their own local affairs, at the price of a partner the capital cannot simply instruct. A resident commissioner would get things built faster, at the price of goodwill. Nothing about the district's place in the country is in question; only the manner of its government is.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Hill Country and Eight Formations
lines: Hill Country and Eight Formations

fields.text:
The army's staff map is pinned to a public wall of the defence ministry for the first time. It shows eight infantry formations spread across a country that is mostly forest, hill and mountain, with marsh along some coasts and dry plains around the capital. It shows three land frontiers, one of them longer than the other two combined, and a district across the water that no formation can reach on foot.

The inventories are honest too: nearly two thousand sets of infantry equipment, about a thousand motor vehicles, a few hundred sets of support equipment and a modest stock of trains. Some of the infantry already trains as mountaineers. Doctrine prefers firepower, because the country will never have numbers. The staff says plainly that it can hold some valleys well and most of the country not at all.

Two schools are forming inside the officer corps. One wants a battalion in every district, raised from local reservists. The other wants a single professional mountain corps that moves to the threat. Before either wins, the government must decide whether the staff map stays on the public wall or goes back into a safe, knowing that the neighbours' attaches read the newspapers too.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Every Aircraft on Two Fields
lines: Every Aircraft on Two Fields

fields.text:
The air staff's report opens with a sentence the ministers will remember: every aircraft Glaceland owns stands on one of two airfields. Seventy-two fighters and twelve ground-attack aircraft are divided between the field beside the capital and the field in District B. Both are known to every map-maker in the region. A single well-planned strike on a clear morning could end the air arm before it flew.

The report is equally blunt about everything else. Radar coverage barely reaches beyond the two fields. Pilots fly too few hours because fuel is rationed by budget rather than by supply, even though the country pumps its own oil. Major overhauls are done abroad and take months. The air arm is proud and capable in small numbers, and it knows exactly how small those numbers are.

The staff offers two remedies that cannot both be afforded. The country could scatter its squadrons across forest strips in the mountain districts, or bury them in concrete at the two fields it already has. The ministers must first decide something easier: whether the air staff may speak publicly about the risk, or whether the report stays among the people who already lose sleep over it.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Ulysses Will Strike
lines: Ulysses Will Strike

fields.text:
In April 1996 the world is told that the asteroid Ulysses will strike the Earth and that nations should prepare. Since the astronomers' announcement of December 1994, Glaceland's committee of astronomers and engineers has watched quietly; now its reports lead every bulletin. Nobody can say where fragments will fall. Glaceland, like every country, must prepare for a danger whose place and scale remain a guess.

The committee divides into two camps. One wants reserves: a year of fuel, grain and medicine in depots across all ten districts, so that whatever falls, the country can feed and fuel itself. The other wants refuges: most districts and most plants lie on the coast, while Districts D and F and the capital lie inland, and moving people is cheaper than storing a year of food.

Public mood swings between calm and fright. Shops in the capital run short of bottled water and candles, and coastal families ask relatives inland whether they have a spare room. The treasury warns that either programme costs as much as the defence budget. Before choosing, the government must decide how to speak about a danger it cannot control: plainly and often, or calmly and rarely.

Provisional gameplay: date anchors only, Official Chronicle rows 1994 / 12.10 and 1996 / 04.20 in tools/lore/chronicle.json; the Glacelandic response is gameplay.

fields.text: Ulysses Breaks Apart
lines: Ulysses Breaks Apart

fields.text:
In July 1999 Ulysses passes through the Earth's Roche limit and begins to break apart. The committee in the capital sits through the night beside its radios and telephones, and district officials stand by in every hall from A to J. Whatever Glaceland prepared over the past three years, reserves or refuges, is now tested against something that does not negotiate.

The first hours are filled with rumours that travel faster than the official bulletins. Coastal towns report lights in the sky that may be fragments or may be aircraft. Telephone exchanges jam. Some families leave for the interior without waiting for any order, while others refuse to leave at all. The ferries to District C are held in harbour, and the district follows the night by radio like everyone else.

By dawn the government must decide how to manage the days that follow. It can keep the emergency apparatus fully mobilised until the danger is certainly past, at a heavy cost in lost work, or stand most of it down as soon as the reports allow and accept the risk of being wrong. Either way, the country will remember how its government behaved on this night.

Provisional gameplay: date anchor only, Official Chronicle row 1999 / 07.08, with the break-up from Super Weapons, Stonehenge, in tools/lore/chronicle.json; what falls near Glaceland is not claimed and the response is gameplay.

fields.text: Three Frontiers, Three Desks
lines: Three Frontiers, Three Desks

fields.text:
The new foreign ministry desks deliver their first joint briefing. Sfaenland shares the longest land frontier with Glaceland, along District A and District F, and is the nearest market for the core plants. Luremia faces District F and the forests of District J. Kaluga touches only a short stretch of District J's mountains. Each relationship has its own history of small disputes and quiet cooperation.

The briefing is candid about how little the capital knows. Customs posts on the frontiers are understaffed, the roads to them are poor, and most local cooperation, on grazing, timber, water and lost travellers, has been arranged by district officials who never told the ministries. The desks expect every neighbour to watch what Glaceland now does with its own empty frontier districts.

Two schools are forming in the ministry. One wants open frontiers with low tariffs and fast crossings, turning the empty frontier districts into trade corridors. The other wants trade under licence, keeping those districts as buffers. First, though, the government must decide how to introduce the new desks to the neighbours: with a public conference or with quiet letters.

fields.text: A Commission Drawn by Lot
lines: A Commission Drawn by Lot

fields.text:
Ten years after the National Administration opened its books, a commission drawn by lot from the district rolls publishes its ledger of the decade. It counts roads laid in the empty districts and plants opened outside the core, hulls launched in District A, aircraft kept flying, preparations made against Ulysses and money owed abroad. It also counts what was promised and never delivered.

The ledger pleases nobody completely. The core districts are richer and so are some of the empty ones, but the gap between them has narrowed less than the speeches claimed. The navy and air arm are better organised and still small. The treasury collects more of what it is owed, though not all of it. District C still waits for its ferries in bad weather.

Whoever holds the seals in 2001 must answer the ledger in public. A full answer, chapter by chapter, would admit failures and give critics a decade of material. A short statement of thanks would look confident and evasive at the same time. The commission has already said it will publish any reply in full beside its own findings.

fields.text: War in Usea
lines: War in Usea

fields.text:
When the ISAF coalition is formed to oppose Erusea, war spreads across Usea. Glaceland is not a party to it and has no wish to become one. Yet within days of the news, shipping insurers raise their premiums, freight rates climb and fuel prices move on every market where Glaceland buys and sells. A war elsewhere arrives in Glacelandic ledgers before it arrives in Glacelandic newspapers.

Merchant owners ask the government what to do. Some of their ships sail routes that touch waters near the war; most do not, but insurers do not distinguish. Exporters worry about contracts and importers about prices. The small navy worries about being asked to protect anything at all. The oil districts, for once, expect higher prices to help rather than hurt.

The government sets up a freight watch to track rates and advise shippers, and must now decide how far to go. It could advise owners to avoid any route near the war, at a cost to trade, or leave the choice to owners and their insurers and accept the risk of a Glacelandic ship caught in the crossfire. Neutrality, the foreign ministry reminds everyone, is a policy that must be practised daily.

fields.text: Who Holds the Seals
lines: Who Holds the Seals

fields.text:
The year opens quietly in Aspneset. An Office of the Crown holds the seals of the principality, the diet returned at New Year has been given no date to sit, and elections are suspended until the palace decides otherwise. Nordlands is calm, comfortable and far from any battlefield, and most citizens see no reason to change an arrangement that has kept it so. More than half of them vote for the crown's friends whenever they are allowed to vote.

Calm is not the same thing as consent. Liberal deputies, backed by roughly a quarter of the electorate, want a cabinet that answers to the diet. The shipping, yard and oil houses of the coast pay most of the country's taxes and would prefer to govern through councils of their own. A circle of palace officials believes the Office should simply be confirmed as the government and stop apologising for its existence.

The secretaries of the Office have drafted a stocktaking of who decides what in the principality. Before it begins, they want a ruling on how it will be conducted. In public, it will be slow, noisy and a platform for every faction. Inside the palace, it will be quick, tidy and distrusted from the first day.

fields.text: Half the Slipways Idle
lines: Half the Slipways Idle

fields.text:
The slipway census lands on the minister's desk with a blunt summary: the Nordlandic coast has more yard capacity than it has orders. Eleven dockyards share the work between Norden Forest, the twin harbours of Djurseryd and Havnaraas, Nyboholm in Tenese and a small yard on the Hait Mountain coast. On an ordinary day a good part of that capacity is idle, and the census counts cranes that have not lifted anything in months.

The yard owners blame cheap foreign competition and ask for subsidies. The admiralty notes that the fleet's escorts and submarines are ageing and could keep several yards busy for a decade, if the treasury paid. The unions want any plan that keeps their members employed and distrust every plan that mentions efficiency. Fitters at the older yards add that repair work, which pays well and needs fewer slipways, has been neglected for years.

The government has not chosen a model for the yards, and it does not need to choose one today. It does need to decide what the census means in public. Published in full, it will start a fierce argument about which yards have a future. Shared only with the owners and the admiralty, it will guide policy quietly while every harbour town assumes the worst.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Oil Beneath the Peninsula
lines: Oil Beneath the Peninsula

fields.text:
The survey teams come back from the Nord Peninsula with maps that change the national budget. The fields under the peninsula hold more oil than every other Nordlandic field combined, and the smaller fields of East Granley, Haugaland and the capital district are richer than the old estimates claimed. For a country that has lived from its yards and its merchant fleet, oil offers a second income that needs no foreign shipowner to stay afloat.

The peninsula itself is thinly settled. It has a single road, an airfield, three arms plants and small towns that are used to being forgotten. Their councils ask what share of the wealth will stay where it is pumped. The oil houses on the coast want leases quickly and say the state is too slow to drill. The treasury wants the revenue but fears an economy that rises and falls with the price of a single product.

Ministers have not chosen how the fields will be owned. They must first decide whether to slow the rush or welcome it. Whatever they say this month will be read as a signal by every bidder, and speculators are already buying land near the old wells in the hope of selling it back to whoever drills.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: A Country Without Conscripts
lines: A Country Without Conscripts

fields.text:
Nordlands raises almost no conscripts. Its manpower law is the lightest any state keeps, and support for war, measured in any way the ministries care to try, is close to nothing. Yet its depots hold three hundred tanks, thousands of trucks, artillery for several divisions and equipment for far more soldiers than it employs. The country is disarmed in its habits and armed in its warehouses.

Nobody planned this. The equipment was bought in years when governments worried more, and the conscripts were released in years when they worried less. Pacifist deputies want the stores sold or scrapped. The general staff wants a reserve system that can use them. Harbour towns, which feel exposed, want someone guarding the oil jetties and the naval harbour, and they do not much mind who.

The defence review must decide what the stores are for before deciding anything else. How it is run will colour the answer: a review led by officers will be trusted by the army and resented by the diet, while a review open to the public will produce a broad consensus and very little equipment policy.

Provisional gameplay.
