fields.text: The Fleet That Stays in Harbour
lines: The Fleet That Stays in Harbour

fields.text:
The admiralty's new doctrine is printed, and the newspapers have already given it a nickname: the fleet that stays in harbour. The doctrine says that a small navy deters best by surviving, keeping its escorts and coastal submarines close to defended bases and sailing only when the odds are good. It is a sensible policy for a country with a long coast, a large merchant fleet and no wish to fight anyone.

It is also an easy policy to mock. Merchant captains ask who will protect them at sea if the warships stay home. Junior officers complain that a navy which never sails never learns. The yards point out that a fleet in being still needs modern hulls, and the treasury points out that modern hulls cost money it would rather not spend on ships designed to wait.

The admirals must now explain the doctrine to the country and to the diet. They can argue it as a deterrent, which will please the general staff and frighten no one abroad, or as a shield for trade, which will please the shipowners and commit the fleet to protecting them whenever they ask.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: A Capital on the Frontier
lines: A Capital on the Frontier

fields.text:
Few capitals sit as close to their neighbours as Aspneset. The West Norden district touches FATO at the crossings into Granley Tips and Gangl, and Wielvakia at Farnlands and Vakia. Trains, trucks and day workers cross every morning. Until now, each crossing has been run by whichever officials happened to be posted there, using forms nobody has revised in decades.

Neither neighbour has given Nordlands cause for alarm in years, which is exactly why the frontier has been neglected. Smuggling is modest, delays are long and disputes go to ministries that answer letters slowly. Merchants on all three sides have learned to pay their way through, and the customs service has learned to let them. East Granley, Hait Mountain and Oregonen have their own crossings and their own habits.

The government proposes shared customs desks with both neighbours as a first step. Before the desks open, it must decide how to describe them. Presented as a convenience for traders, they will be welcomed by merchants and ignored by everyone else. Presented as a security measure, they will reassure the cautious and make both neighbours wonder what Nordlands has heard.

fields.text: War Beyond FATO
lines: War Beyond FATO

fields.text:
In late March 1995 the Belkan War breaks out. Nordlands has no border with Belka, but FATO does, and FATO shares a long frontier with West Norden and East Granley. Within hours the watch room in Aspneset is taking calls from frontier posts, harbour masters and shipping offices that all want to know the same thing: how close will this come?

The first days bring rumours faster than facts. Radio bulletins contradict one another, insurers raise their rates on every lane near the fighting, and the oil houses ask whether tankers bound for ports near the war should keep sailing. The frontier commands report heavy traffic on the FATO side of the line, though nobody can say whether it is refugees, merchants or soldiers.

The government has said nothing yet beyond confirming that Nordlands is not a party to the war. Every faction wants a statement: the houses want reassurance, the pacifists want a declaration, and the admiralty wants authority to watch the harbour approaches more closely. The first decision is narrower and harder: how much of the government's own uncertainty to share with the public.

fields.text: Warships at the Harbour Mouth
lines: Warships at the Harbour Mouth

fields.text:
A warship of one of the belligerents appears off the Norden Forest coast and signals a request to enter harbour for fuel and repairs. Its captain reports minor damage and a sick crew member. The ship is armed, its flag is unmistakable, and its arrival has been noticed by every fishing boat and newspaper on that stretch of coast before the admiralty has finished reading the signal.

Custom allows a neutral port to admit a belligerent warship in distress for a short time and for limited repairs. It does not oblige the port to do so, and every hour the ship spends alongside will be read by the other side as a favour. The harbour master wants instructions. The shipowners want the ship gone before insurers notice. The doctors want the sick sailor ashore.

Whatever the principality decides will become precedent. Other warships, from either side, will ask for the same treatment and point to this one when they do. The admiralty has drafted three replies, and the government has a few hours before the captain stops waiting for an answer and decides the matter alone.

fields.text: Officers Who Serve No Country
lines: Officers Who Serve No Country

fields.text:
On Christmas Day 1995 a group calling itself A World With No Boundaries launches a coup. Its name is its programme: a movement that rejects the borders of every state. The Allied Forces answer it, and on the last day of the year they attack its V2 facilities at Avalon Dam and defeat the rebellion. The news reaches Aspneset in fragments, and none of the fragments is reassuring.

Nordlands has few officers and fewer secrets, but the coup raises an uncomfortable question. A small, comfortable officer corps that has never fought might be exactly the kind of body in which such ideas could take root quietly. The general staff insists that its officers are loyal. The diet's liberals want an inquiry. The palace wants the matter handled without accusing anyone in particular.

The government can order a quiet review of the officer corps, conducted by the general staff itself, or an open inquiry by a committee of the diet with powers to question anyone. A quiet review protects reputations and may miss everything. An open inquiry will find whatever there is to find, and it will humiliate many officers who have done nothing wrong.

fields.text: Pilots Without an Air Force
lines: Pilots Without an Air Force

fields.text:
By the summer of 1998 former top pilots of the Belkan Air Force have found new employers. Various countries hire them to fly as aggressor squadrons, playing the enemy in training so that their own crews learn what a skilled opponent feels like. Agents for some of these pilots are now in Aspneset, offering a contract the Nordlandic air arm never imagined being offered.

The air arm's commanders are enthusiastic. Their pilots have never flown against anyone better than each other, and a few months against veterans would teach them more than years of exercises. The diet is divided. Some deputies object to paying veterans of a war that frightened the whole region, and others note that the pilots are selling their skill, not their politics.

The palace wants a decision before the agents take their offer elsewhere. Whatever the government chooses, the air arm will remember it. A contract buys skill quickly and invites a public argument about whose veterans should teach Nordlandic pilots. A refusal keeps the argument out of the papers and asks the air arm to build its own teachers, slowly.

fields.text: Ulysses Will Strike
lines: Ulysses Will Strike

fields.text:
In April 1996 the President of the FCU tells the world that the asteroid Ulysses will strike the Earth and announces plans to counter it. Nobody can yet say where its fragments will fall. Nordlands has eight coastal districts, one inland capital and a coastline no wall could protect, and the country wakes to the news that its future depends on the arithmetic of orbits.

The advisers divide along familiar lines. Engineers propose shelters dug under the larger cities and stocked for weeks. Planners propose evacuation timetables and early warning, arguing that a few hours of notice, well used, are worth more than tunnels. The treasury observes that either plan costs as much as a decade of fleet construction, and the yards observe that their own orders would be the first delayed.

The public mood swings between panic and denial. Places of worship are crowded, shops sell out of tinned food, and some coastal families talk of moving inland. Before choosing a plan, the government must decide how to speak about a danger it cannot control: openly and immediately, or calmly and only once its plans are ready.

fields.text: Nine Districts, One Treasury
lines: Nine Districts, One Treasury

fields.text:
The district ledger is finished, and it confirms what everyone outside the capital suspected. West Norden and Norden Forest hold most of the population and most of the public spending. The Nord Peninsula, which holds most of the oil, has the fewest schools and the worst roads. Tenese, Oregonen and the twin harbours of Djurseryd and Havnaraas earn much of the shipping income and complain that it is spent elsewhere.

Every district can read the ledger as a grievance. East Granley and Hait Mountain sit on the frontier and feel watched rather than served. Haugaland's villages share their roads with oil trucks and arms convoys. The capital district pays the most tax and is blamed for the most decisions, which its residents consider doubly unfair.

The ministers must decide how the ledger will be used. They could publish it district by district and invite every council to argue its case in public, or keep it inside the ministries and use it to steer spending quietly. The first starts a long argument the capital cannot control; the second leaves every district suspecting that it is being cheated by the others.

fields.text: The Principality at Ten Years
lines: The Principality at Ten Years

fields.text:
Ten years after the crown first took stock of its own powers, an independent commission publishes its review of how Nordlands governs itself. Its members, drawn by lot from judges, harbour officials and district deputies, were given access to every ministry. Their report runs to several volumes, and the summary alone is longer than most newspapers are willing to print.

The findings please nobody completely. The principality is richer, its frontier is quiet and its fleet still exists, which is all the fleet ever promised. But the commission finds too much power in too few offices, too much revenue in a handful of houses and districts, and a younger generation that takes the calm for granted. It warns that the arrangements of the nineties were built for a quiet decade, and the region has not been quiet.

The government must decide how to receive the report. It can publish every volume unedited and accept a season of hostile commentary, or release an approved summary and let the rest gather dust in the archive. Either way the review will frame political argument for years, and the factions have already chosen their favourite paragraphs.

lines: A War on Another Continent

fields.text: Contraband on the Frontier Roads
lines: Contraband on the Frontier Roads

fields.text:
The frontier police, given a week and every spare officer, sweep the back roads between the guarded crossings. They find what everyone expected and a little more: trucks of untaxed fuel heading out, cigarettes and electronics coming in, and a warehouse near the Wielvakian frontier stacked with goods whose papers were signed by officials who should have known better.

The sweep is a success by any measure the police care about. It is also an embarrassment. Several signatures belong to customs officers who have served for decades, and one belongs to a district official with friends in the capital. Merchants on both sides of the frontier are angry that honest trade was held up for a week, and the neighbours' customs services want to know why they were not told in advance.

The government can prosecute everyone the sweep uncovered, publicly and at once, and accept the political damage. Or it can settle quietly, dismissing the officials and recovering the taxes without trials. The first shows that the guarded frontier means what it says. The second keeps the peace with the districts and with both neighbours.

fields.text: The Crown Question
lines: The Crown Question

fields.text:
The session opens in the old throne hall at Gatewood with the usual music and an unusual agenda. For the first time in living memory the clerks have placed the government itself on the order paper. Perbla is a kingdom of four crown lands held together by one throne, a century-old service year and an economy that leans on its arms plants. Each of those pillars now has a faction that wants it rebuilt.

The constitutional camp wants ministers who answer to an elected chamber. The palace party wants the seals returned to a privy council that can act without waiting for votes. A harder faction speaks of order above all, of a crown that governs by decree because elected governments always drift back to greed. Deputies from the outer lands ask whether the crown needs to govern at all, or only to reign.

None of these camps commands a majority today. What the court decides in this first session is not which answer wins, but how the question will be argued: in the open, with the chamber and the press watching, or behind the palace doors. Either way, the arms trusts, the officer corps and the four lands are already counting their friends.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Four Lands, One Throne
lines: Four Lands, One Throne

fields.text:
The census clerks return from the crown lands with trunks of ledgers and a list of complaints. Serenava, the frontier land facing Osea, says it carries the kingdom's airfields and bunker lines but receives little else. Terentio, spread between the desert fields and the northern coast, reports towns that still haul their water by truck. Relentio, home of the great port of Sofern, wants its harbour councils recognised and its customs revenue respected.

Perbla proper, around Gatewood and the old heartland, has its own grievance: it pays most of the taxes and is blamed for most of the decisions. The old charters that bind the four lands disagree with one another about courts, the language of record and who may levy what. Every land can quote a charter that favours it, and most of them do.

Ministers must decide how to present the census. Published in full, it will start a long argument about fairness that the crown cannot control. Kept for the ministries, it will guide policy quietly while every land suspects the worst. The crown lands have lived together for generations; the question is whether they will keep doing so out of loyalty or out of habit.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Unfinished Plants
lines: The Unfinished Plants

fields.text:
The audit teams have walked every arms plant in the kingdom, and their report is long. The last expansion left halls without roofs, presses delivered but never installed, and payrolls for production lines that exist only on paper. Arms output still dominates the economy, which means the waste is not a side issue. In many districts it is the economy.

Economists have warned for years that a sector this large and this fragile could take the whole kingdom down with it if a big customer vanished or a major firm failed. The audit puts numbers on that warning. Some plants can be finished cheaply; others should never have been started. A handful of contractors were paid twice for the same work, and the trusts would very much like that paragraph removed.

The treasury wants the audit to become the foundation of a new industrial model, whatever that model turns out to be. The trusts want it treated as a confidential briefing. The officer corps asks only that nothing be closed before it knows what it would lose. The cabinet has the report on the table and must decide who else gets to read it.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: One Firm, One Kingdom
lines: One Firm, One Kingdom

fields.text:
The study on the national electronics firm arrives with a plain title and an alarming summary. The firm makes nearly every circuit the army uses and most of those in civilian industry, from radios to factory controls. It is famous abroad and proud at home. If it failed, the study concludes, whole sectors would stop within weeks for lack of parts.

The firm's board insists it is healthy and that the study insults a national success. Its few rivals say the firm uses its size to starve them of contracts. The defence staff says it does not care who is right; it wants a second source for anything that keeps an aircraft flying or a radar turning. The university at Gatewood says it could train twice the engineers if it had laboratories outside the firm's gates.

The government now has to decide what kind of partner the crown should be to the kingdom's most important company. It can back the firm as a national champion, or it can work patiently to make the kingdom less dependent on it. Either path takes years, and the firm's board will be reading every line of the cabinet minutes.

fields.text: The Service Year Debate
lines: The Service Year Debate

fields.text:
For more than a century every young Perblan has spent a year in uniform. The policy was built to match the size of Osea's forces, and it has given the kingdom an enormous pool of trained reservists. It has also given it barracks that flood every spring, a training budget larger than some ministries and a year of every worker's youth spent away from fields and factories.

The general staff wants the year kept and modernised; in its view, the frontier with Osea has not moved and neither should the policy. Employers and many families want it shortened or made voluntary, arguing that a growing economy needs young workers more than parade grounds. A third group proposes that conscripts be allowed to serve in civil brigades building roads and wells in the poorer crown lands.

The royal review must hear all of them before it recommends anything. How it is run matters as much as what it concludes: a review led by generals will be trusted by the army and doubted by everyone else, while a review open to employers and families will be trusted by the public and resented in the officers' messes.

fields.text: War Beyond the Frontier
lines: War Beyond the Frontier

fields.text:
In the spring of 1995 the long crisis around Belka becomes open war. Perbla is not a party to it, yet it can hardly stand apart from it in spirit. Belka has been the kingdom's oldest friend for generations, and the Belkan munitions branch at Gatewood employs thousands. Osea, the largest neighbour, sits directly across the Serenava frontier, and the service year was built a century ago to match its army.

The first days bring rumours faster than facts. Radio bulletins contradict each other, foreign embassies ask what Perbla intends, and shipping insurers raise their rates on every lane near the war. Frontier commanders in Serenava report heavy traffic on the far side of the line, though nobody can say whether it is guarding or preparing. In the capital, crowds gather outside newspaper offices waiting for the evening editions.

The crown has opened a war room in Gatewood and placed the frontier commands on watch. It has not yet said where its sympathies lie, and every faction is pressing for a statement. The government's first task is smaller and harder: to decide how much of its own uncertainty it should share with the public.

fields.text: The Old Alliance Debated
lines: The Old Alliance Debated

fields.text:
Behind closed doors, the court takes up the question every officers' mess has argued since the war began: what does Perbla owe Belka? The friendship between the two nations is old enough to be ceremonial and warm enough to be real. Belkan contracts keep the munitions branch at Gatewood busy, and many senior officers trained beside Belkan colleagues. Osea, by long habit, is the neighbour the kingdom plans against.

A loud minority wants more than sympathy. They speak of a second front, of a brother nation in its hour of need, of honour. Others answer that any second front would be fought on Perblan soil, along the Serenava bunkers, against a neighbour many times larger. The ports and converted factories, which trade across the frontier every day, want no part of it. The crown listens to all of them and says very little.

The decision recorded today is a statement of policy, not a declaration of war. Any armed intervention would be a separate and grave act, taken only if the war itself forced the question. What the court can settle now is the tone: how warmly Perbla speaks of its old friend, and how carefully it speaks to its larger neighbour.

fields.text: Ulysses in the Night Sky
lines: Ulysses in the Night Sky

fields.text:
Since the astronomers' warning of December 1994, the asteroid called Ulysses has been a distant worry. In April 1996 it becomes a near one, when the world is told that it will strike the Earth and that nations must prepare. Nobody can yet say where the fragments will fall. Perbla, like every country, has to plan for a danger whose location is still a guess.

The crown's advisers split along familiar lines. Engineers propose deep shelters under the large cities, stocked for weeks. Astronomers and radar specialists propose early warning and evacuation instead, arguing that hours of notice save more lives than concrete. The treasury notes that either plan costs as much as a new arms programme, and the arms trusts note that their own plans would be delayed.

Public mood swings between panic and denial. Places of worship are full, hardware shops sell out of tinned food, and some families on the coast talk of moving inland. The government must decide how to speak about a threat it cannot control, and whether its first priority is calm or preparation. Both, the ministers know, cannot be bought at once.

Provisional gameplay: date anchors only, ACES Chronicle rows 1994 / 12.10 and 1996 / 04.20 in docs/research/CHRONICLE_INDEX.md; Perblan preparations are gameplay.

fields.text: Oil Under Terentio
lines: Oil Under Terentio

fields.text:
The geological survey of the Terentio desert is finished, and its maps are better than anyone hoped. The fields hold far more oil than the old rigs suggested, and the bauxite beds stretch toward Torre Mountain. For a kingdom that has lived on arms contracts, the desert offers a second income that does not depend on anyone else's war.

The question is who will own it. A crown company would keep the revenue at home but drill slowly, managed by ministries with other priorities. Private concessions would bring rigs and foreign capital within a few years but hand the desert's future to shareholders. Terentio's own towns, which have hauled water by truck for generations, want to know what share of the wealth will stay where it is pumped.

Investors are already calling the ministry, and some are offering terms that sound generous until the fine print. The trusts want first claim on the steel and power the new fields will need. Before any model is chosen, the government must decide whether to slow the rush or welcome it, knowing that whatever it says this week will be quoted in every negotiation that follows.

fields.text: Ten Years On
lines: Ten Years On

fields.text:
A decade after the crown question was first opened, an independent panel publishes its review of how the kingdom governs itself. It lists what the chosen order has built, whom it has failed and what it now costs to run. The panel includes judges, economists and deputies from all four crown lands, and its members were chosen by lot rather than by the government of the day.

The findings are mixed in ways every faction can quote. The industrial towns are richer and the frontier is calm, but the outer lands still feel governed from Gatewood, young graduates still leave for jobs abroad, and too many decisions depend on a handful of offices and firms. The panel warns that the next decade will test whether the arrangements of the nineties can bend without breaking.

The government must decide how to answer. It can publish the review unedited and accept a season of hostile headlines, or release an approved summary that highlights success and buries the rest. Either way, the review will set the terms of political argument for the new century, and every faction already has its quotations ready.

fields.text: The Monday Morning Exercise
lines: The Monday Morning Exercise

fields.text:
At six on a Monday morning the treasury opens the sealed rescue plan and runs it as though the national electronics firm had missed its payroll. Banks are told to freeze credit lines, suppliers are told to expect no payment, and the defence staff is asked which aircraft would be grounded first. Nobody outside the exercise is supposed to know.

By noon the gaps are obvious. The emergency credit line takes three days to clear rather than three hours. Two critical radar parts have no second source after all. The plan assumed the firm's managers would cooperate, and in the exercise they did not. By evening a newspaper has the story, and the firm's investors begin a nervous week of phone calls to the ministry.

The exercise has done its job: it found the failures before a real crisis did. Now the government must decide what to do with what it learned. It can close the gaps quietly and deny the leak, or publish the lessons and accept that the firm's reputation will take a knock. The defence staff has already said which it prefers, and the firm's board has said the opposite.

fields.text: A Neighbour at War
lines: A Neighbour at War

fields.text:
In late September 2010 Yuktobania declares war on Osea and attacks an Osean port. Perbla wakes to the news that its largest neighbour, the country its service year was built to match, is fighting a war that has nothing to do with the Serenava frontier. For once, Osea's guns point away from Perbla.

The consequences arrive anyway. Shipping insurers raise rates on every lane that touches Osean waters. Osean buyers call Perblan factories asking for trucks, electronics and munitions, and they want them now. Yuktobanian diplomats ask pointed questions about what Perbla intends to sell. Frontier towns that live on trade with Osea worry about their customers, and harbour masters worry about submarines.

The security council meets in Gatewood to decide the kingdom's posture. Some ministers see a commercial opportunity that may not come again. Others see a trap: a neutral kingdom that sells to one side of a war is no longer neutral in the eyes of the other. The first decision is how to describe Perbla's position in public, before Osean and Yuktobanian newspapers describe it for the kingdom.

fields.text: Drones Over the Harbours
lines: Drones Over the Harbours

fields.text:
On 15 May 2019 drone attacks strike four major Osean naval ports, and on the same day Erusea declares war on Osea. The footage from the Osean harbours is everywhere by evening: small, cheap aircraft slipping past defences built for missiles and bombers. Perbla's own harbours at Sofern and Baleton are smaller, but they are built the same way.

The security council meets the same night. The navy reports that its harbour defences could not reliably stop a swarm of small drones. The engineers at Gatewood argue that most such drones depend on radio links and satellite navigation that could be jammed. The ports' owners ask who will pay for any of it, and the ministers ask how long it would take.

Nobody in the room expects Perbla to be a target. That is precisely what worries the navy: the Osean ports did not expect it either. The government must decide whether to treat this as a distant war's lesson or as an immediate warning, and the answer will shape a decade of spending. Whatever it chooses, the harbour masters want an answer before the summer shipping season begins.

fields.text: Who Governs Relentio
lines: Who Governs Relentio

fields.text:
The chamber meets for its first full session in a hall borrowed from the Sofern harbour councils, because no building in Relentio was designed to hold a national parliament. The ducal office sends its clerk with a short message: the seals are kept, the coast guard is paid and a budget will follow. Everything else, the message says, is for the chamber to argue.

And argue it does. Shipowners from Sofern want a government that moves as quickly as a freight market. Deputies from the Relentio valley around Driscol want protection for the arms halls and the wages they pay. The Torre Mountain districts, smallest of all, want a guarantee that the coast will not outvote them on every question. A few voices ask whether a ducal crown suits a state of merchants at all.

No camp holds a majority today. What the session can decide is how the question will be argued: openly, with the press gallery full and every speech printed, or quietly, in committee rooms where bargains are easier to strike and harder to explain. Either way, the shipping lines, the valley unions and the officer corps are already counting their friends.

fields.text: The Sofern Customs Count
lines: The Sofern Customs Count

fields.text:
For a full season the customs clerks of Sofern have counted everything: every container, sack and barrel that crosses the quays, every receipt issued and every receipt that should have been. Their tally lands on the minister's desk in four thick volumes and a one-page summary that nobody in the harbour wanted written.

The port is busier than the old books admitted. Duty that ought to reach the treasury has leaked through favours, private storage deals and gate staff whose wages never matched their houses. The harbour councils insist that most of the leak is custom rather than crime, and that the port would stall if every old arrangement ended overnight. Shipping agents warn that foreign lines are watching how Relentio treats its largest asset.

The government has to choose how to use what it now knows. It can publish the count and let the press and the chamber chase the missing money, at the cost of a bruising year on the quays. Or it can use the figures quietly to renegotiate with the councils, gaining revenue without headlines and leaving the old arrangements half intact.

fields.text: The First Relentian Budget
lines: The First Relentian Budget

fields.text:
The first Relentian budget is presented to the chamber on a grey morning, printed on paper ordered in a hurry and bound with string. It lists customs receipts, a patchwork of valley taxes and a long column of obligations that the government must honour before it can promise anything new. The finance office reads it aloud in under an hour; the debate takes three weeks.

Deputies from Sofern want lower duties to keep the shipping lines loyal. Valley deputies want credit for the arms halls and their suppliers. Torre Mountain wants its haul road. Everyone wants the coast guard paid and nobody wants to pay for it. Foreign banks send polite letters asking about the state's intentions, and the polite tone fools no one about what the letters mean.

The government must decide what kind of first impression to make. A lean budget with no borrowing would reassure lenders and disappoint almost everyone at home. A budget that borrows to set the ports and the valley moving would please the chamber and test the patience of creditors who have never lent to Relentio before. The finance office has drafted both versions and waits for a decision.

fields.text: Silence in the Valley Halls
lines: Silence in the Valley Halls

fields.text:
The inspection team returns from the Relentio valley and Torre Mountain with notebooks full of numbers and photographs of empty floors. Some halls run three shifts on orders signed long ago. Others stand idle with their machines oiled and covered, waiting for contracts that were meant for a much larger army. A few were never finished at all.

Around Driscol the halls are the economy. Shops, schools and bus routes exist because the plants pay wages, and every rumour of closure empties the cafes. At Torre Mountain the arms lines sit beside the ore beds and a haul road that barely survives each winter. The unions want guarantees, the managers want orders and the banks want to know who will pay if neither arrives.

The government must decide how to speak about the valley before it decides what to do there. A frank statement that some halls will close would let planning begin and frighten thousands of families. A promise that every hall has a future would buy calm now and make every later choice more expensive. The banks are waiting for the answer as eagerly as the unions.

fields.text: Envoys at Gatewood
lines: Envoys at Gatewood

fields.text:
The Relentian envoys travel to Gatewood with a list of practical questions and instructions to avoid grand ones. Who pays the pensions of officials who served the crown lands? Which court hears a dispute between a Sofern shipper and a Perblan buyer? How do freight trains clear a frontier desk that older timetables never had to allow for?

The envoys are received correctly and carefully. Both peoples share courts, schools, family ties and a long habit of doing business together, and neither government wants a quarrel that would block the rails or the quays. Yet both also know that every agreement signed now becomes a precedent, and that their own chambers will read each clause looking for concessions. Officials keep the old shared files open on the table between them, because nobody yet knows which records belong to whom.

The envoys must decide what tone to set. They can ask for a broad settlement covering trade, transit and pensions in one package, which would take longer and risk a single failure sinking everything. Or they can settle small matters one at a time, building trust slowly and leaving the hardest questions for later governments.

fields.text: War on the Shipping Lanes
lines: War on the Shipping Lanes

fields.text:
In the spring of 1995 the crisis around Belka becomes open war. Relentio is not a party to it, and none of its soldiers is anywhere near a front. Its ships are another matter. Within days, freighters bound for Sofern report warships asking for their papers, and insurers in foreign markets publish new war-risk premiums for every lane near the fighting.

The port reacts the way ports always do. Some shipowners lay up their hulls and wait; others raise their rates and sail. Cargo that used to go elsewhere suddenly arrives at Sofern, some of it with paperwork that does not bear close reading. On the third day a freighter under a foreign flag docks with a manifest listing machine parts and a hold that the customs officers are not allowed to see.

The government must decide how hard to look. Holding the ship for a full inspection would show every warring power that Relentian quays are not a convenient back door, and it would start an argument with the ship's owners and their government. Letting it unload with a written warning keeps trade moving and leaves the question of what was in the hold to someone else.

fields.text: The Held Freighter
lines: The Held Freighter

fields.text:
Ten days after the freighter was held, the inspection is complete. Customs officers and marines have opened every container in the hold. Most contain exactly what the manifest promised. Several do not: crated spare parts for military vehicles, packed beneath machine tools and invoiced to a trading company that shares its address with a laundry.

The ship's owners protest that they had no idea, and their government sends a note demanding the vessel's release. Two other governments, on opposite sides of the war, send notes of their own asking what was found. The harbour councils complain that the inspection has frightened other shippers, while the coast guard points out that frightening careless shippers was the whole point.

The parts sit in a Relentian shed and the ship is tied up at a Relentian quay. The government can confiscate the cargo and release the ship, setting a clear rule that will be tested again, or return everything with a formal protest and a fine, keeping the quarrel small and the precedent vague. Whatever it decides will be read in every shipping office on the coast.

fields.text: A Coast Under Ulysses
lines: A Coast Under Ulysses

fields.text:
The announcement of April 1996 turns the asteroid Ulysses from an astronomers' topic into a government's problem. The world is told that the asteroid will strike the Earth and that every nation must prepare, yet nobody can say where its fragments will fall. For a state whose people live almost entirely along the coast, every possible answer is frightening.

Engineers warn about waves as well as impacts: a fragment at sea could push water into the low streets of Sofern and Fraeport. Planners argue for shelters, or for evacuation, or for both, and the treasury reminds them that it cannot buy everything at once. Shipowners ask whether their fleets will be requisitioned. Churches fill, and hardware shops run out of tinned food within a week.

Before it chooses any plan, the government must decide how to speak. It can publish everything it knows and everything it does not, trusting citizens with uncertainty, or it can keep the message calm and short while the experts work. Both approaches have costs, and the first public statement will be quoted back at ministers for years.

fields.text: The Watch Night
lines: The Watch Night

fields.text:
In July 1999 Ulysses passes Earth's Roche limit, and years of preparation turn into nights of watching. Wardens open their posts, ferry and rail crews sleep beside their vehicles, hospital volunteers switch on their generators and observers report every few minutes to the coast guard office. Schools and halls stand open as assembly points, and the trains wait at the platforms with their doors unlocked.

Radio stations stay on the air all night, reading official bulletins between records. Some families go to their assigned places early; others sit on rooftops to watch the sky. Rumours travel faster than reports: a fire on the horizon, a wave sighted off the coast, a ship that has stopped answering. Each one has to be checked before it can be dismissed or acted upon, and the checking exhausts everyone.

The government's plans now meet the real thing. Ministers must decide whether to keep the whole coast on alert until the observatories declare the danger past, at great cost to work and nerves, or to stand most districts down after the first nights, trusting the warning network to call them back if it is needed.

fields.text: An Account of the State
lines: An Account of the State

fields.text:
The panel's report on the state of Relentio is published in one volume with a plain cover. It describes what the government has built since it began governing in its own name: a chamber that meets, a treasury that collects, a coast guard that sails and ports that handle more cargo than the old books ever recorded. It also lists what has not been built.

The valley towns still depend on a handful of buyers. Torre Mountain still feels forgotten by the coast. Young graduates leave for jobs abroad, and too many decisions pass through a few offices and firms. The panel warns that a small state can be agile or fragile, and that the difference lies in whether its institutions can survive a bad year without improvising.

The government must decide how to answer. It can accept the report in full and publish a response to each recommendation, inviting a season of hostile headlines. Or it can thank the panel, highlight its praise and send the criticisms to committee, where they will move slowly if they move at all. The panel members have already said they will tell the press which course the government took.

fields.text: A Trade Mission Returns
lines: A Trade Mission Returns

fields.text:
The trade mission comes home after a month abroad with a folder of business cards, three signed contracts and a much longer list of promises. Valley manufacturers found buyers for rugged vehicles and machine parts. The yard firms found ship operators who want cheaper repairs. The port services sold well everywhere, and the arms halls sold well in places the foreign ministry would rather not discuss.

Every contract comes with a request. One buyer wants credit from the treasury. Another wants a guarantee that deliveries will continue whatever happens at Sofern. A third wants an exclusive agency that would shut out other Relentian firms. The mission leaders insist that small states must say yes more often than large ones; the treasury notes that small states also go bankrupt faster.

The government must decide how to follow up. It can back the new contracts with state export credit, turning promises into orders at some risk to the treasury. Or it can leave the firms to finance their own deals, keeping the state's money safe and accepting that some of the promises will quietly evaporate.

fields.text: An Administration Without a Calendar
lines: An Administration Without a Calendar

fields.text:
The National Administration begins 1991 the way it ended the previous year: governing by ordinance from offices on the capital plain, with no date set for the next election. Its own party, the one that still calls the country a republic, polls almost nobody. The ferries run, the ports collect their dues and the fleet keeps its moorings, but nobody can say on whose mandate any of it happens.

Two great movements fill the space the administration leaves empty. The imperial movement, which wants a Wellowan Empire with one flag and one fleet, claims about half the electorate and fills the port-town halls with petitioners. The union camp, which wants the scattered districts bound together as a United Kingdom under a crown held by their own council, claims nearly all the rest. Both say the administration is a caretaker that has forgotten it was meant to leave.

Senior officials have prepared a statement for the new year. It can promise that the question of government will be settled in public, with hearings in every district and a published record, or it can promise only continuity and ask the country to wait. Neither promise costs anything today. Both will be quoted against the administration for years.

fields.text: The Ferry Season Report
lines: The Ferry Season Report

fields.text:
The district survey comes back as a stack of ledgers from sixteen districts, and the western islands' ledgers arrive last because the ferry carrying them broke down twice. The main island has its capital plain, its industrial districts and a dockyard in the south. Beyond it lie four island districts stretching west and a small islet to the southeast, and most of them have no paved road at all.

The surveyors list the same complaints in different handwriting. Piers built for fishing boats now carry freight. Schools close when the ferry misses a week. Tax offices have files but no clerks, and some districts have clerks but no files. On the northern lowland, the largest district of the main island, villages are separated by marshes that swallow every road the capital has ever paid for.

The surveyors also note that islanders are more patient than the capital deserves. They do not ask for the capital's wealth, only for a timetable that is kept and a road that lasts. The government must decide how to release the survey: as a public promise that will be measured every season, or as an internal plan that can be adjusted without embarrassment.

fields.text: Nine Hundred Hulls
lines: Nine Hundred Hulls

fields.text:
The harbour clerks finish their count of the merchant register and arrive at a number the government had only guessed at: more than nine hundred hulls fly the Wellowan flag. They range from ocean tramps and coastal colliers to ferries, tankers and old trawlers converted to carry freight. Together they earn more foreign currency than every plant on the main island combined.

The count also finds problems. Some owners registered ships that have since been sold abroad without telling anyone. Others pay dues on hulls that were scrapped years ago, to keep their place in the queue for fuel rebates. A handful of entries name owners whose only address is a post office box in a foreign port. Nobody in the harbour offices is sure how many of the nine hundred actually sail.

The shipowners would like the count kept confidential while they put their own books in order. The newspapers have heard about the missing hulls and want names. Whatever the government decides will tell the owners whether the register is a tool of the state or a club they run for themselves, and the owners will remember the answer.

number the government had only guessed at: more than nine hundred hulls fly
the Wellowan flag. They range from ocean tramps and coastal colliers to
ferries, tankers and old trawlers converted to carry freight. Together they earn
more foreign currency than every plant on the main island combined.
The count also finds problems. Some owners registered ships that have since
been sold abroad without telling anyone. Others pay dues on hulls that were
scrapped years ago, to keep their place in the queue for fuel rebates. A handful
of entries name owners whose only address is a post office box in a foreign port.
Nobody in the harbour offices is sure how many of the nine hundred actually
sail.
The shipowners would like the count kept confidential while they put their own
books in order. The newspapers have heard about the missing hulls and want
names. Whatever the government decides will tell the owners whether the
register is a tool of the state or a club they run for themselves, and the owners
will remember the answer.
Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Ghost Hulls
lines: The Ghost Hulls

fields.text:
Three weeks after the register is published, a harbour newspaper prints a list of forty ships that exist only on paper. Some were lost at sea and never struck off; some were sold and renamed abroad; a few appear to have been invented outright to collect fuel rebates. The owners named on the list range from small family firms to two of the largest shipping houses in the capital.

The publication does what the government hoped and what it feared. Honest owners rush to correct their entries, and the harbour offices are flooded with paperwork for the first time in years. The large houses hire lawyers, and their friends in the ministries ask whether the register really needed to be printed in full. Foreign insurers, who read Wellowan newspapers more carefully than anyone expected, quietly raise their premiums.

The prosecutors can pursue the rebate fraud, which would take years and put powerful owners in court, or accept repayment and a fine, which would close the matter within a season. Either way, the register will be cleaner than it has been in a generation, and the owners will know the state is reading it.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: The Western Fields
lines: The Western Fields

fields.text:
The field ledger is complete. It shows three oil-bearing districts on the main island: the western district with its steel works, the capital plain itself and the northeastern marsh. Between them they hold nearly all the nation's oil and steel, worked by wells and furnaces built by different owners at different times for different customers. Nothing about the arrangement was ever planned.

The engineers' summary is blunt. Too much crude leaves the country unrefined, too little steel reaches the dockyard, and the marsh wells lose a season of output to mud every spring. The capital's single fuel depot holds a few weeks of supply for the fleet and the ferries, and nobody has written down who decides when to open it. Three schools of thought have already formed around the ledger, each sure it holds the answer.

Before any model is chosen, the ministry has to decide who will see the ledger. Shared with the owners and the districts, it will start a long argument about royalties and fairness. Kept inside the ministry, it will guide policy quietly while every district suspects the others of being favoured.

fields.text: Six Slips, Three Masters
lines: Six Slips, Three Masters

fields.text:
The dockyard district in the south of the main island has six building slips, and on the morning the inspectors arrive every one of them is claimed by somebody. The navy wants its escort programme restarted. The shipowners want new coasters and ferries for the island routes. The repair crews want the slips cleared so they can stop turning damaged ships away to foreign yards.

The yard managers have a fourth complaint, which is that nobody has asked them. Half their riveters are close to retirement, their cranes were installed when the current escorts were laid down, and their order book is a pile of promises from ministries that change their minds every year. They would like a plan that lasts longer than a budget, and a customer who pays on time.

The government cannot satisfy everyone with six slips. It can let the inspectors fight it out in committee, which will be slow and will leave every party half satisfied, or it can let the yard managers set the priorities for the next season while the larger question is settled. Either choice will be read as a signal by the owners and the admirals alike.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: Belka Sells Its North
lines: Belka Sells Its North

fields.text:
At the end of August 1991 the news from across the narrow sea arrives in a rush: Belka has sold its northern territory to FATO, sold eastern lands to its eastern neighbours and ceded northern islands and the Great Lakes region to the Osean Federation. Shipping agents in the Wellowan ports read the reports twice. Their neighbour to the south is shrinking, and it is selling land rather than losing it in war.

Nobody in the capital knows what the sales mean for Wellow. Some officials expect new customs posts and new flags on the far shore, and new rules for every ship that trades there. Others see a neighbour in financial trouble that will need fuel, ships and credit, and may pay for them badly. A few of the older naval officers simply note that a neighbour reduced this way may one day want to undo it.

The government must decide how loudly to say anything at all. A formal statement would show that Wellow is watching and might be read on the far shore as an opinion. Silence keeps every option open and leaves the ports to guess. The shipowners have already asked which of the new frontiers their masters should prepare for.

fields.text: War Across the Narrow Sea
lines: War Across the Narrow Sea

fields.text:
On 25 March 1995 war breaks out on the continent south of Wellow. The first reports reaching the capital are fragments: Belkan forces moving, air battles over frontier cities, shipping warnings issued and withdrawn within hours. Wellow is not a party to any of it, but the narrow sea between the south coast and Belka is suddenly the busiest and most dangerous water in the region.

The ports react before the ministries do. Shipowners pull their coasters off the southern routes and insurers cancel war cover overnight. Harbour masters on the south coast report unknown aircraft and warships at the edge of the coast watch's sight. In the capital, crowds gather outside newspaper offices, and the imperial and union movements both hold rallies demanding that the government say where it stands.

The cabinet's first decision is smaller than any statement of policy. It must decide whether to put the coast watch, the reserve crews and the radar posts on a war footing now, before anyone can say which way the fighting will go, or to keep the ports calm and the ferries running and wait for clearer news.

fields.text: The First Month of the Watch
lines: The First Month of the Watch

fields.text:
A month after the coast watch went onto a war footing, its commanders send their first report to the capital. Radar posts and lookouts on the south coast have logged hundreds of aircraft and dozens of warships at the edge of their range, most of them heading somewhere else. Twice, damaged aircraft crossed the coastline and came down in the hills before anyone could identify them.

The report is frank about the watch's limits. Its radars cover the southern approaches but not the western islands. Its reserve crews are tired, and the fuel ration for patrol boats runs out before the end of each week. The watch also stopped a fishing boat carrying three civilians who had crossed from the far shore, and nobody had a procedure for what to do with them.

The commanders ask for two things: more patrol fuel, and a rule for people and aircraft that arrive from the war. The ministries can grant the fuel at the expense of the ferries, or write the rules first and leave the patrol boats on their ration a little longer.

fields.text: Light over the Southern Mountains
lines: Light over the Southern Mountains

fields.text:
In the last weeks of the Belkan War instruments on the south coast record something no Wellowan scientist expected to measure outside a textbook. Within hours the news confirms it: nuclear devices have been used in the Waldreich Mountains, far to the south in Belka. Nothing was seen from Wellow, but the sensitive instruments recorded the disturbance, and the meteorologists begin tracking the winds that blow north across the narrow sea toward the south coast and the fishing grounds.

The capital fills with questions faster than the scientists can answer them. Will anything reach the islands? Are the fishing grounds safe? Should children stay indoors? The newspapers print wind maps drawn by amateurs, and pharmacies run out of anything that sounds like protection. The imperial movement demands a national defence against weapons nobody in Wellow possesses, and the union camp demands a public accounting of every reading.

The meteorologists believe the risk to Wellow is small, but they cannot yet prove it. The government can publish every reading as it arrives, including the frightening ones, or release only checked summaries once a day. Trust and calm are both at stake, and the ministers suspect they cannot have both.

fields.text: One Army, Sixteen Districts
lines: One Army, Sixteen Districts

fields.text:
The garrison review lands on the defence minister's desk with a map that every officer in the capital already knew but nobody had drawn. Most of Wellow's infantry formations sit on the main island, within a day's march of the capital plain. The four western island districts and the southeastern islet are defended by a few companies, a coast watch and the hope that nobody tests them.

Moving troops to the islands means ships, and ships belong to the navy or the merchant owners, neither of whom has planned for it. The northwestern highlands of the main island are mountain country where wheeled transport struggles, and the northern lowland is half marsh. The army's equipment was bought for a plain, and most of the nation is not one.

Two schools have formed in the general staff. One wants a battalion raised and kept in every district, so that no island is ever empty. The other wants fewer, better brigades that travel by sea on the ferries and colliers. The minister must decide which school writes the next year's training plan while the larger question is argued.

Provisional gameplay.

fields.text: A Rock with a Name
lines: A Rock with a Name

fields.text:
In December 1994 the International Astronomical Union announces that an asteroid called Ulysses will pass close to the Earth, with a chance of striking it and causing great devastation. In Wellow the announcement is a radio bulletin between the shipping forecast and the evening news. By the next morning it is the only subject in the port taverns.

Nobody can yet say where, or whether, anything will fall. The few astronomers in the capital are suddenly the most quoted people in the country, and they spend most of their interviews explaining what they do not know. Shipowners ask whether ocean routes will close. Island districts ask whether the ferries will still run. The imperial movement asks why Wellow has no rockets of its own.

The government must decide how to speak about a danger that may not arrive for years, and may not arrive at all. It can set up a standing committee to prepare openly, which will keep the subject in the newspapers, or ask the observatories to report privately until there is something certain to announce. Either way, the shipowners will want to know before the public does.

fields.text: Instructors for Hire
lines: Instructors for Hire

fields.text:
By the summer of 1998 former top pilots of the Belkan Air Force are being hired by various countries to fly as aggressor squadrons, playing the enemy so that other air arms can learn to fight one. A contracting agent arrives in the capital with an offer: a squadron of such instructors, with their own aircraft and maintainers, available to the Wellowan air arm on a three-year contract.

The air staff is tempted. Its pilots have never trained against anyone better than themselves, and the instructors would expose every weakness in a season. The foreign ministry is not. Hiring former Belkan pilots, whatever their individual records, will be read on both sides of the narrow sea as a statement, and nobody can say who else these instructors have worked for.

There is a cheaper middle course: send a handful of Wellowan instructors abroad to train against such squadrons elsewhere, and bring the lessons home. It is slower and teaches fewer pilots, but it keeps the contract and its politics out of the capital. The air staff wants an answer before the agent leaves.

fields.text: A Relief Convoy Sails
lines: A Relief Convoy Sails

fields.text:
The chartered relief convoy assembles in the dockyard district: colliers and coasters loaded with grain, fuel, tents and medicine, escorted by a single navy escort flying a relief pennant. Crews were found by volunteer lists posted in every port, and the lists filled faster than the harbour offices could type them up. The owners lent their ships at cost, and some lent them for nothing.

The voyage is long and the destination uncertain. Ports in the stricken regions have their own priorities, and some have no working cranes at all. The convoy's masters carry instructions to unload wherever they are allowed, to take nothing in return and to leave before they become a burden. Insurers have refused to cover the voyage, so the state carries the risk.

When the convoy returns, the government must decide how to tell the story. It can make the voyage a national occasion, with ceremonies in every port and a medal for the crews, or let the crews come home quietly and let the ports tell it themselves. The owners would like the publicity. The crews mostly want sleep.

fields.text: Insurers Price a Distant War
lines: Insurers Price a Distant War

fields.text:
In August 2003 the FCU demands that Erusea withdraw from the railgun complex and San Salvacion, and a new allied force is established. The war that follows is fought on another continent, far from Wellow's waters. Within a week, though, the insurers who cover Wellowan hulls have rewritten their premiums for every route that touches Usea.

Owners face a choice between turning down cargo and paying war-risk premiums that eat most of the profit. Some charterers offer double rates for fuel and supplies bound for the war zone, and do not say whose forces will receive them. The navy points out that Wellow has no escorts to spare for a voyage that long. The ferries, at least, are untouched, and the island districts barely notice.

The government cannot stop a distant war, but it can decide what Wellowan ships may carry into it. It can issue a clear list of forbidden cargo now, or let the register and the insurers sort it out and intervene only when something goes wrong. The shipowners are lobbying for the second, and the newspapers for the first.

fields.text: Fifteen Years of the Register
lines: Fifteen Years of the Register

fields.text:
In the autumn of 2005, with the war over Usea ended and the ports counting their losses and gains, an independent panel publishes a review of how Wellow has been governed since 1991. Its members were drawn by lot from the districts, the shipowners, the dockyard unions and the polytechnic. Its report runs to three volumes and a short summary that every newspaper prints.

The panel finds a country that kept its ships at sea and its ferries running through a Belkan war, an asteroid and a distant continent's war, but one that still governs its outer districts from too far away. The register is cleaner, the yards busier and the fields better managed than they were in 1991. The question of government that opened the period still divides the port towns, whatever answer the capital has given it.

The government must decide how to receive the report. It can adopt the summary as a programme for the next decade and accept being measured against it, or thank the panel and leave the volumes on the shelf. Either way, the report will be quoted in every argument that follows.

fields.text: Nation In Pieces
lines: Nation In Pieces

fields.text: Our nation is in pain. The continued overspending on the military has wrecked our economy, which in turn has caused businesses to downsize, laying off workers, making them spend less, further drying up economic growth, causing company after company to close their doors. Without the goods and services offered by many of these companies, it has gotten harder and harder for our citizens to source food, pay bills, or provide for their families. This, in turn, has caused drastically increased radicalization and polarization of our populace, who turn to radical idealisms as their only hope of change. Even worse, due to our nation being in this state for quite some time, even our resources in the government are now beginning to run thin.

fields.text: People On The Streets
lines: People On The Streets

fields.text: The scope of the protests is far greater than we ever imagined. Nearly every day has some kind of major protest happening somewhere in our country, and crimes have also seen exponential growth compared to when this all began. Masses of people are calling for all sorts of demands, from more reform programs all the way to calls for outright revolution. The silver lining in this is that the sheer mass of protesters makes them unable to unite or organize effectively, making them less of a threat than an organized group. Regardless, this will only buy us some time, as if we continue to leave this issue unresolved they will no doubt find a way to organize.

fields.text: Economy Long Gone
lines: Economy Long Gone

fields.text: Our economy has had negative growth for over a year now, and the effects are extremely obvious. The vast majority of our nation lives below the poverty line, as the middle class has been all but obliterated. More than half of the small businesses in the country have closed, and about a third of the large businesses went bankrupt or were bought out. International companies and investors saw the writing on the wall long ago and have left for greener pastures, meaning there's no external group we can use to leverage ourselves back onto our feet. Worst of all, now our own funds in the government have begun to dry up, and we've had to downsize our own government and print larger amounts of currency to offset our expenses. However, even that is wearing thin and the inflation is devaluing our money faster than we can print enough to compensate it.

fields.text: Mass Exodus
lines: Mass Exodus

fields.text: Unemployment is only the tip of the iceberg. Workers, scientists, doctors, lawyers, even our own officials are emigrating to other countries to find work, and at an alarming rate. The lack of job opportunities in Belka is causing workers to look elsewhere, even outside their home country, to provide for their families. Some are even taking their families with them. Houses run empty and border checkpoints are crowded as people scramble to exit the country. Not only have we lost our workforce, but we will be unable to recover them if we cannot stop this outflow of people. If this keeps up, there won't even be a Belka to revive.

fields.text: Complete Collapse
lines: Complete Collapse

fields.text: It appears, ironically, that our last efforts to take inventory on the crisis pushed us over the tipping point. Our budget this month was unable to meet the expenses, and as a result we, as a nation, are in complete bankruptcy. As our officials find out, many are simply getting up and leaving. We are completely powerless and at the whims of whatever the future brings. The only influence we have is off goodwill alone, and that will not get us far. The future is dark.

fields.text: Government Falls Apart
lines: Government Falls Apart

fields.text: The word is out. The jig is up. Everyone knows about the state of the government, and almost everyone in any position of power has either been forced out or simply walked out. Belka is in a state of anarchy. It is impossible to even tell what is happening in the country because all sources of information we could use is gone or takes orders from someone new now. Dinsmark is empty.

fields.text: New Elections, New Rule
lines: New Elections, New Rule

fields.text: After the collapse of the BCNP's administration, an emergency election was called by the Alternative Wege to regain control of the government. Unsurprisingly, they came out on top, with the BNCP scattered between the DLP, Wege itself, and the rest joining the monarchist movement. With the liberals now in power and promising to fix the mistakes of the past no matter how difficult it may be, a sliver of hope has returned that new leaders may bring about change.

fields.text: Osean Proposition
lines: Osean Proposition

fields.text: Our longtime rival, the Osean Federation, have approached us with an interesting offer. In return for giving several of our eastern territories to the neighboring countries, and selling a portion of the Great Lakes to Osea itself, the Oseans will pay us a rather high sum of money, giving us the ability to start some recovery programs. Osea has even expressed that they would be willing to lease many of the resources in the area to us through a joint resource excavation company. Some in the government are suspicious of this deal, since it's unlikley that Osea would offer us such a deal without a clear benefit to them, but others are hopeful that it could be the beginning of a new era of cooperation between our nations, as well as our lifeline to save our nation. It is a rather humiliating deal to take, but what other choice do we have?

fields.text: Selling Of The Land
lines: Selling Of The Land

fields.text: With all the paperwork in place, we've agreed to the Oseans' proposal and are preparing to remove our forces from the land. The transactions have been made and we now have enough money to get a few programs going. For their cooperation, [BLK.GetLeader] has suggested we take the Oseans up on their joint resource company offer, something that will give us a reliable income from which to rebuild the rest of our country off of.

fields.text: GLRDC Goes Live
lines: GLRDC Goes Live

fields.text: The Great Lakes Resource Development Company opened up today, marking our second cooperation with the Oseans. Early reports have showed us promising amounts of resources in the area, meaning this will likely be a very lucrative deal. Digging has begun and we've invested more of our money into the program to see a profit as quickly as we can. Things are looking up for us, we may just be able to refloat our economy with this.

fields.text: The Results Are In
lines: The Results Are In

fields.text:
They lied to us. 

 The Oseans lied to us about the resources. There weren't even any to begin with in that area. To add insult to injury, we're getting reports in the eastern countries that the territories we sold have plentiful resources in them, that now those countries are exploiting to their full potential. We are now down almost all the money we got from the original deal, and now there does not appear to be any sort of tool or program we can use to save ourselves.

fields.text: Total Anarchy
lines: Total Anarchy

fields.text: After the news of the Osean scam got out, the public has been whirled back into a frenzy, and our attempts at damage control seem to have completely failed. We've run out of money again, and now the [BLK.GetRulingParty] is seeing mass defections to the communists and monarchists. The public is completely uncontrollable and the nation is in complete anarchy.

fields.text: New Power At The Top
lines: New Power At The Top

fields.text: Over the past few days, an intense battle between the DLP and the monarchists ensued across the country, with the DLP now the undisputed dominant power in the country. With the DLP's support in the military assisting them, they have secured control over all apparatuses of state and now are the new leaders of the country, with most of the opposition imprisoned or jailed. With its third government in the last few months, it remains to be seen if the DLP will solve any of the issues plaguing the country.

fields.text: Many People, One Nation, One Goal
lines: Many People, One Nation, One Goal

fields.text: Belka has been wounded, not just by her enemies but also by her own supposed leaders, each of whom pulled her apart seeking their own goals. The failiures of the previous governments showed they were not fit to lead Belka. Now it is our turn. We will unite the people and raise Belka from the ashes, ascendent to the top of the world. With no one left to stand in our way, the DLP will restore Belka to its former glory and beyond. We have much to do, and the people's patience is thin because of the past, so we must waste no time in getting to work. Many of our members have already put forward ideas to start our recovery, which will provide us with a head start on our recovery.

fields.text: The 2 Year Plan
lines: The 2 Year Plan

fields.text: After intense discussion, we have arrived at a conclusion on how to start our reconstruction. While the military is all we have left, and is necessary for our self-preservation, this is exactly what we will use to our advantage. Converting a large amount of our military production into civilan will allow us to start economic growth without many funds to go off of, and our military is powerful enough as it is to ward off any potential invasions from Osea. This will upset the militarist faction in our government, but in all likelyhood they will come around when our economy recovers, which we can use to expand the military from once again.

fields.text: Magic Of Bureaucracy
lines: Magic Of Bureaucracy

fields.text: Through some decisive means, we've found a way to get back at those wretched Oseans. We still technically have a share in the Great Lakes Resource Development Company, but who said we have to use it for that purpose? Using some underhanded methods and pulling strings, we've managed to convert some of the resources used in that project to produce some industry for our own benefit. This will only work for so long before either the Oseans find out and shut down the company, or the company itself dries up, but it's a nice boost, and one that sticks it to the Oseans.

fields.text: Harsh Countermeasures
lines: Harsh Countermeasures

fields.text: Getting jobs for the unemployed is a rather large task, however a mitigation we can use to still get some usable labor is by introducing forced labor and community service for prisoners in our nation. To bolster these numbers, we have criminalized emigration and remaining unemployed, which should hopefully give us an edge against unemployment, at the cost of some public opinion.

fields.text: Regulate Trade Policy
lines: Regulate Trade Policy

fields.text: To recover our economy, we'll need to prompt trade with other nations, but we need to make sure we're gaining a strong profit from it. Rather than allow companies to do free business, we'll make sure that any trade goes through us before it is approved, allowing us to take a cut of the sale, letting us improve the economy itself. With any luck, this process will repeat exponentially, encouraging investors despite the tax of our government on their transactions.

fields.text: Clashes Within The Party
lines: Clashes Within The Party

fields.text: We always expected opposition, at least from the public, and from within our own party to an extent, but we didn't expect it to be around this long. We've begun a number of recovery programs and are already seeing the first fruits of recovery, and yet the militarist faction of our government led by Waldemarr Rald has only dissented louder and louder with each reform that we make, cutting into the military's budget. Unfortunately for us, many of the close-minded officers and generals in the Belkan Armed Forces are seeing these budget cuts as attacks on their livelihood and siding with Rald. It's begun to affect our ability in decision-making, meaning we'll likely need to find a way to please Rald and his militarists.

fields.text: Support In The Military
lines: Support In The Military

fields.text: Almost as soon as we began discussing possible resolutions with Rald, he seems to have disappeared, as well as most of his supporters. We're unsure if they're plotting something, are attempting to force our cabinet into stasis by not meeting the seat count, or if they simply gave up, but in any case it seems the issue resolved itself. Worryingly, many of the heads of the Armed Forces have come forward announcing support for Rald, but despite this outflow of support he has yet to make any appearances.

fields.text: The Coup
lines: The Coup

fields.text: Early yesterday morning, during a regular meeting between Lehmann and several members of the Assembly, a division of the Belkan Army stormed the Dinsmark Parliment Building, capturing those inside and killing any security forces or politicians who resisted. Over the next 24 hours, similar attacks were carried out all across Belkan government buildings with large success, at which point Rald has come forward announcing that a large number of members of the incumbent government were intentionally weakening Belka with the intention of allowing an Osean invasion, and that he has rounded up most of these "traitors" and will be replacing Berthold Lehmann as the head of government. While not many people believe this story, Rald's grip on the military prevents any organized opposition to his new regime.

fields.text: Ein Volk, Ein Nation, Ein Ziel!
lines: Ein Volk, Ein Nation, Ein Ziel!

fields.text: President Rald held a public speech today, calling for the Belkan people to put aside their differences and remember that they are, above all else, Belkans, and that is what matters. Nationalism has always been high after the Osean scam in the Great Lakes, and it seems Rald is capitalizing on this, uniting the people under their nationality. This has alarmed several nations around us, mostly Osea and our former member nations, but domestically this speech has seen Rald's approval ratings increase greatly.

fields.text: Total War
lines: Total War

fields.text: The humliation and shame inflicted on us not just by Osea, but also the foolish conservatives who allowed Belkan territory to secede in the 1987 Federal Law Review, cannot be allowed to stand. Waldemarr Rald held a meeting with his cabinet today promising an immenent revenge war against Osea and the former states, reclaiming lost Belkan territory, as soon as the military is restored back to its former level. While he has not gone public with this information, he has constantly blamed Osea and the other nations for poisoning Belka, and promises citizens that things will be made right. Rald promises to his cabinet a state of 'total war,' as he describes it- 'To wage war with all tools, methods, resources, and weapons that you have at your disposal, to fight tooth and nail with everything you have until victory or annhilation.'

fields.text: Excalibur Online
lines: Excalibur Online

fields.text: Excalibur, the chemical laser anti-ICBM system devised as a part of the large military build-up of the past couple decades, has finally been finished with our efforts. The designs have changed slightly since the original proposed design from 1981, however the core design has remained mostly unchanged. These designs have allowed us to make the design more modular, including swappable lenses for different ranges and targets, as well as heat transferring pipes to allow the main structure to assist in cooling as well as the six primary cooling towers. This also has allowed for possible future improvements on the design, but for now we have a simple choice to make on where to invest the last of the project's leftover budget. We could develop an electronic targeting system that syncs up with radar data, allowing Excalibur to easily target agile objects like aircraft, boosting our air superiority capabilities. We could even invest in a denser power system, allowing the laser to reach higher temperatures and give it the ability to assist in ground attacks. Or we could simply keep it to its original purpose and improve its ICBM destruction capabilities.

fields.text: Avalon Dam Finished
lines: Avalon Dam Finished

fields.text: Started in 1985, the Avalon Dam facility was designed as an undercover top-secret research facility to aid the development of Project Pendragon, our nuclear ICBM program, as well as other classified high-tech projects. While Project Pendragon has already been finished, the facility itself will allow us to develop more weapons and advancements a step above the rest of the world. However, now that this facility has been completed, we must make sure it stays secure. While we could keep the garrison the same as any other military installation, to avoid suspicion, the criticality of the projects being worked on presents a high risk. We could station the former head of Project Pendragon as well as a top ace in the Belkan Air Force, Dr. Anton Kupchenko, head of the "Gault Squadron" at the base, where he could assist in both research and security, as the projects worked on there will likely be continuations of his own work. Alternatively, we could also station the newly-formed Belkan Special Forces at the facility, while this would not allow the research benefits the BSF will likely have a much tighter hold on the facility, making it much more secure, as well as ensure that the BSF will be the first to recieve any new high-tech infantry weapons developed on-site.
